lay_summary: Researchers made a new genetic risk score (a number based on many DNA markers) to find people likely to get peripheral artery disease (PAD), a blood vessel problem that can harm legs. They used genetic and health record data from about 650,000 people in three large studies. People in the top 20% of the score were more likely to have PAD, and about 30% of PAD patients without diabetes, smoking, or kidney disease had a high score. The score predicted PAD about as well as knowing if someone smokes or has diabetes and found a higher chance of severe limb problems. This score might help doctors find and protect people at high risk.

pdr_title: Pregnancy and Diabetic Retinopathy: A Report From the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: In this cross sectional observational study, pregnancy was not associated with higher non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy or proliferative diabetic retinopathy prevalence.Copyright © 2025. Published by Elsevier Inc.
lay_summary: This study checked whether pregnancy raises the chance of diabetic eye disease. Researchers used health data from people in the All of Us program and looked at records at one time (a cross-sectional observational study, meaning they only analyzed existing data). They found pregnancy was not linked to more early diabetic retinopathy (non-proliferative, early damage) or more advanced retinopathy (proliferative, with new abnormal blood vessels). This means pregnant people with diabetes still should get regular eye exams, but pregnancy alone did not increase these eye problems.

pdr_title: Micronutrients and Chronic Pain: A Cross-Sectional Analysis
pdr_journal_title: Pain Practice : The Official Journal of World Institute of Pain
pdr_abstract: Objectives: Awareness about the role of micronutrients in the development of chronic pain has drastically increased. We investigated how serum micronutrient levels differ in subjects with chronic pain compared to pain-free subjects.    Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with subjects from the All of Us database, divided into cohorts of no, mild/moderate, and severe pain based on numeric rating scale scores. We examined serum levels of vitamins D %2825OH-D%29, C, B12, folate, and magnesium-micronutrients found to be involved in chronic pain %2838,006; 656; 62,110; 25,937, and 93,445 subjects, respectively%29 and defined them as normal, deficient, or borderline deficient based on reference ranges. We examined the variation of these findings based on sex and race/ethnicity.    Results: Subjects with severe pain had lower 25OH-D, B12, and folate levels than those with mild/moderate pain and/or without pain %28p < 0.001%29. We found a higher incidence of 25OH-D, vitamin C %28males%29, and magnesium deficiency in subjects with severe pain %28p < 0.05%29. Black and White subjects with severe pain had lower levels of 25OH-D and folate %28p < 0.05 for 25OH-D, NS for folate in Black males, and p < 0.001 for the other groups%29, but lower vitamin B12 only in Whites %28p < 0.001 for females and p < 0.05 for males%29. Asian and Hispanic females also had lower folate %28p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, respectively%29.    Discussion: We found lower 25OH-D, B12, and folate, and a higher incidence of 25OH-D, vitamin C %28males%29, and magnesium deficiency at subjects with chronic pain, more consistent in Blacks and Whites than in Asians and Hispanics. Micronutrient repletion may influence chronic pain

lay_summary: This study looked at whether blood levels of vitamins and minerals (called micronutrients) differ in people with chronic pain. Researchers used a large US health database and grouped people by no, mild/moderate, or severe pain. They compared vitamin D, vitamin C, B12, folate, and magnesium. People with severe pain had lower vitamin D, B12, and folate and more vitamin D, vitamin C (men), and magnesium deficiencies. Differences were strongest in Black and White groups. The findings suggest doctors could check and treat low nutrient levels as part of pain care.

pdr_title: Impacts of sample weighting on transferability of risk prediction models across EHR-Linked biobanks with different recruitment strategies
pdr_abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether using poststratification weights when training risk prediction models enhances transferability when the external test cohort has a different sampling strategy, a commonly encountered scenario when analyzing electronic health record %28EHR%29-linked biobanks.    Methods: PS weights were calculated to align a health system-based biobank, the Michigan Genomics Initiative %28MGI; n = 76,757%29, with a nationally recruited biobank, All of Us %28AOU; n = 226,764%29, which oversamples underrepresented groups. Basic PS weights %28PSBASIC%29 captured age, sex, and race/ethnicity; full PS weights %28PSFULL%29 additionally included smoking, alcohol consumption, BMI, depression, hypertension, and the Charlson Comorbidity Index. Models for esophageal, liver, and pancreatic cancers were developed using EHR data from MGI at 0, 1, 2, and 5 years prior to diagnosis. Phenotype risk scores %28PheRS%29 were constructed using six methods %28e.g., regularized regression, random forest%29 and evaluated alongside covariates, risk factors, and symptoms. Evaluation metrics included the odds ratio %28OR%29 for the top decile vs. the middle 40th-60th percentiles of the risk score distribution and the area under the receiver operating curve %28AUC%29 evaluated in the AOU test cohort when models are trained with and without weighting.    Results: Elastic net and random forest methods generally performed well in risk stratification, but no single PheRS construction method consistently outperformed others. Applying PS weights did not consistently improve risk stratification performance. For example, in liver cancer risk stratification at t = 1, unweighted random forest PheRS yielded an OR of 13.73 %2895 % CI: 8.97, 21.01%29, compared to 14.55 %2895 % CI: 9.45, 22.42%29 with PSBASIC and 13.62 %2895 % CI: 8.90, 20.85%29 with PSFULL.    Conclusion: PS weights do not significantly enhance risk model transferability between biobanks. EHR-based PheRS are crucial for risk stratification and should be integrated with other multimodal data for improved risk prediction. Identifying high-risk populations for diseases like liver cancer early through health history mining shows promise.
lay_summary: This study asked if giving extra weight to some people when training computer risk models helps them work in a different group. Researchers used health record biobanks from Michigan and All of Us and built scores to predict esophagus, liver, and pancreas cancer with several methods. The best models, like random forest, worked well, but weighting the training data did not reliably improve predictions; for liver cancer the top risk group had about 14 times the risk either way. For patients, health-record risk scores can find high-risk people, but adding other types of data will help.

pdr_title: Risk Factors Associated with Gastroenteropancreatic and Lung Neuroendocrine Tumors: A Nested Case-Control Study from The All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention : A Publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, Cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
pdr_abstract: Background: The incidence of neuroendocrine tumors %28NETs%29, which arise primarily in lung and gastroenteropancreatic %28GEP%29 tissues, has risen dramatically in the past fifty years. However, the etiology of NETs remains inconclusive.    Methods: We conducted a nested case-control study using data from the All of Us research program %28version 7; index dates [2000-2022]%29 to compare the odds of diagnosed GEP or lung NETs in the presence or absence of various potential risk factors. One case was matched to five controls without cancer diagnoses by age at consent and sex. We used piecewise structural equation modeling to generate effect estimates.    Results: Of 2,180 individuals %28including 366 with NETs%29, most were non-Hispanic White %2862.8%%29 and female %2861.0 %%29. Individuals with a family history of any cancer %28odds ratios %28OR%29, 1.43; 95% confidence intervals %28CI%29, 1.06 to 1.95, P=0.021%29, a past diagnosis of type 2 diabetes %28OR, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.96, P=0.012%29 and any immune-mediated disease %28OR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.11 to 1.76, P=0.004%29 had higher odds of developing GEP or lung NETs.    Conclusions: This study confirms prior evidence in less diverse cohorts that the risk of developing GEP or lung NETs is significantly associated with having a first-degree relative with any cancer or previous diagnosis of type 2 diabetes.    Impact: Our findings are the first to demonstrate that a pre-existing diagnosis of any immune-mediated disease is a risk factor for developing NETs. Together, our findings suggest that NET development may be influenced by non-modifiable factors as well as modifiable conditions.

lay_summary: This study looked for reasons why certain people get neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) in the lung or gut because these cancers have become more common. Researchers used medical data from 2,180 people (366 had NETs) and compared those with and without NETs. They found that people with a close family member who had cancer, people with type 2 diabetes, and people with immune diseases (when the body’s defense system attacks itself) were more likely to have NETs. This means doctors might watch people with these risks more closely.

pdr_title: AoUPRS: A cost-effective and versatile PRS calculator for the All of Us Program
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND:The All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program provides a comprehensive genomic dataset to accelerate health research and medical breakthroughs. Despite its potential, researchers face significant challenges, including high costs and inefficiencies associated with data extraction and analysis. AoUPRS addresses these challenges by offering a versatile and cost-effective tool for calculating polygenic risk scores %28PRS%29, enabling both experienced and novice researchers to leverage the AoU dataset for large-scale genomic discoveries.METHODS:We evaluated three PRS models from the PGS Catalog %28coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and type 2 diabetes%29 using two distinct approaches in the Hail framework: MatrixTable %28MT%29, a dense representation, and Variant Dataset %28VDS%29, a sparse representation optimized for large-scale genomic data. Computational cost, resource usage, and processing time were compared. To assess the similarity of PRS performance between these two approaches, we compared odds ratios %28ORs%29 and area under the curve %28AUC%29. Lin's concordance correlation coefficient %28CCC%29 was also computed to quantify agreement between PRS scores generated by MT and VDS.RESULTS:The VDS approach reduced computational costs by up to 99.51% %28e.g., from $32 to $0.036 for a 51-SNP score%29 while maintaining PRS estimates that were highly similar to those obtained using the MT approach. Across all three PRS models, AUC comparisons showed minimal differences between MT and VDS, indicating that both approaches yield consistent PRS performance. Agreement between PRS scores calculated by both approaches was further supported by Lin's CCC values ranging from 0.9199 to 0.9944, confirming strong concordance. Empirical cumulative distribution function %28ECDF%29 plots further illustrated the near-identical distribution of PRS values across methods.CONCLUSIONS:AoUPRS enables efficient and cost-effective PRS computation within AoU, providing substantial cost savings while maintaining highly consistent PRS estimates. These findings support the use of AoUPRS for large-scale genomic risk assessment, making the AoU dataset more accessible and practical for diverse research applications. The tool's open-source availability on GitHub, coupled with detailed documentation and tutorials, ensures accessibility and ease of use for the scientific community.© 2025. The Author%28s%29.
lay_summary: This study made and tested AoUPRS, a low-cost tool to calculate polygenic risk scores (PRS) — a measure of genetic risk — using the All of Us health dataset. The team tested three disease scores (heart disease, irregular heartbeat, and type 2 diabetes) using two computer methods: one that keeps all data and one that keeps only needed bits. The method that keeps only needed bits cut computing costs by about 99.5% while giving almost the same scores. This means genetic risk studies can be much cheaper and more accessible, helping future research that may improve health care.

pdr_title: Unlocking the Potential of Wear Time of a Wearable Device to Enhance Postpartum Depression Screening and Detection: Cross-Sectional Study
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND:Postpartum depression %28PPD%29 is a mood disorder affecting 1 in 7 women after childbirth that is often underscreened and underdetected. If not diagnosed and treated, PPD is associated with long-term developmental challenges in the child and maternal morbidity. Wearable technologies, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers %28eg, Fitbit%29, offer continuous and longitudinal digital phenotyping for mood disorder diagnosis and monitoring, with device wear time being an important yet understudied aspect.OBJECTIVE:We aimed to suggest that wear time of a wearable device may provide additional information about perinatal mental health to facilitate screening and early detection of PPD. We proposed that wear time of a wearable device may also be valuable for managing other mental health disorders.METHODS:Using the All of Us Research Program dataset, we identified females who experienced childbirth with and without PPD using computational phenotyping. We compared the percentage of days and number of hours per day females with and without PPD wore Fitbit devices during prepregnancy, pregnancy, postpartum, and PPD periods, determined by electronic health records. Comparisons between females with and without PPD were conducted using linear regression models. We also assessed the correlation between Fitbit wear time consistency %28measured as the maximum number of consecutive days the Fitbit was worn%29 during prepregnancy and PPD periods in females with and without PPD using the Pearson correlation. All analyses were run with Bonferroni correction.RESULTS:Our findings showed a strong trend, although nonsignificant after multiple testing correction, that females in the PPD cohort wore their Fitbits more than those in non-PPD cohort during the postpartum %28PPD cohort: mean 69.9%, 95% CI 42.7%-97%; non-PPD cohort: mean 50%, 95% CI 25.5%-74.4%; P=.02%29 and PPD periods %28PPD cohort: mean 66.6%, 95% CI 37.9%-95.3%; non-PPD cohort: mean 46.4%, 95% CI 20.5%-72.2%; P=.02%29. We found no difference in the number of hours per day females in the PPD and non-PPD cohorts wore their Fitbit during any period of pregnancy. Finally, there was no relationship between the consistency of Fitbit wear time during prepregnancy and PPD periods %28r=-0.05, 95% CI -0.46 to 0.38; P=.84%29; however, there was a trend, though nonsignificant, in Fitbit wear time consistency among females without PPD %28r=0.25, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.49; P=.07%29.CONCLUSIONS:We hypothesize that increased Fitbit wear time among females with PPD may be attributed to hypervigilance, given the common co-occurrence of anxiety symptoms. Future studies should assess the link between PPD, hypervigilance, and wear time patterns. We envision that wear time patterns of a wearable device combined with digital biomarkers such as sleep and physical activity could enhance early PPD detection using machine learning by alerting clinicians to potential concerns and facilitating timely screenings, which may have implications for other mental health disorders.©Eric Hurwitz, Samantha Meltzer-Brody, Zachary Butzin-Dozier, Rena C Patel, Noémie Elhadad, Melissa A Haendel. Originally published in JMIR Formative Research %28https://formative.jmir.org%29, 23.05.2025.

lay_summary: This study asked if Fitbit wear time can help spot postpartum depression (PPD). Researchers looked at women who had babies in a big health study and compared Fitbit use before, during, and after pregnancy. They measured percent of days and hours per day the device was worn. Women with PPD tended to wear Fitbits about 70% of days after birth versus 50% for women without PPD, and about 67% versus 46% during PPD. The pattern was a trend but not proven. If true, wearables plus sleep and activity data could help flag mothers for earlier screening.

pdr_title: Vitiligo and associated comorbidities: A case-control study in the All of Us database
pdr_abstract: Recent research has established an association between vitiligo and other autoimmune diseases. Given the systemic inflammation, there are likely other comorbidities with vitiligo that are not as well established. We identified 1,074 vitiligo patients and 4,296 matched controls in the All of Us database. Conditional logistic regression estimated the odds ratio %28OR%29 and 95% confidence interval %28CI%29 of 29 select comorbid conditions for vitiligo patients compared to matched controls. The Benjamini-Hochberg method was used to adjust p-values. On logistic regression, vitiligo patients had significantly increased likelihoods of atherosclerotic disease %28OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.48-2.14, p<0.001%29, hypertension %28OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.50-2.03, p<0.001%29, and hyperlipidemia %28OR 2.32, 95% CI 1.99-2.72 p<0.001%29. Vitiligo patients additionally carried a significant bone and joint, autoimmune, endocrine, and psychiatric comorbidity burden. This convergence highlights the multifaceted nature of vitiligo, prompting a need for investigating therapeutic approaches capable of addressing both vitiligo and its varied comorbidities.© The Author%28s%29 2025. lay_summary: Researchers studied 1,074 people with vitiligo (a skin condition that causes white patches) and 4,296 similar people without it from the All of Us database to see if vitiligo links to other illnesses. People with vitiligo were about twice as likely to have artery (blood vessel) disease, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. They also had more bone and joint problems, autoimmune conditions (when the immune system attacks the body), hormone problems, and mental health issues. This suggests patients and doctors should watch for these conditions and get regular check-ups.

pdr_title: Progression trajectories of chronic overlapping pain conditions unveiled across two large clinical data warehouses
pdr_abstract: Chronic overlapping pain conditions %28COPCs%29 affect a wide population and incur a substantial disease burden including comorbid mental disorders. Although these comorbidities have been extensively documented, the longitudinal trajectories of their onset, particularly for those with three or more conditions, have been rarely studied. We conducted retrospective cohort studies to identify statistically significant COPCs and mental health trajectories in the All of Us Research Program %28AoU v8, 338,170 persons%29 and the Mayo Data Warehouse %283,957,444 individuals%29. For each trajectory, cases were matched with controls by demographic factors. Logistic regression was then applied to assess the increased likelihood of the final condition given the prior conditions in that sequence. The significant trajectories were visualized as a 'pain forest.' More than 88% of trajectories identified from AoU %28Male: 78, Female: 361%29 were reproducible in the Mayo Data Warehouse data %28Male: 361, Female: 1286%29, with female trajectories encompassing more than 96% of the male trajectories. The findings indicate that chronic low back pain generally occurs earlier than other conditions, while fibromyalgia tends to follow other COPCs. Endometriosis seems to be associated with an increased prevalence of COPCs in women. In addition, longer trajectories are associated with a greater risk of developing additional COPC or mental condition. The results offer new insights into the progression of COPCs and associated mental conditions, which may inform healthcare providers and patients in managing and preventing exacerbation of these conditions.Copyright © 2025 International Association for the Study of Pain.
pdr_grant_number: R21DE031424/DE/NIDCR NIH HHS/United States
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to learn how chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs) — long-term pain problems that happen together — develop over time. They studied medical records from two big databases with 338,170 and about 4 million people and traced condition sequences. More than 88% of patterns in the smaller group were also in the larger group, and women had many more patterns than men. Low back pain usually came first, fibromyalgia came later, and endometriosis in women linked to more COPCs. Longer sequences meant higher risk of more pain or mental health problems. This can help doctors and patients treat problems earlier.

pdr_title: Veteran participation in the All of Us Research Program: applying an intersectionality lens to evaluate participant diversity
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND:Many segments of the population are underrepresented in biomedical research %28UBR%29. Lack of diversity in health research limits understanding of individual and population level differences and risks the generalizability of study results. Examining intersectionality among VA-enrolled Veteran participants in the All of Us Research Program offers a first look at in-depth understanding of Veteran identity.METHODS:Multi-modal approaches to engagement and recruitment were utilized to enroll a diverse cohort of Veterans nationally from 2018 to 2024. All of Us data were analyzed across eight UBR categories and their intersections to highlight the complexity of Veteran identity.RESULTS:Veteran All of Us participants reflect the diversity of Veterans nationwide. All of Us participant metrics shed new light on the diversity of the Veteran population, with over 75 unique UBR combinations identified among participants, and over 90% of participants meeting the criteria for at least one UBR category.CONCLUSIONS:The use of a broad spectrum of engagement approaches was shown to be successful for reaching a more diverse Veteran base, and complex intersectional identities among Veterans are described. Greater understanding of intersectionality and its significance to representation can bolster the adaptation of Veteran engagement methodology in research and broader healthcare settings.© 2025. lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if Veterans in the All of Us Research Program represent the many kinds of Veterans, especially those often left out of health studies. From 2018 to 2024 they used many ways to recruit Veterans and studied eight groups that are usually underrepresented and how they overlap (intersectionality = overlapping identity like race, gender, age, or disability). They found participants matched national diversity, with over 75 different overlap combinations and over 90% in at least one underrepresented group. This shows broad outreach can make research and healthcare fairer for Veterans.
calc_title: Veteran participation in the All of Us Research Program: applying an intersectionality lens to evaluate participant diversity
calc_abstract: BACKGROUND:Many segments of the population are underrepresented in biomedical research (UBR). Lack of diversity in health research limits understanding of individual and population level differences and risks the generalizability of study results. Examining intersectionality among VA-enrolled Veteran participants in the All of Us Research Program offers a first look at in-depth understanding of Veteran identity.METHODS:Multi-modal approaches to engagement and recruitment were utilized to enroll a diverse cohort of Veterans nationally from 2018 to 2024. All of Us data were analyzed across eight UBR categories and their intersections to highlight the complexity of Veteran identity.RESULTS:Veteran All of Us participants reflect the diversity of Veterans nationwide. All of Us participant metrics shed new light on the diversity of the Veteran population, with over 75 unique UBR combinations identified among participants, and over 90% of participants meeting the criteria for at least one UBR category.CONCLUSIONS:The use of a broad spectrum of engagement approaches was shown to be successful for reaching a more diverse Veteran base, and complex intersectional identities among Veterans are described. Greater understanding of intersectionality and its significance to representation can bolster the adaptation of Veteran engagement methodology in research and broader healthcare settings.© 2025. pdr_title: EHR Phenotyping Methods for Measuring Treatment Adherence Among People Living With HIV in All of Us: Towards Disparities and Inequalities in HIV Care Continuum
pdr_journal_title: AMIA ... Annual Symposium Proceedings. AMIA Symposium
pdr_abstract: HIV treatment adherence is among the most important determinants of HIV outcomes. However, only 50% of people living with HIV in the US were retained in care. Measuring HIV treatment adherence in the clinical settings is feasible but when it comes to the growing number of multi-site Electronic Health Records %28EHR%29, there has been a dearth of research for adequate informatics methods to handle EHR. We sought to address this gap by developing a cluster of metrics for measuring HIV treatment adherence via EHR phenotyping methods. Our methods were developed and tested in the All of Us research program. We also performed preliminary analyses to explore disparities in HIV treatment adherence and demographic factors contributing to poor adherence. This study paves the way for systematic data mining and analyses for the HIV care continuum, disparities, and inequality research on All of Us and other EHR normalized with the OMOP Common Data Model.©2024 AMIA - All rights reserved.

lay_summary: The study was done because only about 50% of people with HIV in the US stay in care and we need better ways to measure if people take their medicine. Researchers used the All of Us electronic health records (EHRs) and made computer methods called phenotyping (ways to find and measure health patterns in records) to create and test a set of measures for HIV treatment adherence. Early results showed differences in adherence across groups. This work helps find gaps in care so providers can help people stay on treatment and reduce unfair differences.

pdr_title: Deep Learning-based Time-to-event Analysis of Depression and Asthma using the All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: AMIA ... Annual Symposium Proceedings. AMIA Symposium
pdr_abstract: While there is a growing recognition of the association between depression and asthma, few studies have leveraged deep learning-based %28DL-based%29 models in a retrospective cohort study with a large sample size. We analyzed the association between depression and asthma among 239,161 participants of the All of Us Research Program through DL-based, logistic regression, and Cox Proportional Hazards %28CoxPH%29 models. We used SHAP values to help interpret DL-based models and c-index to evaluate model performance. Results suggest a significant odds ratio for depression in asthma. The c-indices for the CoxPH, DeepSurv, and DeepHit models were 0.619, 0.625, and 0.596, respectively. SHAP indicated a different set of important variables when compared with the CoxPH model. In conclusion, we provide strong evidence of a positive relationship between depression and asthma. Also, DL-based models did not outperform the CoxPH model on the c-index. Sex at birth and income may play important roles in occurrence of depression in asthma patients.©2024 AMIA - All rights reserved.
pdr_grant_number: N/A
lay_summary: Researchers studied 239,161 people in the All of Us program to see if asthma is linked to depression. They used deep learning (computer models that learn patterns) and standard statistical models to predict depression and compared their accuracy. They found clear evidence that people with asthma were more likely to have depression. The model scores were about 62% for the standard model, 63% for one deep learning model, and 60% for another, so deep learning did not do better. Sex at birth and income were important factors. This means doctors should watch for depression in people with asthma.

pdr_title: Perceived Discrimination in Medical Care Settings on A1c Data From the All of Us Program
pdr_journal_title: Health Education & Behavior : The Official Publication of the Society for Public Health Education
pdr_abstract: Approximately 11.3% of the U.S. population has diabetes, mostly type 2 diabetes %28T2DM%29, and maintenance of A1c levels is vital to prevent complications among patients. Perceived discrimination in medical care settings %28PDMS%29 affects patient care, while social support may mitigate its impact. This study aims to explore the influence of PDMS on A1c levels in T2DM patients using the All of Us Research Program, which collects health data from diverse individuals across the United States. Our study included 135 T2DM-diagnosed participants. Measures included demographic info, A1c data, self-rated health, social support, and perceived discrimination. Descriptive and multivariable regression analyses were conducted. Participants were predominantly older, female, non-Hispanic White, and had relatively high levels of education and above-average income levels. Most rated their health positively. Social support, including marital status, was considered. The average A1c level was 6.72 ± 1.54. Notably, 42% experienced high PDMS, correlating with poorer self-rated health. Multivariable regression revealed significant associations between A1c and follow-up time, age, marital status, and PDMS. Specifically, PDMS significantly correlates with poorer A1c, indicating a potential impact on diabetes management. Findings emphasize the need for tailored interventions and anti-discrimination guidelines in clinical practice. Insights from this study inform interventions mitigating discrimination and enhancing diabetes care. Health care providers fostering inclusive environments can improve patient trust and adherence to treatment, leading to better outcomes. Cultivating inclusive environments through health care providers improves patient outcomes. Diverse population inclusion in future studies is crucial.
pdr_grant_number: N/A
lay_summary: This study looked at whether people with type 2 diabetes who felt treated unfairly in medical care had worse blood sugar control. Researchers used data from the All of Us program and studied 135 adults with type 2 diabetes. They checked A1c (a blood test that shows average blood sugar), age, health ratings, social support, and reports of unfair treatment. Average A1c was 6.72. About 42% said they felt high levels of unfair treatment, and those people had worse A1c and poorer health. The finding suggests doctors and clinics should reduce discrimination to help people manage diabetes better.

pdr_title: Association of Pathogenic/Likely Pathogenic Genetic Variants for Cardiomyopathies With Clinical Outcomes: A Multiancestry Analysis in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND:This study aimed to evaluate the prevalence of pathogenic/likely pathogenic cardiomyopathy variant carriers in a multiancestry US population and examine the risk of adverse clinical outcomes.METHODS:This retrospective cohort study included multiancestry US adults aged =18 years with sequencing data from the All of Us Research Program. Pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in cardiomyopathy genes were identified using the ClinVar database. The primary outcome was heart failure. Secondary outcomes included cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia. Outcomes were identified from electronic health records. Interval-censored Cox models, taking age on the timescale, were used to assess the risk of outcomes in pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant carriers with noncarriers as the reference group.RESULTS:Among 167?435 individuals %28median age, 55.2 [39.5-66.3] years; 61.7% female; 40.7% non-European ancestry%29 included, the proportion of pathogenic/likely pathogenic cardiomyopathy variant carriers was 0.7% of the overall population and 0.8%, 0.8%, 0.5%, and 1.2% of European, African, East Asian, and South Asian ancestry individuals, respectively. Over the lifetime, there were 12?867 heart failure events %28205 in carriers and 12?662 in noncarriers%29, with an incidence rate of 3.05 %2895% CI, 2.66-3.49%29 per 1000 person-years in carriers and 1.37 %2895% CI, 1.35-1.40%29 in noncarriers %28HR, 2.30 [95% CI, 2.04-2.60]%29. Cardiomyopathy occurred in 5164 %28161 in carriers and 5003 in noncarriers%29, with an incidence rate of 2.38 %2895% CI, 2.04-2.78%29 per 1000 person-years among carriers and 0.54 %2895% CI, 0.53-0.56%29 in noncarriers %28HR, 4.31 [95% CI, 3.73-4.97]%29. There were 19?405 arrhythmia events %28263 in carriers and 19?142 in noncarriers%29, with an incidence rate of 3.93 %2895% CI, 3.48-4.44%29 per 1000 person-years among carriers and 2.09 %2895% CI, 2.06-2.12%29 in noncarriers %28HR, 2.12 [95% CI, 1.78-2.53]%29.CONCLUSIONS:Pathogenic/likely pathogenic cardiomyopathy variant carriers have an increased risk of heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and arrhythmias. Despite the modest overall prevalence, the associated risks suggest potential benefits of targeted genetic screening for early detection and management.

lay_summary: Researchers studied 167,435 US adults from the All of Us study to see how common harmful gene changes for heart muscle disease are and whether those people had more heart problems. They compared gene test results to medical records. About 0.7% had these gene changes. These people were about twice as likely to get heart failure or irregular heartbeats and about four times more likely to be diagnosed with cardiomyopathy (a disease of the heart muscle). This suggests targeted genetic screening could find at-risk people earlier so they can get care.

pdr_title: Computable phenotypes to identify respiratory viral infections in the All of Us research program
pdr_abstract: Electronic health records %28EHRs%29 contain rich temporal data about respiratory viral infections, but methods to identify these infections from EHR data vary widely and lack robust validation. We developed computable phenotypes by integrating virus-specific International Classification of Diseases %28ICD%29 billing codes, prescriptions, and laboratory results within 90-day episodes. Analysis of 265,222 participants with EHR data from the All of Us Research Program yielded national cohorts of varied size: large cohorts for SARS-CoV-2 %28n?=?28,729%29 and influenza %28n?=?19,784%29; medium cohorts for rhinovirus, human coronavirus, and respiratory syncytial virus %28n?=?1,161-1,620%29; and smaller cohorts for the other viruses %28n?=?238-486%29. Using laboratory results as a reference standard, phenotypes using virus-specific ICD codes and medications had variable sensitivity %288-67%%29 but high positive predictive value %28PPV, 90-97%%29 for most viruses, while influenza virus and SARS-CoV-2 phenotypes had lower PPV %2869-70%%29 that improved with the inclusion of additional ICD codes. Identified infections exhibited expected seasonal patterns matching CDC data. This integrated approach identified infections more effectively than individual components alone and demonstrated utility for severe infections in hospital settings. This method enables large-scale studies of host genetics, health disparities, and clinical outcomes across episodic diseases, with flexibility to optimize sensitivity or PPV depending on the specific research question.© 2025. lay_summary: Researchers built computer rules to find viral infections in electronic health records because methods vary and need testing. They studied 265,222 people in the All of Us study using diagnosis codes (ICD), prescriptions, and lab results over 90-day periods. They found about 29,000 COVID cases and 20,000 flu cases, with hundreds to thousands for other viruses. The rules often missed infections but were usually correct when they flagged one (about 90–97% for most viruses; about 70% for flu and COVID unless more codes were added). This method can help research, tracking, and care.

pdr_title: Racial, ethnic and socioeconomic disparities in healthcare for adult spinal deformity patients
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND:Racial and ethnic disparities in healthcare access remain underexplored among adult spinal deformity %28ASD%29 patients in terms of cost related and non-cost related barriers to care.METHODS:This cross-sectional study analyzed healthcare access and utilization survey data from the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program %28May 6th, 2018-January 30th, 2025%29. The participants included adults aged =?40 years with spinal deformity enrolled online or through partner organizations across the US. The cost and non-cost barriers to health among ASD patients by race and ethnicity were reported. Multivariate logistic regressions were used to analyze the relationship between race and ethnicity and experiencing barriers to care.RESULTS:This study included 7272 ASD patients of which 5635 were White %2874.5%%29 %28median age, 69 years [IQR, 60.0-75.0]%29, 535 Hispanic %287.4%%29 %2860.0 years [51.0-68.0]%29, 538 %287.4%%29 Black %2861.5 years [52.0-69.0]%29 and 564 %287.8%%29 of other race and ethnicity %2865.0 years [55.0-74.0]%29 of whom 528 %287.3%%29 proceeded to undergo correction surgery. Compared to White patients, Black patients had higher odds of reporting delayed general care %28adjusted odds ratio [aOR, 2.5; 95% CI 1.7-3.8%29, follow-up care %28aOR, 1.6; 95% CI 1.1-2.3%29, and prescription filling %28aOR, 1.5; 95% CI 1.1-1.9%29 due to cost. Non-cost barriers for Black patients included lack of transportation aOR, 3.2; 95% CI 2.3-4.3%29 while Hispanic patients had higher odds of reporting delayed care due to childcare %28aOR, 2.9; 95% CI 1.5-5.5%29 and care to an adult %28aOR, 1.8; 95% CI 1.0-3.3%29 responsibilities. Black and Hispanic patients had higher odds of placing importance on having a provider with a similar background %28aOR, 2.4; 95% CI 1.9-3.0; aOR, 3.1, 95% CI 2.4-3.9%29 and of never having had such a provider %28aOR, 4.6; 95% CI 3.2-6.6; aOR, 3.1, 95% CI 2.4-3.9%29, respectively. They also had higher odds of reporting delayed care due to provider background differences %28aOR, 1.9, 95% CI 1.4-2.4; aOR, 1.6, 95% CI 1.2-2.2%29, respectively. Additionally, Hispanic patients had higher odds of reporting not being treated with respect by their provider %28aOR, 1.6; 95% CI 1.0-2.5%29.CONCLUSIONS:Racial and ethnic disparities significantly impact ASD patients with Hispanic and Black patients facing higher rates of cost and non-cost barriers to care. The healthcare practitioners especially those specializing in ASD play a crucial role in recognizing and addressing these disparities to improve healthcare access and outcomes across racial and ethnic groups.LEVEL OF EVIDENCE:Prognostic Level III.© 2025. lay_summary: This study looked at 7,272 adults aged 40 and older with spinal deformities using a national survey to see if race or ethnicity affected access to care. About 75% were White, 7% Hispanic, and 7% Black. Researchers found Black patients more often delayed care or could not fill prescriptions because of cost and had trouble with transportation. Hispanic patients more often delayed care due to childcare or caring for adults and sometimes felt disrespected. The findings mean doctors and health systems should help remove these cost and non‑cost barriers.

pdr_title: PTPN2 and Leukopenia in Individuals With Normal TPMT and NUDT15 Metabolizer Status Taking Azathioprine
pdr_abstract: Leukopenia is a common dose-dependent side effect of azathioprine, often leading to drug discontinuation. Variants in TPMT and NUDT15 are associated with azathioprine-induced leukopenia but only explain 25% of cases. Thus, we aimed to identify novel genetic risk factors among TPMT and NUDT15 normal metabolizers through a genome-wide association study %28GWAS%29. Using BioVU, Vanderbilt's electronic health record linked to genetic data, we assembled a discovery cohort of new users of azathioprine. pdr_title: Sex differences in the confounders influencing the relationships linking socioeconomic factors and cognitive performance with family history of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias
pdr_journal_title: Alzheimer's & Dementia : The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association
pdr_abstract: Introduction: Limited information is available regarding sex differences in the relationship of socioeconomic status and cognitive performance with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias %28ADRD%29 family history.    Methods: Leveraging the UK Biobank %28N = 448,100%29 and All of Us Research Program %28N = 240,319%29, we conducted observational and genetically informed analyses to test the sex-specific associations of socioeconomic factors and cognitive performance with ADRD and its family history.    Results: Observational and genetically informed analyses highlighted that higher socioeconomic status and cognitive performance were associated with reduced ADRD and sibling-ADRD family history. Conversely, these were associated with increased parent-ADRD family history. Sex differences in these relationships were also identified. Additionally, although their sample size was limited, population minorities showed different patterns with respect to ADRD versus parent-ADRD family history.    Discussion: This study highlights sex differences in the misestimated associations of ADRD family history that appear to be related to socioeconomic factors and cognitive performance.    Highlights: Alzheimer's disease family history is differently linked to socioeconomic factors. Observational and genetic analyses highlighted sex differences in these dynamics. Cause-effect relationships could contribute to biases in Alzheimer's disease assessment.      © 2025 The Author%28s%29. lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if men and women differ in how money, schooling, and thinking skills relate to family history of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). They studied about 448,000 people from UK Biobank and 240,000 from All of Us, using health records, thinking tests, and genetic data. They found more money and more schooling, and better thinking, linked to less ADRD and less sibling ADRD, but more parent ADRD. Men and women showed different patterns. This means family history and tests can be influenced by social and sex differences when judging risk.

pdr_title: SLCO1B1 Functional Variants, Bilirubin, Statin-Induced Myotoxicity, and Recent Sub-Saharan African Ancestry: A Precision Medicine Health Equity Study
pdr_abstract: Statin pharmacogenetic implementation guidelines are derived from evidence of primarily Eurocentrically biased study populations. Functional SLCO1B1 variants that are rare in these study populations have not been equitably investigated and are thus missing from guidelines. The objective of this precision medicine health equity study was to determine the clinical validity of understudied candidate functional SLCO1B1 variants common in people with 1,000 Genomes sub-Saharan African superpopulation %281KG-AFR-like%29 genetic similarity. We conducted our analyses using the real-world evidence of participants from three large, electronic health record-linked biobanks. We used bilirubin levels %28as an endogenous substrate of organic anion transporting polypeptide [OATP1B1] function%29 and severe statin-induced myotoxicity phenotypes. Loss-of-function splice variant rs77271279 %28P = 1.1 × 10%28-17%29%29 had the strongest association with elevated total bilirubin levels in Black participants %28mean 84% AFR-like genetic similarity%29 followed by missense variant rs59502379 %28P = 7.4 × 10%28-12%29%29 then missense variant rs4149056 %28P = 6.0 × 10%28-5%29%29. In an exploratory subset of the Black study population who used statins %28n = 77 severe statin-induced myotoxicity cases%29, rs59502379 %28odds ratio [OR] = 2.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08-7.52%29, but not rs77271279 %28OR = 1.75, 95% CI 0.62-4.73%29 was associated with myotoxicity. Sensitivity analyses in participants with >5% AFR-like genetic similarity corroborated these findings. For white participants, rs77271279 and rs59502379 were rare precluding subsequent analyses. Our findings highlight the clinical relevance for understudied SLCO1B1 variants on pharmacogenetic testing panels with a potential immediate impact on reducing the risk of severe statin-induced myotoxicity primarily in Black patients, a group historically excluded from genomic research. Future studies require larger statin user study populations with less heterogeneity by statin type.

lay_summary: This study wanted to check genetic changes in a gene called SLCO1B1 (which helps move some drugs in the body) that are common in people with sub-Saharan African ancestry but not studied before. Researchers used health records and blood tests from large biobanks. They looked at bilirubin (a liver-made chemical) and cases of serious muscle damage from statins. One change (rs77271279) was linked to much higher bilirubin. Another change (rs59502379) was linked to more muscle damage in statin users (77 cases). Testing for these changes could help prevent bad statin side effects in Black patients.

pdr_title: Adaptive Recruitment Resource Allocation to Improve Cohort Representativeness in Participatory Biomedical Datasets
pdr_journal_title: AMIA ... Annual Symposium Proceedings. AMIA Symposium
pdr_abstract: Large participatory biomedical studies - studies that recruit individuals to join a dataset - are gaining popularity and investment, especially for analysis by modern AI methods. Because they purposively recruit participants, these studies are uniquely able to address a lack of historical representation, an issue that has affected many biomedical datasets. In this work, we define representativeness as the similarity to a target population distribution of a set of attributes and our goal is to mirror the U.S. population across distributions of age, gender, race, and ethnicity. Many participatory studies recruit at several institutions, so we introduce a computational approach to adaptively allocate recruitment resources among sites to improve representativeness. In simulated recruitment of 10,000-participant cohorts from medical centers in the STAR Clinical Research Network, we show that our approach yields a more representative cohort than existing baselines. Thus, we highlight the value of computational modeling in guiding recruitment efforts.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to help medical studies include people who match the U.S. population. They tested a computer method to decide how to spread recruiting effort among hospitals so the study group matches the U.S. population by age, gender, race, and ethnicity (representativeness = how much the group matches the population). In computer simulations of 10,000 people using sites in the STAR network, their method made study groups more like the U.S. population than older methods. This matters because fairer, more representative studies can make medical results work better for more people.

pdr_title: Polygenic Risk Scores in Dilated Cardiomyopathy: Towards the Future
pdr_abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Genome-wide association studies %28GWASs%29 have recently shown that common genetic variations significantly affect the risk of developing dilated cardiomyopathy %28DCM%29. This has enabled the development of polygenic scores %28PGSs%29, which aim to aggregate the impact of multiple common genetic variants across the genome to provide an overall genetic risk score for disease manifestation and disease severity. In this review, we discuss the latest findings pertaining to GWASs and PGSs for DCM and various ways in which PGSs could improve the management of patients with DCM or risk of developing DCM. RECENT FINDINGS: In 2024 the two largest GWAS meta-analyses for DCM were published. Notably, both studies produced PGSs that were able to discriminate healthy subjects from DCM patients which brings promise for potential clinical application of the scores. Large-scale GWAS have identified common genetic variants associated with DCM, leading to the development of PGS, which show strong associations with disease risk and hold potential for clinical applications. However, before clinical implementation, further research is needed to explore their utility in real-world settings and across diverse populations.
pdr_grant_number: 03-007-2022-0035/Dutch Heart Foundation/,CVON 2018-30 PREDICT2/Dutch Heart Foundation/
lay_summary: Scientists reviewed large DNA studies that looked for common gene differences linked to dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), a heart condition where the heart becomes weak and enlarged. They combined many small gene effects into polygenic scores (PGS) to estimate risk. Two big studies in 2024 made PGS that could tell apart people with DCM from healthy people. This suggests PGS might help find people at higher risk or guide care, but more testing is needed in real-world settings and in diverse groups before use.

pdr_title: Genomics and multiomics in the age of precision medicine
pdr_abstract: Precision medicine is a transformative healthcare model that utilizes an understanding of a person's genome, environment, lifestyle, and interplay to deliver customized healthcare. Precision medicine has the potential to improve the health and productivity of the population, enhance patient trust and satisfaction in healthcare, and accrue health cost-benefits both at an individual and population level. Through faster and cost-effective genomics data, next-generation sequencing has provided us the impetus to understand the nuances of complex interactions between genes, diet, and lifestyle that are heterogeneous across the population. The emergence of multiomics technologies, including transcriptomics, proteomics, epigenomics, metabolomics, and microbiomics, has enhanced the knowledge necessary for maximizing the applicability of genomics data for better health outcomes. Integrative multiomics, the combination of multiple 'omics' data layered over each other, including the interconnections and interactions between them, helps us understand human health and disease better than any of them separately. Integration of these multiomics data is possible today with the phenomenal advancements in bioinformatics, data sciences, and artificial intelligence. Our review presents a broad perspective on the utility and feasibility of a genomics-first approach layered with other omics data, offering a practical model for adopting an integrated multiomics approach in pediatric health care and research. IMPACT: Precision medicine provides a paradigm shift from a conventional, reactive disease control approach to proactive disease prevention and health preservation. Phenomenal advancements in bioinformatics, data sciences, and artificial intelligence have made integrative multiomics feasible and help us understand human health and disease better than any of them separately. The genotype-first approach or reverse phenotyping has the potential to overcome the limitations of the phenotype-first approach by identifying new genotype-phenotype associations, enhancing the subclassification of diseases by widening the phenotypic spectrum of genetic variants, and understanding functional mechanisms of genetic variations.
lay_summary: This review was done to explain how using a person's genome (their DNA code) together with other biological data can make medical care more precise. The authors looked at new methods like fast DNA sequencing, measurements of proteins and other molecules, and computer tools like artificial intelligence. They found that combining these data types helps doctors understand health and disease better than using genes alone, can find new gene–disease links, and may help prevent illness and tailor treatments, especially for children. For patients, this means earlier, more personalized care and better disease prevention.

pdr_title: Access to oral health care and its social determinants across the lifespan in the United States
pdr_abstract: Disparities in healthcare access, driven by socioeconomic status and social determinants of health %28SDOH%29, contribute to poor health outcomes. While prior studies established the relationship between SDOH and care access, fewer have explored their joint relationships with social satisfaction and health challenges across the lifespan. Rather than assessing direct associations between dental care utilization and physical or mental difficulties, this study examines broader interrelationships among SDOH, access to oral health care, and self-reported health challenges. A cross-sectional study using a lifespan approach-by examining participants within discrete age groups-was conducted on 127,886 individuals aged 18 years and older who participated in the All of Us research program and completed the 'Basics', 'Overall Health' and 'Health Care Access and Utilization' questionnaires. The distribution of participants' SDOH and self-reported health difficulties was presented and stratified by dental care utilization, income group and age across the lifespan. Multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to assess the associations between SDOH and access to oral health care. Across age groups, a consistent trend of disadvantaged social determinants associated with lacking oral health care utilization was noted. Young participants %2818-35 years old%29 were the most likely to report not having received oral health care within the past 12 months %2832.2%%29, worse mental health %2829.6%, fair/poor%29, emotional problems %2831.8%%29, and difficulties in concentrating or remembering %2818%%29. Notably, young adults who did not visit a dentist within 12 months were also more likely to report not visiting a medical doctor %2818.1%%29, being unable to afford copayment %2869%%29, and more frequently using emergency or urgent care %2820.2%%29. No insurance coverage [odds ratio %28OR%29 = 1.67, 95% confidence interval %28CI%29: 1.52-1.84], annual income less than $35,000 %28OR = 3.79, 95% CI: 3.58-4.01%29, and housing instability %28OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.32-1.44%29 were all significantly associated with lack of dental care. This study confirms that SDOH-particularly income and housing instability-significantly impact individuals' ability to afford and access healthcare services, including dental care. These disparities were most pronounced among the youngest age group. Our findings support future policy interventions aimed at integrating dental care into overall healthcare, especially during early adulthood.
lay_summary: This study looked at how social factors (like income, housing, and insurance) affect access to dental care across the life span. Researchers analyzed answers from 127,886 U.S. adults in the All of Us program using questionnaires. Young adults (18–35) were most likely to skip dental visits (32%), report worse mental health (30%), emotional problems (32%), and trouble concentrating (18%). Among young adults who skipped dentists, 18% also skipped medical visits, 69% couldn't afford copayments (small fees), and 20% used emergency care. The findings mean we need better, affordable dental care, especially for young adults.

pdr_title: Machine Learning Approaches to Racial/Ethnic Differences in Social Determinants of Mild Cognitive Impairment and Its Progression to Dementia in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: The Journals of Gerontology. Series B, Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
pdr_abstract: This study examines how social determinants of health %28SDOH%29 influence mild cognitive impairment %28MCI%29 and its progression to dementia across racial/ethnic groups, identifying disparities and key predictors using machine learning approaches. We analyzed data from 83,180 participants aged 50+ in the All of Us Research Program %2865,582 White, 6,207 Black, 4,170 Hispanic, 7,221 Other%29. The sample had mean ages ranging from 62.4 %28Hispanic%29 to 68.1 %28White%29 years, with significant gender disparities %2870.9% Black females vs 46.0% Other females%29. We developed machine learning classification models to predict MCI and its progression to dementia across the four racial/ethnic groups using 18 SDOH, along with key sociodemographic variables. We then applied SHapley Additive exPlanations %28SHAP%29 to quantify each factor's contribution and interpret its risk and protective effects on individual predictions. MCI prevalence was comparable across groups %287.5-8.0%%29, but progression to dementia varied %289.4% Black vs 11.4% Other%29. Perceived stress was the strongest predictor of MCI across all groups, with SHAP values of 15.1% %28White%29, 13.5% %28Black%29, 17.4% %28Other%29, and 19.3% %28Hispanic%29. Predictors of progression to dementia varied by groups: perceived stress %287.0%%29 for Whites, instrumental social support %2814.2%%29 for Hispanics, daily spiritual experience %2834.0%%29 for Blacks, and everyday discrimination %2811.2%%29 for other groups. The findings underscore the need for group-specific interventions addressing stress mitigation for MCI prevention and culturally-tailored support systems to delay dementia progression. This machine learning approach reveals complex SDOH interactions that traditional methods might overlook, particularly for racial/ethnic underrepresented populations.
lay_summary: Researchers used machine learning on 83,180 people aged 50  across four racial/ethnic groups to see how 18 social factors affect mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and its move to dementia. MCI rates were about 7.5–8% in all groups, but dementia progression ranged about 9%–11%. High perceived stress was the strongest predictor of MCI for everyone. Different factors predicted dementia in different groups: help from family or friends for Hispanics, daily spiritual life for Black people, and everyday discrimination for others. This suggests reducing stress and offering group-specific support could help prevent MCI and slow dementia.

pdr_title: Younger Age, Female Sex, Low Income, and Poor Mental Health Are Patient-Perceived Risk Factors for Poor Access to Care for Rotator Cuff Tears
pdr_abstract: To evaluate which patient factors are associated with specific metrics of poor access to care in patients with a rotator cuff tear %28RCT%29. The All of Us Database was utilized to form a cohort of patients with RCT between May 2018 and May 2023. Patients with a diagnosis of RCT using Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine clinical terms were included. The association of RCT diagnosis and patient-specific factors on self-reported outcomes of 'delayed care,' 'could not afford care,' 'skipped medication,' and 'have not seen provider in more than 1 year' were analyzed. Statistical tests performed were univariate regression and multivariable logistic regression. In total, 4,265 patients with RCT who completed the access to care survey were included. In the RCT cohort, 26.7% reported delayed care, 24.9% reported an inability to afford care, 12.1% reported skipped medications, and 1.7% reported not seeing a provider in more than 1 year. Multivariable analysis of patient treatment and demographic features revealed younger age, female sex, lower income, poor physical health, and poor mental health to be strongly associated with higher reported rates of delayed care, inability to afford care, and skipped medications. History of rotator cuff repair, marital status, and sexual orientation were not associated with reported poor access to care. A quarter of patients with rotator cuff tears report delays in overall medical care and inability to afford care. Among patients diagnosed with RCT, patients of younger age, female sex, low income, and poor physical and mental health have higher odds of decreased access to health care. Health care disparities and access to care are topics that should be investigated to reduce them.

pdr_title: Chronic pain prevalence and severity in females before & after menopause versus males in a large multi-center database
pdr_abstract: This observational study aimed to explore the prevalence and severity of chronic pain in menopausal-aged females. We identified participants in the NIH-sponsored All of Us database with a diagnosis of chronic pain. We examined the severity of pain based on numeric rating scale score %28NRS%29. Among those with chronic pain, we generated four sub-cohorts: females ≥ 51 years old who were menopausal, females 18-50 years who were considered pre-menopausal, and age matched male cohorts. The 53,289 participants were separated into four cohorts by age and sex: females 18-50 %2810,269%29, females ≥ 51 %2820,182%29, males 18-50 %284,989%29, and males ≥ 51 %2817,849%29. Both older females and older males had lower pain levels than the sex-matched 18-50 group %28p < 0.001%29. Findings were consistent in White, Black, and non-Hispanic cohorts. When comparing older adults, females ≥ 51 had higher pain levels than males ≥ 51 %28p < 0.001%29. We found that independent of sex, NRS scores were lower in older adults compared to younger cohorts. Older women however had more pain than their male counterparts. These findings have implications for the design of patient-tailored therapeutic treatments and warrant further exploration of physiological and psychosocial causes.
lay_summary: This study looked at how common and how bad long-term pain is in women before and after menopause compared to men. Researchers used a large U.S. health database of 53,289 people with chronic pain and compared four groups by age and sex using a 0–10 pain score. Older adults had lower pain than younger adults, but older women had more pain than older men. The pattern was similar across racial groups. Doctors may need to tailor pain care by age and sex.

pdr_title: Comparative polygenic predispositions of treatment-resistant depression in East Asian and European populations
pdr_journal_title: Neuropsychopharmacology : Official Publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
pdr_abstract: Large-scale genetic studies of treatment-resistant depression %28TRD%29 have been performed majority on European ancestry cohorts, potentially missing important population-specific biological insights. Understanding the genetic predisposition for TRD across populations could provide insights for etiologic heterogeneity. Conducting a cohort study of 106,796 unrelated participants using Taiwan Biobank %28TWBB%29, we investigated the association of polygenic score %28PGS%29 with the development of TRD among patients with depression and explore the concordance of the PGS association between East Asian and European populations. Three binary outcomes were defined, including TRD vs. non-major depressive disorder %28MDD%29, treatment responsive MDD %28trMDD%29 vs. non-MDD, and TRD vs. trMDD. Six PGSs belong to personality domains %28nervous, worry, guilty feelings, neuroticism, tense, and worry embarrassment%29 and compulsive PGS were associated with TRD vs. trMDD in TWBB. The pattern of association was consistent across TRD definitions with different dose, duration, and interrupted window for antidepressant treatment. The estimated strength of PGS association in TWBB is consistent with that in All of US %28AoU%29 %28meta-analytic R2 was 68% for TRD vs. non-MDD, 81% for trMDD vs. non-MDD, and 77% for TRD vs. trMDD%29. PGSs for temperament and education were associated with TRD vs. trMDD in AoU but not in TWBB. There was a moderate to high trans-ancestry concordance for the genetic estimates with TRD, while PGS association for specific traits were not transferable between East Asian and European populations. Genetic research across ancestries and geographic regions is crucial to learn population-specific etiology.
lay_summary: Researchers studied 106,796 people in Taiwan to see if many small genetic differences (a polygenic score, or PGS) help explain why some people have treatment-resistant depression (TRD, when usual medicines do not work). They compared different groups with and without depression and found six PGSs related to personality and compulsive traits linked to TRD in Taiwan. The genetic patterns matched U.S. results about 70–80% of the time, but some links seen in U.S. did not show up in Taiwan. This means genetics help explain TRD, but tests must be checked in different populations before use.

There was a moderate to high trans-ancestry concordance for the genetic estimates with TRD, while PGS association for specific traits were not transferable between East Asian and European populations. Genetic research across ancestries and geographic regions is crucial to learn population-specific etiology.

pdr_title: Factors associated with acute unscheduled care visits for asthma in the all of US dataset
pdr_journal_title: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine
pdr_abstract: Asthma exacerbations can cause patients to visit the emergency department %28ED%29 without prior appointments. This study analyzed factors associated with unscheduled ED visits among asthma patients by examining the All of Us Research Program dataset. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the All of Us database %282018-2024%29. Electronic health records %28EHR%29 were utilized to identify asthma patients based on physician-reported asthma diagnoses. Patients were divided into three groups based on ED visit frequency during the study period: General Asthma Patients %28no ED visits%29, Single ED Visit Asthma Patients %28one visit%29, and Frequent ED Visit Asthma Patients %28more than one visit%29. Python and R were utilized to perform a multinomial logistic regression analysis in order to examine demographic factors, social determinants, healthcare accessibility, neighborhood conditions and comorbidities. The research included 47, 227 asthma patients from a total participant pool of 409,420 individuals. The study included 33,046 %2870.0 %%29 General Asthma Patients with no ED visit record, 4779 %2810.1 %%29 Single ED Visit Asthma Patients with a single reported visit and 9402 %2819.9 %%29 Frequent ED Visit Asthma Patients with two or more ED visits. Factors significantly associated with frequent ED visits included income less than $10,000/year %28OR = 1.42; 95 % CI [1.25-1.61]%29, Black/African American race %28OR = 2.08; 95 % CI [1.61-2.68]%29, chest pain %28OR = 2.31; 95 % CI [2.16-2.48]%29, hypertension %28OR = 1.19; 95 % CI [1.11-1.28]%29, respiratory tract infections %28OR = 1.60; 95 % CI [1.50-1.71]%29, anxiety %28OR = 1.17; 95 % CI [1.08-1.28]%29, living near abandoned buildings %28OR = 1.20; 95 % CI [1.14-1.26]%29, and perceived daytime neighborhood unsafety %28OR = 1.07; 95 % CI [1.02-1.13]%29. Protective factors included higher income %28>$200,000/year, OR = 0.55; 95 % CI [0.42-0.70]%29, insurance coverage %28OR = 0.65; 95 % CI [0.58-0.71]%29, older age %28OR per year = 0.99; 95 % CI [0.99-0.99]%29, and male sex %28OR = 0.86; 95 % CI [0.81-0.92]%29. Female patients and younger age were associated with increased likelihood of ED visits. The frequency of unscheduled ED visits for asthma patients was significantly influenced by social determinants which include race, socioeconomic status, neighborhood factors, and specific comorbidities. Understanding these disparities can aid in the improvement of asthma management and the development of targeted interventions to address these critical factors.
lay_summary: Researchers used medical records from the All of Us program (2018–2024) to learn why some people with asthma visit the emergency room (ER). They studied 47,227 people: 70% had no ER visits, 10% had one, and 20% had two or more. People with very low income, being Black, chest pain, high blood pressure, lung infections, anxiety, living near abandoned buildings, or feeling their neighborhood unsafe were more likely to have frequent ER visits. Having high income, insurance, being older, or male made ER visits less likely. Helping social and health needs could reduce ER trips for asthma.

pdr_title: Changes in mental health care utilisation before and during the COVID-19 pandemic among people living with HIV in the USA: a retrospective cohort study using the All of Us dataset
pdr_abstract: Despite the profound impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on people living with HIV %28PLWH%29 mental health, large-scale, real-world data on mental healthcare utilisation and associated factors among PLWH remain limited. This study explores mental healthcare utilisation and associated factors among PLWH during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a retrospective cohort design, we identified and included 4575 PLWH through computational phenotyping based on relevant Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model concept sets from the All of Us programme between March 2018 and March 2022. Mental healthcare utilisation was measured using the yearly count of mental healthcare visits and compared between pre-pandemic %282018-2020%29 and during the pandemic %282020-2022%29. Incidence rate ratios %28IRRs%29 from the Poisson generalised linear mixed models were used to examine associations between mental healthcare utilisation, history of COVID-19 infection, demographic factors, pre-existing chronic conditions and socioeconomic status. Annual number of mental healthcare visits among PLWH decreased significantly during the pandemic compared with pre-pandemic %28IRR=0.89, p<0.001%29. COVID-19 infection %28IRR=1.35, p<0.001%29, pre-existing comorbidities %28one comorbidity: IRR=5.49; two or more: IRR=10.4, p<0.001%29 and Medicaid health insurance %28IRR=1.29, p=0.007%29 were associated with a higher number of visits. Middle-aged group participants %28aged 30-39: IRR=2.35, p=0.002; 40-49: IRR=3.49, p<0.001 and 50-64: IRR=2.07, p=0.004%29 had higher visit numbers compared with the youngest group %2818-29 years%29. Compared with white participants, black or African American %28IRR=0.71, p=0.002%29 and those with employer-sponsored or union-sponsored insurance %28IRR=0.54, p<0.001%29 had fewer visits. This study reveals a decrease in mental healthcare utilisation and diverse experiences of mental healthcare among PLWH during the COVID-19 pandemic. Addressing these disparities is crucial, particularly during public health emergencies.
lay_summary: This study used US health records for 4,575 people with HIV from 2018–2022 to compare yearly mental health visits before and during COVID-19. Visits fell 11%. People who had COVID had about 35% more visits. Those with one health problem had about five times as many visits and those with two or more had about ten times as many. Middle-aged adults used more care than 18–29 year olds. Black people and those with employer insurance used fewer visits. This shows mental care fell and access was uneven, so we need fairer, easier care during emergencies.

pdr_title: Validation of the American Heart Association Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events Equations in Diverse Socioeconomic Groups: The All of Us Cohort
pdr_journal_title: Journal of the American Heart Association
pdr_abstract: In 2023, the American Heart Association PREVENT %28Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events%29 equations were introduced as a tool to improve cardiovascular disease %28CVD%29 risk prediction. This study tests their performance in a diverse socioeconomic cohort. We analyzed All of Us participants aged 30 to 79 years without baseline CVD who had required PREVENT input data over a 5.4-year follow-up. Discrimination was assessed using Harrell's C-statistic, with calibration by comparing predicted and observed 5-year CVD rates across 10-year risk deciles. Mean data are ±SD. We examined 9010 individuals %28mean age, 63.0±11.0 years; 45.5% male%29. Racial and ethnic composition was 61.7% non-Hispanic White, 17.2% non-Hispanic Black, 4.5% multiracial/other, 1.3% non-Hispanic Asian, and 11.2% Hispanic or Latino. The 'other' race/ethnic category reflects participants who self-identified as 'other' in response to the, 'Which category describes you?' item in the Basics survey. Over a mean follow-up of 3.6±1.8 years, 9.0% experienced a cardiovascular event. The mean 10-year predicted risks were 0.23±0.17 for total CVD, 0.13±0.10 for atherosclerotic CVD %28ASCVD%29, and 0.19±0.17 for heart failure. The predicted-to-observed rate ratios were 5.3 for CVD and 3.3 for ASCVD. The C statistic for the overall sample was 0.732 %2895% CI, 0.718-0.752%29 for CVD, 0.716 %2895% CI, 0.698-0.741%29 for ASCVD, and 0.777 %2895% CI, 0.757-0.800%29 for heart failure. The PREVENT equations showed strong discrimination across all strata in this national cohort. Overprediction of CVD events likely reflects baseline differences in comorbidity burden between the PREVENT development cohort and this All of Us cohort, particularly due to the exclusion of individuals missing estimated glomerular filtration rate, a variable not routinely collected and likely missing, not at random. Strong discrimination supports potential clinical utility, though further work is needed to improve calibration in this population.
lay_summary: Researchers tested new American Heart Association heart risk equations (a calculator that estimates chance of heart problems) on 9,010 adults ages 30–79 in the All of Us study who had no prior heart disease. They followed people for about 3.6 years and compared predicted 10‑year risk to real events. Nine percent had a heart problem. The tool was good at telling who was higher or lower risk (about 73–78% at that job) but it overestimated how many people would get sick. This means it can help rank risk but needs adjustment before doctors use the exact numbers.

pdr_title: Adults With Congenital Heart Disease Have an Increased Prevalence of Autoimmunity
pdr_abstract: Adult congenital heart disease %28ACHD%29 individuals have increased risk of noncardiac comorbidities including cancer and infections. Whether they are at increased risk of autoimmunity is unknown. The purpose of this study was to understand the association of ACHD and risk for autoimmunity. A case-control study was performed using All of Us, a nationwide biomedical database. In 2024, we queried autoimmune conditions and ACHD individuals ≥18 year of age with congenital heart disease %28CHD%29 diagnoses determined using SNOMED, International Classification of Diseases %28ICD%29-9-CM, and ICD-100-CM classifications. ACHD individuals were matched 1:20 to controls for age, race, sex, smoking, and obesity. We examined subcategories of mild/moderate/severe CHD. Among 287,012 participants, 2941 ACHD %281.02%%29 individuals %28mean age 62 years, 55.3% female%29 were identified. ACHD individuals had increased odds of autoimmunity %28OR: 1.95; P < 0.05%29, both systemic %28OR: 1.94; P < 0.05%29 and organ specific %28OR: 1.54; P < 0.05%29 conditions. Sixty-nine percent had sufficient detail to be classified into mild/moderate/severe CHD; severe group was smaller and younger %28n = 162, mean age = 47.6 years%29 compared to mild %28n = 1169, mean age = 63.8%29 and moderate %28n = 703, mean age = 61.8 years%29 groups. Mild and moderate CHD were associated with autoimmunity %28OR: 1.93; P < 0.05 and OR: 1.56; P < 0.05, respectively%29. The entire severe CHD group did not show an increase in odds of autoimmunity %28OR: 1.45; P = 0.168%29. When the groups were subdivided by age, severe ACHD individuals ≥60 years did show increased odds of autoimmunity %28OR: 2.71; P < 0.05%29. ACHD individuals showed a nearly 2-fold increased odds of developing autoimmune conditions, both for systemic and organ-specific autoimmunity, which persisted among those with simple/moderate CHD. In an age-related analysis, the severe CHD group ≥60 years has a similar risk.
lay_summary: This study asked if adults born with heart defects (ACHD) have more autoimmune disease. Researchers looked at a U.S. health database of 287,012 adults and found 2,941 people with congenital heart disease and matched them to similar adults without it. They checked medical codes for autoimmune illnesses. People with ACHD were about twice as likely to have an autoimmune disease, including both whole-body and organ-specific types. The increase was seen in those with mild or moderate heart defects, and in people with severe defects who were 60 or older. This means doctors should watch ACHD patients for autoimmune problems.

pdr_title: Socioeconomic Factors Impact the Perception of Healthcare Experiences in Patients with Cirrhosis
pdr_abstract: Suboptimal patient-provider relationship is a significant contributor to healthcare disparities. Minority populations report fewer favorable interactions, which may lead to poorer outcomes and engagement in care. Patients with chronic diseases are especially at risk. We aimed to study perceptions of healthcare providers and experience among those with cirrhosis. The nationally representative database, All of Us, was queried. The primary outcome was 'favorable healthcare experiences,' defined as whether providers asked for opinions, demonstrated respect, and were easy to understand. The secondary outcome was 'unfavorable healthcare experiences,' defined as whether patients felt they were treated with less courtesy, received poorer service, or not listened to. We compared the experience between income levels and other demographic variables. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for a priori covariates. 5753 patients with cirrhosis were included with a mean age of 58. The majority were male %2851%%29, White %2852%%29, and US-born %2884%%29. On multivariable analysis, compared to those earning > $150 k annually, participants with $10-35 k and < $10 k reported significantly lower odds of finding providers easy to understand %28OR 0.40 [0.17-0.96] and OR 0.37 [0.15-0.94], respectively%29 and higher odds of feeling they were treated with less courtesy %28OR 3.10 [1.06-9.03] and OR 4.13 [1.30-13.1], respectively%29. After further controlling for education, participants with an annual income of $10-35 k and < $10 k still reported higher odds of feeling they received poorer service than others %28OR 3.87 [1.09-13.71] and OR 5.01 [1.26-19.8], respectively%29. Compared to men, women felt that they were not listened to %28OR 1.90 [1.37-2.63]%29. Patients with cirrhosis from various backgrounds report significantly different experiences with providers. Notably, those with lower income endorsed more unfavorable interactions. We identified areas for interventions to strengthen the patient-provider relationship among patients with chronic liver disease.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if people with cirrhosis (long-term liver disease) feel respected and understood by their healthcare teams. They looked at answers from 5,753 people in a national database about whether doctors asked their opinions, showed respect, were easy to understand, or treated them with less courtesy, poorer service, or did not listen. People who made under $35,000 a year were much more likely to say providers were hard to understand and treated them worse. Women were more likely than men to say they were not listened to. This shows care needs to improve for low-income patients and women.
