pdr_title: The human glucocorticoid receptor variant rs6190 increases blood cholesterol and promotes atherosclerosis
pdr_abstract: Elevated cholesterol poses cardiovascular risks. The glucocorticoid receptor %28GR%29 harbors a still undefined role in cholesterol regulation. Here, we report that a coding SNP in the gene encoding the GR, rs6190, is associated with increased cholesterol in women according to UK Biobank and All of Us %28NIH%29 datasets. In SNP-genocopying mice, we found that the SNP enhanced hepatic GR activity to transactivate Pcsk9 and Bhlhe40, negative regulators of LDL and HDL receptors, respectively. In mice, the SNP was sufficient to elevate circulating cholesterol across all lipoprotein fractions and the risk and severity of atherosclerotic lesions on the proatherogenic hAPOE*2/*2 background. The SNP effect on atherosclerosis was blocked by in vivo liver knockdown of Pcsk9 and Bhlhe40. Also, corticosterone and testosterone were protective against the mutant GR program in cholesterol and atherosclerosis in male mice, while the SNP effect was additive to estrogen loss in females. Remarkably, we found that the mutant GR program was conserved in human hepatocyte-like cells using CRISPR-engineered, SNP-genocopying human induced pluripotent stem cells. Taken together, our study leverages a nonrare human variant to uncover a GR-dependent mechanism contributing to atherogenic risk, particularly in women.
lay_summary: This study tested whether a common DNA change (called rs6190) in the glucocorticoid receptor (a protein that senses stress hormones) gene affects cholesterol and artery disease. Researchers looked at human health records and then made mice and human liver cells with the same change. The variant raised blood cholesterol and made artery plaques worse in mice, and was linked to higher cholesterol in women. Turning off two liver genes (Pcsk9 and Bhlhe40) stopped the bad effects. These results can help find people at higher heart risk and point to liver targets for new treatments.

pdr_title: Polygenic Risk Prediction for Normal-Tension Glaucoma
pdr_abstract: Normal-tension glaucoma %28NTG%29 is a subtype of glaucoma characterized by optic nerve damage in the setting of normal intraocular pressure. Polygenic risk scores %28PRSs%29 have shown potential to assist with risk prediction in glaucoma, but to date no comprehensive studies have evaluated the predictive ability of PRSs for NTG. We utilized genome-wide association study %28GWAS%29 summary data for NTG from a European cohort to estimate the variant weights and construct PRSs. The PRSs were computed using both the SBayesRC and clumping and thresholding %28C+T%29 methods in 317 European ancestry NTG cases and 634 controls from the National Institutes of Health All of Us dataset. To validate our findings, we used the Genetics of Glaucoma %28GOG%29 dataset for NTG cases %28n = 89%29 and the QSkin Sun and Health Study %28QSkin%29 dataset for controls %28n = 267%29. We applied the SBayesRC method, which incorporates genome functional annotation, to compare results across both studies. Logistic regression was performed to assess the association between PRSs and NTG. SBayesRC analysis demonstrated that the NTG PRS was significantly associated with NTG, yielding an odds ratio per standard deviation of 1.53 %2895% confidence interval [CI], 1.32-1.77; P = 6.86 × 10⁻9%29 in the All of Us dataset and 1.83 %2895% CI, 1.42-2.38; P = 4.01 × 10⁻6%29 in the combined GOG and QSkin dataset. The C+T method produced results similar to those for SBayesRC. Despite the limited sample size of current NTG GWASs, our findings suggest that NTG-specific PRSs hold promise for risk prediction. Future large-scale GWASs for NTG may enable the development of clinically relevant PRSs, improving early detection and personalized risk assessment for this challenging phenotype.
lay_summary: This study tested whether genetic risk scores (scores that add up many small gene effects) can predict normal-tension glaucoma (NTG). Researchers used genetic data from about 950 European-ancestry people (317 with NTG, 634 without) and checked results in about 350 more people. People with higher genetic scores were about 50% more likely to have NTG in the first group and about 80% more likely in the second. The two ways of making scores gave similar results. This could help find people at risk earlier, but bigger studies are needed.

pdr_title: Evaluating Misalignment Between Emergency Department and Discharge Diagnoses
pdr_journal_title: Studies in Health Technology and Informatics
pdr_abstract: This study examined diagnostic discrepancies between emergency department %28ED%29 and inpatient care using three distinct datasets: the All of Us Research Program, a synthetic VA dataset, and TriNetX. Inclusion criteria focused on patients admitted through the ED, with diagnoses compared at two levels: category %28530+ categories%29 and body system %2822 categories%29. A many-to-many comparison was used for the All of Us and TriNetX datasets, while a one-to-one comparison was used for the VA dataset due to its limited diagnosis records. The analytical datasets comprised patients with chronic cardiopulmonary conditions, with All of Us containing 599 patients, TriNetX 1,562 patients, and the VA dataset 12,621 patients. High mismatch rates were consistently observed. At the category level, no matches were seen in 19.10% of All of Us cases, 20.30% of TriNetX cases, and 58.30% of VA cases. For the body system level, no matches occurred in 7.78%, 7.70%, and 30.30% of cases, respectively. Partial matches were more common in patients with high comorbidities and inaccurate diagnoses were associated with longer hospital stays.
lay_summary: This study checked whether emergency room (ER) diagnoses matched final hospital diagnoses. Researchers used three health record datasets with 14,782 patients who had chronic heart or lung problems. They compared early and final diagnoses by disease category and by body system. At the category level, no match happened in about 19%, 20%, and 58% of cases; by body system, no match happened in about 8%, 8%, and 30%. Mismatches were more common in people with many other health problems and led to longer hospital stays. This means hospitals should double-check diagnoses to help patients get safer, faster care.

pdr_title: Sleep duration and timing are associated with next-day physical activity: Insights from two large-scale wearable sensor studies
pdr_journal_title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
pdr_abstract: Sleep and physical activity %28PA%29 are pillars of health. However, the temporal dynamics between these two behaviors remain poorly understood. This research aims to examine the independent and interactive between- and within-person associations of sleep duration and sleep onset timing on next-day PA duration in two large, longitudinal samples of adults under free-living conditions. In the primary study, participants %28N = 19,963; 5,995,080 person-nights%29 wore a validated biometric device %28WHOOP%29 for 1 y %2801/09/2021 to 31/08/2022%29. Objective sleep and PA metrics were derived from the wrist-worn device. Generalized additive mixed models assessed between- and within-person associations between sleep and PA variables, adjusted for age, sex, Body Mass Index, weekday/weekend, seasonal effects, biometric feedback, and autocorrelated errors. Between participants, longer sleep duration and later sleep onset timing were associated with decreased moderate-to-vigorous PA %28MVPA%29 and overall PA duration %28ps < 0.001%29. Within participants, sleeping shorter-than-usual and falling asleep earlier-than-usual were associated with increased next-day MVPA and overall PA, whereas sleeping longer-than-usual, or falling asleep later-than-usual, showed the opposite relationship %28ps < 0.001%29. Next-day MVPA duration was highest following earlier-than-usual sleep onset timing combined with one's typical sleep duration. Results were consistent but smaller in magnitude in the external validation study %28N = 5,898; 635,477 person-nights%29 using Fitbit data from the All of Us Research Program. Individuals may sacrifice time in one health behavior for time in the other. Interventions promoting exercise and holistic public health messaging should consider the temporal dynamics between sleep and next-day PA outcomes.

lay_summary: This study asked how sleep length and bedtime affect how much people move the next day. Researchers used wrist wearables on about 20,000 people for a year and on about 6,000 people in a second group. Devices recorded sleep and physical activity. People who usually slept longer or went to bed later moved less than others. When a person slept less or went to bed earlier than their usual, they moved more the next day. The results suggest changing sleep timing could help increase daily activity.

pdr_title: Exploring depression treatment response by using polygenic risk scoring across diverse populations
pdr_abstract: Treatment-resistant depression %28TRD%29, usually defined as limited or no response to at least two antidepressants, occurs in approximately one-third of individuals diagnosed with major depressive disorder %28MDD%29. Studies of individuals of European ancestry highlight a genetic overlap between TRD and MDD. We analyzed two large and diverse biobanks, the UCLA ATLAS Community Health Study %28ATLAS%29 and the All of Us Research Program %28AoU%29, to test for associations between a polygenic score for major depression %28MDD-PGS%29 and TRD. Compared to treatment responders, TRD individuals have higher MDD-PGS across all ancestries. MDD-PGS was significantly associated with response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in individuals of European and Hispanic/Latin American genetic ancestries in both biobanks. In AoU, a decreased MDD-PGS was observed in response to tricyclics or serotonin modulators in individuals of European American ancestry and in response to serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors in individuals of African American ancestry. ATLAS found that MDD-PGS showed lower odds of responding to atypical agents than did TRD in MDD-affected individuals belonging to the Hispanic/Latin American group, MDD-PGS was associated with atypical agents. Overall, by leveraging larger sample sizes from two diverse biobanks, we provide new insights into antidepressant response and treatment specificity for MDD in individuals of diverse genetic ancestries.
lay_summary: This study wanted to know if a genetic risk score (a number that adds up many small gene risks) can help predict who won’t get better with usual antidepressants. Researchers used health and DNA records from two large, diverse U.S. biobanks with people of European, Hispanic/Latino, and African ancestry. They found that people with treatment-resistant depression (no help after two or more drugs; about one-third) had higher genetic risk scores. The score also matched how people did on certain drug types, like SSRIs, in some ancestry groups. This could help doctors choose better medicines for different people.

In AoU, a decreased MDD-PGS was observed in response to tricyclics or serotonin modulators in individuals of European American ancestry and in response to serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors in individuals of African American ancestry. ATLAS found that MDD-PGS showed lower odds of responding to atypical agents than did TRD in MDD-affected individuals belonging to the Hispanic/Latin American group, MDD-PGS was associated with atypical agents. Overall, by leveraging larger sample sizes from two diverse biobanks, we provide new insights into antidepressant response and treatment specificity for MDD in individuals of diverse genetic ancestries.

pdr_title: Hearing Loss Is Associated With Depression and Dysthymia in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: To investigate the association between hearing loss and depressive disorders in a large national cohort. Cross-sectional epidemiologic study. Adults ≥ 18 years old from the federally initiated All of Us Research Program were analyzed. The exposure was bilateral sensorineural hearing loss %28SNHL%29 defined by ICD-10 code %28H90.3%29. The outcomes were depressive disorders defined by major depressive disorder %28ICD-10 codes F32-33%29 and dysthymia %28ICD-10 code F34.1%29. The odds of depression or dysthymia in subjects with and without hearing loss were assessed with univariable and multivariable regression, controlling for known confounding variables %28age, sex, race, ethnicity, education, hypertension, and type II diabetes%29. Out of the 375,438 participants with complete data, the mean %28SD%29 age was 55 years %28±17%29. 61.7% of subjects identified as female. The cohort included 25,260 %286.7%%29 individuals with a bilateral SNHL diagnosis. After controlling for covariates, the odds of major depressive disorder diagnosis were 2.05 times %2895% CI 1.99-2.11; p < 0.001%29 higher for those with hearing loss compared to those without hearing loss. After controlling for covariates, the odds of dysthymia diagnosis were 2.68 times %2895% CI 2.50-2.88; p < 0.001%29 higher for those with hearing loss compared to those without hearing loss. In the All of Us Research Program, bilateral SNHL is strongly associated with major depressive disorder and dysthymia. This supports the growing body of literature linking psychological disorders, specifically depression, with hearing loss. Future studies should look at stratified analyses, enabled by the massive sample size in the All of Us Research Program.

pdr_title: Comorbidities and systemic steroids drive pneumonia risk in inflammatory bowel disease: Propensity score-matched cohort study
pdr_journal_title: World Journal of Gastrointestinal Pharmacology and Therapeutics
pdr_abstract: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease %28IBD%29 are at an increased risk of bacterial pneumonia, contributing to significant morbidity and mortality. While previous studies have identified various risk factors, including medications and comorbidities, the independent contribution of IBD to pneumonia risk remains unclear. We hypothesized that the increased pneumonia risk is primarily driven by factors other than IBD itself. To investigate the relative contributions of IBD, comorbidities, and medications to pneumonia risk in patients with IBD. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the All of Us Research Program database %282010-2022%29. We matched 2810 participants with IBD 1:1 with controls using four propensity score models: %281%29 Demographics/Lifestyle only; %282%29 Plus comorbidities; %283%29 Plus medications; and %284%29 All factors combined. Then we used Cox proportional hazards models to assess pneumonia risk and logistic regression to evaluate risk factors. In the primary analysis of 5620 matched participants, IBD was not independently associated with increased pneumonia risk [hazard ratio %28HR%29 = 1.07, 95%CI: 0.84-1.35] when matched for all factors. However, participants with IBD had significantly higher risk %28HR = 2.08, 95%CI: 1.56-2.78%29 when matched only for demographics and lifestyle factors. Within the IBD cohort, a high comorbidity burden %28Charlson Comorbidity Index ≥ 10%29 [odds ratio %28OR%29 = 12.20, 95%CI: 6.69-23.00] and systemic steroid use %28OR = 2.26, 95%CI: 1.21-4.64%29 were independently associated with increased pneumonia risk. Comorbidities and systemic steroids, rather than IBD itself, drive pneumonia risk. Management should focus on these factors and prioritize vaccination in high-risk patients.

lay_summary: Researchers used health records from 2010–2022 to see if people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) get more pneumonia. They compared 2,810 people with IBD to 2,810 similar people without IBD. After accounting for other health problems and medicines, IBD alone did not raise pneumonia risk. But without those adjustments, IBD looked like it doubled risk. In people with IBD, other health problems made pneumonia about 12 times more likely and using steroids that affect the whole body about twice as likely. This means doctors should control other illnesses, avoid steroid use when possible, and give vaccines to high-risk patients.

pdr_title: The Effect of Patient-Provider Relationships on Compliance in Uncontrolled Diabetic Patients
pdr_abstract: Background Effective patient-provider communication is critical for managing chronic diseases like diabetes mellitus %28DM%29. This study examines whether patient attitudes toward their healthcare providers influence diabetes management and compliance, comparing individuals with poorly managed diabetes mellitus %28PM DM%29 and those without DM %28No DM%29.  Methods Data from the All of Us Research Program was analyzed. After excluding incomplete responses, the final sample included 1903 PM DM patients and 94,218 No DM patients. Patient perceptions of respect, involvement in medical decision making, and provider interactions were assessed. Bivariate analysis was used to identify responses that were independently associated with PM DM. Variables found to be independently associated with PM DM at p<0.10 were entered into a multivariable model, and backwards stepwise binary logistic regression was used to find the model of best fit. Variables found to be significant %28p<0.05%29 in the multivariable model were retained.  Results Patients who felt disrespected by providers were significantly more likely to have poorly managed diabetes %28OR = 1.396, 95% CI: 1.189, 1.639, p<0.05%29. Counterintuitively, patients who reported always being asked for their opinion in treatment decisions were likely to have PM DM %28OR = 1.466, 95% CI: 1.235, 1.740, p<0.05%29. Patients who were not nervous to see their provider were also more likely to have PM DM %28OR = 1.365, 95% CI: 1.152, 1.618, p<0.05%29. Conclusion Findings suggest that positive provider interaction does not always translate to better disease control. Future studies should explore how communication styles and shared decision-making impact long-term adherence to diabetes treatment.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether how patients feel about their doctors affects diabetes care. Researchers used survey data from the All of Us program, comparing 1,903 people with poorly controlled diabetes to 94,218 without diabetes. People who felt disrespected were about 40% more likely to have poor diabetes control. Surprisingly, those who said they were always asked their opinion were about 45% more likely to have poor control, and people not nervous to see their provider were about 35% more likely. This means friendly talks alone may not ensure better diabetes care, so patients should ask for clear treatment plans.

pdr_title: Prevalence and Correlates of Lipoprotein%28a%29 Testing in a Diverse Cohort of U.S. Adults
pdr_abstract: Once-per-lifetime lipoprotein%28a%29 [Lp%28a%29] testing is recommended by multiple professional societies during cardiovascular disease risk assessment. The purpose of this study was to assess the prevalence and identify correlates of Lp%28a%29 testing in a real-world, diverse sample. Participants were ≥18 years of age from the All of Us Research Study who shared electronic medical record information through 2022 %28N = 266,612%29. Completion of Lp%28a%29 testing was defined by the following: presence of Lp%28a%29 values, Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms or Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes electronic health record listings for Lp%28a%29 testing, or an Internal Classification of Diseases-10 code for elevated Lp%28a%29. Multivariable logistic regression assessed the association of demographic, socioeconomic, and clinical variables with Lp%28a%29 testing. The mean age was 52 years, 61% were women, and 53% were non-Hispanic White. A total of 2,172 %280.8%%29 underwent Lp%28a%29 testing, 86% of whom had clinical cardiovascular disease. Compared to non-Hispanic White individuals, non-Hispanic Black individuals %28OR: 0.68, 95% CI: 0.58-0.81%29 had 32% lower odds of Lp%28a%29 testing. Less than high school education %28OR: 0.34, 95% CI: 0.25-0.44%29, unemployment %28OR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.68-0.85%29, and disability %28OR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.65-0.91%29 were associated with a 23% to 66% lower odds of Lp%28a%29 testing. Among clinical factors, non-Lp%28a%29 lipid abnormality %28OR: 5.64, 95% CI: 4.72-6.79%29 and prevalent cardiovascular disease %28OR: 3.21, 95% CI: 2.76-3.74%29 were strongly associated with Lp%28a%29 testing. The prevalence of Lp%28a%29 testing among US adults is exceedingly low, especially for non-Hispanic Black individuals and those with socioeconomic risk. These results underline the importance of emphasizing health equity in Lp%28a%29 testing expansion.

pdr_title: Examining Reasons for Using Non-Primary Care Providers as Usual Source of Health Care: Insights From the All of Us Study
pdr_abstract: Having a primary care usual source of care %28USC%29 is associated with better population health outcomes. However, the percent of adults in the United States %28US%29 with a usual primary care provider is declining. We sought to identify factors associated with establishing a USC at an urgent care clinic or emergency department as opposed to primary care. We analyzed data from 57,152 participants in the All of Us study who reported having a USC. We used the Andersen Behavioral Model of Health Services Use framework and multivariable logistic regression to examine associations among predisposing, enabling, and need factors, according to the source of usual care. An urgent care clinic, minute clinic, or emergency department was the source of usual care for 6.3% of our sample. The odds of seeking care at this type of facility increased with younger age, lower educational attainment, and better health status. Black and Hispanic individuals, as well as those who reported experiencing discrimination in medical settings or that their provider was of a different race and ethnicity, were also less likely to have a primary care USC. Financial concerns, being anxious about seeing a provider, and the inability to take time off from work also increased the likelihood of having a non-primary care USC. Improving the rates of having a primary care USC among younger and healthy adults may be achievable through policies that can improve access to convenient, affordable primary care. Efforts to improve diversity among primary care providers and reduce discrimination experienced by patients may also improve the USC rates for racial and ethnic minority groups.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know why some adults use urgent care or the ER as their usual place for health care instead of a regular doctor. They looked at survey data from 57,152 people in the All of Us study who said they had a usual source of care (USC). About 6% used urgent care, minute clinics, or the ER as their USC. Younger people, those with less education, healthier people, Black and Hispanic people, and people who felt discriminated against or who worried about costs or taking time off work were more likely to use non‑primary care. Making primary care easier to get, cheaper, and less biased could help more people have a regular doctor.

pdr_title: Evaluating Genomic and Clinical Risk Factors for Alzheimer's Disease in Individuals with Hypertension
pdr_abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer's disease %28AD%29 is a progressive neurodegenerative condition whose growing prevalence has become an increasingly important public health concern as the population ages. The lack of a definitive cure elevates the importance of identifying risk factors that are crucial for prevention efforts. Hypertension %28HTN%29 and obesity have emerged as two highly widespread, interrelated conditions that have independently been associated with AD risk. Despite extensive research into AD pathology, the impact of obesity in a hypertensive population is not well explored. This study aims to investigate how obesity and blood pressure control within a hypertensive population may interact with genomic risk and environmental factors to influence AD incidence. Methods: A retrospective cohort of matched AD and normal patients diagnosed with HTN and taking anti-HTN drugs %28n = 1862%29 from the All of Us database was analyzed. In this hypertensive cohort, obesity was significantly associated with increased AD risk. Genome-wide association studies %28GWASs%29 were conducted on hypertensive AD individuals %28n = 1030%29 and identified six single nucleotide variants %28SNVs%29 that were associated with AD development in this population. Results: Obesity and Area Deprivation Index, a measure of socioeconomic status, were significantly associated with elevated AD risk within the hypertensive cohort. GWAS analysis identified six SNVs significantly associated with AD development among the hypertensive cohort. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that among hypertensive individuals, comorbid obesity and the Area Deprivation Index confer greater AD risk. These results highlight the critical need for obesity prevention and management strategies as part of Alzheimer's risk reduction efforts.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if obesity, genes, and neighborhood poverty change Alzheimer’s risk in people with high blood pressure. They looked at medical and genetic records from 1,862 people with high blood pressure, and ran genetic scans on 1,030 people who had both high blood pressure and Alzheimer’s. They found that obesity and a higher Area Deprivation Index (a measure of neighborhood disadvantage) were linked to more Alzheimer’s, and six single-letter DNA changes (single nucleotide variants) were tied to the disease. This suggests managing weight and improving community conditions may lower Alzheimer’s risk for people with high blood pressure.

pdr_title: Sociodemographic, health-related, and clinical characteristics and their associations with mortality among all of us participants compared with the United States general population
pdr_abstract: The large and diverse All of Us Research Program offers tremendous opportunities for health research. However, results may not be generalizable to the U.S. population due to the program's targeted recruitment efforts. We compared All of Us participants to those from the nationally representative continuous 1999-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey %28NHANES%29 with respect to: overall mortality rates; the distribution of sociodemographic, health-related, and clinical characteristics; the association of each characteristic with mortality estimated using Cox proportional-hazards models; and population attributable fractions %28PAFs%29 for each characteristic and mortality. All of Us participants were older, less likely to be Non-Hispanic White, had more years of education, and had a higher prevalence of major chronic conditions than NHANES. Mortality rates were generally lower for All of Us participants, especially at older ages. The direction of associations in All of Us and NHANES matched for almost all comparisons, but differed in magnitude for some conditions, primarily clinical diagnoses. PAFs were generally higher in All of Us. Predictors of mortality in All of Us do not consistently generalize to the U.S. population. Analytical approaches are needed to address non-representativeness and mitigate potential biases associated with the selection into the All of Us cohort.
lay_summary: This study looked to see if people in the All of Us research program are like the U.S. population. Researchers compared All of Us volunteers to a national health survey from 1999–2018. They checked peoples’ backgrounds, health conditions, and deaths using statistical risk models that follow people over time. All of Us members were older, more racially diverse, had more schooling, and more chronic illnesses, but they died less often, especially when older. Risk factors worked the same way but were stronger or weaker for some conditions. This means scientists must adjust for these differences before using All of Us results for everyone.

pdr_title: Food Insecurity in Hidradenitis Suppurativa: A Cross-Sectional Analysis from the Population-Based All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa %28HS%29 is a chronic inflammatory cutaneous disease associated with obesity and low socioeconomic status that can have a significant impact on quality of life. Food insecurity %28FI%29 is associated with a higher likelihood of having a chronic health condition. This cross-sectional study was undertaken to assess the association between HS and FI. We performed secondary analysis of a cross-sectional survey of individuals 18 years and older registered in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program in May 2024. The study sample was limited to those who had completed the Children's HealthWatch Hunger Vital Sign™ FI screening survey, validated for use in adults in 2017. HS status was assessed among study participants based on ICD-9/10 diagnosis code %28705.83 or L73.2%29. Multivariable logistic regression was used to characterize the association between HS diagnosis and food security status, adjusting for sex, race and ethnicity, age, and income. Among participants with HS, 37/134 %2827.6%%29 screened positive for FI. In comparison, among those without HS, 6,278/56,967 %2811%%29 screened positive. In an adjusted multivariable logistic regression, HS was associated with significantly higher odds of FI %28OR: 1.70, 95% CI: 1.09-2.60%29. Study results demonstrated a significant association between HS and FI. Further research is needed to understand specific factors mediating the relationship between HS and FI. The study highlights an opportunity for dermatologists to take an active role in screening for FI in patients with HS and in providing resources as necessary.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether people with hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), a long‑term skin disease, are more likely to have food insecurity (not having enough food or money for food). Researchers analyzed adult survey data from the NIH All of Us program using a short screening tool for food insecurity. They found about 28% of people with HS had food insecurity compared with 11% without HS, and the link stayed even after accounting for age, sex, race, and income. Doctors treating HS should ask about food access and help connect patients to resources.

pdr_title: Genetic disease risks of under-represented founder populations in New York City
pdr_abstract: The detection of founder pathogenic variants, those observed in high frequency only in a group of individuals with increased inter-relatedness, can help improve delivery of health care for that community. We identified 16 groups with shared ancestry, based on genomic segments that are shared through identity by descent %28IBD%29, in New York City using the genomic data of 25,366 residents from the All Of Us Research Program and the Mount Sinai BioMe biobank. From these groups we defined 7 as founder populations, mostly communities currently under-represented in medical genomics research, such as Puerto Rican and Garifuna. The enrichment analysis of ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic %28P/LP%29 variants in each group identified 201 of these damaging variants across the seven founder populations. We confirmed disease-causing variants previously reported to occur at increased frequencies in Ashkenazi Jewish and Puerto Rican genetic ancestry groups, but most of the damaging variants identified have not been previously associated with any such founder populations, and most of these founder populations have not been described to have increased prevalence of the associated rare disease. Twenty-two of 47 variants meeting Tier 2 prenatal screening criteria %281/100 carrier frequency within these founder groups%29 have never previously been reported. We show how population structure studies can provide insights into rare diseases disproportionately affecting under-represented founder populations, delivering a health care benefit but also a potential source of stigmatization of these communities, who should be part of the decision-making about implementation into health care delivery.

pdr_title: Epidemiology and Comorbidities of Psychodermatologic Conditions
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery
pdr_abstract: Psychodermatologic conditions include primary psychodermatologic disorders %28PPDs%29, psychological conditions manifesting with dermatologic symptoms, and psychophysiological disorders, dermatologic conditions influenced by psychological stress. Despite their clinical significance and considerable impact on quality of life, the comprehensive epidemiology and neuropsychiatric comorbidity profiles of these disorders remain limited. To evaluate the prevalence and comorbidity profiles of psychodermatologic conditions in a diverse, population-based cohort. A nested, case-control study was conducted using data from the All of us research program. From 287,011 eligible participants, 984 patients with PPDs %28trichotillomania, skin picking disorder, dermatitis artefacta, body dysmorphic disorder, delusions of parasitosis%29 and 40,535 patients with psychophysiological disorders %28psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, acne vulgaris, hidradenitis suppurativa, vulvodynia%29 were identified using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes. Each patient was paired with 4 controls based on age, sex, and race/ethnicity using nearest-neighbor propensity score matching. Multivariable logistic regression calculated adjusted odds ratios %28aOR%29 and 95% confidence intervals to evaluate associations with various neuropsychiatric comorbidities. PPDs showed low point prevalences %28range: ≤0.01-0.17%%29 but demonstrated markedly higher odds of neuropsychiatric comorbidities, including depressive disorders %28range: aOR, 5.72-13.94%29, anxiety disorders %28range: aOR, 5.96-8.40%29, and personality disorders %28range: aOR, 8.67-13.56 Psychophysiological disorders had higher prevalence rates %28range: 0.14%-5.72%%29 but showed more moderate associations, including depressive disorders %28range: aOR, 2.24-3.13%29, neurodevelopmental disorders %28range: aOR, 1.20-2.36%29, and sleep-wake disorders %28range: aOR, 2.25-3.95%29. Findings reveal distinct but overlapping comorbidity profiles between PPDs and psychophysiological disorders, emphasizing the need for tailored interventions that address the psychosocial and biological complexities of these conditions.
lay_summary: This study looked at how common skin problems tied to mental health (psychodermatologic) are and what mental health issues come with them. Researchers used health data from 287,011 people and found 984 with primary psychodermatologic disorders (like hair pulling or skin picking) and 40,535 with stress-linked skin diseases (like psoriasis or acne). Primary disorders were rare (under 0.2%) but often had much higher rates of depression, anxiety, and personality problems. Stress-linked skin diseases were more common (about 0.1%–5.7%) and linked to more depression, developmental, and sleep problems. The results say doctors should check both skin and mental health.

pdr_title: Association between Nucleoside and Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor Use and Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Risk in All of Us
pdr_abstract: To assess the association between the systemic use of nucleoside and nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors %28NRTIs%29 and primary open-angle glaucoma %28POAG%29. Retrospective cohort study. Individuals aged ≥40 years with linked electronic health record %28EHR%29 data in the National Institutes of Health %28NIH%29 All of Us dataset. Participants with a diagnosis of POAG before the use of NRTIs were excluded. A cohort of 1:10 NRTI users to nonusers was created using a propensity score matching design, considering age, race, sex at birth, human immunodeficiency virus %28HIV%29 diagnosis, hepatitis B diagnosis, and family history of POAG. A multivariable logistic regression model was used to adjust for residual imbalance. Sensitivity analyses were performed for self-reported eye doctor visits. Diagnosis of POAG. Among the 305 441 All of Us participants aged ≥40 years with a linked EHR, we identified 718 individuals %280.24%%29 with NRTI use, excluding participants with a diagnosis of POAG before NRTI exposure. The rate of POAG in the NRTI users was 4.32% %28N = 31%29. The rate of POAG in the propensity score-matched control group %28N = 7180%29 was 2.00% %28N = 144%29. Use of NRTI was associated with an increased risk of POAG %28odds ratio [OR], 2.21; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.48-3.28; P < 0.001%29. When adjusting for residual imbalance of family history of POAG, HIV diagnosis, and hepatitis B diagnosis, use of any NRTIs remained significantly associated with an increased risk of developing POAG %28OR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.22-2.77; P = 0.004%29. After matching and adjusting for self-reported eye doctor visits, NRTIs remained significantly associated with POAG risk %28OR, 2.30; 95% CI, 1.07-4.96; P = 0.033%29. Use of NRTIs was associated with a higher risk of POAG with propensity score matching for covariates and adjusting for residual imbalances. The author%28s%29 have no proprietary or commercial interest in any materials discussed in this article.
lay_summary: This study asked whether taking nucleoside or nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs, medicines for HIV and hepatitis B) is linked to primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG, a common eye disease that can cause vision loss). Researchers checked health records of people 40 and older and compared 718 NRTI users to 7,180 similar nonusers. POAG happened in 4.3% of users versus 2.0% of nonusers. The higher rate stayed after checking for other differences. People on NRTIs may benefit from regular eye exams to catch glaucoma early.

pdr_title: APOE ε4 and Risk of Intracranial Hemorrhage in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Taking Apixaban
pdr_abstract: The APOE ε4 variant is causally linked to cerebral amyloid angiopathy and is a risk factor for intracranial hemorrhage %28ICH%29 among warfarin-treated patients with atrial fibrillation. Nevertheless, its impact on those treated with apixaban remains unknown. To test the hypothesis that APOE ε4 allele carriership is associated with an increased risk of ICH in patients with atrial fibrillation taking apixaban. This cohort study involved data from the All of Us Research Program, a longitudinal, population-based study in the United States. Inclusion criteria were age older than 50 years, history of atrial fibrillation, and anticoagulation with apixaban. Participants with a history of ischemic stroke or ICH were excluded. Up to 3 years of follow-up data were available. Data were collected from 2017 to 2022 and analyzed from November 2023 to December 2024. APOE ε2, ε3, and ε4 were ascertained using variants rs429358 and rs7412. APOE ε4 was modeled dichotomously %28noncarriers [no alleles] vs carriers [1 or 2 alleles]%29. Incident ICH, including any new intraparenchymal, subdural, or subarachnoid hemorrhage after initiation of apixaban therapy. Of 413 477 All of Us participants, 2038 were eligible. Their mean %28SD%29 age was 71 %289%29 years; 918 %2845%%29 were female, 1120 %2855%%29 were male, and 1710 %2883%%29 had European ancestry. Among these participants, 483 %2823.7%%29 were carriers of at least 1 APOE ε4 allele. After a median follow-up of 2.9 years, 26 participants sustained an ICH %28cumulative incidence, 1.5%; 95% CI, 1.0%-2.2%%29, of whom 12 %28cumulative incidence, 3.1%; 95% CI, 1.7%-5.3%%29 were carriers and 14 %28cumulative incidence, 1%; 95% CI, 0.6%-1.7%%29 were noncarriers %28P = .007%29. Multivariable Cox proportional hazard models confirmed this association: compared with noncarriership, APOE ε4 carriership was associated with a 3-fold increase in the risk of ICH %28hazard ratio, 3.07; 95% CI, 1.42-6.65%29. APOE information improved the discrimination of risk prediction scores %28C statistic of 0.74 and 0.68 for models with and without APOE, respectively; P = .03%29. Further research is needed to evaluate whether cerebral amyloid angiopathy mediates the observed association and whether APOE e4 information improves clinical decision-making about anticoagulation therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation. The latter is important now that APOE information is used in clinical settings to guide antiamyloid treatment for Alzheimer disease and has been returned to millions of persons by direct-to-consumer genotyping companies.

lay_summary: This study looked to see if people with an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) who carry the APOE ε4 gene variant have more brain bleeds while taking the blood thinner apixaban. pdr_title: A Model for Rapid Innovation for Engagement, Enrollment, and Data and Sample Collection in a Diverse Cohort Study: Insights from All of Us Participant Labs
pdr_abstract: To improve engagement and retention of a cohort that reflects the US population within the All of Us Research Program, we created and implemented an innovation infrastructure and initiatives. All of Us participant laboratories %28APLs%29 established innovation-specific processes to rapidly ideate, select, implement, and evaluate cost-effective innovative initiatives, while mitigating risks. This was done within 4 priority areas: accelerating enrollment, enhancing engagement and retention, improving biospecimen collection, and broadening data types. Participants within the All of Us Research Program were engaged in this research between April 6, 2022 and May 6, 2024. We present a summary of APL processes and portfolio along with 5 specific initiatives that rapidly tested innovative ways to increase task completion and broaden biospecimen submission accessibility. Each initiative's cost-benefit profile was evaluated by a committee of program leadership. Findings include the following: %281%29 offering compensation increased task completion, the degree of which was dependent on the context and amount of compensation; and %282%29 adding evening and weekend blood donation appointment times and distributing saliva collection kits through community partners increased donations from participants who have been historically underrepresented in biomedical research. On average, program staff predicted initiative effect sizes would be more than double their actual effect. We found that large research studies can rapidly innovate to meet program goals, including a focus on diversity. We identified specific strategies and tactics to improve health research engagement and retention, with a focus on historically underrepresented in biomedical research communities, which can be used by numerous health research studies.
lay_summary: The All of Us study tested new ways to get more people to join, stay, and send samples from April 6, 2022 to May 6, 2024. Teams tried five quick ideas and looked at cost and benefit. Paying people helped more tasks get done, and offering evening and weekend blood appointments and giving saliva kits through community groups brought more donations from groups usually left out. Staff thought the ideas would work twice as well as they did. These simple changes can help health studies include more kinds of people and make research fairer.

pdr_title: Patterns of Basal Cell Carcinoma Presentation in the NIH All of Us Database
pdr_abstract: To examine risk factors for the development of eyelid, face, and body basal cell carcinoma %28BCC%29 within the National Institutes of Health All of Us database. Around 7342 patients with BCC and 29,728 age-matched controls were included. Patients with genetic syndromes predisposing to BCC, and patients with a history of solid organ transplants were excluded. Outcomes examined included tumor location, ethnicity, age, smoking, alcohol intake, income, and access to care. Univariate and multivariate regression analyses were performed to examine the association between BCC on different areas of the body and race as well as the effect of modifiable risk factors. Almost 48.7% %283623%29 of patients had BCC on the body %28nonface%29, 47.2% had BCC on the face %283505%29, and 4.1% %28304%29 had BCC of the eyelid. White race %28OR, 11.79; CI, 5.99-27.73; p < 0.001%29 and male sex %28OR, 1.23; CI, 1.14-1.33; p < 0.001%29 were nonmodifiable risk factors for BCC and overall, patients with facial BCC were significantly older %28p < 0.001%29 than those with body BCC. Nonwhite patients with BCC were younger, and significantly more likely to have nonfacial BCC %28p < 0.001%29. On multivariate analysis, alcohol intake also showed a dose-dependent increased risk for BCC %28OR, 1.54; CI, 1.14-2.13; p < 0.001%29 of the face. Nonwhite patients were significantly younger and more likely to be diagnosed with nonfacial BCC. Thus, we hypothesize that BCC pathogenesis may not be as closely related to cumulative sun exposure as for white patients. Alcohol intake is an important modifiable risk factor.
lay_summary: The NIH All of Us database included 7,342 people with basal cell carcinoma (BCC), a common skin cancer, and 29,728 controls to study where BCC appears and what affects risk. Researchers looked at tumor site, race, age, sex, and alcohol use. About 49% of tumors were on the body, 47% on the face, and 4% on the eyelid. White people and men were more likely to get BCC. Nonwhite patients were younger and more often had body tumors. More alcohol was linked to more face tumors. Cutting back on alcohol and regular skin checks may help.

pdr_title: Predicting Weight Loss After Vertical Sleeve Gastrectomy Using a Whole-genome Sequencing-derived Polygenic Risk Score in the All of Us Cohort
pdr_abstract: To create a genome-wide polygenic risk score %28PRS%29 to improve prediction of a 12-month percentage weight loss %28WL%29 after vertical sleeve gastrectomy %28VSG%29. Variability in post-VSG WL is not well explained by clinical factors. The All of Us program provides access to a 414,830 short-read whole-genome sequencing resource, enabling unbiased discovery of genetic predictors after VSG. VSG counts, demographic, anthropomorphic and vital sign information were obtained from the linked electronic health record. The discovery cohort %28DC%29 included participants from version 7 carried into version 8 while the validation cohort %28VC%29 included those newly added to v8. We defined good responders and nonresponders as having WL±1SD from the mean. Following quality filtering, we applied a 2-stage penalized-regression, followed by elastic-net logistic regression, to identify 1583 stable variants and derive β-weights. We then tested this PRS on the DC into a prediction model. We identified 395 participants in the DC and 336 participants in the VC, respectively. Of these, VSG, 44 were classified as good responders %28≥37% WL%29 and 55 as nonresponders %28≤19% WL%29. In the VC, 55 were classified as good responders and 48 as nonresponders. Adding the PRS to models to clinical predictors increased the area under the curve following logistic regression by 0.03; P <4.3 × 10 -14 , random forest by 0.03; P <9.1 × 10 -7 , decision tree by 0.05; P = 1.2 × 10 -3 , and gradient boosting by 0.08; P <8.3 × 10 -10 . Use of short-read whole-genome sequencing from All of Us %28AoU%29 can be effectively used to generate PRS to enhance predictive WL accuracy. This work has implications for outcomes of both bariatric surgery and other surgical procedures.
lay_summary: This study tested whether a score made from many genes (a polygenic risk score, PRS) can help predict how much weight people lose one year after vertical sleeve gastrectomy (VSG), a common weight-loss surgery. Researchers used whole-genome data and health records from the All of Us project. They built the score with 395 people and tested it in 336 more. The PRS used 1,583 genetic spots and made predictions a bit better, improving accuracy by about 3–8 percentage points. This could help doctors and patients better predict likely weight loss after surgery.

pdr_title: Socio-demographic and clinical factors associated with the receipt of anti-obesity medication prescriptions and metabolic and bariatric surgery among eligible all of Us participants
pdr_abstract: There is a paucity of data on socio-economic characteristics associated with the use of anti-obesity medications %28AOM%29 and metabolic and bariatric surgery %28MBS%29 when accounting for clinical factors. This study characterized factors associated with the receipt of AOM prescriptions and MBS. A cross-sectional study was conducted using the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research %28v.8%29 data. Patients with obesity who received AOM or MBS between 2017 and 2023 were included. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics, while multivariable regression examined factors associated with the receipt of the treatments. Only 6.6% of 183 424 patients for AOM analysis, received an AOM prescription, while 1.8% underwent MBS among 93 146 patients. Being a man %28vs. woman, adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 0.62, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.59-0.65%29, Medicare insurance holder %28vs. private, aOR = 0.78, 95% CI, 0.72-0.84%29, retiree %28vs. employed, aOR = 0.70, 95% CI, 0.66-0.75%29 and high school degree holders %28vs. college, aOR = 0.85, 95% CI, 0.80-0.90%29 were associated with lower odds of receiving AOM. Being single %28vs. married, aOR = 0.84, 95% CI, 0.74-0.96%29, retired %28vs. employed, aOR = 0.63, 95% CI, 0.49-0.80%29, with body mass index %28BMI%29 35- < 40 %28vs. ≥45, aOR = 0.13, 95% CI, 0.11-0.15%29 were associated with lower odds of MBS. Patients with dyslipidaemia and obstructive sleep apnoea had higher odds of receiving both treatments. Disparities in obesity treatment exist. Male sex, older age, lower income and lower BMI were associated with lower odds of treatment, while dyslipidaemia and obstructive sleep apnoea were associated with higher odds.
lay_summary: This study looked at health records from 2017–2023 to find which social and medical factors are linked to getting weight-loss medicines or weight-loss surgery. Researchers checked about 183,000 people for medicines and 93,000 for surgery. Only 6.6% got medicines and 1.8% had surgery. Men, older people, retirees, people on Medicare, and those with less education or lower income were less likely to get these treatments. People with high blood fats (dyslipidemia) or sleep breathing problems (obstructive sleep apnea) were more likely to get them. This means some groups may not be getting fair access to obesity care.

pdr_title: Replicated blood-based biomarkers for myalgic encephalomyelitis not explicable by inactivity
pdr_abstract: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome %28ME/CFS%29 is a common female-biased disease. ME/CFS diagnosis is hindered by the absence of biomarkers that are unaffected by patients' low physical activity level. Our analysis used semi-parametric efficient estimators, an initial Super Learner fit followed by a one-step correction, three mediators, and natural direct and indirect estimands, to decompose the average effect of ME/CFS status on molecular and cellular traits. For this, we used UK Biobank data for up to 1455 ME/CFS cases and 131,303 controls. Hundreds of traits differed significantly between cases and controls, including 116 significant for both female and male cohorts. These were indicative of chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and liver disease. Nine of 14 traits were replicated in the smaller All-of-Us cohort. Results cannot be explained by restricted activity: via an activity mediator, ME/CFS status significantly affected only 1 of 3237 traits. Individuals with post-exertional malaise show stronger biomarker differences. Single traits could not cleanly distinguish cases from controls. Nevertheless, these results keep alive the future ambition of a blood-based biomarker panel for accurate ME/CFS diagnosis.
lay_summary: This study looked for blood signs that show myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Scientists compared up to 1,455 people with ME/CFS to 131,303 people without it using UK Biobank data and statistical methods. They found hundreds of blood and cell differences, with 116 seen in both women and men, and 9 of 14 tested traits were replicated elsewhere. Most differences were not due to low activity; only 1 of 3,237 traits linked to inactivity. People whose symptoms worsen after activity showed stronger differences. The findings suggest blood tests may help diagnose ME/CFS in the future.

pdr_title: Sex and racial differences in prevalence and clinical characteristics of people living with LDLR and PCSK9 familial hypercholesterolemia genetic variants: Data from the All of Us Research program
pdr_abstract: Data on the prevalence and clinical characteristics of people with Familial hypercholesterolemia %28FH%29 genetic variants across sex and diverse racial and ethnic groups in the United States are limited. Using data from the All of Us research program, we examined the prevalence and clinical characteristics of FH variant carriers in a diverse U.S. population. LDLR and PCSK9 FH genetic variants were identified using the ClinVar database. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease %28ASCVD%29 and lipid-lowering therapy %28LLT%29 use were ascertained from electronic health records. Prevalence, ASCVD burden, and LLT use among FH variant carriers were estimated and stratified by sex, race, and ethnicity. Among 245,388 participants %28mean age 51.8 years, 59.3 % women, 51.3 % non-Hispanic White, 20.4 % non-Hispanic Black, 3 % non-Hispanic Asian, 19.3 % Hispanic%29, 448 were identified as FH genetic variant carriers, yielding a prevalence of 1 in 546 %2895 % CI: 1/602- 1/500%29. Prevalence was highest among Asian non-Hispanics %281 in 286%29 and lowest in Hispanics %281 in 694%29; p-value = 0.003. Males had a higher prevalence of FH variants than females %281 in 485 vs. 1 in 602, p-value = 0.03%29. Regardless of LDL-C levels, FH variant carriers had a higher prevalence of ASCVD history than those without FH variants %28p-value = 0.04%29. Black non-Hispanics, Asian non-Hispanics, and Hispanics had lower ASCVD prevalence and LLT use than White non-Hispanics. ASCVD prevalence was higher in males with FH variants than females %2825 % vs. 18 %, p-value = 0.04%29. Significant racial, ethnic, and sex disparities exist in the prevalence, ASCVD burden, and LLT use among FH variant carriers. Further targeted efforts, including increased genetic testing, are needed to improve FH detection and optimize treatment, particularly in racial and ethnic minority groups where LLT use remains inadequate.

lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know how common familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), a genetic condition that raises bad cholesterol, is across sexes and races. They used genetics and health records from 245,388 people to find LDLR and PCSK9 variants and check heart disease and cholesterol medicine use. They found 448 carriers, about 1 in 546 people. Rates were highest in non-Hispanic Asians (1 in 286) and lowest in Hispanics (1 in 694). Men had more carriers and more heart disease than women. Black, Asian, and Hispanic groups got less treatment than White people. More testing and better care for minorities are needed.

pdr_title: Investigating the Relationship Between Social Support and Health Care Barriers Among Sexually and Gender Diverse Young Adults in the United States
pdr_abstract: Purpose: Recognizing the necessity of supportive health care systems, we used strengths-based approaches to explore the potential protective nature of social support against health care barriers among sexually and gender diverse %28SGD%29 young adults. Methods: Using data spanning May 2018 to July 2022 from the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program, we created a sample of and produced descriptive estimates for 2417 SGD young adults between 20 and 35 years of age. Using logistic regressions, we calculated adjusted odds ratios %28aORs%29 and 95% confidence intervals %28CIs%29 to measure the association between two outcomes-delaying health care and reported discrimination in medical settings-and instrumental/emotional social support. We adjusted for age, gender identity, race and ethnicity, housing stability, and income. Results: Of our sample, 70.8% endorsed at least one reason for delaying care, and 45.0% reported discrimination in medical settings 'rarely' or more frequently, with significant differences by gender identity, sexual orientation, race and ethnicity, housing stability, income, and education for both outcomes. More social support was associated with fewer reasons for delaying health care %28instrumental: aOR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.71-0.86; emotional: aOR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.63-0.79%29 and fewer reports of discrimination in medical settings %28instrumental: aOR = 0.72, 95% CI 0.66-0.78; emotional: aOR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.58-0.70%29. Conclusion: Our results suggest that social support might serve as a protective factor against health care barriers for SGD young adults. More strengths-based research is needed to understand intersectionality in SGD health care.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if having people who help you (social support) makes it easier for sexually and gender diverse young adults to get health care. They looked at survey answers from 2,417 people ages 20–35 collected from 2018 to 2022. They checked if people delayed care or felt treated unfairly in medical places and how much help or emotional support they had. About 71% had delayed care and 45% said they faced discrimination. People with more help and emotional support were less likely to delay care or report discrimination. This means stronger social support may help reduce health care problems.

pdr_title: Sociodemographically differential patterns of chronic pain progression revealed by analyzing the all of us research program data
pdr_abstract: The differential progression of ten chronic overlapping pain conditions %28COPC%29 and four comorbid mental disorders across demographic groups have rarely been reported in the literature. To fill in this gap, we conducted retrospective cohort analyses using All of Us Research Program data from 1970 to 2023. Separate cohorts were created to assess the differential patterns across sex, race, and ethnicity. Logistic regression models, controlling for demographic variables and household income level, were employed to identify significant sociodemographic factors associated with the differential progression from one COPC or mental condition to another. Among the 139 frequent disease pairs, we identified group-specific patterns in 15 progression pathways. Black or African Americans with a COPC condition had a significantly increased association in progression to other COPCs %28CLBP- > IBS, CLBP- > MHA, or IBS- > MHA, OR≥1.25, adj.p ≤ 4.0x10-3%29 or mental disorders %28CLBP- > anxiety, CLBP- > depression, MHA- > anxiety, MHA- > depression, OR≥1.25, adj.p ≤ 1.9x10-2%29 after developing a COPC. lay_summary: This study looked at how long-term pain problems and mental health issues change over time in different groups. Researchers used health records from the All of Us program (1970–2023) to follow how one condition led to another across sex, race, and income. Out of 139 disease pairs, 15 showed group-specific patterns. Black adults were more likely to develop more pain or mental health problems after a pain condition. Women were more likely to get chronic low back pain after anxiety or depression. People with the lowest incomes had higher risk of worsening pain or new mental illness. This means doctors should use social info to help prevent and treat pain earlier.
calc_title: Sociodemographically differential patterns of chronic pain progression revealed by analyzing the all of us research program data

Separate cohorts were created to assess the differential patterns across sex, race, and ethnicity. Additionally, the lowest income bracket was associated with an increased risk of developing another COPC from a COPC (CLBP- > MHA, IBS- > MHA, MHA- > CLBP, or MHA- > IBS, OR≥1.44, adj.p ≤ 2.6x10-2) or from a mental disorder (depression- > MHA, depression- > CLBP, anxiety- > CLBP, or anxiety- > IBS, OR≥1.50, adj.p ≤ 2.0x10-2), as well as developing a mental disorder after a COPC (CLBP- > depression, CBLP- > anxiety, MHA- > anxiety, OR≥1.37,adj.p ≤ 1.6x10-2). pdr_title: Incident cytopenia and risk of subsequent myeloid neoplasm in age-related clonal hematopoiesis: a multi-biobank case-control study
pdr_abstract: Cross sectional studies have demonstrated patients with clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential %28CHIP%29 are at increased risk of developing multiple adverse outcomes, including cytopenia and myeloid neoplasm %28MN%29. One prior study suggests cytopenia or cytosis is a required intermediate step in disease progression from CHIP to MN. We analyzed genomic sequencing data from the NIH All of Us Research Program, Vanderbilt's BioVU repository, and UK Biobank participants %28N = 805,249%29. The study period ranged from 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2023. Genetic mutations, demographic data, laboratory values, and MN outcomes were used to create a case-control study to estimate the risk of incident cytopenia and MN among cases with CHIP and matched controls without CHIP. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, the study cohort contained 9374 cases with CHIP and 24,749 matched controls without CHIP. Among the 34,123 participants, 190 %280.56%%29 developed incident cases of MN and 4151 %2812.1%%29 developed an incident cytopenia. Individuals with CHIP at enrollment who subsequently developed a cytopenia progressed to MN at a rate of 0.5% per year, compared to 0.05% per year for those with CHIP and normal cell counts. Longitudinal analysis across three cohorts demonstrated an increased risk of cytopenia in CHIP patients and identified those at the highest risk of progression. Cytopenia risk factors included smoking %28HR = 1.17, 95% CI: [1.05-1.32], P = 5.87 × 10-3%29, male sex %28HR = 1.45, 95% CI: [1.30-1.62], P = 2.17 × 10-11%29, variant allele frequency ≥0.20 %28HR = 1.36, 95% CI: [1.21-1.54], P = 7.56 × 10-7%29, age ≥65 %28HR = 1.41, 95% CI: [1.25-1.57], P = 3.98 × 10-9%29, mean corpuscular volume ≥100 fL %28HR = 2.12, 95% CI: [1.68-2.68], P = 2.58 × 10-10%29, red cell distribution width ≥15% %28HR = 2.59, 95% CI: [2.26-2.98], P = 1.14 × 10-40%29, mutations in high-risk CHIP genes %28HR = 1.48, 95% CI: [1.26-1.75], P = 2.39 × 10-6%29, and ≥2 CHIP mutations %28HR = 1.95, 95% CI: [1.61-2.36], P = 9.73 × 10-12%29. Longitudinal analysis across three large cohorts found that it is rare for patients with CHIP to develop MN without first developing cytopenia. The risk for MN among patients with CHIP resides almost entirely among those with cytopenia. These findings suggest that cytopenia is a critical step in progression from CHIP to MN, underscoring its utility as an endpoint in cancer prevention trials for CHIP patients. lay_summary: This study tested whether low blood counts help turn CHIP (when some blood cells have DNA changes) into blood cancer. Researchers studied gene and lab data from over 34,000 people in three biobanks, including about 9,000 with CHIP. About 12% got low blood counts and 0.6% got blood cancer. People with CHIP who developed low counts got cancer about ten times more often than those with normal counts. Smoking, being male, older age, certain blood test changes, and risky or multiple gene mutations raised low-count risk. Checking blood counts can help find and stop cancer early.

pdr_title: Diseases Common in Persons With Cystic Fibrosis Among CFTR Heterozygotes
pdr_abstract: Cystic fibrosis is one of the most commonly diagnosed autosomal recessive disorders in the US. It is estimated that more than 10 million individuals are heterozygous for a pathogenic CFTR gene variant in the US %28heterozygotes%29. The phenotypic risk of these heterozygotes is not well defined, particularly among populations of predominantly non-European genetic ancestry. Understanding disease risk across each population can improve management strategies for all. To examine associations of diseases across the phenome with CFTR heterozygotes. The All of Us Research Program is a US-based ongoing longitudinal cohort study whose enrollment started nationally in 2018. In this genetic association study, whole-genome sequencing data were linked to electronic health records %28EHRs%29 and surveys. Participants were 18 years and older. Similarity to genetic ancestral groups was genetically inferred using All of Us data and 2 large reference datasets, the 1000 Genomes Project and Human Genome Diversity Project. This analysis was conducted between February and April 2025. A single pathogenic CFTR variant. The main variables included clinical diagnoses documented in EHRs. Multivariable-adjusted phenome-wide association studies were performed. The main measures were odds ratios %28ORs%29, indicating risk for a particular disease or condition. Overall, 363 pathogenic variants were identified in the cohort. Among 317 964 adult participants %2855.7% female; mean [SD] last age in EHR, 56.1 [16.9] years%29, 7957 heterozygotes and 280 995 noncarriers were identified. Participants were followed up through EHRs with a mean %28SD%29 follow-up of 12.4 %289.0%29 years. The genetically inferred ancestral distribution of the cohort was 18.0% African, 16.2% American or Admixed American, 2.1% East Asian, 53.4% European, 0.3% South Asian, and 0.4% West Asian. Frequencies of heterozygotes varied by groups of genetic similarity to reference populations: 3.62% in participants most genetically similar to a European reference population %28n = 169 812%29, 1.35% in participants most genetically similar to an African reference population %28n = 57 297%29, and 1.86% in participants most genetically similar to an Admixed American reference population %28n = 51 483%29. A total of 2909 phenotypes were analyzed. No statistically significant associations were identified in heterozygotes of all populations combined or within each genetic ancestral group. Among 52 cystic fibrosis-associated diseases, although an elevated risk of respiratory diseases and infections was observed in some heterozygotes %28allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis [OR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.27-4.95]; bronchiectasis [OR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.00-1.47]; pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae [OR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.05-2.26]; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [OR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.05-1.24]; asthma [OR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01-1.15]; and Pseudomonas infection [OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.03-1.74]%29, effect sizes of these associations were several orders of magnitude lower than those found in homozygotes or predicted compound heterozygotes. In this genetic association study, most heterozygotes did not appear to have a substantially higher risk of cystic fibrosis-associated diseases during their adulthood compared to noncarriers. Additional studies are needed to investigate the underlying factors for the elevated risk of respiratory and infectious diseases in some heterozygotes.

lay_summary: This study asked if people who carry one bad cystic fibrosis (CF) gene copy (carriers) have more health problems. Researchers used whole-genome tests linked to medical records from 317,964 U.S. adults and found 7,957 carriers (about 2.5%). They checked almost 3,000 health conditions over about 12 years. Overall, carriers did not have much higher risk of cystic fibrosis related diseases. A few carriers had slightly more lung and infection problems, but these were much smaller than in people with CF. For most people, being a carrier does not mean big health risks in adulthood.

pdr_title: Integrating a conceptual consent permission model from the informed consent ontology for software application execution
pdr_journal_title: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science Proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
pdr_abstract: We developed a simulated process to show a software implementation to facilitate an approach to integrate the Informed Consent Ontology, a reference ontology of informed consent information, to express implicit description and implement conceptual permission from informed consent life cycle. An early study introduced an experimental method to use Semantic Web Rule Language %28SWRL%29 to describe and represent permissions to computational deduce more information from the Informed Consent Ontology %28ICO%29, demonstrated by the use of the All of Us informed consent documents. We show how incomplete information in informed consent documents can be elucidated using a computational model of permissions toward health information technology that integrates ontologies. Future goals entail applying our computational approach for specific sub-domains of the informed consent life cycle, specifically for vaccine informed consent.
lay_summary: The researchers wanted to help computers understand and use people’s medical consent forms. They built a test system that used the Informed Consent Ontology (a way to organize consent information) and computer rules (SWRL, a set of rules computers use to draw conclusions). They tried it on real All of Us consent documents. The system could find and fill in missing consent details and work out what actions were allowed. This could help health software respect patients’ wishes and may be useful for vaccine consent in the future.

pdr_title: Impact of APOE4-related dementia risk in underrepresented groups from the All of Us research program
pdr_journal_title: Alzheimer's & Dementia : The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association
pdr_abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records %28EHRs%29, 'dementia' diagnostic codes, and genetic data from All of Us were used to see if there is a higher risk of dementia and an attenuated impact of apolipoprotein ε4 %28APOE4%29 on Alzheimer's disease %28AD%29 risk in Black and Hispanic/Latino groups. Participants included 9,784 Hispanic/Latinos, 14,937 Non-Hispanic Blacks %28NHB%29, and 60,388 Non-Hispanic Whites %28NHWs%29 ≥age 60 without an initial dementia diagnosis. There was a significantly higher risk of developing a dementia diagnosis in Hispanic/Latino and NHB participants than NHW participants and comparably increased dementia hazard ratios in the Hispanic/Latino, NHB, and NHW APOE4 carriers than non-carriers %28hazard ratio [HR] [95% confidence interval {CI}] 1.54 [1.25-1.91], 1.25 [1.00-1.57], and 1.55 [1.40-1.72]%29. Compared to NHW individuals, Hispanic/Latino and NHB individuals are at higher risk of developing a 'dementia diagnosis' and comparably higher risk in APOE4 carriers than non-carriers. Plasma AD biomarkers could clarify the proportion of dementia cases with and without AD and the impact of APOE4 on AD in these groups. Hispanic/Latino and non-Hispanic Black individuals have a higher risk of all-cause dementia. The impact of apolipoprotein ε4 %28APOE4%29 on dementia risk was similar in the studied ethnoracial groups. Plasma biomarkers could inform the risk of Alzheimer's disease %28AD%29 and impact of APOE4 in these groups.

pdr_title: Hormone Therapy Usage Is Associated With Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Prostate Cancer Patients of the All of Us Research Program Cohort
pdr_abstract: Hormone therapy %28HT%29 has greatly improved overall survival for prostate cancer patients, but may also influence cardiovascular health in an already high-risk population. This retrospective cohort study examined participants in the All of Us Research Program with prostate cancer, had no prior history of adverse cardiovascular events, and were either treated or not treated with HT. HT was defined as GnRH agonists, GnRH antagonists, abiraterone, androgen antagonists, or androgen receptor pathway inhibitors. We defined adverse cardiovascular event as myocardial infarctions, heart failure, or strokes. Time to adverse cardiovascular event was defined using longitudinal electronic health record data. We evaluated whether HT use affected the risk of adverse cardiovascular events using a Cox regression model adjusted for established cardiovascular risk factors. The final cohort included 5156 participants. After adjustment for cardiovascular risk covariates, HT treatment was associated with increased risk of adverse cardiovascular event %28HR: 1.22; 95% CI: 1.01-1.48; p = 0.03%29. In participants with pre-treatment dyslipidemia, HT usage was associated with increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events %28HR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.19-1.95; p < 0.001%29. In participants without pre-treatment dyslipidemia, no association was found %28HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.71-1.30; p = 0.81%29. Our results show that HT-associated cardiovascular risk may be synergistically amplified by dyslipidemia. These results suggest that risk stratification by dyslipidemia status may improve cardiovascular outcomes for prostate cancer survivors.

lay_summary: This study looked at 5,156 U.S. men with prostate cancer in the All of Us database to see if hormone therapy (HT) affects heart health. Researchers checked medical records for new heart attacks, heart failure, or strokes after treatment. Overall, men who got HT had about a 22% higher chance of such events. Men who already had high blood fats (dyslipidemia = high cholesterol or triglycerides) had about a 52% higher chance with HT, while men without high fats did not. This suggests checking and treating high blood fats may lower heart risk for patients on HT.
calc_title: Hormone Therapy Usage Is Associated With Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Prostate Cancer Patients of the All of Us Research Program Cohort
calc_abstract: Hormone therapy (HT) has greatly improved overall survival for prostate cancer patients, but may also influence cardiovascular health in an already high-risk population. This retrospective cohort study examined participants in the All of Us Research Program with prostate cancer, had no prior history of adverse cardiovascular events, and were either treated or not treated with HT. HT was defined as GnRH agonists, GnRH antagonists, abiraterone, androgen antagonists, or androgen receptor pathway inhibitors. We defined adverse cardiovascular event as myocardial infarctions, heart failure, or strokes. Time to adverse cardiovascular event was defined using longitudinal electronic health record data. We evaluated whether HT use affected the risk of adverse cardiovascular events using a Cox regression model adjusted for established cardiovascular risk factors. The final cohort included 5156 participants. After adjustment for cardiovascular risk covariates, HT treatment was associated with increased risk of adverse cardiovascular event (HR: 1.22; 95% CI: 1.01-1.48; p = 0.03). In participants with pre-treatment dyslipidemia, HT usage was associated with increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events (HR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.19-1.95; p < 0.001). In participants without pre-treatment dyslipidemia, no association was found (HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.71-1.30; p = 0.81). Our results show that HT-associated cardiovascular risk may be synergistically amplified by dyslipidemia. These results suggest that risk stratification by dyslipidemia status may improve cardiovascular outcomes for prostate cancer survivors.

pdr_title: Improved breast cancer risk prediction using chromosomal-scale length variation
pdr_abstract: Early diagnosis of breast cancer leads to higher long-term survival rates. The development of a germline genetic test, or polygenic risk score, to identify women at high risk of breast cancer holds the potential to reduce cancer deaths. However, current tests based on SNPs do not perform much better than predictions based on family history and perform significantly worse in populations with non-European ancestry. We have developed an alternative method to characterize a genome, called chromosomal-scale length variation, which can be applied to polygenic risk scores. The objective of this paper is to characterize a breast cancer genetic risk score based on chromosomal-scale length variation using the NIH All of Us dataset in different self-identified racial groups when trained on different populations. We used the NIH All of Us dataset to compile a dataset with 4,533 women who have been diagnosed with breast cancer %28including 440 who self-identified as Black%29 and 44,518 women who have not. We acquired, through All of Us, genetic information for each of these women. We computed a set of 88 values for each woman in the dataset, representing the chromosomal-scale length variation parameters. These numbers are average log R ratios for four different segments from each of the 22 autosomes. We used machine learning algorithms to find a model that best differentiates the women with breast cancer from the women without breast cancer based on the set of 88 numbers that characterize each woman's germline genome. The best model had an AUC of 0.70 %2895% CI, 0.67-0.73%29 in the All of Us population. Women who scored in the top quintile by this model were nine times more likely to have breast cancer when compared to women who scored in the lowest quintile. In conclusion, we found that this method of computing genetic risk scores for breast cancer is a substantial improvement over SNP-based polygenic risk scores. In addition, we compared models trained on populations of only White women and only Black women. We found that the models trained only on White women performed better than models trained only on Black women when tested on only White women. We did not see a significant difference between the two models when tested on only Black women.
lay_summary: The researchers wanted a better genetic test to find women at higher risk for breast cancer. They used the NIH All of Us data with 4,533 women who had breast cancer and 44,518 who did not. For each woman they measured 88 numbers called chromosomal-scale length variation (big patterns of DNA size differences) and used computers to learn which patterns matched cancer. The test was moderately accurate (about 70% by a common measure). Women in the top fifth were nine times more likely to have breast cancer. This could help find high-risk women earlier.
