pdr_title: The genetics of cannabis lifetime use
pdr_journal_title: Neuropsychopharmacology : Official Publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
pdr_abstract: Cannabis is one of the most commonly used drugs in the world, and use is trending alarmingly higher. We aimed to examine the genetic basis of cannabis lifetime use %28CanLU%29 and its genetic relationships with a variety of psychiatric- and physical health-related phenotypes. We conducted a multi-ancestral genome-wide association study %28GWAS%29 of CanLU using data from All of Us in five genetic populations. We meta-analyzed the results of EUR participants with previously published CanLU data %28total effective sample size: 258,823%29, and conducted a set of post-GWAS analyses, including genetic correlation analysis using LDSC, local genetic correlation analysis with LAVA, Mendelian randomization %28MR%29 to assess causality, and phenomewide association analysis. We found 11 independent variants significantly associated with CanLU, most prominently CADM2*rs7609594 %28p=7.4×10-20%29. CanLU was genetically correlated with traits related to openness to experience and risk taking, including substance use and sexual behaviors. MR demonstrated that most of these traits had a bidirectional causal relationship with CanLU, and six were locally genetically correlated with CanLU in a region that maps to CADM2. Genetic correlations sometimes differed from those previously observed for cannabis use disorder. Our results highlight the distinct genetic architecture of CanLU, and support the genetic, and biological, differentiation between CanLU and cannabis use disorder. Genetic correlations between CanLU and other risk taking- and substance use-related traits indicate a broad mutual genetic mechanism underlying these traits, and suggest involvement of CADM2. These findings provide potential targets for future prevention and intervention strategies for substance use and risk-taking behaviors.
lay_summary: This study looked at why some people ever try cannabis by studying genes in about 259,000 people. Scientists scanned many genes to find links and found 11 DNA differences, especially near the gene called CADM2. They saw that the same genes linked to trying cannabis are also linked to being open to new experiences, taking risks, other drug use, and sexual behaviors. The results suggest these traits and cannabis use can influence each other. The study also showed trying cannabis has different genetics than having a cannabis problem. This may help make better prevention and treatment plans.

pdr_title: Real-world effects of using gnomAD 4.1.0 and AllofUs population reference datasets on reporting of variants of uncertain significance
pdr_journal_title: Genetics in Medicine : Official Journal of the American College of Medical Genetics
pdr_abstract: PURPOSE: Clinical testing of rare genetic variants relies on population genomic datasets as a source of evidence. New datasets from the Genome Aggregation Database %28gnomAD%29 and AllofUs Research Program are many-fold larger than prior datasets, and the latter includes highly detailed phenotype data. The effect of these datasets on variant classification and reporting for highly-penetrant pediatric-onset disease is not well characterized, but one likely effect is to reduce reporting of variants of uncertain significance %28VUS%29.    METHODS: We retrospectively identified VUS previously reported by our CAP/CLIA certified laboratory and evaluated whether they are still reportable provided new reference datasets.    RESULTS: By examining allele counts in new datasets, we identified 24 variants that are likely no longer reportable. Additionally, the AllofUs phenotype data suggest an additional 10 VUS are no longer reportable. Overall, we find that nearly one fifth of VUS %2834/173, 19.6%%29 are no longer reportable.    CONCLUSION: We conclude that the use of these new datasets is likely to reduce reported VUS for highly-penetrant pediatric-onset disease. This may be further augmented through updated gene-specific thresholds and improved accessibility of AllofUs phenotype data.

pdr_title: Cross-ancestry discovery of genetic risk variants for lean metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND: The presence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease %28MASLD%29 in lean patients challenges the traditional association between fatty liver and obesity. While genome-wide association studies %28GWAS%29 have identified key genetic variants linked to hepatic steatosis, most have focused on Western obese populations and were based on the former non-alcoholic fatty liver disease %28NAFLD%29 criteria. Genetic studies targeting lean MASLD, particularly among the Taiwan Han Chinese population, remain limited. This study addresses this knowledge gap by investigating the genetic architecture of lean MASLD in a Taiwan Han Chinese cohort.    METHODS: We analyzed data from the Taiwan Biobank, integrating genomic data with abdominal ultrasound findings to define lean MASLD cases with BMI less than 23. A total of 1,720 lean MASLD individuals and 5,331 lean controls were included. A metabolic risk score ranging from 1 to 5 was calculated for each participant, reflecting the number of metabolic criteria met for MASLD classification. GWAS was conducted using logistic regression, adjusting for age, sex, and top 10 principal components. Conditional analyses were used to identify independent signals. Significant variants were replicated using data in the All of Us Research Program %281,017 lean MASLD and 1,553 lean healthy%29.    RESULTS: Lean MASLD patients exhibited significantly worse metabolic profiles than lean controls. GWAS identified 47 genome-wide significant variants, predominantly in PNPLA3 and SAMM50, with rs9625962 in PNPLA3 emerging as the most significant and independent variant. These associations were replicated in the All of Us lean MASLD cohort, affirming their cross-population relevance. Notably, the C allele of rs9625962 increased the risk of MASLD in both lean and non-lean individuals. In the lean MASLD group, fibrosis risk scores %28FIB-4 and NFS%29 positively correlated with the metabolic risk scores.    CONCLUSION: This study identified significant associations between genetic variants in PNPLA3 and SAMM50 and lean MASLD in the Taiwan Han Chinese population. The variant rs9625962 exhibited pleiotropic effects, contributing to MASLD regardless of BMI category, triglyceride levels, and liver function profiles. The replication of all significant variants in the All of Us dataset underscores the robustness and generalizability of our findings. These results highlight the importance of genetic factors in lean MASLD pathogenesis and support further investigation into gene-environment interactions.
lay_summary: This study asked why some thin people get metabolic fatty liver disease. Scientists compared 1,720 lean patients with the disease to 5,331 lean healthy people using genome scans and liver ultrasound, and checked findings in another group (1,017 patients, 1,553 controls). They found 47 DNA changes linked to the disease, mostly in two genes called PNPLA3 and SAMM50, with one called rs9625962 raising risk in both thin and heavier people. Higher metabolic risk also linked to more liver scarring. The results show genes help cause fatty liver in thin people and could help with screening and care.

pdr_title: Understanding the Comorbidities Among Psychiatric Disorders, Chronic Low Back Pain, and Spinal Degenerative Disease Using Observational and Genetically Informed Analyses
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND: Psychiatric disorders and symptoms are associated with differences in pain perception and sensitivity. These differences can have important implications in treating spinal degenerative disease %28SDD%29 and chronic low back pain %28CLBP%29.    METHODS: Leveraging UK Biobank %28UKB%29 %28n = 402,072%29 and All of Us Research Program %28AoU%29 %28n = 157,415%29 data, we investigated the effects linking psychiatric disorders to SDD and CLBP. We applied multinominal regression models, polygenic risk scoring, and one-sample Mendelian randomization %28MR%29 to triangulate the effects underlying the observed associations. We also performed gene ontology and drug-repurposing analyses to dissect the biology shared among mental illnesses, SDD, and CLBP.    RESULTS: When we compared individuals affected only by SDD, those affected only by CLBP, and those affected by both conditions with control participants, observational and genetically informed analyses highlighted that the strongest effects across the 3 case groups were observed for alcohol use disorder, anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder. Additionally, schizophrenia and its polygenic risk score appeared to have an inverse relationship with CLBP, SDD, and their comorbidity. One-sample MR highlighted a potential direct effect of internalizing disorders on the outcomes investigated that was particularly strong on SDD. Our drug repurposing analyses identified histone deacetylase inhibitors as targeting molecular pathways shared by psychiatric disorders, SDD, and CLBP.    CONCLUSIONS: These findings support that the comorbidity among psychiatric disorders, SDD, and CLBP is due to the contribution of direct effects and shared biology linking these health outcomes. These pleiotropic mechanisms, together with sociocultural factors, play a key role in shaping the SDD-CLBP comorbidity patterns that have been observed across the psychopathology spectrum.
lay_summary: This study asked how mental illnesses relate to spine wear-and-tear and long-term low back pain. Researchers looked at medical and genetic data from about 560,000 people and used statistical and genetics tests. They found alcohol use disorder, anxiety, depression, and PTSD were most linked to spinal degeneration, chronic low back pain, or both. Schizophrenia was linked to lower chances of these problems. Genetic tests suggested anxiety and depression may directly raise risk, especially for spinal degeneration. They also found a drug type that might affect shared biology (these drugs change how genes work). Treating mental health may help prevent or manage back problems.

pdr_title: Associations between pre-pandemic housing insecurity and reports of anxiety and depression in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic: an analysis of the All of Us Research Program cohort
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND: Housing insecurity is an important social determinant of health that has been linked to poor mental health. The beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic marked a time of major upheaval and has been linked to worsening experiences with anxiety and depression. It is not well understood how pre-pandemic housing insecurity may be associated with trajectories of anxiety and depression in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic.    METHODS: Using data from the NIH All of Us Research Program, we estimated the correlation between pre-pandemic housing insecurity and repeated measures of anxiety and depression symptoms between May and July 2020. We combined data from baseline surveys and the COVID-19 Participant Experience Survey %28COPE%29 and used generalized linear models with a logit link to estimate results.    RESULTS: Our sample included 37,535 participants. Those who reported housing insecurity prior to the start of the pandemic were significantly more likely to report moderate-to-severe symptoms of anxiety %28AOR 1.630, p<.001%29 and depression %28AOR 1.877, p<.001%29 across all months. Trajectories of anxiety and depression symptoms did not differ between May and July 2020 for those who reported housing insecurity versus those who did not.    CONCLUSIONS: This study examined how experiences and trajectories of anxiety and depression symptoms differed by housing insecurity status among a novel large national sample. Experiencing housing insecurity prior to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with a greater likelihood of moderate-to-severe anxiety and depression from May to July 2020, and this difference was consistent over time.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether people who had housing problems before COVID-19 had more anxiety and depression in the first months of the pandemic. Researchers used survey answers from 37,535 people in the All of Us study, comparing reports from before the pandemic with surveys in May–July 2020. People with pre-pandemic housing insecurity (problems like unstable housing or trouble paying rent) were more likely to have moderate-to-severe anxiety and depression across all months. This means helping with housing and mental health could reduce suffering during crises.

pdr_title: Socioeconomic trends of adult strabismus in the United States: an analysis of the All of Us database
pdr_journal_title: Journal of AAPOS : The Official Publication of the American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
pdr_abstract: PURPOSE: To determine associations of income and education level with a diagnosis of strabismus and to identify socioeconomic variables that may affect timely access to diagnosis.    METHODS: Annual income, high level of education completed, and ZIP code income, high school completion, poverty, and socioeconomic deprivation metrics were collected from 413,360 participants in the database. A χ2 test was used to determine significant differences in distributions of income, education, and ZIP code metrics in 3,734 strabismus patients compared with the overall database.    RESULTS: Participants living in ZIP codes with lower multidimensional deprivation indices %28less deprivation%29 are more likely to be diagnosed with strabismus. Participants with annual income below $10,000 %2810.10%%29 or who completed education between fifth grade and a high school diploma or GED %2820.06%%29 are less likely to receive a diagnosis for certain strabismus subtypes. Participants with annual income over $200,000 %287.07%%29, advanced degrees %2827.02%%29, living in ZIP codes with higher income, and higher high school completion rates were more likely to be diagnosed with certain strabismus subtypes.    CONCLUSIONS: Participants diagnosed with strabismus tend to have higher incomes, an advanced degree, and reside in more affluent ZIP codes, whereas those with lower income and education levels are less likely to be diagnosed. These findings reveal potential socioeconomic disparities in access to ophthalmic diagnostic services and care. Findings emphasize the importance of addressing socioeconomic barriers in eye care to enable equitable access.
lay_summary: This study looked for links between income, education, and diagnosis of strabismus (misaligned or crossed eyes). Researchers used income, education, and ZIP code data from 413,360 people and compared 3,734 people with strabismus. People in richer areas, with incomes over $200,000 or advanced degrees were diagnosed more often, while those earning under $10,000 or with only up to high school were diagnosed less often. The results suggest people with lower income or education may not get diagnosed as often, so better access to eye care is needed.

CONCLUSIONS: Participants diagnosed with strabismus tend to have higher incomes, an advanced degree, and reside in more affluent ZIP codes, whereas those with lower income and education levels are less likely to be diagnosed. These findings reveal potential socioeconomic disparities in access to ophthalmic diagnostic services and care. Findings emphasize the importance of addressing socioeconomic barriers in eye care to enable equitable access.

pdr_title: Epidemiology of strabismus among adults in the United States: insights from the All of Us database
pdr_journal_title: Journal of AAPOS : The Official Publication of the American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
pdr_abstract: PURPOSE: To determine the prevalence of adult-diagnosed strabismus and its associations with sex, age, and race in a large, diverse population database in the United States.    METHODS: Sex, age, and race data were collected from 413,457 individuals in the All of Us database. The χ2 test with post hoc pairwise comparisons was used to determine significant differences in distributions of sex, age, and race data in 3,734 strabismus patients compared with the overall database.    RESULTS: There is a higher proportion of males among patients with strabismus compared with the overall database %2843.34% vs 38.34% [P < 0.001]%29. There is a significantly higher proportion of patients aged over 65 years among patients with strabismus compared with the overall database %2845.77% vs 24.7% [P < 0.001]%29. There is also a significantly different racial distribution of individuals with strabismus compared with the overall database %28P < 0.001%29. Pairwise comparisons showed a significantly lower proportion of Asian individuals among patients with strabismus or heterotropia, a lower proportion of Black individuals with most subtypes, and a higher proportion of White individuals among patients with any strabismus.    CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that there is a lower proportion of females, Asian, and Black participants with diagnosed strabismus compared with the overall population in the All of Us database. These findings may indicate that strabismus affects patient populations differently, or that there is differential access to care and diagnosis of strabismus across sex, age, and race.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at medical records from 413,457 adults to find who was diagnosed with strabismus (misaligned or crossed eyes). They compared 3,734 people with strabismus to the whole group. More men were diagnosed (43% vs 38%) and many were over 65 years old (about 46% vs 25%). Fewer Asian and Black people were diagnosed, and more White people were diagnosed. This could mean the condition really affects groups differently or that some groups have less access to eye care and diagnosis. The findings suggest we need better eye screening and fair access to care.

pdr_title: Associations Between Sexual Orientation and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction in Sexual Minority Populations
pdr_journal_title: Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology : The Official Clinical Practice Journal of the American Gastroenterological Association
pdr_abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Sexual and gender minority %28SGM%29 individuals %28e.g., those identifying as Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Other [LGBTQ+]%29 are disproportionately affected by psychological distress and trauma, all recognized risk factors for disorders of gut-brain interaction %28DGBIs%29. This suggests a potentially higher burden of DGBIs in SGM populations. However, the relationship between SGM status and DGBIs has not been well characterized in large-scale clinical datasets.    METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis using All of Us database to identify the relationship between sexual orientation and presence of bowel DGBIs. Eligible participants were adults %28≥18 years%29 who completed a sexual orientation survey and had gastrointestinal diagnostic data available. Participants self-identified as straight, gay or lesbian, or bisexual. Outcomes included irritable bowel syndrome %28IBS%29, functional diarrhea, and chronic constipation, identified using ICD-10 codes. Chi-square tests and multivariable logistic regression models were used to assess associations between sexual orientation and DGBIs, stratified by gender and adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, and psychological factors. Interaction analyses were conducted to assess whether the association between sexual orientation and DGBIs differs between men and women. Missing data were imputed using multiple imputation by chained equations %28MICE%29 to address missing covariate data under a Missing at Random %28MAR%29 assumption, and sensitivity analyses with pooled results were compared with complete-case analyses to support robustness.    RESULTS: Among 386,242 eligible participants, 3.58% %28n=13,843%29 identified as gay or lesbian, and 4.09% %28n=15,788%29 as bisexual. Gay or bisexual men had significantly higher odds of being diagnosed with IBS %28aOR 1.55, 95%CI 1.36-1.76%29, functional diarrhea %28aOR 1.82, 95%CI 1.36-2.38%29, chronic constipation %28aOR 1.33, 95%CI 1.08-1.63%29, and a composite DGBI outcome of any of these diagnoses %28aOR 1.49, 95%CI 1.33-1.66%29 compared to straight men. Among women, there were no statistically significant associations between sexual orientation and any of the DGBI diagnoses or the composite outcome. Interaction analyses demonstrated that these associations were significantly stronger among men, particularly for any DGBI, functional diarrhea, and IBS.    CONCLUSIONS: Sexual orientation was independently associated with DGBI diagnoses among men, with no significant associations observed among women. These findings underscore the importance of considering gender-specific patterns when evaluating gastrointestinal health in sexual minority populations and highlight the need for tailored, inclusive approaches to DGBI care and research.
lay_summary: Because sexual minority people often face more stress and trauma that can affect health, this study looked at whether sexual orientation is linked to common gut-brain disorders (stomach and bowel problems tied to the brain). Researchers reviewed health records from 386,242 adults in the All of Us database who reported their sexual orientation. They checked for diagnoses of irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhea. Gay and bisexual men were more likely than straight men to have these gut problems. No clear differences were seen among women. This suggests doctors should be aware and offer inclusive, tailored care.

pdr_title: Gender differences in non-fatal suicidal behaviors linked to concurrent use of cannabis and opioids
pdr_abstract: Cannabis and opioids are among the most misused substances in the U.S. Growing evidence suggests gender differences in how substance use impacts mental health, particularly non-fatal suicidal behaviors. This study investigates whether the joint effect of cannabis and opioid use on non-fatal suicidal behaviors differs between men and women METHODS: We extracted data on US citizens from the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program %28N = 152,930; ages 18-49%29 and used logistic regression models to assess whether cannabis and opioid uses and their interaction were associated with non-fatal suicidal behaviors %28suicidal ideation, attempts, or self-harm%29, controlling for demographic and psychiatric variables RESULTS: In the study population, 3.2 % of participants used cannabis, 2.3 % used opioids, and 2.5 % experienced non-fatal suicidal behaviors. We found that the co-use of cannabis and opioids was associated with a smaller-than-expected increase in non-fatal suicidal behaviors overall and among women, suggesting an attenuated rather than additive risk %28β = -0.58 overall; β = -0.87 in women; both p < 0.001%29. In men, however, this joint effect did not significantly differ from additivity %28β = -0.29, p = 0.07%29, indicating a potential greater vulnerability CONCLUSIONS: These findings underscore gender-specific differences in the relationship between polysubstance use and suicidality, with implications for tailoring suicide risk screening and intervention programs. Understanding how cannabis and opioid co-use influences non-fatal suicidal behaviors differently across genders is crucial for developing targeted prevention efforts. Future research should explore the biological, psychological, and social mechanisms driving these disparities to inform more effective harm reduction strategies and mental health interventions.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether using both cannabis (marijuana) and opioids (pain medicines) affects non-fatal suicidal thoughts or actions differently for men and women. Researchers used health and survey data from 152,930 U.S. adults ages 18–49 and used math models to compare groups while accounting for other factors. About 3.2% used cannabis, 2.3% used opioids, and 2.5% had suicide-related behaviors. Using both drugs raised risk less than expected overall and in women, but men did not show this smaller effect and may face higher risk. This means doctors and prevention programs should watch people who use both drugs, especially men.

pdr_title: Meta-evolutionary exome analysis identifies novel type 2 diabetes mellitus genes in the UK Biobank and all of us
pdr_abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus %28T2DM%29 risk is heavily influenced by genetics, yet current association tests have explained only parts of its heritability. We developed MEVA %28Meta-Evolutionary Action%29, a meta-analytic framework that integrates three complementary methods-EAML, Sigma-Diff, and GeneEMBED-to assess the functional burden of protein-coding variants using evolutionary data. MEVA was applied to exome data from 28,115 T2DM cases and 28,115 controls in the UK Biobank %28UKB%29, identifying 101 genes %28p<1e-5%29. MEVA outperformed its component methods, each of which substantially outperformed a conventional burden test %28MAGMA%29, in recovering known T2DM genes %28AUROC=0.925%29 and maintaining robustness in progressively smaller cohorts %28AUROC=0.917%29. MEVA showed significant enrichment for T2DM-related loci %28p=6.8e-10, p=2.0e-34%29, protein interactions %28z=4.6, z=4.2%29, pathways %28p=1.3e-6, z=2.0%29, phenotypes %28p=1.3e-21, z=9.1%29, and literature mentions %28z=7.2%29. Replication in 16,915 T2DM cases and 16,915 controls from All of Us %28AoU%29 yielded 99 genes %28p<1e-5%29, 23 of which were also recovered in the UKB cohort - far exceeding random chance. These included established genes %28SLC30A8, WFS1, HNF1A%29 and less-characterized candidates %28NRIP1, ADAM30, CALCOCO2, TUBB1, ZFP36L2, WDR90%29. Notably, NRIP1 loss-of-function variants were associated with increased T2DM risk in both the UKB %28OR = 1.09, FDR=5.4e-4%29 and AoU %28OR = 1.09, FDR=0.046%29, and TUBB1 and CALCOCO2 gain-of-function variants showed consistent risk effects %28FDR<0.05%29. Pathway analyses revealed convergence on endoplasmic reticulum chaperone complexes %28FDR=0.02%29 and Hippo signaling %28FDR=8.5e-4%29. Finally, all 177 candidate genes were functionally prioritized using ten orthogonal criteria to guide experimental follow-up. These results demonstrate that combining complementary, impact-aware association tests increases sensitivity, improves replication, and expands the catalog of genetic risk factors for T2DM.
lay_summary: Researchers made a new computer method called MEVA that checks how damaging protein changes might be by comparing them across species. They used MEVA on protein-coding DNA from people with and without type 2 diabetes: 28,115 cases and 28,115 controls in UK Biobank and 16,915 cases and 16,915 controls in All of Us. MEVA found about 100 genes in each group and 23 genes in both, including known diabetes genes and new ones like NRIP1 and CALCOCO2. Some gene changes were linked to higher diabetes risk. This helps scientists pick genes to study for future tests or medicines.

pdr_title: Evaluation of Disparities in Management of Chronic Rhinosinusitis by Race and Ethnicity: An All of Us Research Program Study
pdr_abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate disparities in the management of chronic rhinosinusitis %28CRS%29 across racial, ethnic, and gender groups, focusing on treatment patterns and associated comorbidities.MethodsThis cross-sectional study analyzed data from 28,278 adults with CRS in the NIH All of Us Research Program between 2018 and 2022. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess associations between demographic variables, associated comorbidities, and receipt of treatments including systemic steroids, leukotriene modifiers, antibiotics, biologics, and sinus surgery.ResultsBlack individuals had higher odds of receiving systemic steroids %28OR: 1.59, P<.0001%29 and antibiotics %28OR: 1.67, P<.0001%29, but were less likely to receive biologics %28OR: 0.30, P=.051%29. Non-Hispanic individuals were more likely to receive systemic steroids %28OR: 1.54, P<.001%29 and antibiotics %28OR: 1.54, P=.0007%29, but were less likely to undergo sinus surgery %28OR: 0.67, P=.016%29. Male sex was associated with reduced odds of receiving systemic steroids %28OR: 0.86, P<.0001%29, leukotriene modifiers %28OR: 0.81, P<.001%29, and antibiotics %28OR: 0.91, P<.001%29 but increased odds of undergoing surgery %28OR: 1.37, P<.0001%29. Presence of nasal polyps and comorbid asthma strongly predicted use of biologics %28ORs: 4.39 and 13.83, respectively, P<.0001%29 and surgical intervention %28ORs: 13.13 and 1.34, respectively, P<.0001%29.ConclusionSignificant racial, ethnic, and gender disparities exist in the treatment of CRS, independent of comorbidities. These findings highlight the need for equity-focused strategies to ensure timely access to advanced therapies and to address structural barriers that may influence treatment allocation.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if people of different races, ethnic groups, or genders get different care for long‑term sinus inflammation (chronic rhinosinusitis). They looked at medical data for 28,278 adults from 2018–2022. They found Black people were more likely to get steroid pills or shots and antibiotics, but less likely to get newer targeted drugs (biologics). Non‑Hispanic people got more steroids and antibiotics but less surgery. Men got less medicine but more surgery. Having nasal polyps or asthma made getting biologics or surgery much more likely. This shows care is unequal and needs fairer access.

pdr_title: A highly accurate risk factor-based XGBoost multiethnic model for identifying patients with skin cancer
pdr_abstract: While individuals of European descent have a higher risk of skin cancer, other ancestries tend to have more advanced disease at diagnosis, resulting in outcome disparities. We examine the diverse All of Us dataset and identify genetic ancestries, lifestyle, social determinants of health and PDE5a inhibitor use as independent risk factors for skin cancer. We integrate these risk factors into a highly accurate XGBoost multiethnic model for identifying patients with skin cancer. Analyses of Shapley scores and interactions indicate the presence of strong non-linear associations between age and other risk factors, in particular cancer history, genetic ancestry and annual income, and suggest a stronger dependence on genetic and social determinants in younger individuals. Our XGBoost multiethnic model offers a precision medicine approach for early skin cancer detection in ethnically diverse patients, which could reduce outcome disparities in individuals of non-European ancestries.
lay_summary: This study looked at a large, diverse health database to find who is more likely to have skin cancer. Researchers used known risk factors and built a machine learning model (XGBoost) to spot people with skin cancer. They found that genetic ancestry, lifestyle, social factors like income, past cancer, age, and use of certain drugs (PDE5a inhibitors, e.g., Viagra) were linked to skin cancer. The model worked well across different ethnic groups and showed younger people relied more on genetic and social factors. The model could help doctors find skin cancer earlier in diverse groups and reduce unfair outcomes.

pdr_title: Chromosome 12 and Environmental Factors in Parkinson's Disease: An All of Us Data Analysis
pdr_abstract: Background/Objectives: Parkinson's disease %28PD%29 is a neurodegenerative disease that develops with age and is related to a decline in motor function. Studies suggest that the causes may be based on genetic dysfunction including PARK gene mutations and environmental factors.    Methods: To explore those factors, we used multivariable logistic regression to obtain odds ratios %28ORs%29 and adjusted ORs by using the All of Us Dataset which contains genomic, blood test, and other environmental data.    Results: On Chromosome 12, there were 3709 candidate genetic polymorphisms %28GPs%29 that are associated with PD. Of those GPs, fourteen GPs had high ORs which are similar to the OR of the PARK8 gene G2019S mutation. Of those 3709 GPs, a 2.00-fold change in OR was observed in five GPs located at bases 53,711,362 %28OR = 4.86, 95% CI [1.46, 16.18]%29, 31,281,818 %28OR = 4.37, 95% CI [1.02, 18.82]%29, 101,921,705 %28OR = 5.38, 95% CI [1.23, 23.51]%29, 47,968,795 %28OR = 7.82, 95% CI [1.81, 33.83]%29, and 112,791,809 %28OR = 8.05, 95% CI [1.85, 35.05]%29 by calcium, Vitamin D, and alcohol intake and were statistically significant.    Conclusions: The results suggest that the progression of some PD caused by certain GPs can be delayed or prevented by the environmental factors above. In February 2025, All of Us released the CT Dataset v.8 which has a 50% increase in the number of participants. Potentially, it may be possible to research more GPs and environmental factors. In future studies, we would like to explore other environmental factors and GPs on other chromosomes. It is believed that specific GPs may tailor current treatments and qualify patients for clinical trials. Additionally, genetic knowledge may help increase accuracy in clinical trials.
lay_summary: This study looked for DNA differences on chromosome 12 and everyday factors that might affect Parkinson’s disease. Researchers analyzed DNA, blood tests, and health survey data from people in the All of Us study using statistical methods. They found 3,709 small DNA differences linked to Parkinson’s, with 14 especially strong ones. Five spots showed about a 4 to 8 times higher chance of Parkinson’s when combined with calcium, vitamin D, and alcohol use. This suggests that changing diet or drinking habits and knowing your genes might help delay or prevent some cases.

Of those 3709 GPs, a 2.00-fold change in OR was observed in five GPs located at bases 53,711,362 (OR = 4.86, 95% CI [1.46, 16.18]), 31,281,818 (OR = 4.37, 95% CI [1.02, 18.82]), 101,921,705 (OR = 5.38, 95% CI [1.23, 23.51]), 47,968,795 (OR = 7.82, 95% CI [1.81, 33.83]), and 112,791,809 (OR = 8.05, 95% CI [1.85, 35.05]) by calcium, Vitamin D, and alcohol intake and were statistically significant.    Conclusions: The results suggest that the progression of some PD caused by certain GPs can be delayed or prevented by the environmental factors above. In February 2025, All of Us released the CT Dataset v.8 which has a 50% increase in the number of participants. Potentially, it may be possible to research more GPs and environmental factors. In future studies, we would like to explore other environmental factors and GPs on other chromosomes. It is believed that specific GPs may tailor current treatments and qualify patients for clinical trials. Additionally, genetic knowledge may help increase accuracy in clinical trials.

pdr_title: Healthcare Access and Utilization: Understanding Racial Disparities in Primary Hyperparathyroidism
pdr_abstract: Introduction: Previous studies have demonstrated racial disparities in healthcare access and utilization for patients with primary hyperparathyroidism %28PHPT%29. To refine current interventions and enhance patient outcomes, it is important to understand the reason behind such disparities, which we aimed to identify in this study.    Materials And Methods: Patients diagnosed with PHPT who completed the Healthcare Access and Utilization Survey within the All of Us database were included. Data were collected on patient demographics and survey responses. A chi-square test and analysis of variance test compared differences between racial groups.    Results: A total of 23.6% %28n = 243%29 of patients delayed medical care, and 37.3% %28n = 384%29 could not afford care. Paying out of pocket %2810.3%%29 and nervousness %288.6%%29 were the most common reasons for delaying care. Prescription medications were the most common item patients could not afford %2810.7%%29. Asian patients were more likely to delay care due to being unable to take time off work when compared to Black and White patients %2823.5% versus 6.4% and 4.9%, P < 0.001%29. Black patients were less likely to afford the following compared to White and Asian patients: prescription medications %2812.8% versus 9.3% versus 11.8%, P < 0.001%29, follow-up care %289.2% versus 3.4% versus 0%, P < 0.001%29, and specialist care %2811.0% versus 4.1% versus 0%, P < 0.001%29. Asian and Black patients were more likely to find patient-physician concordance important when compared to White patients %2882.4% versus 79.8% versus 69.9%, P < 0.001%29.    Conclusions: The racial background of PHPT patients within our cohort was associated with differences in reported reasons for delaying or being unable to afford care. Understanding the unique challenges faced by each racial group is crucial to creating targeted interventions that can improve healthcare access and utilization.
lay_summary: This study asked people with primary hyperparathyroidism (a gland disease) in the All of Us database about their access to care. About 24% delayed care and 37% could not afford care. Paying out of pocket (10%), feeling nervous (9%), and not affording medicines (11%) were common problems. Asian patients more often delayed care because they could not take time off work (about 24% versus 6% and 5%). Black patients more often could not pay for medicines, follow-up, or specialist visits. The study says we need targeted help to make care fairer for each group.

pdr_title: Association of psychiatric comorbidities with chronic urticaria: a nested case-control study in the All of Us research program
pdr_abstract: Background: Chronic urticaria %28CU%29 is characterized by recurring itchy hives lasting more than six weeks, with or without angioedema. Although CU patients are known to have an increased likelihood of psychiatric comorbidities, research exploring this connection in diverse populations remains limited.    Objectives: This study investigates the association between CU and psychiatric disorders using the All of Us %28AoU%29 database, a nationwide initiative designed to enhance research in underrepresented populations.    Methods: We conducted a nested case-control study among US adults in the AoU program from May 6, 2018 to February 26, 2025. SNOMED codes were used to identify CU cases that were then matched 4:1 to controls by age, sex, ethnicity, and smoking status. Psychiatric comorbidities were assessed using logistic regression models adjusted for hypothyroidism, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis.    Results: We identified 1171 CU cases and 4684 matched controls. CU was significantly associated with increased odds of ADHD %28OR, 3.61; 95% CI, 2.62-4.96%29, anxiety %28OR, 3.48; 95% CI, 3.03-3.99%29, depression %28OR, 3.26; 95% CI, 2.84-3.75%29, dysthymia %28OR, 3.67; 95% CI, 2.89-4.66%29, insomnia %28OR, 3.27; 95% CI, 2.77-3.86%29, psychological stress %28OR, 3.92; 95% CI, 3.09-4.96%29, PTSD %28OR, 3.25; 95% CI, 2.53-4.17%29, and substance use disorder %28OR, 2.13; 95% CI, 1.74-2.62%29.    Conclusions: These findings highlight the psychiatric burden associated with CU and demonstrates the importance of routine psychiatric screenings for CU patients to allow early intervention. Prospective studies investigating additional psychiatric disorders and underlying mechanisms will help clarify meaningful associations and guide appropriate psychiatric screening and management.
lay_summary: This study looked at adults in the All of Us research program to see if people with chronic urticaria (long‑lasting itchy hives) have more mental health problems. Researchers compared 1,171 people with chronic hives to 4,684 similar people without hives. They found people with chronic hives were about 2 to 4 times more likely to have ADHD, anxiety, depression, long‑term low mood (dysthymia), trouble sleeping, high stress, PTSD, or substance use problems. The results say doctors should check people with chronic hives for mental health issues so they can get help sooner.

pdr_title: Racial disparities in clonal hematopoiesis and their impact on hematologic malignancies
pdr_abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential %28CHIP%29 is a known risk factor for hematologic malignancies %28HM%29, but its distribution and clinical implications across diverse ancestries remain poorly characterized. In this study, we investigated CHIP and its progression to HM in a large, racially diverse cohort from the All of Us Research Program, comprising 245,388 participants. We identified 10,446 CHIP driver mutations in 9,476 individuals. Our analysis revealed clear racial disparities in CHIP prevalence and mutational profiles: African American %28AA%29 individuals had higher odds of CHIP and exhibited distinct mutation patterns compared to White American %28WA%29 individuals. Consistent with prior studies, CHIP was associated with an increased risk of HM, particularly myeloid malignancies. Notably, ancestry influenced the subtype of myeloid malignancy observed; CHIP was more strongly linked to myeloproliferative neoplasms in AA individuals compared with WA individuals. These findings demonstrated significant racial differences in CHIP biology and HM progression, highlighting the need for ancestry-informed approaches to CHIP risk assessment and HM prevention.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether CHIP (when blood stem cells grow with certain mutations) differs by race and raises cancer risk. Researchers studied 245,388 people and found 10,446 CHIP mutations in 9,476 people. African Americans had more CHIP and different mutation patterns than White Americans. CHIP raised the chance of blood cancers, especially myeloid cancers. In African Americans, CHIP was more often linked to myeloproliferative neoplasms (a subtype that makes too many blood cells). This means doctors may need race-aware ways to find CHIP and prevent blood cancers.

pdr_title: Inequities in Neuropsychiatric Outcomes After Brain Trauma in the All of Us Database
pdr_abstract: Importance: Traumatic brain injury %28TBI%29 is an important public health concern, with disparities in post-TBI neuropsychiatric diagnoses %28NPDs%29 observed across Black or African American and White populations.    Objective: To examine the incidence of NPDs following TBI in the US and assess how socioecologic factors are associated with population-level differences.    Design, Setting, And Participants: This retrospective cohort study used data from the All of Us Research Program, version 7, including available electronic health record data from participants aged 18 years or older enrolled between May 6, 2018, and July 1, 2022, with an established TBI diagnosis based on diagnostic codes and criteria from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Department of Defense, and clinical expertise. Data were analyzed between June 24, 2024, and January 23, 2025.    Exposure: Social and structural determinants of health.    Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcomes assessed were incident NPDs following TBI grouped into 10 diagnostic clusters according to phecode categories. Competing-risk models %28subdistribution hazard ratio [HR] with 95% CI%29 and Heckman-type selection models %28β [SE]%29 were used.    Results: The study included 8714 participants %28mean [SD] age, 49.0 [17.9] years; 4700 women [54.5%]%29 with TBI and was limited to participants self-identifying as Black or African American %28hereafter, Black%29 %282192 [25.2%]%29 or White %286522 [74.8%]%29 race. White participants had a lower adjusted risk of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders %28adjusted HR [AHR], 0.49 [95% CI, 0.35-0.69]%29, posttraumatic stress disorder %28AHR, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.52-0.86]%29, substance use disorders %28AHR, 0.51 [95% CI, 0.42-0.62]%29, and headache disorders %28AHR, 0.78 [95% CI, 0.67-0.91]%29 compared with Black participants. Models accounting for selection bias revealed a lower adjusted likelihood of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders %28β [SE],-0.24[0.07]%29 and headache disorders %28β [SE],-0.10[0.03]%29 in White participants. Higher social deprivation was associated with a lower likelihood of mood disorders %28β [SE],-0.65[0.14]%29, anxiety disorders %28β [SE],-0.85[0.13]%29, posttraumatic stress disorder %28β [SE],-1.06[0.22]%29, any dementia %28β [SE],-1.03[0.22]%29, and headache disorders %28β [SE],-0.52[0.14]%29 but a higher likelihood of sleep disorders %28β [SE],0.34[0.08]%29.    Conclusions And Relevance: This cohort study found that post-TBI NPDs varied across populations, with a higher likelihood of psychotic and headache disorders among Black All of Us participants. These findings highlight the utility of social determinants of health for better understanding disparities in post-TBI outcomes, underscoring the need for additional efforts to address these disparities.

pdr_title: Association between neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio and Alzheimer's disease in large biobank cohorts
pdr_abstract: BackgroundNeutrophil to lymphocyte ratio %28NLR%29 is an inflammatory biomarker for chronic disease that also may provide evidence for peripheral innate immune activation in Alzheimer's disease %28AD%29 pathogenesis.ObjectiveThe objective of this study is to assess the association between NLR and AD as a biomarker or potential causal step for AD pathogenesis.MethodsCohorts used for analysis include the UK Biobank %28n=207100; n=2198 AD cases%29 and the All of Us research program %28AoU, n=45202; n=263 AD cases%29 which allowed for a larger sample size than most previous studies. Cox proportional hazard models were used to assess the association between NLR and AD, including in models adjusting for factors in the UK Biobank Dementia Risk Score. A Mendelian randomization analysis was performed to assess the potential causality between NLR and AD.ResultsNLR was associated with AD in the UK Biobank %28HR: 1.03 per 1 SD, 95% CI: 1.01-1.05%29 but not in AoU %28HR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.92-1.14%29. A fixed effects model resulted in a pooled HR: 1.03 %2895% CI: 1.02-1.05%29. These effects were robust to adjustment for C-reactive protein, APOE ε4 genotype status, APOE ε2 genotype status, and other AD risk factors. The MR analysis was performed with 214 NLR-associated variants but was not significant %28IVW estimate: -0.001, p: 0.99%29.ConclusionsFindings provide evidence for NLR as a biomarker for AD but not as a causal risk factor.
lay_summary: The researchers wanted to know if the neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR), a blood test that shows inflammation, is linked to or causes Alzheimer's disease. They looked at over 250,000 people from two large studies (207,100 in UK Biobank, 45,202 in All of Us), using statistical models and a genetic test that checks if one thing causes another. They found a small link in the UK group and overall (about a 3% higher risk with higher NLR), but the genetic test showed NLR does not cause Alzheimer's. This means NLR might help show who is at higher risk, but lowering NLR may not stop the disease.

manual_title: Guideline-concordant antibiotic prescribing for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) due to drug-resistant pathogens in the All of Us database
pdr_title: Guideline-concordant antibiotic prescribing for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia %28CABP%29 due to drug-resistant pathogens in the I%28content=['All of Us']%29 database
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Clinical and Translational Science
pdr_abstract: Introduction: Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia %28CABP%29 contributes significantly to mortality and healthcare costs worldwide. The use of guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy for CABP is associated with improved outcomes.    Methods: This was a retrospective cohort study of inpatients with CABP due to MRSA or P. aeruginosa in the All of Us database. The proportion of patients on guideline-concordant antibiotics or guideline-discordant antibiotics was compared within groups based upon patient age, sex, self-reported race, ethnicity, marital status, alcohol use, and tobacco use. Guideline concordance was determined using the 2019 IDSA/ATS CABP guidelines. Associations were further analyzed using multivariate logistic regression.    Results: A total of 336 patients with CABP due to MRSA %28152%29 or P. aeruginosa %28184%29 were included. Guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy was prescribed to 70% of CABP-MRSA patients and for 57% of CABP-P. aeruginosa patients. Independently predictive factors of guideline-concordant antibiotic prescribing for CABP-P. aeruginosa patients were Non-Hispanic Black %28NHB%29 vs. Non-Hispanic White %28NHW%29 race %28odds ratio = 0.30, 95% confidence interval = 0.12 - 0.75%29.    Conclusion: In the All of Us database, the majority of CABP-MRSA and CABP-P. aeruginosa patients were prescribed guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy. Race was independently predictive of guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy for patients with CABP-P. aeruginosa, but not CABP-MRSA. NHB patients were less likely to receive guideline-concordant antibiotic therapy than NHW patients when treated for CABP-P. aeruginosa.
lay_summary: This study looked at hospital patients with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) caused by MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the All of Us database to see if they got antibiotics that match 2019 medical guidelines. Researchers reviewed 336 patients (152 with MRSA, 184 with P. aeruginosa). About 70% of MRSA patients and 57% of P. aeruginosa patients received guideline-matching antibiotics. Black patients were less likely than White patients to get guideline-matching treatment for P. aeruginosa. This shows a racial gap in care that should be fixed to make treatment fairer and better.

pdr_title: Machine learning-derived genetic risk scores identify IL21 as a predictor of response to omalizumab and dupilumab in asthma
pdr_abstract: Rationale: Genetic risk scores %28GRS%29 of Th1/2/17-related loci may be associated with response to biologics. We leveraged previously published machine learning-derived GRSs associated with plasma proteins from the INTERVAL/UK-Biobank study.    Methods: We assessed 42 Th1/2/17-related GRSs and SNPs for association with response %28≥50% reduction in exacerbations%29 to biologics in 172 White patients with moderate-to-severe asthma in the Mass General Brigham Biobank %28MGBB: 92 omalizumab, 38 mepolizumab, 42 dupilumab%29. Replication was sought in 243 individuals in the All of Us %28AoU%29 cohort %28111 omalizumab, 58 mepolizumab, 74 dupilumab%29. Models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, baseline exacerbations, and principal components 1-10. AUROC was used to evaluate top predictors; type I error was assessed using random GRS sets %28target FDR ≤20%%29.    Results: Females comprised a large proportion; mean BMI was 28-35 kg/m2. IL21 GRS was associated with omalizumab response in MGBB %28OR: 1.7, 95% CI: 1.03-2.87%29 with similar direction in AoU %281.5, 0.91-2.45%29. IL21 also predicted dupilumab response in MGBB %282.4, 1.05-5.44%29 but in the opposite direction in AoU %280.57, 0.31-1.06%29. They used computer-made scores in 172 White patients treated with omalizumab, mepolizumab, or dupilumab and checked results in 243 people from another group. A score linked to the IL21 gene predicted better response to omalizumab in both groups and to dupilumab in one group. No score predicted response to mepolizumab. This finding could help doctors choose the right asthma drug.

pdr_title: Migraine is associated with a higher risk of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke: an analysis of the I%28content=['All of Us']%29 database
pdr_abstract: Background: While prior studies suggest an increased risk of stroke among individuals with migraine, particularly those with migraine with aura, data on how specific migraine characteristics and comorbidities influence this risk across diverse populations remain limited. The All of Us database provides a unique opportunity to address this gap given its large sample size and inclusion of historically underrepresented groups.    Methods: A cross-sectional case-control analysis using multivariable regression models accounting for vascular risk factors and comorbidities was performed to compare the risk of stroke between individuals with and without migraine, odds ratios %28OR%29 using a 95% confidence interval %28CI%29 were calculated.    Results: Within the All of Us database, 31,444 individuals received a migraine diagnosis [female=25,374/81%, male=5,391/17%, other=679/2%; mean %28std%29 age=54.9 %2815.6%29] and 379,283 did not have a migraine diagnosis [female=222,104/59%, male=149,182/39%, other=7,997/2%; mean %28SD%29 age=55.9 %2817.2%29]. The migraine group had a greater proportion of women %2881% vs. 59%%29, a higher proportion of white individuals %2861% vs. 55%%29 and fewer African American individuals %2815% vs. 19%%29. Compared to the non-migraine group, individuals with migraine had higher rates of comorbidities, including depression %2846% vs. 12%%29, diabetes %2816% vs. 7%%29, tobacco use %2836% vs. 15%%29, hyperlipidemia %2852% vs. 24%%29, hypertension %2854% vs. 26%%29, and atrial fibrillation %283% vs. 2%%29.A multivariable regression model adjusted for differences between group demographics and comorbidities found that compared to those without migraine, individuals with migraine had a higher risk of overall stroke [OR 1.97, 95% CI %281.88, 2.07%29], ischemic stroke [OR 1.38, 95% CI %281.24, 1.53%29] and hemorrhagic stroke [OR 1.75, 95% CI %281.60, 1.92%29]. Individuals with chronic migraine had a higher risk of overall stroke compared to the non-migraine group [OR 2.56, 95% CI %28 2.32, 2.84%29] and compared to episodic migraine [OR 1.90, 95% CI %281.81, 2.00%29]. Those with migraine with aura had a higher risk of stroke compared to individuals with migraine without aura [OR 1.33, 95% CI %281.20, 1.48%29].    Conclusions: Individuals with migraine, particularly those with chronic migraine had a higher risk of stroke compared to those without migraine and compared to individuals with episodic migraine. The risk of stroke was higher in those with migraine with aura compared to those with migraine without aura even after adjusting for vascular comorbidities. Our analysis, using data from the All of Us database, confirms previous findings and suggests that while vascular comorbidities are more prevalent in those with migraine, they do not fully account for the increased risk of stroke.
lay_summary: This study used the All of Us database to compare 31,444 people with migraine to 379,283 people without migraine, adjusting for other health problems, to check stroke risk. People with migraine had about twice the chance of any stroke and higher risk of both blocked-artery strokes and bleeding in the brain. Those with chronic migraine had higher risk than those with episodic migraine, and people with migraine with aura (warning signs like flashes or tingling) had higher risk than those without aura. People with migraine should talk with their doctor about stroke risk and heart health.

pdr_title: Implications of a New Obesity Definition Among the All of Us Cohort
pdr_abstract: Importance: A recent Lancet Commission proposed an obesity definition that integrates body mass index %28BMI [calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared]%29 with anthropometric measures, marking a paradigm shift in how obesity is conceptualized and classified.    Objective: To determine the clinical implications of the new definition of obesity.    Design, Setting, And Participants: This population-based longitudinal cohort study leveraged data from the All of Us cohort. Participants in All of Us with complete anthropometric data were enrolled between May 31, 2017, and September 30, 2023, with a median follow-up of 4.0 %28IQR, 1.7-4.7%29 years.    Exposure: Obesity classified by traditional and new definitions.    Main Outcomes And Measures: Obesity was defined by the new framework using sex- and race-specific thresholds as %281%29 BMI above the traditional obesity threshold plus at least 1 elevated anthropometric measure or BMI greater than 40 %28BMI-plus-anthropometric obesity%29 or %282%29 at least 2 elevated anthropometric measures with BMI below the traditional obesity threshold %28anthropometric-only obesity%29. Obesity was categorized as clinical or preclinical based on organ dysfunction and/or physical limitation.    Results: Among 301 026 individuals %28183 633 [61.0%] female; median age, 54 [IQR, 38-65] years%29, 206 361 %2868.6%%29 had obesity according to the new definition vs 128 992 %2842.9%%29 according to the traditional definition, due to inclusion of individuals with anthropometric-only obesity. Among the overall cohort, 108 650 individuals %2836.1%%29 had clinical obesity according to the new definition; this prevalence increased with age, as 24 498 of 45 018 individuals 70 years or older %2854.4%%29 had clinical obesity. Compared with no obesity, odds ratios of organ dysfunction were 3.31 %2895% CI, 3.24-3.37%29 for BMI-plus-anthropometric obesity and 1.76 %2895% CI, 1.73-1.80%29 for anthropometric-only obesity per the new definition. In longitudinal analyses, clinical obesity conferred elevated risks of incident diabetes %28adjusted hazard ratio [AHR], 6.11; 95% CI, 5.67-6.60%29, cardiovascular events %28AHR, 5.88; 95% CI, 5.38-6.43%29, and all-cause mortality %28AHR, 2.71; 95% CI, 2.41-3.05%29 compared with no obesity or organ dysfunction. Preclinical obesity was also associated with increased risks of incident diabetes %28AHR, 3.32; 95% CI, 3.08-3.58%29 and cardiovascular events %28AHR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.27-1.55%29, albeit to a lesser degree.    Conclusions And Relevance: In this cohort study, adoption of the new definition of obesity significantly increased obesity prevalence with major implications for clinical practice and public policy. The new framework effectively stratified individuals at high risk of organ dysfunction and long-term complications while introducing anthropometric-only obesity and preclinical obesity as distinct entities warranting further study.

Researchers used 301,026 adults from the All of Us study followed about 4 years. The new definition found obesity in 68.6% versus 42.9% with the old rule. pdr_title: Disruptions of healthcare visits and viral suppression for people living with HIV during the COVID-19 pandemic in the US
pdr_abstract: Background: Existing studies have documented the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the utilization of health services among people living with HIV %28PLWH%29, including reduced access to medical consultations, antiretroviral therapy %28ART%29 uptake, and viral load monitoring. However, few studies have investigated the pandemic’s effect on clinical outcomes—such as viral suppression rates—particularly within U.S. settings. Using a nationwide data source, this study aims to examine the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on healthcare visits and viral suppression outcomes of PLWH.    Methods: This retrospective cohort study used data from All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program, a nationwide cohort designed to be broadly representative of the U.S. population, particularly groups historically underrepresented in biomedical research. Data from more than 340 sites, deposited into AoU and harmonized into a release set spanning January 2018 through December 2021, were used for this study. Using CD4 count or viral load measures as proxies for health care visits, we employed generalized linear mixed regression interrupted time series %28ITS%29 models with a log link to assess the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the number of healthcare visits and viral suppressions, comparing data two years before and after the onset of the pandemic. Among 7,667 PLWH identified, 1,772 who had at least one CD4 count or viral load measure were included in the healthcare visit analysis, and 1,382 who had at least one viral load measure were included in the viral suppression analysis.    Results: For the outcomes of interest, the total number of healthcare visits dropped from 7,902 %28average of 4.90 per person%29 before pandemic to 5,252 %28average of 3.70 per person%29 after the pandemic. Similarly, the total number of viral suppression events declined from 2,361 %28average of 1.98 per person%29 before pandemic to 1,893 %28average of 1.88 per person%29 after pandemic. Compared to the pre-COVID-19 period, the number of healthcare visits among PLWH significantly decreased %28adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=0.80, 95%CI: 0.75–0.86%29 whereas the number of viral suppression events did not change significantly %28aOR=1.10, 95%CI: 0.97–1.25%29 after the pandemic. Older individuals had lower odds of healthcare visits, while those with Medicaid insurance and individuals with more comorbidities were more likely to have healthcare visits. Regarding viral suppression, older individuals, Hispanic or Latino participants, and those who were married or living with partners were more likely to achieve viral suppression, whereas individuals with a greater number of comorbidities were less likely to achieve viral suppression.    Conclusions: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted healthcare visits and contributed to suboptimal viral suppression among underrepresented HIV populations. Targeted interventions are needed to ensure continuous engagement in HIV care during unprecedented health crises.
lay_summary: This study looked at how COVID-19 affected doctor visits and virus control for people with HIV in the U.S. Using national health records from 2018–2021, researchers compared two years before and after the pandemic for about 1,800 people for visits and 1,400 for virus tests. Clinic visits fell by about one-third. The share of people with the virus under control (viral suppression) stayed roughly the same. Older people had fewer visits; people with many health problems had more visits but less virus control. The findings mean we need better ways to keep HIV care going during crises.

pdr_title: Population-scale gene-based analysis of whole-genome sequencing provides insights into metabolic health
pdr_abstract: In addition to its coverage of the noncoding genome, whole-genome sequencing %28WGS%29 may better capture the coding genome than exome sequencing. Here we sought to exploit this and identify new rare, protein-coding variants associated with metabolic health in WGS data %28n=708,956%29 from the UK Biobank and All of Us studies. Identified genes highlight new biological mechanisms, including protein-truncating variants %28PTVs%29 in the DNA double-strand break repair gene RIF1 that have a substantial effect on body mass index %282.66kgm-2, s.e. 0.43, P=3.7×10-10%29. UBR3 is an intriguing example where PTVs independently increase body mass index and type 2 diabetes risk. Furthermore, PTVs in IRS2 have a substantial effect on type 2 diabetes %28odds ratio 6.4 %283.7-11.3%29, P=9.9×10-14, 34% case prevalence among carriers%29 and were also associated with chronic kidney disease independent of diabetes status, suggesting an important role for IRS2 in maintaining renal health. Our study demonstrates that large-scale WGS provides new mechanistic insights into human metabolic phenotypes through improved capture of coding sequences.
lay_summary: This study looked for rare gene changes that affect metabolism by analyzing whole-genome DNA from 708,956 people. Researchers searched for protein-truncating variants (PTVs), which are changes that break a protein. They found PTVs in RIF1 linked to about 2.7 units higher body mass index (BMI, a measure of body fat), UBR3 PTVs that raised BMI and diabetes risk, and IRS2 PTVs where 34% of carriers had diabetes and they also had more kidney disease even without diabetes. These results could help find new ways to assess and treat metabolic illness.

pdr_title: Building analytical capacity for research at Federally Qualified Health Centers through the I%28content=['All of Us']%29 Research Program
pdr_abstract: The National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program %28All of Us or program%29 aims to better understand the complexity of diseases, prevention and treatment at the individual level. To accomplish this, one of the program components is to build a longitudinal cohort of one million or more volunteers in the United States and its territories through which clinical, environmental, genetic, and behavioral data are collected. Federally Qualified Health Centers %28FQHCs%29 play a crucial role in enrolling participants in the program and while FQHCs have the dedication, leadership, and wherewithal to operationalize a national longitudinal data collection, their local resources are limited by funding and scope for conducting research. This paper describes the evolution of FQHC research landscape, from building capacity for descriptive, to exploratory operational research, and moving toward biomedical research. As programs such as All of Us continue to ensure that focus on precision medicine is reflected in both data collection and research, continuing to advance the research landscape within health centers is crucial. By developing this capacity, we are developing a research infrastructure that will continue to grow, supporting advancements in precision medicine for improving health outcomes.
lay_summary: This paper explains how the All of Us program helped community health centers (FQHCs) get better at doing research. Purpose: to build local research skills so centers can collect long-term health, environment, behavior, and genetic data from many people. Methods: the authors describe how centers moved from simple data work to more advanced studies. Key findings: FQHCs can grow their research ability, supporting precision medicine. Practical importance: stronger local research means better care and fairer access to new medical discoveries for their patients.

pdr_title: Semiparametric efficient estimation of small genetic effects in large-scale population cohorts
pdr_abstract: Population genetics seeks to quantify DNA variant associations with traits or diseases, as well as interactions among variants and with environmental factors. Computing millions of estimates in large cohorts in which small effect sizes and tight confidence intervals are expected, necessitates minimizing model-misspecification bias to increase power and control false discoveries. We present TarGene, a unified statistical workflow for the semi-parametric efficient and double robust estimation of genetic effects including $ k $-point interactions among categorical variables in the presence of confounding and weak population dependence. $ k $-point interactions, or Average Interaction Effects %28AIEs%29, are a direct generalization of the usual average treatment effect %28ATE%29. We estimate genetic effects with cross-validated and/or weighted versions of Targeted Minimum Loss-based Estimators %28TMLE%29 and One-Step Estimators %28OSE%29. The tests showed the method finds small effects more accurately, keeps false findings low, and handles related people in the data. This helps scientists find real genetic links faster and avoid wrong leads in health research.

pdr_title: Comparative Analysis of White and African American Groups Reveals Unique Lipid and Inflammatory Features of Diabetes
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
pdr_abstract: Diabetes is a metabolic and inflammatory disease that disproportionately affects African American populations, yet clinical diagnostics often rely on biomarkers discovered and validated predominantly in White cohorts. This study investigates race-specific lipid and inflammatory features of diabetes to uncover biologically distinct disease signatures that may contribute to disparities in diagnosis and management. We analyzed clinical parameters from a well-matched subset of the HANDLS cohort %28N = 40%29 and conducted targeted plasma lipidomics and multiplex cytokine profiling across African American and White individuals from the HANDLS cohort with and without diabetes. Then we validated key findings using a large and diverse cohort of African American and White individuals with type 2 diabetes from the NIH AllofUs program %28N = 17,339%29. Our results reveal racially divergent signatures of diabetes. White individuals with diabetes exhibited elevated Cholesterol:HDL ratios, triglycerides, and classical inflammatory markers such as hs-CRP. In contrast, African American individuals with diabetes displayed minimal lipid elevations but showed increased Th17-related cytokines1. These differences were independent of statin use, age, and body mass index. Additionally, correlations between lipid to cytokine ratios and the glycemic marker hemoglobin A1C differed sharply by race, suggesting that the pathophysiology of diabetes is not uniform across populations. Our findings challenge standard diabetes biomarkers and emphasize the need for more inclusive diagnostic frameworks. By identifying population-specific biological patterns of diabetes, this study provides important insight into the roots of persistent health disparities and underscores the value of precision approaches to equitable diabetes care.

pdr_title: Using Data from All of Us to Examine Cardiovascular Risk
pdr_abstract: The American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 %28LE8%29 metrics of blood pressure, body mass index, glucose, cholesterol, smoking, diet, sleep, and physical activity are measurable outcomes to gauge cardiovascular health in individuals and populations.Objective: To determine the utility of using the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program data to quantify LE8 contemporary in a United States cohort. This was a cross-sectional observational study of primary %28participant-reported and researcher-measured%29 and secondary %28electronic health records%29 data from Version 7 All of Us data. Adults aged 20-100 years were included. Our primary outcome was percent of participants with complete data for all LE8 cardiovascular health indicators within one year of enrollment. We used All of Us researcher measured blood pressure and body mass index, health record serum glycosylated hemoglobin %28HbA1c%29, total, and non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and participant-reported cigarette use, age, race, and sex data. We described the availability of LE8 in the dataset, then calculated sex differences in LE8 using independent samples t-tests with equal variance, or Wilcoxon rank sum test, or chi-square tests. There were no data for diet, sleep, or physical activity. The final sample with complete data was 56,565 primarily middle aged adults, and over half were female. Overall, the sample had higher mean systolic blood pressure, high mean body mass index indicating obesity, and average to high HbA1c, indicating few participants meet the definition of ideal cardiovascular health. Nearly half of participants reported lifetime cigarette use of ≥100 cigarettes. Data for non-high-density cholesterol was missing in half of participants. Compared to males, females were younger by 4.2 years, had lower average systolic and diastolic blood pressure, higher mean body mass, higher total cholesterol, lower median HbA1c, and fewer reported lifetime cigarette use. Important data for modifiable lifestyle factors of diet, physical activity, and sleep are missing from the All of Us dataset. We recommend adding these missing variables to future surveys. Nevertheless, this snapshot of cardiovascular health shows that, on average, adults in the United States had poorer than recommended cardiovascular health for cardiovascular disease risk.
lay_summary: Researchers used data from the NIH 'All of Us' program to see if it could measure heart health using the Life's Essential 8. They looked at 56,565 adults aged 20–100 from surveys, medical records, and measurements like blood pressure and BMI (body mass index). They found no data for diet, sleep, or physical activity, and half lacked a key cholesterol test. Many people had high blood pressure, obesity-level BMI, and raised blood sugar. Nearly half had smoked 100 or more cigarettes. This means many U.S. adults have worse heart health than recommended and the dataset needs more lifestyle data.

pdr_title: Alcohol consumption among patients diagnosed with genitourinary cancers
pdr_abstract: To characterize alcohol consumption and binge-drinking patterns among individuals with GU cancers %28prostate, kidney, bladder and testicular%29 compared to a propensity-matched cohort without cancer in a large, nationally diverse population. We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional study utilizing data from the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program. Matching accounted for age, sex assigned at birth, smoking status, comorbidities and education/marital status. The primary outcome was self-reported drinking frequency. The secondary outcomes were self-reported binge-drinking frequency and Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test %28AUDIT-C%29 scores. Drinking and binge-drinking among individuals with GU malignancy %28N = 11 522%29 closely resembled those of matched controls %28N = 47 747%29, with the majority %2853%%29 consuming at least 2-4 drinks per month. There was no significant association between GU cancer diagnosis and increased drinking frequency %28OR: 0.99; p = 0.65%29, binge-drinking frequency %28OR: 0.85; p: 0.055%29 or AUDIT-C %28OR: 0.99; p =0.65%29. Individuals diagnosed with kidney cancer had reduced odds of higher alcohol use %28OR: 0.76; p < 0.001%29 and AUDIT-C score %28OR: 0.83; p < 0.001%29 compared to controls. In this large cohort, including traditionally underrepresented minorities, alcohol use was highly prevalent among those with GU malignancies. Drinking behaviours were similar to individuals without cancer, underscoring the need for integration of lifestyle-focused interventions into survivorship care, as alcohol remains a common and modifiable behaviour with wide-ranging health implications.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if people with genitourinary (GU) cancers (urinary and reproductive organs) drink more alcohol than similar people without cancer. They used a large U.S. health database to compare people with GU cancers to matched people without cancer and asked about usual drinking, binge drinking (drinking a lot at once), and a brief alcohol screen. Most people (53%) drank at least 2–4 drinks per month, and drinking habits were similar between groups. People with kidney cancer drank less. This means alcohol use is common after GU cancer and should be part of follow-up care.

pdr_title: The association between glaucoma and dementia in a national cohort of All of Us participants
pdr_abstract: To assess the association between glaucoma and its subtypes and incidence of dementia and its subtypes across APOE genotypes in the National Institutes of Health %28NIH%29 All of Us Research Program. Retrospective longitudinal cohort study. A cohort of individuals with linked electronic health record %28EHR%29 data in the All of Us dataset, with every individual with a glaucoma diagnosis matched with four control participants. Participants diagnosed with dementia prior to glaucoma were excluded. A 1:4 cohort of participants with a glaucoma diagnosis and control participants was created using a propensity score matching design that considered age, race, ethnicity, and sex. Among participants with whole-genome sequencing data, APOE was genotyped to stratify for sub-analyses. Multivariable Cox regression model was used to adjust for residual imbalance in comorbidities: hypertension, obesity, depression, traumatic brain injury, type 2 diabetes, and hearing loss. Incidence of dementia and its subtypes. Among the 393497 All of Us participants with linked EHRs, we identified 9444 individuals %282.40%%29 with glaucoma diagnoses %28excluding participants with diagnoses of dementia before glaucoma%29 and 37776 matched controls without glaucoma. During the observation period %28median: 6.5 years, inter-quartile range: 3.3 to 10.7 years%29, dementia was diagnosed in 1127 %282.39%%29 individuals. Glaucoma was associated with a significantly increased risk of all-cause dementia %28adjusted HR %28aHR%29: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.08-1.40%29, Alzheimer's disease %28aHR: 1.60, 95% CI: 1.26-2.02%29, and vascular dementia %28aHR: 1.38, 95% CI: 1.04-1.83%29. Among glaucoma subtypes, primary open-angle glaucoma %28POAG, N=5756%29 and normal-tension glaucoma %28NTG, N=1106%29 was linked to elevated risk of Alzheimer's disease %28POAG: aHR: 1.48, 95% CI: 1.11-1.96; NTG: aHR: 1.87, 95% CI: 1.09-3.18%29, while angle-closure glaucoma %28N=3150%29 showed no significant association %28aHR=1.49, 95% CI: 0.91-2.27%29. Glaucoma was associated with an increased risk of all-cause dementia across the three APOE genotypes assessed, with the greatest increased risk observed in ε2ε3 %28N=4965, aHR: 1.76, 95% CI: 1.11-2.79%29, followed by ε3ε3 %28N=23667, aHR: 1.45, 95% CI: 1.19-1.75%29 and ε3ε4 %28N=8544, aHR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.09-1.87%29. Glaucoma was associated with a higher risk of dementia with varying associations among glaucoma and dementia subtypes across APOE genotypes.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if people with glaucoma (an eye disease) get dementia more often. They used health records from a large US study, matched people with glaucoma to similar people without it, followed them about 6.5 years, and checked a dementia gene (APOE). About 2% were diagnosed with dementia. People with glaucoma had higher dementia risk: about 23% more overall, about 60% more for Alzheimer’s, and about 38% more for vascular dementia. Two glaucoma types (open-angle and normal-tension) linked to higher Alzheimer’s risk. This means people with glaucoma should watch for memory problems and get brain health checks.
