pdr_title: Age-Dependent Contributions of Rare and Common Genetic Variation in Atrial Fibrillation
pdr_abstract: Genetic variation contributes to atrial fibrillation %28AF%29, but its impact may vary with age. The All of Us Research Program contains whole-genome sequencing of data from 100 574 adult participants with linked electronic health records. We assessed clinical, monogenic, and polygenic associations with AF in a cross-sectional analysis, stratified by age: <45 years %28n=22 290%29, 45 to 60 years %28n=26 805%29, and >60 years %28n=51 659%29. AF was defined as ≥2 Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine-Clinical Terms codes on separate days. We identified pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in 145 cardiac genes with dominant inheritance and calculated a previously established polygenic risk score. Adjusted for known clinical factors, multivariable analysis quantified associations between monogenic and polygenic factors and AF in each age group. Among 100 574 participants %28mean age 59±16 years%29, 7811 %287.8%%29 had AF, while 92 763 %2892%%29 did not. Monogenic pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were associated with AF across all age groups, most strongly in participants aged <45 years %28odds ratio, 2.1 [95% CI, 1.2-3.2]; P=0.007%29. In contrast, the polygenic risk score was not associated with AF in this youngest group %28odds ratio, 1.0 [95% CI, 0.9-1.2]; P=0.650%29 but was in older groups %28odds ratio 1.3 [95% CI, 1.2-1.4]; P<0.001 for both ages 45-60 and >60 years%29. Clinical factors were significantly associated with AF %28C-index, 0.84 [0.83-0.84]; P<0.001%29, with marginal improvement when monogenic and polygenic data were added %28C-index, 0.86 [0.86-0.87]; P<0.001%29. In hazard-based time-to-event analysis, monogenic variants were associated with earlier onset, whereas the polygenic risk score was not associated with age of onset. In this large cross-sectional study, monogenic variants were associated with AF throughout life, particularly in younger participants, whereas polygenic risk was associated with AF only in older participants. While genetic information added only marginal improvements to AF risk discrimination beyond existing clinical risk factors, monogenic variants were associated with an earlier age of onset in participants with AF.
lay_summary: They studied 100,574 adults with gene sequencing and medical records to see how rare (single‑gene) and common (many‑gene) genetic changes affect atrial fibrillation (AF), an irregular heartbeat, at different ages. AF was present in 7.8% of people. Rare (single‑gene) harmful variants were linked to AF at all ages and were especially common in people under 45. The many‑gene risk score was linked to AF only in people over 45. Single‑gene variants were tied to earlier AF. This suggests single‑gene testing may help young patients, while broad genetic scores add little beyond usual medical risk factors.

pdr_title: Whole genome sequence analysis of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol across 246 K individuals
pdr_abstract: Rare genetic variation provided by whole genome sequence datasets has been relatively less explored for its contributions to human traits. Meta-analysis of sequencing data offers advantages by integrating larger sample sizes from diverse cohorts, thereby increasing the likelihood of discovering novel insights into complex traits. Furthermore, emerging methods in genome-wide rare variant association testing further improve power and interpretability. Here, we conduct the largest meta-analysis of whole genome sequencing for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol %28LDL-C%29, a therapeutic target for coronary artery disease, analyzing data from 246 K participants and integrating 1.23B variants from the UK Biobank and the Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine %28TOPMed%29 program. We identify numerous rare coding and non-coding gene associations related to LDL-C, with replication across 86 K participants in All of Us. Our findings are based on single-variant analyses, rare coding and non-coding variant aggregation tests, and sliding window approaches. Through this comprehensive analysis, we identify 704 novel single-variant associations, 25 novel rare coding variant aggregates, 28 novel rare non-coding variant aggregates, and one novel sliding window aggregate. This study provides a meta-analysis framework for large-scale whole genome sequence association analyses from diverse population groups, yielding novel rare non-coding variant associations.
lay_summary: This study looked for rare DNA changes that affect LDL cholesterol, the 'bad' cholesterol that can cause heart disease. Researchers combined whole genome data from 246,000 people and checked findings in 86,000 more. They searched single spots in DNA and groups of rare changes in parts that make proteins (coding) and parts that do not (non-coding). They found 704 new single DNA links, plus 25 new rare coding groups and 28 new rare non-coding groups, and one extra region. These discoveries may help doctors find new treatments and better predict heart risk.

Here, we conduct the largest meta-analysis of whole genome sequencing for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), a therapeutic target for coronary artery disease, analyzing data from 246 K participants and integrating 1.23B variants from the UK Biobank and the Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine (TOPMed) program. We identify numerous rare coding and non-coding gene associations related to LDL-C, with replication across 86 K participants in All of Us. Our findings are based on single-variant analyses, rare coding and non-coding variant aggregation tests, and sliding window approaches. Through this comprehensive analysis, we identify 704 novel single-variant associations, 25 novel rare coding variant aggregates, 28 novel rare non-coding variant aggregates, and one novel sliding window aggregate. This study provides a meta-analysis framework for large-scale whole genome sequence association analyses from diverse population groups, yielding novel rare non-coding variant associations.

pdr_title: Association of Autoimmune Disease with Melanoma and Non-Melanoma Skin Cancers
pdr_abstract: This study examines the association between autoimmune diseases and melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer using data from the All of Us Research Program. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis including 419,789 participants using multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for sociodemographic variables, comorbidities, and immunosuppressant use. We found significant associations between melanoma and Sjögren's syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease %28IBD%29, vitiligo, and autoimmune thyroiditis. Non-melanoma skin cancer risk was elevated in Sjögren's, IBD, and Type 1 diabetes mellitus. Notably, our finding of increased melanoma and basal cell carcinoma risk in vitiligo contrasts with prior studies. These differences may reflect increased genetic diversity in our cohort or confounding by immune checkpoint inhibitor use. Our findings demonstrate increased risk of both melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer in patients with select autoimmune diseases, highlighting the importance of heightened surveillance in high-risk autoimmune populations and the need for future research into immune-related mechanisms driving skin cancer susceptibility.
lay_summary: Researchers used health data from the All of Us program to see if autoimmune diseases are linked to skin cancers. They looked at 419,789 people and used statistics to adjust for age, sex, other illnesses, and immune-suppressing medicines. They found higher melanoma risk in people with Sjögren's syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), vitiligo (a skin condition causing loss of color), or autoimmune thyroid disease. Non-melanoma skin cancers were more common in people with Sjögren's, IBD, or type 1 diabetes. This means people with these autoimmune conditions may need more regular skin checks.

pdr_title: Association of Ptosis with Mental Health Conditions in Adults from a Large United States Research Database
pdr_abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between blepharoptosis %28ptosis%29 and the prevalence of mental health disorders in adults, including anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and substance use/addictive disorders. Cross-sectional study using data from the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program. The study included 4,411 adults diagnosed with ptosis and 4,411 propensity score-matched controls, matched by age, sex, race, education, and income. A 1:1 propensity score-matched analysis was performed, comparing adults with ptosis to matched controls. Logistic regression was used to adjust for potential confounders, including body mass index, elevated blood pressure, and blood glucose levels. Prevalence rates of anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and substance use/addictive disorders. The primary outcome was the association between ptosis and any mental health disorder. Adults with ptosis exhibited significantly higher rates of mental health disorders compared to controls, including anxiety %2846.8% vs. 28.9%%29, depression %2844.9% vs. 27.8%%29, bipolar disorder %285.8% vs. 3.6%%29, schizophrenia spectrum disorders %281.8% vs. 1.1%%29, and substance use/addictive disorders %2823.4% vs. 17.0%%29. The prevalence of any mental health disorder was significantly higher in the ptosis group %2863.4% vs. 44.8%, p < 0.001%29. After adjustment, ptosis was associated with increased odds of any mental health disorder %28aOR: 1.92, 95% CI, 1.76-2.10%29 and each specific mental health disorder. Ptosis is associated with a significantly higher prevalence of mental health disorders, suggesting it may be an independent risk factor. Mental health screenings and psychosocial support should be considered for patients with ptosis. Further research is needed to explore causal mechanisms and stratify risk based on ptosis etiology and severity. This study may be subject to Berkson's bias, wherein individuals with ptosis may have more frequent health care encounters, increasing the likelihood of being diagnosed with psychiatric conditions.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at whether droopy eyelids (ptosis) are linked to mental health problems. They compared 4,411 adults with ptosis to 4,411 similar people using a large U.S. health database. People with ptosis had higher rates of anxiety (46.8% vs 28.9%), depression (44.9% vs 27.8%), bipolar disorder (5.8% vs 3.6%), schizophrenia (1.8% vs 1.1%), and substance use problems (23.4% vs 17.0%). Overall, 63.4% with ptosis had a mental health disorder versus 44.8% of others. This means doctors should consider mental health screening and support for patients with ptosis, though more study is needed because these patients may see doctors more often and get diagnosed more.

pdr_title: Artificial Intelligence Models to Identify Patients at High Risk for Glaucoma Using Self-reported Health Data in a United States National Cohort
pdr_abstract: Early glaucoma detection is key to preventing vision loss, but screening often requires specialized eye examination or photography, limiting large-scale implementation. This study sought to develop artificial intelligence models that use self-reported health data from surveys to prescreen patients at high risk for glaucoma who are most in need of glaucoma screening with ophthalmic examination and imaging. Cohort study. Participants enrolled from May 1, 2018, to July 1, 2022, in the nationwide All of Us Research Program who were ≥18 years of age, had ≥2 eye-related diagnoses in their electronic health record %28EHR%29, and submitted surveys with self-reported health history. We developed models to predict the risk of glaucoma, as determined by EHR diagnosis codes, using 3 machine learning approaches: %281%29 penalized logistic regression, %282%29 XGBoost, and %283%29 a fully connected neural network. Glaucoma diagnosis was identified based on International Classification of Diseases codes extracted from EHR data. An 80/20 train-test split was implemented, with cross-validation employed for hyperparameter tuning. Input features included self-reported demographics, general health, lifestyle factors, and family and personal medical history. Models were evaluated using standard classification metrics, including area under the receiver operating characteristic curve %28AUROC%29. Among the 8205 patients, 873 %2810.64%%29 were diagnosed with glaucoma. Across models, AUROC scores for identifying which patients had glaucoma from survey health data ranged from 0.710 to 0.890. XGBoost achieved the highest AUROC of 0.890 %2895% confidence interval [CI]: 0.860-0.910%29. Logistic regression followed with an AUROC of 0.772 %2895% CI: 0.753-0.795%29. Explainability studies revealed that key features included traditionally recognized risk factors for glaucoma, such as age, type 2 diabetes, and a family history of glaucoma. Machine and deep learning models successfully utilized health data from self-reported surveys to predict glaucoma diagnosis without additional data from ophthalmic imaging or eye examination. These models may eventually enable prescreening for glaucoma in a wide variety of low-resource settings, after which high-risk patients can be referred for targeted screening using more specialized ophthalmic examination or imaging. The author%28s%29 have no proprietary or commercial interest in any materials discussed in this article.
lay_summary: The study tested whether computer programs could use people’s health surveys to find those at high risk for glaucoma (an eye disease that can cause vision loss). Researchers used 8,205 U.S. adults with survey answers and medical records; 873 (about 11%) had glaucoma. They trained three machine‑learning models (computer programs that learn patterns) using age, health, lifestyle, and family history. The models identified glaucoma cases correctly about 71% to 89% of the time, and age, type 2 diabetes, and family history were key clues. This approach could help prescreen people so those at high risk get eye exams sooner.

pdr_title: Artificial Intelligence Models to Identify Patients with High Probability of Glaucoma Using Electronic Health Records
pdr_abstract: Early detection of glaucoma allows for timely treatment to prevent severe vision loss, but screening requires resource-intensive examinations and imaging, which are challenging for large-scale implementation and evaluation. The purpose of this study was to develop artificial intelligence models that can utilize the wealth of data stored in electronic health records %28EHRs%29 to identify patients who have high probability of developing glaucoma, without the use of any dedicated ophthalmic imaging or clinical data. Cohort study. A total of 64 735 participants who were ≥18 years of age and had ≥2 separate encounters with eye-related diagnoses recorded in their EHR records in the All of Us Research Program, a national multicenter cohort of patients contributing EHR and survey data, and who were enrolled from May 1, 2018, to July 1, 2022. We developed models to predict which patients had a diagnosis of glaucoma, using the following machine learning approaches: %281%29 penalized logistic regression, %282%29 XGBoost, and %283%29 a deep learning architecture that included a 1-dimensional convolutional neural network %281D-CNN%29 and stacked autoencoders. Model input features included demographics and only the nonophthalmic lab results, measurements, medications, and diagnoses available from structured EHR data. Evaluation metrics included area under the receiver operating characteristic curve %28AUROC%29. Of 64 735 patients, 7268 %2811.22%%29 had a glaucoma diagnosis. Overall, AUROC ranged from 0.796 to 0.863. The 1D-CNN model achieved the highest performance with an AUROC score of 0.863 %2895% confidence interval [CI], 0.862-0.864%29. Investigation of 1D-CNN model performance stratified by race/ethnicity showed that AUROC ranged from 0.825 to 0.869 by subpopulation, with the highest performance of 0.869 %2895% CI, 0.868-0.870%29 among the non-Hispanic White subpopulation. Machine and deep learning models were able to use the extensive systematic data within EHR to identify individuals with glaucoma, without the need for ophthalmic imaging or clinical data. These models could potentially automate identifying high-risk glaucoma patients in EHRs, aiding targeted screening referrals. Additional research is needed to investigate the impact of protected class characteristics such as race/ethnicity on model performance and fairness. The author%28s%29 have no proprietary or commercial interest in any materials discussed in this article.
lay_summary: This study wanted to find people at high risk for glaucoma so they can get eye care sooner. Researchers looked at health records (electronic health records, EHRs) from 64,735 adults with eye visits. They used three types of artificial intelligence (AI) that only used non-eye data like medicines and lab tests. About 11% had glaucoma and the AI models could identify them about 80–86% of the time. This could help doctors flag people for eye exams, but more work is needed to make sure the tools are fair for all groups.

pdr_title: The Etiology of Autism Spectrum Disorder and Gender Dysphoria
pdr_journal_title: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. Annual International Conference
pdr_abstract: This paper investigates the genetic correlations between Autism Spectrum Disorder %28ASD%29 and Gender Dysphoria %28GD%29 using network science techniques applied to data from the National Institute of Health's All of Us research program. Despite extensive research on the genetic etiology of ASD and the phenotypic overlaps between ASD and GD, a genetic component linking the two has not been explored thoroughly. Our study addresses this gap by integrating phenotypic data and genetic variations, specifically single nucleotide polymorphisms %28SNPs%29, to construct a network graph that reveals potential genetic intersections between these conditions. We identify a single gene linking ASD and GD, indicating a potential genetic overlap. This finding is significant as the gene has been associated with several psychiatric conditions, including ASD.Clinical relevance-The study's methodology extends existing research by combining phenotypic and genetic data to analyze the comorbidity of two different conditions. Our results not only provide insights into the genetic correlations between ASD and GD but also demonstrate the utility of network science in medical research. The approach used here could be generalized to other conditions, offering a new way to understand genetic relationships in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders.
lay_summary: This study looked for shared genes between autism and gender dysphoria. Researchers used health and genetic data from the All of Us program. They built networks that linked traits to single-letter DNA changes called SNPs (small genetic differences). They found one gene connecting autism and gender dysphoria, and that gene is also tied to other mental health conditions. This suggests a possible genetic overlap and that the method can find links between conditions. More research could help explain why they sometimes occur together and improve care.

pdr_title: Cancer Risk and Estimated Lithium Exposure in Drinking Groundwater in the US
pdr_abstract: Lithium is a naturally occurring element in drinking water and is commonly used as a mood-stabilizing medication. Although clinical studies have reported associations between receiving lithium treatment and reduced cancer risk among patients with bipolar disorder, to our knowledge, the association between environmental lithium exposure and cancer risk has never been studied in the general population. To evaluate the association between exposure to lithium in drinking groundwater and cancer risk in the general population. This cohort study included participants with electronic health record and residential address information but without cancer history at baseline from the All of Us Research Program between May 31, 2017, and June 30, 2022. Participants were followed up until February 15, 2023. Statistical analysis was performed from September 2023 through October 2024. Lithium concentration in groundwater, based on kriging interpolation of publicly available US Geological Survey data on lithium concentration for 4700 wells across the contiguous US between May 12, 1999, and November 6, 2018. The main outcome was cancer diagnosis or condition, obtained from electronic health records. Stratified Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate the hazard ratios %28HRs%29 and 95% CIs for risk of cancer overall and individual cancer types for increasing quintiles of the estimated lithium exposure in drinking groundwater, adjusting for socioeconomic, behavioral, and neighborhood-level variables. The analysis was further conducted in the western and eastern halves of the US and restricted to long-term residents living at their current address for at least 3 years. A total of 252 178 participants were included %28median age, 52 years [IQR, 36-64 years]; 60.1% female%29. The median follow-up time was 3.6 years %28IQR, 3.0-4.3 years%29, and 7573 incident cancer cases were identified. Higher estimated lithium exposure was consistently associated with reduced cancer risk. Compared with the first %28lowest%29 quintile of lithium exposure, the HR for all cancers was 0.49 %2895% CI, 0.31-0.78%29 for the fourth quintile and 0.29 %2895% CI, 0.15-0.55%29 for the fifth quintile. These associations were found for all cancer types investigated in both females and males, among long-term residents, and in both western and eastern states. For example, for the fifth vs first quintile of lithium exposure for all cancers, the HR was 0.17 %2895% CI, 0.07-0.42%29 in females and 0.13 %2895% CI, 0.04-0.38%29 in males; for long-term residents, the HR was 0.32 %2895% CI, 0.15-0.66%29 in females and 0.24 %2895% CI, 0.11-0.52%29 in males; and the HR was 0.01 %2895% CI, 0.00-0.09%29 in western states and 0.34 %2895% CI, 0.21-0.57%29 in eastern states. In this cohort study of 252 178 participants, estimated lithium exposure in drinking groundwater was associated with reduced cancer risk. Given the sparse evidence and unknown mechanisms of this association, follow-up investigation is warranted.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if natural lithium (a metal sometimes used as medicine) in groundwater affects cancer risk. They studied 252,178 U.S. adults with medical records and addresses, estimated local lithium from well tests, and followed people about 3.6 years; 7,573 were diagnosed with cancer. People in areas with more lithium had much lower cancer risk—about 70% lower in the highest versus lowest areas—and this held for men and women and in different regions. This does not prove lithium prevents cancer; more research is needed and people should not take lithium for cancer prevention.

pdr_title: Is the Association of Cannabis Use and Stroke Frequency-Dependent: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of the NIH All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: International Journal of Stroke : Official Journal of the International Stroke Society
pdr_abstract: Background: The relationship between cannabis use and stroke prevalence remains incompletely characterized, with most studies limited by binary exposure classification. We examined the frequency-dependent association of cannabis use and stroke prevalence by subtype in a large, diverse national cohort.    Aims: Our primary aim was to explore the relationship between cannabis use frequency and the adjusted prevalence of ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke. pdr_title: Intersection of race and ethnicity with perceptions of health status and literacy in adult patients with spinal deformity: insights from the all of us research program
pdr_abstract: Purpose: This study evaluated racial disparities in health perception, health literacy, and barriers to care in patients with adult spinal deformity %28ASD%29.    Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study using the National Institutes of Health All of Us survey database. Adult patients with spinal deformities were identified using ICD-9/10 codes and categorized by race: non-Hispanic White %28NHW%29, non-Hispanic Black %28NHB%29, and Hispanic or Latino %28HL%29. Survey responses regarding demographics, socioeconomic status, health status, health perceptions, health literacy, and barriers to healthcare were compared between groups.    Results: In our cohort of 9271 patients, 69.7% were NHW, 15.7% were NHB, and 14.6% were HL. NHW patients reported the highest education, annual income, employment, married status, and home ownership %28p<0.001%29. HL patients reported both the highest and lowest fatigue %28p<0.001%29. NHB patients reported more pain %28p<0.001%29, while the HL cohort reported more emotional problems %28p<0.001%29. NHW patients accomplished more everyday activities %28p<0.001%29. HL patients had the worst self-perceptions of health %28p<0.001%29 and the least health literacy %28p<0.001%29. NHW patients were the least worried about paying for care %28p<0.001%29; however, they more often reported delaying prescriptions to save money %28p=0.041%29 and not being able to afford dental or specialist care %28p<0.001%29, deductibles %28p=0.003%29, or copays %28p<0.001%29. NHB patients experienced more transportation issues %28p<0.001%29, and HL patients experienced more issues with childcare or getting time off work %28p<0.001%29.    Conclusion: Our study points to racial disparities in self-perception of health, literacy, and barriers to care among ASD patients.

pdr_title: Patient-Provider Relationships Influence Reception of Postmastectomy Breast Reconstruction: An Analysis of the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Although existing literature has comprehensively investigated socioeconomic disparities in postmastectomy breast reconstruction, the effect of patient-provider relationships on the receipt of breast reconstruction is still not completely described. This study incorporates a large national data platform to investigate the effect of such interactions on the likelihood of reconstruction after mastectomy.    Methods: Patients who underwent mastectomy were identified in the All of Us Research Program, a large and diverse United States patient registry. Patient-provider relationships were quantified through a series of survey questions assessing themes of respect, understanding, and apprehension from patient-provider interactions. The main outcome of interest was the receipt of breast reconstruction, which was assessed with multivariable logistic regression %28P < .05%29.    Results: The final cohort included 547 patients with complete survey data. The rate of postmastectomy breast reconstruction was 47.3%. Patient perceptions of receiving respectful treatment by providers 'most of the time' %28OR: 0.47, 95% CI, 0.30-0.74, P = .0012%29 and 'some of the time' %28OR: 0.21, 95% CI, 0.05-0.89, P = .034%29 predicted lower odds of breast reconstruction when compared to 'always.' Nervousness about seeing a health care provider was also associated with lower odds of breast reconstruction %28OR: 0.51, 95% CI, 0.27-0.96, P = .034%29.    Conclusion: Despite increasing volume of breast reconstruction in the United States, the receipt of such reconstruction may still be influenced by aspects of the patient-provider relationship. This analysis supports the importance of cultivating patient-centered relationships for patients with breast cancer.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether the way patients and doctors get along affects whether women get breast reconstruction after mastectomy (breast removal surgery). Researchers used survey answers from 547 U.S. patients in the All of Us registry. About 47% had reconstruction. People who said they were always treated with respect were more likely to get reconstruction than those respected only some or most of the time. People who felt nervous about seeing providers were less likely to get reconstruction. This means kinder, more supportive doctor care may help more patients get the choices they want.

pdr_title: Biological Sex and Chronic Rhinosinusitis Diagnosis and Biomarkers
pdr_abstract: Importance: The inflammation-modulating properties of sex hormones provide a pathophysiological basis for anticipating sex-based differences in chronic rhinosinusitis %28CRS%29, but the role of biological sex has not been thoroughly studied.    Objectives: To investigate sex differences in CRS diagnosis and biomarkers.    Design, Setting, And Participants: This cross-sectional study used data from the All of Us Research Program, a large national dataset of US adults, collected from partner health care organizations including academic medical centers, Veterans Affairs facilities, and community health centers. From May 2018 to October 2023, a total of 393 596 participants with electronic health records were considered for inclusion; those with incomplete data were excluded. Data analysis was conducted from April to September 2025.    Exposures: Participant sex was the primary exposure, and covariates included demographics, socioeconomic status, risk factors, and comorbidities.    Main Outcomes And Measures: CRS diagnosis, stratified into CRS with nasal polyps %28CRSwNP%29 and without nasal polyps %28CRSsNP%29, and CRS biomarkers.    Results: The analysis included 258 245 participants, of whom 38.4% were male and 61.6% were female and most %2857.3%%29 were 50 years or older. After controlling for covariates, female sex was associated with an increased odds of CRSsNP among those younger than 60 years %28odds ratio [OR], 1.44; CI with Holm-Bonferroni correction [CIH-B], 1.35 to 1.54%29 and 60 years or older %28OR, 1.32; CIH-B, 1.23 to 1.40%29, but a lower odds of CRSwNP %28OR, 0.63; CIH-B, 0.52-0.76%29 compared to males. Compared to male participants, female participants had a lower concentration of serum eosinophils %28β, -0.35; CIH-B, -0.44 to -0.25%29 and IgE %28β, -99.73; CIH-B, -190.49 to -8.96%29 among participants with CRSsNP after controlling for covariates, as well as lower eosinophils among participants with CRSwNP %28β, -0.41; CIH-B, -0.80 to -0.01%29. Analyzing CRS prevalence by age group revealed a downtrend among female participants 60 years or older, despite an upward trend at younger age groups, with regression analysis demonstrating a negative interaction effect between female sex and age 60 years or older with odds of CRSsNP %28OR, 0.91; CIH-B, 0.84 to 0.99%29.    Conclusions And Relevance: This cross-sectional study found that female sex was associated with a higher odds of CRSsNP, but a lower odds of CRSwNP compared to males. Biomarker analysis indicated a possible female disposition for nontype 2 inflammation.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if being male or female changes the chance of having chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS), long-lasting sinus inflammation. They studied health records for 258,245 U.S. adults from 2018–2023. About 61.6% were female. Women were more likely to have CRS without nasal polyps (small growths) and less likely to have CRS with polyps than men. Women also had lower blood levels of markers linked to allergic inflammation (eosinophils and IgE). Older women (60 ) had fewer cases without polyps. These findings may help doctors better diagnose and treat sinus disease.

pdr_title: Evaluating the association between upstream perceived individual and neighborhood determinants of health and intensity of breast cancer screening
pdr_abstract: Exposure to negative perceived individual and neighborhood determinants disproportionately impacts marginalized groups and can profoundly shape health behavior. We assessed the hypothesized relationship between exposure to adverse perceived individual and neighborhood determinants and rates of mammography. In this cohort study, we identified 31,568 female participants aged 40-74 without history of breast cancer in the All of Us Research Program. Participant-reported levels of perceived stress, everyday discrimination, perceived neighborhood physical disorder, perceived neighborhood social cohesion, and receipt of mammography were ascertained in the linked participant survey and electronic health record data. 52% of participants had at least one mammogram during follow-up. Women reporting high stress were screened at lower rates compared to low stress individuals. Higher discrimination %28IRR=0.92, 95% CI=0.88, 0.95%29 and higher perceived stress %28IRR=0.84, 95% CI=0.79, 0.90%29 were both respectively associated with lower breast cancer screening rates, while perceived neighborhood physical disorder and social cohesion were not. Women reporting high stress and discrimination were also less likely to be compliant with screening guidelines. The associations between the determinants and breast cancer screening rates did not differ by race and ethnicity. Women who report highest levels of discrimination and stress may face additional barriers obtaining breast cancer screening.
lay_summary: This study was done to see if feeling stressed or treated unfairly affects breast cancer screening. Researchers looked at 31,568 women aged 40–74 in the All of Us study using surveys and medical records. They checked if women had mammograms and asked about stress (feeling overwhelmed) and discrimination (being treated unfairly). About 52% had at least one mammogram. Women with higher stress or more discrimination got screened less often; neighborhood problems did not affect screening. This suggests stressed or discriminated women may need extra help to get regular mammograms.

pdr_title: Advancing methods for multi-ancestry genomics
pdr_abstract: Genomics research has historically been biased toward individuals of European ancestry, which has the potential to exacerbate health inequities %28Martin, A.R. et al. Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities%29. To reduce these disparities, current efforts in human genetics emphasize the inclusion of diverse populations %28All of Us Research Program Investigators, The 'All of Us' Research Program%29. Here, we highlight recent preprints that focus on the intricacies of researching participants with multiple genetic ancestries.
lay_summary: This paper was written because gene studies have mostly used people with European family origins and that can make health care less fair. The authors looked at recent unpublished studies about people with mixed genetic backgrounds. They explain problems and new ways to study these groups. They note that including more diverse people can help make genetic tools work better for everyone. This matters because fairer gene research can lead to better health care for more people.

manual_title: An Example Analysis for a Gender-inclusive Approach in Sport and Exercise Science Research using Fitbit Outcomes from the All of Us Research Program Dataset
pdr_title: An Example Analysis for a Gender-inclusive Approach in Sport and Exercise Science Research using Fitbit Outcomes from the I%28content=['All of Us']%29 Research Program Dataset
pdr_abstract: Prevalence studies with wearable devices are used to understand disparities in health-related physical activity behaviors and whether interventions are efficacious. However, studies have been limited to a binary definition of sex. This example analysis aimed to demonstrate how researchers can investigate differences in data beyond the sex-gender binary. Using a cross-sectional analysis of the All of Us Research Program dataset, participants' self-identified gender was categorized into Cisgender Female %28n = 10,401%29, Additional Options %28n = 27%29, Non-binary %28n = 84%29, Transgender %28n = 17%29, and Cisgender Male %28n = 4,470%29. Fitbit data on active calories, steps, sedentary minutes, and very active minutes were analyzed following a valid statistical decision framework found in the companion editorial to this paper. Data were checked for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and because data were not normally distributed, homogeneity was evaluated using the Brown-Forsyth test. The omnibus test for significant group differences was determined using the Kruskal-Wallis test, with significance accepted at p < 0.05. Effect sizes %28ES%29 for omnibus test results were calculated using Epsilon squared. Results provide evidence for differences in physical activity metrics among gender groups %28p < 0.001; active calories ES = 0.069, steps ES = 0.005, and very active minutes ES = 0.026%29. Cisgender males had higher active calories, steps, and very active minutes than cisgender females %2840% more%29 and non-binary individuals %2845% more%29. No differences were observed among other gender groups studied. These findings highlight that activity patterns vary beyond traditional binary classifications, emphasizing the need for gender-inclusive research in sport and exercise science. Specifically, the disparities observed underscore the importance of nuanced interpretations and tailored recommendations for diverse populations, addressing systemic gaps in supporting gender-diverse individuals in health and exercise behaviors.
lay_summary: Researchers used Fitbit data from about 15,000 adults in the All of Us study to see if activity patterns differ across more gender groups, not just male and female. They compared steps, active calories, very active minutes, and sitting time across five gender categories. Cisgender men (whose gender matches the sex they had at birth) had about 40% more steps, active calories, and very active minutes than cisgender women and about 45% more than non-binary people. This shows research and exercise advice should include more gender groups to better help everyone.

pdr_title: Genome-wide association studies of lifetime and frequency of cannabis use in 131,895 individuals
pdr_abstract: Cannabis is one of the most widely used drugs globally. We performed genome-wide association studies %28GWASs%29 of lifetime %28N=131,895%29 and frequency %28N=73,374%29 of cannabis use. For lifetime cannabis use, we identified two loci, one near CADM2 %28rs35827242, p=4.63E-12%29 and another near GRM3 %28rs12673181, p=6.90E-09%29. For frequency of cannabis use, we identified one locus near CADM2 %28rs4856591, p=8.10E-09; r2=0.76 with rs35827242%29. Lifetime and frequency of cannabis use were heritable %2812.88 vs. 6.63%%29 and genetically correlated with previous GWASs of lifetime use and cannabis use disorder %28CUD%29, as well as other substance use and cognitive traits. Polygenic scores %28PGSs%29 for lifetime and frequency of cannabis use predicted cannabis use phenotypes in All of Us participants. A phenome-wide association study using a PGS for lifetime cannabis use to interrogate a hospital cohort replicated prior associations with substance use and mood disorders, and uncovered novel associations with celiac and infectious diseases. This work demonstrates the utility of pre-addiction phenotypes in cannabis use genomic discovery.

calc_title: Genome-wide association studies of lifetime and frequency of cannabis use in 131,895 individuals
calc_abstract: Cannabis is one of the most widely used drugs globally. We performed genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of lifetime (N=131,895) and frequency (N=73,374) of cannabis use. For lifetime cannabis use, we identified two loci, one near CADM2 (rs35827242, p=4.63E-12) and another near GRM3 (rs12673181, p=6.90E-09). For frequency of cannabis use, we identified one locus near CADM2 (rs4856591, p=8.10E-09; r2=0.76 with rs35827242). Lifetime and frequency of cannabis use were heritable (12.88 vs. 6.63%) and genetically correlated with previous GWASs of lifetime use and cannabis use disorder (CUD), as well as other substance use and cognitive traits. Polygenic scores (PGSs) for lifetime and frequency of cannabis use predicted cannabis use phenotypes in All of Us participants. A phenome-wide association study using a PGS for lifetime cannabis use to interrogate a hospital cohort replicated prior associations with substance use and mood disorders, and uncovered novel associations with celiac and infectious diseases. This work demonstrates the utility of pre-addiction phenotypes in cannabis use genomic discovery.

pdr_title: Fast and robust invariant generalized linear models
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics : A Joint Publication of American Statistical Association, Institute of Mathematical Statistics, Interface Foundation of North America
pdr_abstract: Statistical integration of diverse data sources is an essential step in the building of generalizable prediction tools, especially in precision health. The invariant features model is a new paradigm for multi-source data integration which posits that a small number of covariates affect the outcome identically across all possible environments. Existing methods for estimating invariant effects suffer from immense computational costs or only offer good statistical performance under strict assumptions. In this work, we provide a general framework for estimation under the invariant features model that is computationally efficient and statistically flexible. We also provide a robust extension of our proposed method to protect against possibly corrupted or misspecified data sources. We demonstrate the robust properties of our method via simulations, and use it to build a transferable prediction model for end stage renal disease using electronic health records from the All of Us research program.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to make medical prediction tools that work well across different places and messy data. They created a fast, flexible method based on the 'invariant features' idea (some factors affect outcomes the same everywhere). They tested it with computer simulations and used it on electronic health records to predict end stage kidney disease. The method stayed accurate even when some data were wrong. This means doctors and patients may get more reliable risk predictions across hospitals, even when data are imperfect.

pdr_title: A clinical algorithm to identify people with the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase p.Val68Met variant at risk for diabetes undertreatment
pdr_abstract: Purpose: To develop an algorithm using routine clinical laboratory measurements to identify people at risk for systematic underestimation of glycated hemoglobin because of p.Val68Met glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase %28G6PD%29 deficiency.    Methods: We analyzed 122,307 participants of self-identified Black race across 4 large cohorts with blood glucose, glycated hemoglobin, and red cell distribution width measurements from a single blood draw. In UK Biobank, we used recursive partitioning to train 2 models to predict possible and likely G6PD deficiency. We validated the algorithm in NIH AllofUs, Vanderbilt BioVU, and the Million Veterans Program. In the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative with clinical but no genetic data, we created a cohort of 48,031 participants with type 2 diabetes and no genetic data to test whether predicted risk for G6PD deficiency was associated with incident diabetic retinopathy.    Results: G6PD deficiency predictions in hemizygous males showed precision/recall of 31%/81% for possible and 81%/10% for likely deficiency. In homozygous females, precision/recall was 6%/76% for possible and 34%/13% for likely deficiency. Patients with diabetes having predicted possible deficiency demonstrated 1.4-fold higher 20-year retinopathy rates %2814.3% vs 11.2%, P = .003%29.    Conclusion: We report a simple clinical algorithm that enables health care systems to identify people who may benefit from G6PD genotyping and glucose-based diabetes monitoring.

pdr_title: Residential radon exposure and incident myocardial infarction and stroke risks in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Radon, a naturally occurring radioactive gas, is ubiquitous in the environment. Little is known about radon's impact on cardiovascular disease %28CVD%29. This study aims to evaluate the association between residential radon exposure and incident myocardial infarction %28MI%29 and stroke.    Methods: This cohort study included participants with electronic health records %28EHR%29 and residential address information from the All of Us Research Program between May 31, 2017, and October 1, 2023. Residential radon exposures were estimated from a 2024 high-resolution model incorporating over six million measurements across the USA. The main outcome was MI and stroke diagnosis or condition, obtained from EHR. Stratified Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate the hazard ratios %28HRs%29 and 95% CIs for the risk of incident MI and stroke for log-2 transformed radon exposure and quartiles of radon exposure, adjusting for sociodemographic, behavioral, and clinical covariates. Sex- and smoker-stratified analyses were conducted. Penalized spline models were used to estimate the nonlinear association.    Results: A total of 304,050 participants were included. The mean %28SD%29 age was 58.5 %2812.9%29 years old. Among them, 59.2% were female, 18.2% non-Hispanic Black, and 59.0% non-Hispanic White. The median radon exposure was 1.14 pCi/L %28interquartile range: 0.90-1.71 pCi/L%29. Over 950,895 person-years, 1334 MI and 1869 stroke cases were identified. Per doubling of radon exposure was associated with increased risks for incident MI %28HR=1.46, 95% CI 1.04-2.08%29 and stroke %28HR=1.60, 1.02-2.49%29. Participants in the third and fourth quartiles had a significantly higher risk for MI and stroke compared to the lowest quartile. Specifically, the fourth quartile was associated with HR=2.20 %2895% CI 1.18-4.10%29 for MI and HR=2.38 %2895% CI 1.16-4.89%29 for stroke. Associations persisted across sexes and current smoking status. Nonlinear analyses revealed steep risk increased starting at 1 pCi/L, plateauing at 1.5 pCi/L.    Conclusions: In this cohort study of 304,050 participants, residential radon exposure was significantly associated with elevated risks for incident MI and stroke. Our results suggest that risks may emerge at levels well below this action level. These findings call for further research incorporating household-level exposure measures and lifetime residential histories to confirm the association.
lay_summary: Researchers studied 304,050 U.S. adults using health records and a map of home radon levels to see if radon (a natural radioactive gas) raises heart attack or stroke risk. They found people with higher radon at home had more heart attacks and strokes: when radon was twice as much, heart attack risk rose by about 46% and stroke risk by about 60%, and people in the highest radon group had about twice the risk. Risk rose near 1 pCi/L (a radon measurement) and leveled off at 1.5 pCi/L. People should test their homes and reduce radon if it's high.

pdr_title: Exploring the Use of Wearable Data in the Congenital Heart Disease Population Using the All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society. Annual International Conference
pdr_abstract: Wearable devices, such as smart watches, smart rings, accelerometer-based step counters, compact blood pressure monitors, and continuous glucose sensors have enabled the continuous measurement of physiological signals. Studies have demonstrated that wearable health technologies can provide valuable physiological feedback to subjects and clinicians about health trajectories and can aid in the detection of health anomalies. Wearable devices have the potential to provide more frequent remote physiologic measurements for congenital heart disease %28CHD%29 patients - people who are born with a range of structural and functional cardiovascular abnormalities. In this paper, differences in activity levels, defined by step count and activity minutes, between patients diagnosed with congenital heart diseases and those without were evaluated within relevant subgroups %28age range, sex at birth, race, ethnicity, BMI status, state%29 using the All of Us Research Program. A cohort of 537 patients diagnosed with some form of CHD was created. Fitbit metrics like the average number of steps and activity minutes %28lightly active, fairly active, very active, and sedentary%29 between January 2015 to December 2019 were compared across a CHD and non-CHD cohort %2836,071 people%29. Using factorial ANOVA, the results demonstrate a statistically significant difference in the number of steps walked by CHD and non-CHD subjects. In addition, sex assigned at birth and BMI have the highest contribution %28when compared to CHD diagnosis and various subgroups%29 to the difference in steps counted, followed by geographic location, age range, and then CHD diagnosis. The implications of these findings are that the number of steps, which are a surrogate for the amount of physical activity achieved by a subject, are much smaller for CHD patients than for non-CHD subjects.Clinical relevance- The population of people with congenital heart disease %28CHD%29 is expected to increase over the next 25 years and routine monitoring for these individuals is crucial for their health trajectories. Wearable devices represent supplemental devices that can help clinicians track the health status of CHD patients.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if wearable devices (like Fitbits) show activity differences in people born with heart problems (congenital heart disease). They used data from the All of Us program from 2015–2019 and compared Fitbit step counts and activity minutes from 537 people with CHD and 36,071 people without CHD. People with CHD walked fewer steps than those without. Differences in steps were influenced most by sex at birth and body size (BMI, a measure of weight for height), then location and age. This suggests wearables could help doctors watch CHD patients' activity.

pdr_title: Improving polygenic risk prediction performance by integrating electronic health records through phenotype embedding
pdr_abstract: Large-scale biobanks provide comprehensive electronic health records %28EHRs%29 that capture detailed clinical phenotypes, potentially enhancing disease prediction. However, traditional polygenic risk score %28PRS%29 methods rely on simplified phenotype definitions or predefined trait sets, limiting their ability to represent the complex structures embedded within EHRs. To address this gap, we introduce EHR-embedding-enhanced PRS %28EEPRS%29, leveraging phenotype embeddings derived from EHRs to improve PRSs using only genome-wide association study %28GWAS%29 summary statistics. Employing embedding methods such as Word2Vec and GPT, we conducted EHR-embedding-based GWASs and identified a cardiovascular cluster via hierarchical clustering of genetic correlations. Across 41 traits in the UK Biobank, EEPRS consistently outperformed single-trait PRSs, particularly within this cluster. PRS-based phenome-wide association studies further demonstrated robust associations between EHR-embedding-based PRS and circulatory system diseases. We then developed EEPRS_optimal, a data-adaptive method that uses cross-validation to select the best embedding, yielding additional improvements. We also developed MTAG_EEPRS for multi-trait PRSs, which further improved prediction accuracy compared to single-trait PRSs and MTAG_PRS. Finally, we validated the benefits of EEPRS in the All of Us cohort for seven selected diseases. Overall, EEPRS represents a robust and interpretable framework, enhancing single-trait and multi-trait PRSs by integrating EHR embeddings.
lay_summary: Purpose: The study tested if adding detailed electronic health records (EHRs) can make genetic risk scores work better.     Methods: Researchers turned EHRs into simple number summaries ('embeddings') using tools like Word2Vec and GPT. They combined these with genetic risk scores from large genetic studies and checked results in two big health databases.    Key findings: The new method (EEPRS) predicted disease risk better for many traits, especially heart-related problems. A tuned version worked even better and results held up in a separate group.    Practical importance: This approach could help doctors spot higher-risk people earlier and guide prevention or care.

pdr_title: Cross-sectional analysis of delays in care and interactions with healthcare providers among transgender and gender diverse individuals
pdr_abstract: Introduction: Timely access to positive, culturally competent healthcare experiences may be critical for transgender and gender diverse %28TGD%29 individuals. However, gaps remain in our understanding of TGD individuals' access to these experiences. Our aim was to determine whether TGD individuals' likelihood of reporting delays in care and positive healthcare provider interactions differs from that of cisgender people.    Methods: We analyzed survey data from 89,133 participants who enrolled in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program from 5/6/2018 to 4/1/2021. Unadjusted and adjusted logistic regressions were performed to assess the association of gender with delays in care in the past 12 months and provider interactions.    Results: After adjustment, TGD individuals were more likely than cisgender men to report eight of nine reasons for care delays and more likely than cisgender women to report two of nine reasons. TGD individuals were more likely than cisgender men %28OR: 2.20, 95% CI: 1.88-2.58, p<.001%29 or women %28OR: 1.45, 95% CI: 1.24-1.70%29 to report delaying care for any reason enquired about on the survey. TGD individuals were less likely than cisgender men to report all three types of positive healthcare provider interactions and were less likely than cisgender women to report two of three types of positive interactions.    Conclusion: Our findings indicate that TGD individuals may be more likely than cisgender people to experience delays in care and less likely to experience positive healthcare provider interactions. This suggests a critical need to increase TGD individuals' access to supportive, culturally competent healthcare providers.
lay_summary: This study asked if transgender and gender diverse (TGD) people face more delays and worse health care. About 89,000 people in a national health study completed a survey from 2018–2021 and researchers compared answers by gender. TGD people were more likely to delay care for many reasons; they were about twice as likely as cisgender men and about 1.5 times as likely as cisgender women to delay care. They also reported fewer positive experiences with health providers. This shows we need more supportive, culturally competent (understands and respects different genders) care so TGD people get care when needed.

pdr_title: Characterizing rurality using the All of Us Research Program data
pdr_abstract: Rural communities experience disproportionately higher rates of chronic diseases, less access to healthcare services, and poorer health outcomes compared to their urban counterparts in the United States. However, inconsistencies in how rurality is defined across biomedical research, including limitations in geographic detail within large-scale datasets, present significant challenges for reliably studying rural health outcomes. This study aimed to develop and apply an operational rurality scale using 3-digit ZIP codes to characterize rural participation in the All of Us Research Program and to examine associations between rurality, delayed care, and healthcare affordability. Publicly available information from the Federal Office of Rural Health Policy and the Environmental Systems Research Institute was integrated to generate a continuous rurality scale at the 3-digit ZIP code level. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test identified statistically significant differences in the geographic distribution of those who had delayed access to care %28P<0.001%29 and those with difficulties affording care %28P<0.001%29. The proposed continuous rurality scale is reproducible and extensible in several ways within the All of Us Workbench, as it provides a framework for categorizing participants by geolocation and facilitates standardized analyses of rurality-related research questions.
lay_summary: Researchers made a new way to measure how rural a place is using the first three digits of ZIP codes and data from the All of Us research program. They combined public maps and federal rural data to create a continuous rurality scale. They used it to compare where people reported delaying care or having trouble affording care and found clear geographic differences. The scale can be reused by other researchers in the All of Us Workbench. This helps study rural health better and could guide efforts to improve access to care for rural communities.

The proposed continuous rurality scale is reproducible and extensible in several ways within the All of Us Workbench, as it provides a framework for categorizing participants by geolocation and facilitates standardized analyses of rurality-related research questions.

pdr_title: Frailty and Physical Activity: A Compositional Isotemporal Substitution Analysis from the All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Frailty, Sarcopenia and Falls
pdr_abstract: Objectives: The objective of this study was to quantify the impact of shifting time away from sedentary behavior to physical activity on frailty in older adults.    Methods: Participants from the All of Us Research Program with Fitbit data were included in the analysis. Fitbit data was used to measure time spent in sleep, sedentary behavior, light-intensity physical activity, and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. Frailty was assessed using a 33-item frailty index. A compositional isotemporal substitution model was created to assess the estimated effects of substituting 30 minutes of sedentary behavior with an equal amount of time in physical activity on frailty.    Results: Reductions in frailty index were seen by shifting 30 minutes from sedentary behavior to light activity %28-0.003 [95% CI: -0.004, -0.002]%29 and moderate-to-vigorous activity %28-0.016 [-0.017, -0.014]%29. Lower odds of frailty were also seen from shifting time from sedentary behavior to light activity or moderate-to-vigorous activity. Associations between physical activity and frailty were generally more pronounced in those participants who were frail or pre-frail than in those who were robust.    Conclusions: Shifting time from sedentary behavior to physical activity is associated with lower odds of frailty, and shifting time to higher intensity activities may have a greater benefit to frailty.
lay_summary: Researchers asked whether moving 30 minutes a day from sitting to activity could lower frailty (frailty means having more health problems) in older adults. They used Fitbit data from a large U.S. study to measure sleep, sitting, light activity, and harder activity. Replacing 30 minutes of sitting with light activity lowered frailty a little, while replacing it with moderate-to-vigorous activity lowered frailty about five times more. The benefit was larger for people already frail or partly frail. For the public, even 30 minutes less sitting daily may help.

pdr_title: Long-read sequencing identifies FGF14 repeat expansions in Parkinson's disease
pdr_abstract: Pathogenic GAA repeat expansions in FGF14 are an established cause of late-onset cerebellar ataxia, but have not been linked to Parkinson's disease %28PD%29. Given emerging evidence that repeat expansions in ataxia-associated genes like RFC1, can contribute to atypical or familial forms of PD, we investigated whether FGF14 expansions might play a similar role. Using long-read whole-genome sequencing, we analyzed 411 individuals with PD and 197 neurologically healthy controls from the PPMI cohort, together with 1,429 additional controls from the NIH CARD initiative, the 1000 Genomes Project, and the All of Us program, representing globally diverse populations. We identified pathogenic FGF14 GAA repeat expansions in five individuals with PD and one control. All five individuals fit the clinical criteria of PD and showed typical patterns of neurodegeneration on DaTSCAN imaging; α-synuclein aggregation was confirmed by a positive seeding assay among four individuals with available data. These findings broaden the phenotypic spectrum of FGF14 repeat-associated disease and suggest a rare, previously unrecognized genetic contributor to PD. To our knowledge, this is the first report implicating FGF14 in PD and underscores the utility of long-read sequencing for detecting hidden forms of pathogenic variation in unresolved cases.
lay_summary: Researchers looked for extra copies of a small DNA code (GAA repeat expansions) in the FGF14 gene because this change causes ataxia (balance and coordination problems) and might also cause Parkinson’s disease. They used long-read sequencing (a way to read long stretches of DNA) to study 411 people with Parkinson’s and 1,626 people without neurological disease from many groups. They found the FGF14 GAA expansion in 5 people with Parkinson’s and 1 control. Those five had typical Parkinson’s signs on brain scans and protein tests. This suggests a rare genetic cause of Parkinson’s and may help diagnose some patients.

pdr_title: Investigation of the transcriptional impact of rare germline JAK/STAT variants found in a Tyrolean alpine community
pdr_abstract: The impact of most missense variants in immune regulatory genes on steady-state immune transcriptome expression in healthy individuals in real-world conditions remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the transcriptional impact of 21 germline variants in JAK, TYK2, and STAT family genes identified within a healthy Austrian alpine cohort. Of the 98 participants 35 carried only one variant and 32 carried two or more variants. Allele frequencies %28AF%29 of these germline mutations, based on the gnomAD and All of Us databases, ranged from approximately 10-6 for three very rare variants to approximately 10-1 for the most common. In silico prediction tools combined with surveying COSMIC and the NIH ClinVar databases were used to explore links with known disease. Thirteen of the 21 variants were reported in the COSMIC database, suggesting gain-of-function activity. Structural analysis revealed clear mechanistic basis for few variants, although some appeared to have modest structural effects in agreement with their weak GOF phenotypes.
lay_summary: Purpose: The researchers wanted to see if rare inherited changes in JAK/STAT immune genes affect gene activity in healthy people. Methods: They studied 21 gene variants found in 98 people from an Austrian alpine town. They used computer prediction tools, cancer and clinical databases (COSMIC, ClinVar), and looked at protein structure to guess effects. Key findings: 35 people had one variant; 32 had two or more. Thirteen variants appeared in COSMIC and likely make the genes work more (gain-of-function). Some changes showed clear structural effects; others only small ones. Practical importance: These results help us know how rare gene changes might alter immune activity in healthy people and inform disease risk and monitoring.

pdr_title: Sex differences in cardiovascular disease and associated factors in people living with HIV: Evidence from All of Us program
pdr_abstract: Background: People living with HIV %28PLWH%29 face a higher risk of cardiovascular disease %28CVD%29, with significant sex differences in outcomes. However, it is unclear whether these differences are driven by distinct risk factor profiles or by a differential impact of shared risk factors. This study aimed to identify factors associated with CVD among PLWH and to specifically assess for effect modification by sex using a large, diverse nationwide database.    Methods: We utilized data from the All of Us Research Program %28AoU%29. The primary outcome was a composite of coronary artery disease or stroke. We used multivariable logistic regression to identify factors associated with CVD in the overall cohort. To assess for effect modification, we introduced interaction terms between sex and key covariates. Subsequently, sex-stratified analyses were performed to explore these differences.    Results: Among 6464 PLWH %284608 men and 1856 women%29, women had a higher prevalence of CVD than men %2824.8% vs. 21.9%, p=0.011%29. We identified significant interaction effects between sex and several key risk factors, including hypertension, unemployment and hyperlipidaemia %28p<0.05 for all%29. In stratified analyses comparing women to men within these risk groups, the association of hypertension with CVD was substantially stronger in women than in men %28adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=4.928, 95% CI: 2.827-8.586%29. Similarly, the effects of unemployment and hyperlipidaemia on CVD were more pronounced in women. In fully stratified models, a detectable viral load was a significant risk factor for CVD only among men %28aOR=1.524, 95% CI: 1.130-2.049%29.    Conclusions: While many traditional and HIV-specific CVD risk factors are shared between men and women living with HIV %28WLWH%29, our findings reveal that the magnitude of their effect is not uniform. The impact of key risk factors, particularly hypertension, is substantially greater in women, suggesting a heightened vulnerability to these exposures. These findings underscore the critical need for sex-specific risk assessments and aggressively tailored prevention strategies for PLWH.
lay_summary: Because people with HIV can have more heart disease and men and women may be different, researchers studied 6,464 people with HIV from a large U.S. health database. They compared 4,608 men and 1,856 women by looking at medical records for heart attack, blocked arteries, or stroke. More women had these problems (24.8%) than men (21.9%). High blood pressure, unemployment, and high cholesterol were much more linked to heart disease in women. Detectable virus in the blood was linked to heart disease only in men. This suggests care should focus on these risks, especially for women.

pdr_title: S4-Multi: enhancing polygenic score prediction in ancestrally diverse populations
pdr_abstract: Polygenic scores %28PGSs%29 have shown promise in advancing precision medicine by capturing the additive effects of common genetic variants to assess inherited disease risk. However, their predictive accuracy remains limited in non-European populations. We enhanced our previously developed Bayesian polygenic model, Select and Shrink with Summary Statistics %28S4%29, by introducing a multi-ancestry extension %28S4-Multi%29 to improve prediction accuracy across African, American, East Asian, European, and South Asian ancestries. By leveraging simulated data and biobank cohorts from UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan, All of Us Research Program, and Global Biobank Meta-Analysis Initiative, we benchmarked S4-Multi against leading methods for predicting type 2 diabetes, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, asthma, and stroke. In simulation tests, S4-Multi outperformed its single-ancestry version, achieving over 1.6 times greater accuracy in non-European populations, and matched or exceeded top performing methods across all tested ancestry groups. In biobank tests, S4-Multi matched the performance of the best methods, varying by ancestry and phenotype. We find that S4-Multi achieves comparable performance using 9% to 77% fewer genetic variants than competing models, highlighting potential for robust performance in clinical settings with limited available genomic data.
lay_summary: The study tested a new method called S4‑Multi to improve genetic risk scores for people from five ancestry groups. Researchers used computer simulations and health databases (biobanks) to predict type 2 diabetes, breast and colorectal cancer, asthma, and stroke. In simulations S4‑Multi was about 60% more accurate in non‑European groups and matched or beat top methods across ancestries. In real biobank data it performed as well as the best methods while using 9%–77% fewer genetic markers (small DNA pieces). This could make genetic risk testing fairer and cheaper for more people.

pdr_title: Impact of integrase strand transfer inhibitors on cardiovascular disease in people with HIV
pdr_abstract: Purpose: Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors %28INSTIs%29 are effective and well-tolerated in HIV treatment, but their cardiovascular impact remains uncertain. This study evaluated the association between INSTI-based antiretroviral therapy %28ART%29 and cardiovascular disease %28CVD%29 risk in people with HIV %28PWH%29.    Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic health records and survey data from the All of Us research program. Adults with HIV on continuous ART for ≥ 1 year, free of CVD at baseline and within one year of ART initiation, were included. INSTI exposure was categorized by regimen status. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the association between INSTI use and CVD. A subgroup analysis examined INSTI-naïve individuals who later switched to INSTI-based ART.    Results: Among 2175 PWH, 437 %2820.09 %%29 experienced CVD events; 1715 %2878.85 %%29 used INSTIs. INSTI-only %28aHR = 0.65, 95 % CI: 0.50-0.83%29 and partial-INSTI use %28aHR = 0.34, 95 % CI: 0.27-0.42%29 were linked to lower CVD risk. In the INSTI-naïve cohort %28N = 1300%29, switching to INSTIs reduced CVD risk %28aHR = 0.32, 95 % CI: 0.25-0.40%29. Older age %28≥ 70%29 increased CVD risk.    Conclusions: INSTI-based ART may lower CVD risk among PWH. Further research is needed to validate these findings.    Summary: INSTI-based ART was associated with reduced cardiovascular disease risk among people with HIV, suggesting potential cardioprotective effects that warrant further investigation.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if a common class of HIV drugs called integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) affects heart disease risk. They looked at medical records and surveys for 2,175 adults with HIV who were on treatment at least one year. About 20% had heart problems and about 79% used INSTIs. People taking only INSTIs or who switched to INSTI drugs later had fewer heart events. Older people had higher heart risk. This suggests INSTI-based treatment might lower heart disease risk, but patients should talk with their doctor before changing medicines.

pdr_title: Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Degenerative Lumbar Disc Disease: A Population-Based Study Using the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: BackgroundDegenerative lumbar disc disease %28DLDD%29 can contribute to substantial low back pain and radicular leg pain. Emerging evidence suggests that racial and ethnic disparities in DLDD care could impact clinical outcomes, yet these trends remain largely unexplored. This study investigates differences in health literacy, access to care, and healthcare utilization among patients with DLDD using the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program.MethodsAdults diagnosed with DLDD were identified from the AoU database using ICD-9 and ICD-10 diagnostic codes. Participants were stratified by race and ethnicity into White, Black, Hispanic, and Other. Demographics, socioeconomic status, health literacy %28BRIEF score%29, healthcare access, and treatment utilization across racial and ethnic groups were compared across cohorts using chi-square analyses. Multivariate logistic regressions evaluated these outcomes while adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic status.ResultsIn total, 30,775 participants with DLDD were identified. Most participants were 65+ years %2862.8%%29 and female %2865.3%%29, with 74.0% self-identifying as White, 10.7% as Black, 8.1% as Hispanic, and 7.2% as Other. Compared to Whites, Black and Hispanic participants were significantly more likely to report limited health literacy %28White = 15.3%, Black = 22.2%, Hispanic = 28.1%, Other = 21.3%, P < 0.001%29. In addition, they were more likely to be denied insurance coverage %289.7%, 10.5%, 14.5%, 13.8%%29 and report difficulty affording care, including prescription medications %2811.5%, 20.9%, 19.0%, 18.9%%29 and follow-up visits %286.2%, 10.0%, 10.7%, 9.3%%29 %28all P < 0.001%29. Finally, Black participants, in particular, were more likely to receive nonoperative treatments such as physical therapy %2825.7%, 28.2%, 23.1%, 25.9%%29, steroid injections %2814.4%, 16.7%, 12.8%, 12.4%%29, and opioids %2849.1%, 53.4%, 42.5%, 48.3%%29 compared to White participants %28all P < 0.001%29. Many of these disparities persisted in multivariate models after adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic covariates.ConclusionDisparities in DLDD are multifactorial, reflecting the intersection of age, sex, race/ethnicity, comorbidities, and social determinants of health. Despite most participants being Medicare-eligible, minority groups continued to report access and affordability barriers, suggesting the role of underinsurance and coverage gaps. These findings underscore the need for targeted interventions to improve access, promote education, and ensure equitable treatment of DLDD across minority populations.
lay_summary: This study looked at 30,775 adults with degenerative lumbar disc disease (wear-and-tear in the lower back that causes pain) to see if care differed by race and ethnicity. Researchers compared White, Black, Hispanic, and other groups for health knowledge, insurance access, and treatments. Black and Hispanic people were more likely to have limited health knowledge (about 22% and 28% vs 15% for Whites), be denied coverage or struggle to pay for medicines and visits, and Black patients more often received therapy, injections, and opioids. This shows we need better access, clearer education, and fair treatment for minority patients.
