pdr_title: Measuring the accuracy of electronic health record-based phenotyping in the All of Us Research Program to optimize statistical power for genetic association testing
pdr_journal_title: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
pdr_abstract: Objective: Accurate phenotyping is an essential task for researchers utilizing electronic health record %28EHR%29-linked biobank programs like the All of Us Research Program to study human genetics. However, little guidance is available on how to select an EHR-based phenotyping procedure that maximizes downstream statistical power. This study aims to estimate accuracy of three phenotype definitions of ovarian, female breast, and colorectal cancers in All of Us %28v7 release%29 and determine which is most likely to optimize downstream statistical power for genetic association testing.    Materials And Methods: We used empirical carrier frequencies of deleterious variants in known risk genes to estimate the accuracy of each phenotype definition and compute statistical power after accounting for the probability of outcome misclassification.    Results: We found that the choice of phenotype definition can have a substantial impact on statistical power for association testing and that no approach was optimal across all tested diseases. The impact on power was particularly acute for rarer diseases and target risk alleles of moderate penetrance or low frequency. Additionally, our results suggest that the accuracy of higher-complexity phenotyping algorithms is inconsistent across Black and non-Hispanic White participants in All of Us, highlighting the potential for case ascertainment biases to impact downstream association testing.    Discussion: EHR-based phenotyping presents a bottleneck for maximizing power to detect novel risk alleles in All of Us, as well as a potential source of differential outcome misclassification that researchers should be aware of. We discuss the implications of this as well as potential mitigation strategies.
lay_summary: Purpose: The study checked how well three ways of finding cancer cases in electronic health records (EHRs) work in the All of Us research program and which way helps find gene links best.    Methods: The team looked at known harmful gene changes for ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancer and used those rates to estimate how accurate each EHR method was and how that affects the chance to detect gene-disease links.    Key findings: Choice of method strongly changes the chance to find real gene links. No single method worked best for all cancers. Problems were bigger for rare cancers and uncommon risk genes. The methods worked differently for Black versus non-Hispanic White participants, which could cause bias.    Why it matters: Researchers should pick and check EHR methods carefully to avoid missed discoveries and unfair results, and use strategies to reduce bias.

pdr_title: The Moderating Effect of Social Support on the Association Between Healthcare Discrimination and Quality of Life in Persons with Type 2 Diabetes
pdr_abstract: Background/Objectives: Healthcare discrimination poses significant challenges to the health-related quality of life %28HRQoL%29 of people living with type 2 diabetes %28T2D%29. However, the role of social support in alleviating these effects has not been fully explored. Drawing on Cohen and Wills' social support buffering model, this study examined whether social support moderates the association between healthcare discrimination and HRQoL among individuals with T2D. Methods: We analyzed data from 5180 adults with T2D enrolled in the All of Us Research Program. Healthcare discrimination was assessed using the modified Everyday Discrimination Scale %28mEDS%29, social support with the Medical Outcomes Study Social Support Survey %28MOS-SSS%29, and HRQoL %28physical and mental domains%29 with the PROMIS Global Health Scale. Moderation analyses were conducted through linear regression models. Results: Greater exposure to healthcare discrimination was associated with poorer physical and mental HRQoL. Social support demonstrated a significant moderating effect on mental HRQoL: as social support increased, the negative association between healthcare discrimination and mental well-being weakened. However, this buffering effect was not observed for physical HRQoL. Conclusions: Findings suggest that social support can mitigate the adverse mental health consequences of healthcare discrimination among individuals with T2D. Interventions aimed at strengthening social support networks warrant investigation as potential strategies to improve the mental HRQoL of people with T2D who encounter discrimination in healthcare environments.
lay_summary: This study looked at 5,180 adults with type 2 diabetes to see if friends and family help reduce harm from unfair treatment in healthcare. Using surveys and statistical tests, researchers found that people who faced more healthcare discrimination had worse physical and mental quality of life. Strong social support helped protect mental well-being but did not help physical health. This means building better support networks may help people with diabetes cope mentally when they face unfair care, and health systems should work to stop discrimination.

pdr_title: Genetic Risk Scores, Perceived Neighborhood Disorder, and Sleep Duration
pdr_abstract: Study Objectives: Most studies of neighborhood context and sleep health emphasize direct effects and fail to account for the role of genetics. In this paper, we draw on the socioecological model to examine the interplay of genetics, neighborhood context, and sleep health. We specifically examine the independent and joint effects of genetic risk scores %28GRS%29 and perceived neighborhood disorder on sleep duration.    Methods: We combine genomic and cross-sectional survey data from the All of Us Research Program, a non-probability sample of 22,575 adults of European ancestry living in the United States. We use the sleep duration-increasing risk allele count for 78 genome-wide SNPs to construct weighted GRS. Our analyses include an index of perceived neighborhood disorder and an objective measure of sleep duration based on wrist actigraphy.    Results: GRS are inversely associated with neighborhood disorder, positively associated with continuous sleep duration, and inversely associated with the odds of short sleep. Neighborhood disorder is inversely associated with continuous sleep duration and positively associated with the odds of short and long sleep. The association between GRS and sleep duration %28continuous and categorical%29 is invariant across levels of neighborhood disorder.    Conclusions: Our analyses confirm the independent direct effects of GRS and neighborhood disorder on sleep duration. Our findings extend the socioecological model by assessing the role of genetics in the study of neighborhood context and sleep health. Although we revealed a gene-environment correlation between GRS and perceived neighborhood disorder, there was little indication of genetic confounding and no evidence of gene-environment interaction.
lay_summary: Purpose: The study looked at how genes and how people see their neighborhood affect how long they sleep. Methods: Researchers used health and DNA data from 22,575 U.S. adults. They counted many small genetic risks for longer sleep, asked people about neighborhood problems, and measured sleep with a wrist device. Key findings: Both genes and neighborhood problems separately changed sleep time. People with more “sleep” genes slept longer; people who saw more neighborhood disorder slept less (and were more likely to have too little or too much sleep). Genes worked the same in good and bad neighborhoods. Practical importance: Both biology and neighborhood matter for sleep, so fixing local conditions can help people sleep better.

pdr_title: Alcohol use-specific treatment initiation among patients undergoing surgical procedures: A retrospective cohort analysis
pdr_abstract: Background: Alcohol use is common in surgical patients and linked to morbidity and mortality. Yet, alcohol screening and treatment are frequently overlooked in perioperative care. This study examines how patient risk for unhealthy alcohol use is associated with the likelihood of receiving any treatment for the purpose of alcohol risk reduction or cessation.    Methods: All records from surgical patients with quantifiable Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Consumption %28AUDIT-C%29 scores in the All of Us Research Program, a precision medicine-focused database harmonizing surveys and electronic health records, were evaluated. The association between treatment for at-risk alcohol use, including psychotherapy and pharmacologic therapy, and categorical AUDIT-C risk was estimated using adjusted multivariable logistic regression models.    Results: Any alcohol use treatments were initiated in 0.5% of patients within 90days of a procedure. Patients in high-risk and severe-risk AUDIT-C groups had significantly increased odds of receiving any treatment %28aOR 2.37, 95% CI 1.06, 4.74; aOR 10.1, 95% CI 6.02, 16.8%29. Similarly, participants with an alcohol use disorder %28AUD%29 diagnosis were nine times more likely to receive any treatment than those without a diagnosis %28aOR 9.33, 95% CI 5.97, 14.70%29. Yet only 0.7% of high-risk, 4% of severe-risk AUDIT-C participants, and 1.7% of participants diagnosed with AUD received any treatment.    Conclusions: Surgical patients with identified severe risk for unhealthy alcohol consumption are more likely to receive perioperative alcohol-specific treatment. However, even for high-risk patients, the provision of perioperative treatments to reduce alcohol intake is rare. Future work should focus on overcoming barriers to reduce unhealthy alcohol use after surgery.
lay_summary: This study checked whether surgical patients who drank at risky levels got help to stop or cut down. Researchers looked at medical records and alcohol screening scores and used statistics to compare risk groups. They found only 0.5% of patients started alcohol treatment within 90 days of surgery. People at highest risk were more likely to get help, but still very few did (0.7% high-risk, 4% severe-risk, 1.7% with diagnosed alcohol use disorder). This shows a big missed chance to help patients before and after surgery.

pdr_title: Association between diabetic retinopathy and neurodegenerative diseases in the All of Us research program
pdr_abstract: Purpose: While diabetic retinopathy %28DR%29 has previously been linked to neurodegenerative diseases, it remains unclear whether DR independently reflects neurodegenerative diseases beyond those attributable to diabetes itself. In this study, we leveraged data from the All of Us Research Program to assess whether DR serves as an independent marker of neurodegenerative disease among individuals with diabetes.    Methods: A matched case-control, cross-sectional study was conducted using data from the All of Us Research Program %28US-based EHR database%29. Three groups %28exactly matched by age, sex, and race%29 were created and compared: individuals with both DR and DM %28DR+DM, n = 7629%29, individuals with DM but no DR %28DM-only, n = 22,887%29, and individuals without DM %28n = 22,887%29. Outcomes included dementia, Alzheimer's disease %28AD%29, Parkinson's disease %28PD%29, and multiple sclerosis %28MS%29. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed, adjusting for demographics, comorbidities and diabetes-related mediators.    Results: In multivariable analysis, DM-only was associated with increased odds of dementia %28adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.28, 95 % CI: 1.08-1.51; p = 0.004%29. However, DR in the setting of DM %28DM+DR vs. DM-only%29 was not associated with further increased odds of neurodegenerative disease outcome in multivariate models %28aOR for dementia 1.18, 95 % CI: 0.94-1.49%29. No significant associations were identified for AD, PD, or MS %28all p ≥ 0.10%29.    Conclusion: Diabetic retinopathy was not associated with increased rates of neurodegenerative diseases beyond that conferred by diabetes itself, and the relationship may be mediated by diabetes severity and related comorbidities.
lay_summary: This study asked if an eye problem from diabetes (diabetic retinopathy, DR) shows extra risk for brain diseases beyond having diabetes. Using U.S. health records, researchers matched three groups: people with diabetes and DR, people with diabetes without DR, and people without diabetes. They checked for dementia, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and MS. They found diabetes raised the chance of dementia, but having DR did not add extra risk compared to diabetes alone. This means managing diabetes and other health issues is more important than DR as a warning sign for these brain diseases.

pdr_title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease is Associated with Pericarditis: A Cross-Sectional Study in an NIH-Sponsored, Nationwide Database
pdr_abstract: Introduction Inflammatory bowel disease %28IBD%29 is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting approximately 2.39 million individuals in the United States. IBD is associated with extraintestinal manifestations %28EIMs%29, among which pericarditis is prominent, comprising 70% of cardiac EIMs. The onset of pericarditis in these patients is primarily attributed to IBD medication-related adverse effects and is predominantly documented through case reports. This highlights the need for an epidemiological study in a large, propensity-matched cohort, given the significant morbidity and mortality of pericarditis. Methods Using the National Institutes of Health's %28NIH%29 All of Us Research Program, we conducted a cross-sectional study and propensity-matched 5,178 IBD cases to 15,534 controls %281:3%29. We compared demographics, clinical characteristics, prevalence of autoimmune diseases, and rates of pericarditis. Logistic regressions assessed the association between IBD and pericarditis, adjusting for confounders %28p < 0.15%29, and a sensitivity analysis confirmed the association %28p < 0.001%29. A Kaplan-Meier analysis compared the incidence of pericarditis in various IBD severity cohorts, including mild %28n=620%29 and moderate/severe %28n=1,908%29, stratified by IBD medication exposure. Results Pericarditis was significantly more prevalent in IBD cases %281.3% vs. 0.6%; absolute risk difference %28ARD%29 0.7%, 95% confidence interval %28CI%29 0.37%-1.03%%29, with significant associations in univariable %28odds ratio %28OR%29 2.2, 95% CI 1.6-3.0, p < 0.001%29 and multivariable analyses %28OR 1.9, 95% CI 1.3-2.6, p < 0.001%29. IBD preceded pericarditis in 65% of cases. There was no difference in pericarditis-free survival between mild and moderate/severe cohorts %28p = 0.90%29. Conclusion This study uniquely provides evidence of a significant association between IBD and pericarditis, establishing pericarditis as a clinically significant EIM in a large, diverse U.S. cohort, independent of disease severity. This highlights the need for heightened screening to enhance pericarditis management and patient outcomes.
lay_summary: Purpose: The study looked to see if people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) get pericarditis (heart lining inflammation) more often. Methods: Researchers used a large U.S. health database and matched 5,178 people with IBD to 15,534 similar people without IBD. They compared how often pericarditis happened. Key findings: Pericarditis was more common in people with IBD (1.3% vs. 0.6%). In most cases, IBD came before the heart problem. Importance: Doctors should watch IBD patients for heart inflammation to help catch and treat it early.

pdr_title: Barrett's esophagus-associated genetic loci in African Americans: a case-control study using the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background And Aims: Barrett's esophagus is the only known precursor lesion to esophageal adenocarcinoma %28EAC%29. Barrett's esophagus and EAC are less common in African Americans than in non-Hispanic Whites. Studies in European populations have identified Barrett's esophagus-associated risk loci; however, none have examined loci in African Americans cohorts. We conducted a case-control targeted replication study to investigate previously identified Barrett's esophagus risk loci in an African Americans cohort in the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program.    Methods: We abstracted phenomic and genomic data from 108 African Americans with Barrett's esophagus and 778 African Americans controls in the AoU database. We examined 16 single-nucleotide polymorphisms %28SNPs%29 identified in individuals of European origin in the largest Barrett's esophagus genome-wide association study to date. We conducted a logistic regression, adjusting for age, sex, and global ancestry, to assess associations between SNPs and Barrett's esophagus/control status. The nonreplication of most loci and differences in association patterns suggest distinct genetic factors influence Barrett's esophagus in admixed populations. These findings underscore the need for discovery and replication in diverse populations.

pdr_title: The association between loneliness and quality of life in cancer survivors: All of Us research program
pdr_journal_title: Quality of Life Research : An International Journal of Quality of Life Aspects of Treatment, Care and Rehabilitation
pdr_abstract: Introduction: Cancer survivors may experience loneliness, which can impair the capacity to self-regulate lifestyle behaviors, induce systemic inflammation, and deteriorate mental and physical health. Previous studies have found an association between loneliness and health outcomes in the general population, but few studies have examined health effects of loneliness among cancer survivors and its differential effects by sociodemographic characteristics.    Methods: In a cross-sectional analysis of All of Us Research program data, we examined the association between loneliness %28defined using the UCLA-3 items loneliness scale%29 and overall quality of life and four other health outcomes among cancer survivors aged≥18 years in the United States %28N=17,367%29.    Results: Lonely cancer survivors were more likely to have fair/poor overall quality of life, severe pain, severe fatigue, and fair/poor physical and mental health compared to non-lonely cancer survivors, controlling for multiple health behaviors and sociodemographic factors. Models stratified by sociodemographic characteristics generally showed similar results, but differences existed between some age, sex, and living arrangement subgroups. For example, the association between loneliness and fair/poor mental health was stronger among older survivors %28≥65 years, AOR=5.30; 95% CI=4.30-6.54%29 than younger survivors %2818-39 years, AOR=3.07; 95% CI=1.95-4.85%29; p for difference<0.05. The association between loneliness and severe fatigue was stronger among survivors living alone %28AOR=3.15; 95% CI=2.33-4.25%29 than survivors living with others %28AOR=2.16; 95% CI=1.81-2.59%29; p<0.05.    Conclusions: Loneliness generally showed adverse association with all evaluated health outcomes, but the magnitude of associations varied between certain subpopulations. Results of this study suggest the need for screening and monitoring of loneliness among cancer survivors.
lay_summary: This study used survey data from 17,367 U.S. cancer survivors to see if feeling lonely is linked to worse health. Researchers measured loneliness with a short questionnaire and checked quality of life, pain, tiredness, and physical and mental health. Lonely survivors were more likely to have poor quality of life, bad pain, severe fatigue, and poor physical and mental health. The link was stronger for some groups (for example, older adults and people who live alone). The findings suggest doctors should check for loneliness and offer support to improve survivors’ health.

pdr_title: Assessing the generalizability of prevalence estimates from the all of us research program
pdr_abstract: The National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program %28All of Us%29 aims to enhance precision medicine by collecting multimodal data from one million or more participants. Because All of Us prioritizes enrollment from populations for which there is limited data on health outcomes using nonprobability sampling methods, prevalence estimates may not reflect those of the general U.S. population. This study examines the challenges of estimating electronic health record-based disease prevalence from All of Us and offers a framework and novel R package %28waou%29 to help researchers consider these complex issues. We investigated the application of three weighting techniques to improve generalizability for dementia, type 2 diabetes, and depression prevalence estimates. Using data from All of Us alongside the National Health Interview Survey as a benchmark, we found that weighting approaches yielded more representative estimates for dementia and type 2 diabetes, yet amplified bias for depression. Waou is presented as a tool to facilitate the application of these methodologies, empowering researchers to critically evaluate the generalizability of their estimates. This work underscores the need for careful consideration of bias in epidemiological research when using the All of Us dataset for population-level inferences.
lay_summary: This study checked if disease rates from the All of Us research program match U.S. population rates. Researchers used health record data and tried three ways of giving people different weights so the study group looks more like a national health survey. The weighting made estimates better for dementia and type 2 diabetes but made depression estimates worse. They also made a free tool called waou to help other researchers test this. The work warns people to be careful when using All of Us to estimate how common diseases are in the whole country.

pdr_title: Depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder in association with cardiovascular disease among patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Objectives: Both mental health conditions, such as depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder %28PTSD%29, and cardiovascular disease %28CVD%29 events are increased in patients with rheumatoid arthritis %28RA%29 and systemic lupus erythematosus %28SLE%29. We assessed associations and interactions between mental health conditions, RA and/or SLE %28RA/SLE%29, and CVD risk.    Method: Patients with RA/SLE in All of Us Research Program were matched 1:20 to patients without either. We calculated hazard ratios %28HR, 95% confidence intervals%29 for associations of baseline depression, anxiety, or PTSD with incident CVD, adjusting for socioeconomic and comorbid factors, repeating for RA and SLE separately. We tested for interactions between RA/ SLE and mental health conditions influencing CVD risk.    Results: Among 5,543 patients with RA/SLE, matched to 110,860 patients without RA/SLE, 31.7% vs. 15.2% had mental health conditions. Matching factor-adjusted CVD event HR was the highest among those with RA/SLE and mental health conditions vs. those with neither %282.91, 2.52-3.36%29. After full adjustment, this decreased to 1.59 %281.37-1.85%29. While similar associations were observed for RA and SLE, higher risks were among patients with mental health conditions and SLE %282.08, 1.60-2.71%29 vs. RA %281.41, 1.17-1.70%29. No statistical interactions between mental health conditions and RA/SLE influencing CVD risks were detected.    Conclusions: In this large US cohort, patients with RA/SLE and mental health conditions had the highest CVD risks compared to those with either condition or none. Strategies are needed to address mental health conditions that contribute to excess CVD risk for patients with RA/SLE. Key points • Patients with RA/SLE and mental health conditions had the highest CVD incidence, compared to those with either RA/SLE or any of the mental health conditions alone. • Adjustment for sociodemographic factors and comorbidities attenuated this relative CVD risk. • No significant interactions were found between RA/SLE and mental health conditions influencing observed CVD risks.

pdr_title: Dysphagia in heart failure: Demographics, nutritional status, and patient-reported outcomes
pdr_journal_title: Heart & Lung : The Journal of Critical Care
pdr_abstract: Background: Dysphagia, or difficulty swallowing, is an often underrecognized comorbidity in individuals with heart failure %28HF%29, which can potentially affect nutrition, symptom burden, and overall well-being. Patients with HF may experience dysphagia due to the anatomical proximity of the heart and esophagus. Cardiac remodeling, such as cardiomegaly and left ventricular dilation, can result in external compression of the esophagus, disrupting normal swallowing function. Despite these plausible mechanisms, there is limited large-scale data on evaluating the prevalence and clinical impact of dysphagia in HF populations.    Objectives: This study aimed to compare nutritional status, health perception, quality of life, and fatigue among HF patients with and without dysphagia.    Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on HF patients enrolled in the All of Us Research Program. Nutritional status was assessed using serum albumin levels, body weight, and body mass index %28BMI%29. Health perception and fatigue were evaluated through responses to the Overall Health Survey.    Results: Within the analysis of the All of Us Research Program, 14,243 participants with HF were identified, of which 2,903 %2820.4%%29 reported dysphagia after excluding those with a history of cerebrovascular accidents. The HF cohort was predominantly aged ≥65 years %2853.2%%29, predominantly non-Hispanic or Latino %2881.7%%29, and mainly White %2851.3%%29, with a slight female predominance %2855.1%%29. Among participants with available left ventricular ejection fraction %28LVEF%29 data, 64.1% had preserved ejection fraction %28>50%%29. Dysphagia was more frequently observed in older individuals and women, and it was associated with significantly lower body weight %28mean 89.3 vs. 93.5 kg%29 and serum albumin levels %2835.3 g/L vs. 36.2 g/L; p < 0.001%29, despite both groups having BMI %28mean ∼32 kg/m², indicating Class I obesity%29. Individuals with dysphagia consistently reported poorer general, physical, and mental health, along with lower quality of life; and greater fatigue severity compared to those without dysphagia %28all p < 0.001%29.    Conclusions: Dysphagia is a prevalent and clinically significant comorbidity in patients with HF, especially in those with preserved ejection fraction and advanced age. HF patients with dysphagia experience worse nutritional status and patient-reported outcomes compared to those without dysphagia. These findings underscore the need for routine screening for dysphagia and a comprehensive nutritional assessment to improve management and outcomes in HF populations.
lay_summary: This study looked at people with heart failure to see how common trouble swallowing (dysphagia) is and how it affects health. Researchers reviewed data from 14,243 heart-failure patients in the All of Us program. About 20% reported dysphagia. Those with swallowing problems were older, more often women, and many had normal heart pumping but still had worse nutrition (lower weight and blood protein). They also reported poorer overall, physical, and mental health and more fatigue. The takeaway: doctors should check heart-failure patients for swallowing problems and address nutrition to help their health.

pdr_title: Health Literacy and Awareness of Family Health History in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: We quantified the association between health literacy and awareness of family health history using a nationwide cross-sectional study of 286,293 All of Us Research Program participants. Awareness of family health history was constructed as a binary outcome %281 = none at all vs. 0 = some/a lot%29. Health literacy %28adequate vs. limited%29 was measured by the Brief Health Literacy Screening Tool. Modified Poisson regression models estimated unadjusted and adjusted prevalence ratios %28PRs%29. Model 1 estimated the unadjusted relationship. Model 2 controlled for demographic factors. Model 3 further controlled for socioeconomic status. Models 4-6 further adjusted for health insurance, self-rated health status, and number of chronic health conditions, respectively. The average age was 53 years %28SD = 17%29, with 4% who self-reported no awareness of family health history and 17% who had limited health literacy. Without controlling for confounders, participants with limited health literacy were 3.06 %2895% CI: 2.95-3.17%29 times more likely than those with adequate health literacy to report no awareness of family health history. This significant association persisted but attenuated in Models 2 %28adjusted PR [aPR]: 2.04, 95% CI: 1.96-2.12%29 and 3 %28aPR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.37-1.49%29. The association remained stable in Models 4-6 with the sequential addition of health insurance coverage %28aPR: 1.42, 95% CI: 1.37-1.48%29, self-rated health status %28aPR: 1.42, 95% CI: 1.36-1.47%29, and number of chronic health conditions %28aPR: 1.42, 95% CI: 1.36-1.48%29. These findings indicate that increasing health literacy may increase awareness of family health history, which is vital for delivery of personalized healthcare and active patient participation in precision medicine.
lay_summary: This study looked at 286,293 U.S. adults to see if being able to understand health information (health literacy) affects knowing your family’s health history. People answered questions about their health knowledge and family illnesses. Four percent said they knew nothing about their family health history and 17% had limited health literacy. After accounting for age, income, insurance, and health, people with limited health literacy were about 42% more likely to know nothing about family health history. Improving health literacy could help people and doctors make better, more personalized health choices.

pdr_title: Association of chronic disease risk and physical activity measured by wearable devices in the All of Us program
pdr_abstract: Background: Physical activity plays an important role in preventing chronic diseases, but most studies rely on self-reported or short-term data that fail to capture habitual behavior. This study utilizes Fitbit data to investigate the relationship between physical activity and various chronic diseases.    Methods: We analyzed data from 22,019 participants in the All of Us Research Program who shared at least six months of Fitbit activity data linked with electronic health records. Various physical activity patterns were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards and logistic regression models, adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index %28BMI%29. To test robustness, sensitivity analyses were conducted using obesity defined by BMI, applying a two-year exclusion window for outcome diagnoses to mitigate potential reverse causation, and incorporating lifestyle covariates %28smoking and alcohol use%29 under a simplified directed acyclic graph %28DAG%29 framework to address residual confounding.    Results: Here, we show that higher physical activity levels are associated with lower risks of multiple chronic conditions. Higher daily step counts were negatively associated with obesity and type 2 diabetes, while greater elevation gains and longer vigorous activity are associated with lower risks of conditions such as morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and major depressive disorder. All sensitivity analyses yield consistent results, supporting the robustness of findings against reverse causation and lifestyle confounding.    Conclusions: Higher physical activity and lower sedentary time may help prevent diverse chronic diseases. These findings demonstrate the potential of large-scale wearable data to inform personalized prevention and population health strategies.
lay_summary: Researchers used Fitbit data from 22,019 people who shared at least six months of activity linked to their health records. They studied steps, elevation gain, and vigorous activity using models that adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index, and ran extra checks to ensure results were robust. They found more daily steps tied to lower risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes, while climbing more and doing more vigorous activity linked to lower risks of severe obesity, sleep apnea, and major depression. Being more active and sitting less may help prevent many chronic diseases, and wearables can guide prevention.

pdr_title: Dysphonia Is Associated With Anxiety and Depression in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Objectives: Previous studies have examined the relationship between dysphonia and mental health, but often in small samples and not across age groups. In this large national epidemiological study, we examine if dysphonia is related to anxiety and depression generally and across cohorts of different ages.    Methods: This is a cross-sectional analysis of adults≥18years old in the All of Us dataset. The exposure was dysphonia %28ICD-10 code R49.0%29, and the outcomes were anxiety %28ICD-10 F41%29 and depression %28ICD-10 F32-33%29. We performed multivariable logistic regression analyses, controlling for age, gender, race, ethnicity, insurance, education, smoking history, alcohol use, and medical comorbidities. A sub-analysis compared depression and anxiety odds across two and five age groups.    Results: Of 283,137 adults in our sample, the mean age was 56years %28standard deviation 16years%29. Sixty-one percent identified as female. pdr_title: Discovery of obesity genes through cross-ancestry analysis
pdr_abstract: Gene discoveries in obesity have largely relied on homogeneous populations, limiting their generalizability across ancestries. Here, we conduct a gene-based rare variant association study of BMI on 839,110 individuals from six ancestries across two population-scale biobanks. A cross-ancestry meta-analysis identifies 13 genes, including YLPM1, RIF1, GIGYF1, SLC5A3, and GRM7, that confer about three-fold risk for severe obesity, are expressed in the brain and adipose tissue, and are linked to obesity traits such as body-fat percentage. While YLPM1, MC4R, and SLTM show consistent effects, GRM7 and APBA1 show significant ancestral heterogeneity. Polygenic risk additively increases obesity penetrance, and phenome-wide studies reveal additional associations, including YLPM1 with altered mental status. These genes also influence cardiometabolic comorbidities, including GIGYF1 and SLTM towards type 2 diabetes with or without BMI as a mediator, and altered levels of plasma proteins, such as LECT2 and NCAN, which in turn affect BMI. Our findings provide insights into the genetic basis of obesity and its related comorbidities across ancestries and ascertainments.
lay_summary: This study looked for genes that raise risk for obesity across different ancestry groups. Researchers analyzed rare gene changes tied to body mass index (BMI) in 839,110 people from six ancestries in two health databases. They found 13 genes (for example MC4R and YLPM1) that roughly triple the chance of severe obesity, work in brain and fat, and link to body fat. Some genes had the same effects across groups, others did not. These genes also relate to diabetes and to thinking or mood. The findings help spot people at high risk and guide prevention and treatments.

pdr_title: A common 19 bp APOE enhancer deletion is protective against Alzheimer's disease in African Americans
pdr_abstract: The APOE-ε4/ε4 genotype is the strongest genetic risk factor for sporadic Alzheimer's disease, though the relative risk is diminished in individuals with African ancestry. Through analysis of phased APOE alleles, we identify a 19bp deletion approximately 1.1kb distal to the APOE 3'UTR in a SPI1 microglial transcription factor binding site. The deletion is present in 60% of African American APOE-ε4 homozygotes and reduces Alzheimer's disease odds ratio relative to individuals without the deletion. The deletion also delays Alzheimer's disease onset in APOE-ε4/ε4 cases with local African ancestry at APOE. The All of Us dataset confirms reduced Alzheimer´s disease risk associated with the deletion and identifies additional variants between APOE and APOC1 that disentangle APOE-ε4 neurological and lipid-related phenotypes. Functional assays reveal that the 19bp deletion abolishes SPI1 repression at this region. Collectively, these findings describe a protective allele at APOE in African Americans that mediates APOC1 expression, reducing relative Alzheimer´s disease risk.

pdr_title: Evaluating the impact of family history and polygenic risk scores on cardiometabolic disease risk
pdr_abstract: Background: Cardiometabolic diseases %28CMD%29 are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. While both family history %28FH%29 and polygenic risk scores %28PRS%29 are predictive of CMD risk, few studies have systematically evaluated their independent and joint effects. This study aimed to quantify the individual contributions of FH and PRS, as well as their combined impact on CMD risk.    Methods: We conducted an analysis of more than 120,000 adults from the All of Us Research Program with available genotypic, phenotypic, and FH data. CMDs including type 2 diabetes %28T2D%29, obesity, hypertension %28HTN%29, and coronary artery disease %28CAD%29 were ascertained from electronic health records. FH was derived from self-reported survey responses, and family history scores %28FHS%29 were constructed by weighting the number and degree of affected relatives. PRSs were computed using validated multi-ancestry PRS weights from the PGS catalog. Cox proportional hazard regression was used to assess associations of FH, FHS, and PRS independently and jointly with CMD in the overall cohort and stratified by genetic ancestry. We also tested for FHS×PRS interactions and conducted mediation analysis.    Results: Positive FH was significantly associated with increased risk of all CMDs, with the strongest effect observed for obesity %28HR 2.07, 95% CI:2.02-2.12%29. FHS showed the strongest association with T2D %28HR 1.34, 95% CI:1.32-1.37%29. Higher PRS values were also associated with elevated disease risk, most strongly for T2D %28HR 2.13, 95% CI:2.07 -2.18%29. FHS and PRS associations were attenuated in the African ancestry population. A statistically significant interaction between FHS and PRS was observed for obesity %28p<0.001%29. Individuals with a positive FH and high PRS have greater than 2.5-fold risk of developing CMDs compared to those with negative FH and an intermediate PRS. Mediation analysis indicated that PRS accounted for between 13 and 16% of the total effect of FHS across all traits.    Conclusions: Both FH and PRS are associated with CMD risk and provide complementary but distinct insights into disease risk. PRS adds predictive value beyond FH and partially mediates its effect. Integration of both measures may enhance risk stratification and guide precision prevention strategies.
lay_summary: This study used data from over 120,000 adults to see how family history and polygenic risk scores (PRS, which add up many small genetic risks) affect the chance of type 2 diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure, and heart artery disease. Researchers used health records, surveys about relatives, and genetics. Both family history and PRS raised disease risk; family history about doubled obesity risk and PRS had the strongest link to diabetes. People with both had more than 2.5 times the risk. PRS explained about 13–16% of the family history effect. Using both could help guide prevention.

pdr_title: Perceived Discrimination, Communication, and Healthcare Utilization following Gastrointestinal Surgery: A Moderated Mediation Analysis
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery : Official Journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract
pdr_abstract: Background: In the US, perceived discrimination in healthcare settings %28PDHS%29 has been linked with delayed care due to nervousness. Surgery represents a high-stakes, vulnerable period leaving lasting impressions on future utilization. We aimed to assess the association between PDHS and delayed care, and evaluate mediating and moderating roles of patient-clinician communication %28PCC%29 and sociodemographic factors, respectively.    Methods: We included adults who underwent gastrointestinal %28GI%29 procedures before completing the Healthcare Access & Utilization survey in the All of Us Research Program. Associations were examined using structural equation modeling %28SEM%29; variance decomposition quantified contributions of sociodemographic moderators.    Results: Among 1,866 participants %2846.4% hepatopancreatobiliary; 41.6% colorectal; 12.0% esophagogastric%29, median age was 62.0 years %28IQR 52.0-70.0%29; the majority was female %28n=1,306, 70.3%,%29 and non-Hispanic White %28n=1,571, 84.2%%29. Participants who delayed care were more often 18-44 years %2839.0% vs. 11.6%%29 and less frequently married %2855.5% vs. 63.5%%29 %28both p<0.05%29. In adjusted SEM, higher PDHS was associated with worse PCC %28β -0.46, 95%CI -0.56-0.36%29 and greater odds of delayed care %28aOR 1.55, 95%CI 1.20,2.01%29. PCC mediated 14.8% of the PDHS-delayed care association. PDHS %2857.9%%29, age %289.6%%29, and income %284.3%%29 contributed most to PCC variance. Delayed care was associated with higher odds of poor quality of life %28aOR 2.65%29, poor mental health %28aOR 2.65%29, and poor physical health %28aOR 2.24%29 %28all p<0.001%29.    Conclusion: PCC mediated the relationship between discrimination and healthcare delays due to nervousness, with sociodemographic factors moderating this effect. Higher PDHS and worse PCC increased odds of delayed care, leading to worse health and quality of life.
lay_summary: This study checked whether feeling discriminated against in healthcare makes people delay care after gastrointestinal (stomach and bowel) surgery, and if talking with doctors explains it. Researchers studied 1,866 adults who had surgery and completed a survey. Those who felt discriminated against reported poorer communication with doctors and were more likely to delay care. Poor communication explained about 15% of the link. People who delayed care were more than twice as likely to report poor physical and mental health and worse quality of life. The findings show better communication and less discrimination could help people get care sooner.

pdr_title: Associations between obesity, metabolic syndrome and glaucoma in the National Institutes of Health 'All of Us' research programme
pdr_abstract: Background/Aims: The literature surrounding the relationship between obesity and glaucoma is conflicting. The aim of this study was to examine associations between obesity, metabolic syndrome %28MetS%29 and glaucoma prevalence in the National Institutes of Health All of Us %28AoU%29 research programme.    Methods: 156362 individuals over age 40 were included in analyses. Obesity was defined by %281%29 body mass index %28BMI%29 and %282%29 central obesity based on waist circumference %28WC%29. MetS was defined as ≥3 of the following: central obesity %28CO%29, triglycerides ≥150mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol %28<40mg/dL for men and <50mg/dL for women%29, blood pressure ≥130/85mm Hg and fasting glucose ≥100mg/dL or non-fasting glucose ≥140mg/dL. Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score %28MSSS%29 was captured as a continuous measure of MetS. Logistic regression models examined associations between %281%29 BMI, %282%29 CO, %283%29 WC, %284%29 MetS, %285%29 MSSS and glaucoma prevalence.    Results: Overweight %28OR 0.80 %2895% CI 0.74 to 0.86%29%29 and obese %28OR 0.79 %2895%CI 0.74 to 0.85%29%29 individuals based on BMI and those with CO %28OR 0.87 %2895%CI 0.83 to 0.93%29%29 and increased WC %28OR 0.97 %2895%CI 0.95 to 0.99%29%29 had lower odds of glaucoma compared with non-overweight individuals. Individuals with MetS %28OR 1.35 %2895%CI 1.27 to 1.44%29%29 and higher MSSS %28OR 1.19 %2895%CI 1.16 to 1.22%29%29 had increased odds of glaucoma compared with individuals without MetS.    Conclusion: In AoU, higher BMI and increased WC were associated with a lower likelihood of glaucoma, while MetS was associated with an increased likelihood of glaucoma.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know how body weight and metabolic health relate to glaucoma. They studied 156,362 adults over 40 and compared BMI, waist size, and metabolic syndrome (a group of problems like high blood pressure, high blood sugar, low good cholesterol, and belly fat) with glaucoma. Overweight or obese people had a 20% lower chance of glaucoma and larger waists had a small lower chance. But people with metabolic syndrome were 35% more likely to have glaucoma and worse metabolic scores raised risk 19%. This means people and doctors should watch metabolic health, not just weight, to protect eyesight.

pdr_title: Population-scale sequencing resolves determinants of persistent EBV DNA
pdr_abstract: Epstein-Barr virus %28EBV%29 is an endemic herpesvirus implicated in autoimmunity, cancer and neurological disorders. Although primary infection is often subclinical, persistent EBV infection can drive immune dysregulation and long-term complications. Despite the ubiquity of infection, the determinants of EBV persistence following primary exposure remain poorly understood, although human genetic variation partially contributes to this phenotypic spectrum1-3. Here we demonstrate that existing whole genome sequencing %28WGS%29 data of human populations can be used to quantify persistent EBV DNA. Using WGS and health record data from the UK Biobank %28n=490,560%29 and All of Us %28n=245,394%29, we uncover reproducible associations between blood-derived EBV DNA quantifications and respiratory, autoimmune, neurological and cardiovascular diseases. We evaluate genetic determinants of persistent EBV DNA via genome association studies, revealing heritability enrichment in immune-associated regulatory regions and protein-altering variants in 148 genes. Single-cell and pathway level analyses of these loci implicate variable antigen processing as a primary determinant of EBV DNA persistence. Further, relevant gene programs were enriched in B cells and antigen-presenting cells, consistent with their roles in viral reservoir and clearance. Human leukocyte antigen genotyping and predicted viral epitope presentation affinities implicate major histocompatibility complex class II variation as a key modulator of EBV persistence. Together, our analyses demonstrate how re-analysis of human population-scale WGS data can elucidate the genetic architecture of viral DNA persistence, a framework generalizable to the broader human virome4.

lay_summary: This study looked at why Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a common virus, stays in some people's blood. Researchers used DNA from about 490,000 people in the UK Biobank and 245,000 in All of Us (reading all their DNA) to measure EBV in blood and link it to health records. They found lasting EBV DNA was tied to lung, autoimmune, brain, and heart problems, and to differences in 148 human genes. Genes that help immune cells show pieces of the virus were most important. It may help find people at higher risk and guide new treatments.
calc_title: Population-scale sequencing resolves determinants of persistent EBV DNA
calc_abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is an endemic herpesvirus implicated in autoimmunity, cancer and neurological disorders. Although primary infection is often subclinical, persistent EBV infection can drive immune dysregulation and long-term complications. Despite the ubiquity of infection, the determinants of EBV persistence following primary exposure remain poorly understood, although human genetic variation partially contributes to this phenotypic spectrum1-3. Here we demonstrate that existing whole genome sequencing (WGS) data of human populations can be used to quantify persistent EBV DNA. Using WGS and health record data from the UK Biobank (n=490,560) and All of Us (n=245,394), we uncover reproducible associations between blood-derived EBV DNA quantifications and respiratory, autoimmune, neurological and cardiovascular diseases. We evaluate genetic determinants of persistent EBV DNA via genome association studies, revealing heritability enrichment in immune-associated regulatory regions and protein-altering variants in 148 genes. Single-cell and pathway level analyses of these loci implicate variable antigen processing as a primary determinant of EBV DNA persistence. Further, relevant gene programs were enriched in B cells and antigen-presenting cells, consistent with their roles in viral reservoir and clearance. Human leukocyte antigen genotyping and predicted viral epitope presentation affinities implicate major histocompatibility complex class II variation as a key modulator of EBV persistence. Together, our analyses demonstrate how re-analysis of human population-scale WGS data can elucidate the genetic architecture of viral DNA persistence, a framework generalizable to the broader human virome4.

pdr_title: Social determinants of health and health-related quality of life among cancer survivors: Analyses of the all of us and NHANES cohorts
pdr_journal_title: European Journal of Oncology Nursing : The Official Journal of European Oncology Nursing Society
pdr_abstract: Purpose: Health-related quality of life %28HRQoL%29 is a critical aspect of cancer survivorship, influenced by various social determinants of health %28SDoH%29 such as economic stability, education, and healthcare coverage. Understanding the association between these determinants and HRQoL is essential for developing interventions that improve the well-being of cancer survivors.    Methods: Cross-sectional analyses were conducted using data from 19,725 adults with cancer, including 15,754 from the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program and 3971 from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey %28NHANES%29. HRQoL outcomes were assessed pairwise with individual SDoH and using a cumulative SDoH risk score using binary logistic regression models.    Results: Higher economic stability, education, and healthcare coverage were significantly associated with better HRQoL outcomes. In the AoU cohort, those with higher family income were more likely to report very good %28OR: 1.67; CI: 1.40-2.00%29 or excellent %28OR: 1.85; CI: 1.54-2.21%29 quality of life. Similar trends were observed for excellent physical health %28OR: 1.58; CI: 1.45-1.72%29 and mental health %28OR: 1.45; CI: 1.28-1.64%29. The NHANES cohort showed consistent findings for excellent overall health %28OR: 2.79; CI: 2.06-3.77%29, physical health %28OR: 1.61; CI: 1.31-1.96%29, and mental health %28OR: 1.60; CI: 1.29-1.98%29. Participants with fewer negative SDoH factors reported significantly better outcomes across all HRQoL dimensions.    Conclusions: These findings underscore the association between SDoH and cancer survivors' HRQoL, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions and policies to address the adverse effects of negative SDoH factors. Reducing disparities is crucial for improving the quality of life of cancer survivors.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see how social factors (like money, schooling, and health insurance) affect quality of life for people who survived cancer. They looked at data from 19,725 adult cancer survivors (15,754 in All of Us and 3,971 in NHANES) and compared these social factors with people's reports of physical and mental health. People with higher income, more education, and health coverage reported better overall, physical, and mental health. Those with fewer negative social factors did better. This means fixing social gaps could help cancer survivors feel and live better.

pdr_title: Improving polygenic score prediction for underrepresented groups through transfer learning
pdr_abstract: The advent of large biobanks has substantially increased the accuracy of polygenic scores %28PGS%29. However, most existing PGSs were derived from European-ancestry data and often exhibit reduced predictive performance when applied to individuals of non-European ancestries. Transfer Learning offers a promising strategy to address this limitation by leveraging information learned in one population to improve prediction in another. Here, we introduce GPTL, an R package that implements three Transfer Learning based approaches for developing PGS: %281%29 gradient descent with early stopping, %282%29 a penalized regression model that shrinks variant-effect estimates toward prior values, and %283%29 a Bayesian method with a finite-mixture prior that enables integration of multiple prior sources of information. Using both simulated data and real data from the UK-Biobank and All of Us, we demonstrate that PGS generated with GPTL's Transfer Learning algorithms consistently outperform single-ancestry PGS and, in many settings, match or exceed the performance of multi-ancestry ensemble-based PGS. Our software can be used with either individual genotype-phenotype data or summary statistics from genome-wide association studies.
lay_summary: This study was done because genetic risk scores (polygenic scores, a number that estimates genetic risk) made from European data work less well for people from other ancestries. The authors made an R software tool called GPTL that uses transfer learning (learning from one group to help another). They tested it with simulated data and real data from UK Biobank and All of Us. GPTL improved prediction compared to single-ancestry scores and often matched or beat multi-ancestry methods. This can help make genetic risk estimates more accurate for underrepresented groups.

pdr_title: The Mediating Role of Frailty in Healthcare Utilization Among Sexual and Gender Minorities: A Comparison of Generalist, Specialist, and Mental Health Visits
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Applied Gerontology : The Official Journal of the Southern Gerontological Society
pdr_abstract: This study examined whether frailty mediates the relationship between sexual and gender minority %28SGM%29 status and three types of outpatient healthcare utilization among adults aged 50 and older in the All of Us Research Program %282017-2022%29. We estimated controlled direct effects of SGM status across generalist, specialist, and mental health visits. Healthcare utilization and SGM status were self-reported, and frailty was measured using a survey-based deficit accumulation index. Both SGM status and frailty were independently associated with increased rates of all outpatient visit types. Regarding mediation, our results suggest that if all participants were robust, SGM adults would still have higher healthcare utilization compared to cisgender heterosexual older adults. This indicates that factors beyond frailty influence patterns of healthcare use in this population and highlights the importance of identifying additional determinants to ensure that older SGM adults receive appropriate and responsive care.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether being frail explains why older sexual and gender minority (SGM) adults use more outpatient care. Researchers studied people 50  in the All of Us program (2017–2022). They used self-reported sexual/gender identity and doctor visits, and a frailty score (count of health problems). Both SGM status and frailty were linked to more general, specialist, and mental health visits. But frailty did not fully explain the extra use: even if everyone were robust, SGM adults still used more care. This means other reasons drive their higher use and care should be tailored.

pdr_title: Social determinants disadvantage score and liver health in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Social determinants of health %28SDOH%29 are crucial in shaping liver health outcomes, yet comprehensive assessments that span key SDOH domains are lacking. To address this knowledge gap, we developed a Social Determinants Disadvantage Score %28SDDS%29 and examined its association with major adverse liver conditions. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 117,783 participants from the All of Us Research Program. The SDDS was systematically constructed using validated questionnaires covering economic stability, education, healthcare access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. Each question was scored on a 0 %28most advantage%29 to 1 %28most disadvantage%29 scale. Total SDDS was calculated as the mean of all questions, ranging from 0 to 1. We used logistic regression models to estimate odds ratios %28ORs%29 and 95% confidence intervals %28CIs%29 for the associations of SDDS with total and individual adverse liver conditions, including steatotic liver disease %28SLD%29, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis %28MASH%29, alcoholic liver disease %28ALD%29, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma %28HCC%29, chronic hepatitis B virus %28HBV%29, chronic hepatitis C virus %28HCV%29, and hepatic failure based on the Electronic Health Record. Higher SDDS was associated with a higher risk of adverse liver conditions. The highest SDDS quintile %28most disadvantaged%29 compared to the lowest SDDS quintile had an OR =1.67 %2895% CI: 1.55-1.79%29 for total adverse liver condition risk after adjusting for age, sex, race, and other covariates. Similar associations were observed for individual liver conditions. Per 10% higher SDDS, the adjusted OR %2895% CI%29 was 1.25 %281.22-1.29%29 for SLD, 1.27 %281.19-1.35%29 for MASH, 1.15 %280.99-1.34%29 for ALD, 1.31 %281.25-1.39%29 for cirrhosis, 1.35 %281.15-1.59%29 for HCC, 1.24 %281.14-1.35%29 for HBV infection, 1.40 %281.33-1.48%29 for HCV infection, and 1.35 %281.21-1.50%29 for hepatic failure. Consistent associations were found for disadvantages in individual SDOH domains, score excluding missingness, and score with selected factors. The SDDS provides a comprehensive, validated tool for assessing SDOH and their associations with liver health. Our findings highlight significant associations between social disadvantage and the prevalence of adverse liver conditions, emphasizing the need for future longitudinal studies to inform targeted interventions.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if social disadvantages hurt liver health. They gave a social disadvantage score to 117,783 people in a large US study using questions about money, education, health care, neighborhood, and community. They checked medical records for liver problems. People with more disadvantage had more liver disease. Those most disadvantaged had about 67% higher chance of any bad liver problem than those least disadvantaged. Each 10% worse score was tied to about 25–40% higher risk for specific liver diseases. This shows social conditions affect liver health and may help target prevention.

pdr_title: Associations Between Objective Sleep Characteristics From Wearable Physiologic Monitors and Incident Atrial Fibrillation
pdr_abstract: Background: Previous research suggests a link between sleep and atrial fibrillation %28AF%29. Most published studies are limited by the use of self-reported data or absence of information regarding sleep architecture. The predictive role of objectively measured sleep parameters for incident AF remains underexplored.    Objectives: The objective of the study is to examine associations between objectively measured sleep parameters, including total sleep duration and sleep stages and incident AF in a large, diverse cohort.    Methods: We analyzed data from 52,952 participants in the All of Us Research Program with wearable-derived sleep data and no baseline AF, followed for a median of 935 days. Subjects with total sleep under 3 hours or over 16 hours were excluded. Incident AF %28n = 437; 0.84%%29 was identified via electronic health records. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate HRs adjusted for demographic, behavioral, and clinical covariates.    Results: Incident AF was associated with older age, male sex, White race, smoking, and comorbidities %28all P < 0.001%29. Longer total sleep duration was linked to increased AF risk, particularly >9 hours %28HR vs 6-9h: 1.47; 95% CI: 1.12-1.94%29. Duration of deep and rapid eye movement sleep was inversely associated with AF, whereas light sleep and nonmain sleep ≥2 hours were associated with increased risk %28HR: 1.65; 95% CI: 1.23-2.20 vs 1-2 hours%29.    Conclusions: Wearable-derived sleep parameters are independently associated with AF risk. Prolonged total and nonmain sleep, reduced deep and REM sleep, and increased light sleep are independently associated with incident AF, supporting their potential role in AF risk stratification and prevention.
lay_summary: This study looked at 52,952 people without atrial fibrillation (AF) at the start, using sleep data from wearable devices and health records for about 2.5 years. It found 437 new AF cases (0.84%). People who slept more than 9 hours, had more light sleep, or extra nonmain sleep like long naps had a higher chance of AF. People with more deep sleep or REM sleep (rapid eye movement, when we dream) had a lower chance. These results suggest wearable sleep data may help spot and reduce AF risk.

pdr_title: Assessing the comorbidity between asthma and depression through polygenic risk scoring and time-to-event models
pdr_abstract: Background: Patients with asthma have an increased risk of developing depression, affecting their quality of life. To date, the processes contributing to this comorbidity remain unclear.    Methods: We integrated two large genome-wide association studies %2888,486 patients with asthma and 447,859 controls; 412,024 patients with depression and 1,587,577 controls%29 with cross-sectional and longitudinal information available from the All of Us Research Program %28N=87,167%29 through polygenic risk scoring %28PRS%29, Cox proportional-hazards models, one-sample Mendelian randomization %28MR%29, and gene-set and drug-repurposing analyses.    Results: We observed that depression PRS was associated with increased asthma risk %28hazard ratio, HR=1.13, 95% CI=1.09-1.17%29, also when accounting for comorbidity status %28HR=1.08, 95% CI=1.04-1.12%29. Conversely, the effect of asthma PRS was null after accounting for comorbidity status. One-sample MR analysis showed an effect of depression genetic liability on asthma, ranging from beta=0.36±0.03 when considering a linear relationship to beta=3.21±0.31 when considering possible nonlinear relationships. Conversely, the effect of asthma genetic risk on depression was null after accounting for potential confounders. The gene-set analyses showed that asthma and depression polygenic risks share biological processes, molecular functions, and cellular components related to the immune system and the lung-brain axis.    Conclusions: Genetic predisposition contributes to asthma-depression comorbidity through direct effects and shared pathogenic processes. These findings highlight the potential to develop targeted interventions to prevent and treat the co-occurrence of respiratory and neuropsychiatric disorders.
lay_summary: The study asked if inherited genes link asthma and depression. Researchers used large genetic studies and health records from 87,167 people. They used genetic risk scores (a measure of inherited risk) and follow-up models to see who later got asthma or depression. They found that higher genetic risk for depression raised the chance of later having asthma, but genes for asthma did not clearly raise depression risk after checking overlap. The two conditions share immune and lung–brain biological links. This could help doctors prevent or treat both conditions together.

pdr_title: Using large biobanks for psychiatric genomic research: Consistency of clinical and genetic aspects of recorded depression across US states in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Large biobanks offer unprecedented data for psychiatric genomic research, but concerns exist about representativeness and generalizability. This study examined depression prevalence and polygenic risk score %28PRS%29 associations in the All of Us data to assess potential impacts of nonrepresentative sampling.    Methods: Depression prevalence and correlates were analyzed in two subsamples: those with self-reported personal medical history %28PMH%29 data %28N = 185,232 overall; N = 114,739 with genetic data%29 and those with electronic health record %28EHR%29 data %28N = 287,015 overall; N = 206,175 with genetic data%29. PRS weights were estimated across ancestry groups. Associations of PRS with depression were examined by state and ancestry.    Results: Depression prevalence varied across states in both PMH %2816.7-35.9%%29 and EHR %280.2-45.8%%29 data. Concordance between PMH and EHR diagnoses was low %28kappa: 0.29, 95% CI: 0.30-0.30%29. Overall, one standard deviation increase in depression PRS was associated with lifetime depression based on PMH %28odds ratio [OR] = 1.05, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.04-1.07%29 and EHR %28OR = 1.05, 95% CI: 1.04-1.07%29. Results were generally consistent by ancestry, with the strongest signal for European ancestry %28PMH: OR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.08-1.12; EHR: OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.05-1.10%29. Associations between PRS and lifetime depression were largely consistent and significant associations varied minimally %28ORs = 1.06-1.45%29 by state of residence in both subsamples.    Conclusions: Recorded depression prevalence by state in All of Us demonstrates a wide range, likely reflecting recruitment differences, EHR data completeness, and true geographic variation; yet PRS associations remained relatively stable. As studies like All of Us expand, accounting for sample composition and measurement approaches will be crucial for generating actionable findings.
lay_summary: Researchers checked whether depression records and a genetic risk score (PRS, a number from many genes) were similar across US states. They used self-reports (185,000 people) and medical records (287,000 people). Depression rates varied by state: 17–36% in self-reports and 0.2–46% in records, and the two sources did not match well. Higher genetic risk meant a slightly higher chance of depression (about 5% more overall and about 10% in people of European ancestry), and this pattern was similar across states. Big studies can help, but results can change based on who joins and how health data are recorded.
calc_title: Using large biobanks for psychiatric genomic research: Consistency of clinical and genetic aspects of recorded depression across US states in the All of Us Research Program

This study examined depression prevalence and polygenic risk score (PRS) associations in the All of Us data to assess potential impacts of nonrepresentative sampling.    Methods: Depression prevalence and correlates were analyzed in two subsamples: those with self-reported personal medical history (PMH) data (N = 185,232 overall; N = 114,739 with genetic data) and those with electronic health record (EHR) data (N = 287,015 overall; N = 206,175 with genetic data). Associations between PRS and lifetime depression were largely consistent and significant associations varied minimally (ORs = 1.06-1.45) by state of residence in both subsamples.    Conclusions: Recorded depression prevalence by state in All of Us demonstrates a wide range, likely reflecting recruitment differences, EHR data completeness, and true geographic variation; yet PRS associations remained relatively stable. As studies like All of Us expand, accounting for sample composition and measurement approaches will be crucial for generating actionable findings.

pdr_title: Associations between loneliness severity and depression and suicidal ideation among older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic
pdr_abstract: Objectives: The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated loneliness among older adults. This study evaluates the relationship between loneliness, depression, and suicidal ideation in this population during the early pandemic by utilizing data from the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program.    Method: We analyzed cross-sectional data from 17,084 individuals aged ≥65 enrolled in the AoU Research Program who completed a COVID-19 related survey in May 2020. Participants were categorized into loneliness quartiles based on their UCLA Loneliness Scale Short Form-8 scores. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests assessed demographic differences. Poisson regression models with robust standard errors tested associations between loneliness quartiles and both depression and suicidal ideation, adjusting for age, gender, race, ethnicity, education, marital status, employment status, housing status, health insurance status, and social support.    Results: Among 17,084 participants %28mean age 72.0years [SD 5.3], 55% female, 89% White%29, we found a clear stepwise pattern: as loneliness increased, so did the risk of depression and suicidal ideation. Compared to the lowest loneliness quartile, those in the highest loneliness quartile were approximately 25 times more likely to experience moderate-to-severe depression %28adjusted relative risk [aRR]=25.09, 95% CI: 16.63-37.84%29 and 44 times more likely to report suicidal ideation %28aRR = 44.31, 95% CI: 19.69-99.71%29. Intermediate loneliness levels %28quartiles 2-3%29 also showed elevated risks %28depression aRRs: 2.45, 7.33; suicidal ideation aRRs: 4.03, 11.87%29.    Conclusion: Increasing levels of loneliness were associated with greater risk of depression and suicidal ideation among older adults during the early pandemic, underscoring the need for targeted loneliness interventions for this vulnerable population.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether feeling lonely was linked to depression and thinking about suicide in 17,084 adults age 65 and older who answered a survey in May 2020. Researchers grouped people by how lonely they felt using a short loneliness survey and compared rates of depression and suicidal thoughts. People with the highest loneliness were about 25 times more likely to have serious depression and about 44 times more likely to have suicidal thoughts than the least lonely. This suggests we need programs to reduce loneliness to protect older adults’ mental health.

pdr_title: Investigation into EHR data coverage in the All of Us Research Program via linkage to health insurance claims
pdr_abstract: In 2020, the All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program Data Completeness Task Force identified several challenges in the state of program health data, including the high likelihood that Electronic Health Record %28EHR%29 data from recruitment institutions is missing a significant portion of care received by participants. To improve data availability, the AoU Data Completeness Task Force recommended efforts to work with industry partners to better understand the degree of missingness within AoU EHR data, with an initial focus on claims data. In this study we describe efforts from AoU's collaboration with Swoop, a commercial analytics company holding health insurance claims data for over 80% of Americans, to assess the degree to which health insurance claims data can fill out the complete picture of care received by AoU participants. Using record linkage to link between individual participant AoU EHR data and their respective insurance claims, we quantitatively assess the amount of missing health data in both Swoop claims data and AoU EHR data over a decade long sample, identifying trends in data missingness based on participant characteristics. Our analysis demonstrates that AoU would greatly benefit from ingestion of claims data, gaining an estimated 16 million %2890 per person%29 unique diagnosis codes, 17.8 million %2899 per person%29 unique procedure codes, and 9.4 million %2853 per person%29 unique drug codes through linkage to claims data.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at how much health information is missing from the All of Us program's medical records (EHRs). They linked EHRs to health insurance billing records (claims) from Swoop, which covers over 80% of Americans, across ten years. The added claims data gave about 16 million diagnosis entries (about 90 per person), 17.8 million procedure entries (about 99 per person), and 9.4 million drug entries (about 53 per person). This shows insurance data can fill many gaps and give patients and researchers a much clearer picture of the care people actually receive.

pdr_title: Multi-trait and multi-ancestry genetic analysis of comorbid lung diseases and traits improves genetic discovery and polygenic risk prediction
pdr_abstract: While respiratory diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease %28COPD%29 and asthma share many risk factors, most studies investigate them in isolation and in predominantly European-ancestry populations. Here, we conducted the most powerful multi-trait and multi-ancestry genetic analysis of respiratory diseases and auxiliary traits to date, identifying 25 new loci associated with lung function in individuals of East Asian ancestry. Using these results, we developed PRSxtra %28cross-trait and cross-ancestry%29, a multi-trait and multi-ancestry polygenic risk score %28PRS%29 approach that leverages shared components of heritable risk via pleiotropic effects. PRSxtra significantly improved the prediction of asthma, COPD and lung cancer compared to trait- and ancestry-matched PRSs in a multi-ancestry cohort from the All of Us Research Program, especially in diverse populations. Our results present a new framework for multi-trait and multi-ancestry studies of respiratory diseases to improve genetic discovery and polygenic prediction.

pdr_title: Perceived Neighborhood Environment and Objectively Assessed, Habitual Physical Activity Among US Adults: An All of Us Research Program Study
pdr_abstract: Introduction: The purpose of this study was to assess the associations between perceived socioenvironmental neighborhood attributes and objectively assessed habitual physical activity among US adults as well as whether associations vary by sociodemographic characteristics.    Methods: We used data from the All of Us research program, a longitudinal cohort study of a diverse sample of Americans. Perceived neighborhood social cohesion, physical and social disorder, walkability, and sociodemographic characteristics were self-reported. Habitual physical activity was ascertained using Fitbit-derived step counts over ≥24 weeks. Generalized additive mixed-effects models were used to test the associations between perceived socioenvironmental neighborhood attributes and daily step counts.    Results: Among participants %28n = 6716%29, average daily step count was 7274.1 %28SD = 3353.6%29. Social cohesion %28B = 117.15, SE = 30.12, P < .001%29 and walkability %28B = 72.74, SE = 31.43, P = .021%29 were positively associated with step count. The association of social cohesion with step count was moderated by age, being strongest among younger adults %28B for interaction term = -5.43, SE = 2.00, P = .001%29, whereas the association between walkability and step count was moderated by income, being strongest for the lowest income group %28B = -211.57, SE = 90.92, P = .020%29. Despite not finding main effects on step count for perceived physical disorder, age- and income-moderated effects were observed, with opposite-direction associations found for low %28inverse%29 versus mid-upper income %28direct%29 %28B = 229.66, SE = 94.48, P = .015%29 and for younger %28inverse%29 versus older %28direct%29 adults %28B for interaction term = 4.48, SE = 2.01, P = .030%29.    Conclusions: Perceived neighborhood social cohesion, walkability, and physical disorder are associated with habitual physical activity among US adults. Age and income moderated the associations between neighborhood attributes and physical activity.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether people's views of their neighborhood affect how much they walk. Researchers studied 6,716 U.S. adults and used Fitbit step counts for 24 weeks. People reported neighborhood social cohesion (how connected neighbors feel), walkability (how easy it is to walk), and physical disorder (things like graffiti, litter, or broken buildings). Average steps were about 7,274 a day. Higher social cohesion and better walkability were linked to more steps. The links were strongest for younger adults (cohesion) and for lower-income people (walkability). This means friendlier, more walkable neighborhoods may help people be more active.

pdr_title: Disability and Health Care Interactions in Patients with Celiac Disease in the United States: An Analysis of All of Us Cohort
pdr_abstract: Backgrounds And Aims: Celiac disease %28CeD%29 presents with various gastrointestinal and systemic comorbidities, causing significant social and health burdens. Given the substantial symptom burden and lack of therapeutic options beyond the gluten-free diet, patients with CeD may have limited or unsatisfying interactions with healthcare providers.    Methods: Using the All of Us Research Program, we analyzed five categories of surveys: basic, lifestyle, overall health, social factors of health, and healthcare access and utilization, for participants with self-reported or electronic health records-documented CeD. To increase diagnostic accuracy, we excluded CeD patients without compatible HLA haplotypes or with a polygenic risk score associated with a low probability of CeD. Each patient with CeD was matched to cohort participants without CeD using the following matching parameters: age, genetically inferred ancestry, and sex.    Results: Individuals with CeD %28n=1816%29 were more likely to report severe fatigue %2812.0% vs. 8.4%%29, frequent specialist visits %28≥13 per year: 6.6% vs. 4.3%%29, and negative interactions with healthcare. On multivariate logistic regression, the following symptoms and healthcare interactions were independently associated with CeD: fatigue severity %28OR=1.19, 95% CI [1.11-1.27]%29, more frequent medical specialist visits OR=1.69, 95% CI: 1.51-1.90, and negative provider interactions were all positively associated with increased likelihood of CeD.    Conclusions: Participants with CeD reported significantly greater functional limitations, higher difficulty assessing care, and a higher degree of fatigue, compared to participants without CeD, underscoring the need to integrate social determinants of health and patient-reported experiences into clinical management.
lay_summary: This study looked at 1,816 people with celiac disease to see how they interact with doctors and health care, and compared them to similar people without the disease using surveys, health records, and genetic checks to make sure they really had celiac disease. People with celiac disease reported more severe tiredness (12% vs 8%), more frequent doctor visits to specialists (6.6% vs 4.3%), and more negative experiences with healthcare. They also had more trouble with daily activities and getting care. The study shows people with celiac disease may need better support from doctors and the health system.
