pdr_title: Trends in Use of Obesity Medications and Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Among All of Us Participants From 2003 to 2023
pdr_abstract: Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the trends in antiobesity medication %28AOM%29 and metabolic and bariatric surgery %28MBS%29 use relative to the 2013 American Medical Association %28AMA%29 declaration of obesity as a chronic disease and semaglutide approval in 2021 in the United States.    Methods: We employed a repeated cross-sectional design to analyze national electronic health records %28EHR%29 of US adults %28≥18years%29 with obesity %28BMI ≥30kg/m2%29 or overweight %28BMI ≥27kg/m2%29 with ≥1 comorbidity for AOM and those with BMI ≥35kg/m2 for MBS, using the All of Us dataset. We used interrupted time-series models to evaluate trends from January 1, 2003, to October 1, 2023.    Results: AOM rates increased by 0.31%/year %2895% CI, 0.25%, 0.37%%29 after 2013 and further increased by 1.42%/year %2895% CI, 1.16%, 1.68%%29 after 2021. MBS use declined by 0.10%/year %2895% CI, -0.15%, -0.04%%29 before 2013. Semaglutide approval was not associated with MBS use decline after 2021. After 2013, patients with BMI ≥40kg/m2 experienced a larger increase in AOM use %280.50% [95% CI, 0.40%, 0.61%]%29 vs. <40kg/m2 %280.25%/year [95% CI, 0.20%, 0.30%]%29 and stable MBS use.    Conclusions: The declaration increased AOM use and, to a lesser extent, MBS use. Semaglutide approval increased AOM use but had no impact on MBS use.
lay_summary: The study looked at U.S. health records from 2003–2023 to see how often adults with overweight or obesity used weight-loss medicines or had weight-loss surgery before and after two events: the 2013 decision to call obesity a chronic disease and the 2021 approval of semaglutide (a weight-loss drug). Use of anti-obesity medicines rose slowly after 2013 (about 0.3% per year) and faster after 2021 (about 1.4% per year). People with very high BMI (≥40) had larger increases in medicine use. Surgery did not rise after 2021. This means more people are using medicines for weight loss, so talk with your doctor about options.

pdr_title: Scalable and accurate rare-variant association tests for whole genome sequencing time-to-event analysis in large biobanks
pdr_journal_title: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
pdr_abstract: Whole genome sequencing %28WGS%29 studies in large biobanks provide an unprecedented opportunity to study the rare-variant %28RV%29 effects on the natural history of human diseases by analyzing censored time-to-event %28TTE%29 phenotypes, such as age at disease diagnosis, disease progression, and lifespan. Unlike existing methods developed for continuous and categorical phenotypes, rare-variant association tests %28RVATs%29 for TTE phenotypes in large biobanks face several major challenges, including heavy censoring, cryptic relatedness, and population structure. We introduce GATE-STAAR %28Genetic Analysis of Time-to-Event phenotypes via the variant-Set Test for Association using Annotation infoRmation%29, a powerful and computationally efficient frailty model framework for RVATs of TTE phenotypes in large biobanks. GATE-STAAR accounts for high censoring rates, cryptic relatedness, and population structure in large biobanks, while incorporating multifaceted variant functional annotations to improve power and result interpretability. We propose a rare-variant saddlepoint approximation method to effectively address heavy censoring in WGS TTE analysis. We demonstrate through extensive simulations that GATE-STAAR is powerful while maintaining proper control of type I error rates. We apply GATE-STAAR to analyze the WGS data of approximately 400,000 UK Biobank participants of white British ancestry across a variety of TTE phenotypes, and validate the findings using participants of European ancestry from the All of Us Research Program. These analyses uncover RV associations with age at diagnosis of a range of diseases.
lay_summary: This study made a fast and accurate test to find rare DNA changes (rare variants) that affect when health events happen (time-to-event, like age at diagnosis). The team tested the method on whole genome data from about 400,000 UK Biobank participants and checked results in another large group. The method handles people who have not yet had the event (censoring) and relatedness between people. It found rare variants linked to age at diagnosis for many diseases. This will help researchers discover genes that could improve prevention, diagnosis, or treatment.

pdr_title: A multilevel analysis of LGBT-relevant laws and sexual and gender minority mental health: evidence for the protective role of inclusive policies
pdr_abstract: Background: Sexual and gender minority %28SGM%29 individuals experience elevated rates of depression and anxiety, largely attributed to chronic exposure to stigma, discrimination, and social exclusion. Less is known about whether state-level policy climates may buffer the mental health impacts of stress among SGM populations.    Methods: We used data from the All of Us Research Program %282020–2022%29 to examine whether state-level LGBTQ policy climates; measured using the Movement Advancement Project %28MAP%29 Total Tally Score %28range: –18.5 to 38.5%29, moderated associations between general perceived stress %28PSS-10%29 and symptoms of depression and anxiety. Multilevel modeling assessed within- and between-state associations and cross-level interactions between policy climate and stress. Subgroup analyses tested whether moderation effects varied across demographic groups %28e.g., marital status, gender identity%29. Final samples included N=6,430 %28depression%29 and N=6,392 %28anxiety%29.    Results: A more inclusive state LGBTQ policy climate significantly moderated the association between perceived stress and mental health symptoms, reflecting a weaker stress–depression association %28β=–.023, SE=.010, p=.020%29 and a weaker stress–anxiety association %28β=–.032, SE=.009, p<.001%29. Moderation was stronger for divorced SGM individuals compared with married individuals %28β=–.091, SE=.033, p=.006%29.    Conclusion: State-level LGBTQ policy climates were statistically associated with variation in the strength of stress–mental health relationships among SGM adults. These findings highlight the relevance of structural environments for SGM mental health. Future longitudinal research should evaluate how changes in policy climates shape stress processes and mental health trajectories over time. lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if state laws that protect LGBT people help keep them mentally healthy. They used 2020–2022 All of Us data on about 6,400 sexual and gender minority (SGM) adults and measured stress, depression, anxiety, and how inclusive each state's laws were. In states with more inclusive laws, stress was less likely to lead to depression or anxiety. This protective effect was especially strong for divorced SGM people. The findings suggest that inclusive state policies may help reduce the mental harm of stress for LGBT people and should be considered by lawmakers and communities.
calc_title: A multilevel analysis of LGBT-relevant laws and sexual and gender minority mental health: evidence for the protective role of inclusive policies
calc_abstract: Background: Sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals experience elevated rates of depression and anxiety, largely attributed to chronic exposure to stigma, discrimination, and social exclusion. Less is known about whether state-level policy climates may buffer the mental health impacts of stress among SGM populations.    Methods: We used data from the All of Us Research Program (2020–2022) to examine whether state-level LGBTQ policy climates; measured using the Movement Advancement Project (MAP) Total Tally Score (range: –18.5 to 38.5), moderated associations between general perceived stress (PSS-10) and symptoms of depression and anxiety. Multilevel modeling assessed within- and between-state associations and cross-level interactions between policy climate and stress. Subgroup analyses tested whether moderation effects varied across demographic groups (e.g., marital status, gender identity). Final samples included N=6,430 (depression) and N=6,392 (anxiety).    Results: A more inclusive state LGBTQ policy climate significantly moderated the association between perceived stress and mental health symptoms, reflecting a weaker stress–depression association (β=–.023, SE=.010, p=.020) and a weaker stress–anxiety association (β=–.032, SE=.009, p<.001). Moderation was stronger for divorced SGM individuals compared with married individuals (β=–.091, SE=.033, p=.006).    Conclusion: State-level LGBTQ policy climates were statistically associated with variation in the strength of stress–mental health relationships among SGM adults. These findings highlight the relevance of structural environments for SGM mental health. Future longitudinal research should evaluate how changes in policy climates shape stress processes and mental health trajectories over time. pdr_title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease-induced Inflammation Augments Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential through Ref-1
pdr_abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential %28CHIP%29 is characterized by age-related somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells %28HSC/Ps%29 and is correlated with an increased risk of myeloid malignancies, elevated inflammatory pathways in circulating myeloid cells, higher all-cause mortality, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease. The pathophysiology of inflammatory bowel disease %28IBD%29 is intrinsically linked to heightened inflammation. Nevertheless, the presence of CHIP in IBD and its role in the pathophysiology of IBD remains poorly elucidated. In the UK Biobank, CHIP was associated with an increased incidence of IBD. Females with CHIP had a 1.33-fold higher risk, which was further validated in All of Us data base %28ßOR = 1.29%29. For Crohn's disease, DNMT3A mutations conferred a 1.81-fold increased incidence in females compared to non-DNMT3A-carriers, which rose to 2.09 for large clones %28variant allele fraction ≥10%%29. In contrast, for ulcerative colitis, TET2 large clones were significantly associated, and only among individuals under 45. These associations were further identified using two-sample Mendelian randomization. In a mouse model of CHIP-IBD, HSC/Ps with Dnmt3a mutation demonstrated significantly worse pathophysiology compared to controls, due in part to heightened expression of Apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 %28APE1%29 in the bone marrow and colon. Treatment with the APE1/Ref-1 inhibitor APX3330 ameliorated CHIP-IBD driven by the Dnmt3a mutation.

pdr_title: Integrating Polygenic Scores with Clinical, Lifestyle, and Social Risk Factors to Improve Heart Failure Risk Prediction
pdr_journal_title: Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing. Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing
pdr_abstract: Heart failure %28HF%29 is highly prevalent, high-burden disorder with its prevalence expected to increase. Early detection of HF can reduce morbidity and mortality; therefore, novel early detection methods are needed. Polygenic scores %28PGS%29 can combine common variants across the genome and provide phenotype-specific risk scores. However, there are also many well-known, non-genomic risk factors of HF, in the clinical, lifestyle, and social determinant of health %28SDOH%29 domains, and it is not clear how genetic and non-genetic risk factors collectively contribute to HF risk. To address this question, we assessed whether combining HF PGS with clinical, lifestyle, and SDOH risk factors improves risk prediction. Leveraging data from the All of Us Research Program %28n = 22,275%29, clinical risk factors were aggregated into a clinical risk score %28CRS%29 while lifestyle and SDOH risk factors were aggregated into a polyexposure score %28PXS%29. Feature selection was conducted with LASSO regression and statistical significance thresholding from logistic regression models %28p < 0.05%29. Features were included in the model if they were statistically significant and important in ≥ 95% of 1000 iterations. To assess model performance, logistic regressions with HF case/control status were conducted with each risk score individually, as well as integrated models. The integrated model %28PGS + CRS + PXS%29 performed better than individual risk scores %28AUROC = 0.763, AUPRC = 0.047, F1 score = 0.062, balanced accuracy = 0.683%29. To assess the validity of the CRS and PXS, an integrated model with the PGS along with clinical and exposure risk factors as independent features was also evaluated. Based on AUPRC and F1 score, this integrated risk model %28PGS + CRS risk factors + PXS risk factors%29 performed better than the combining the PGS with the CRS and PXS %28AUROC = 0.738, AUPRC = 0.047, F1 score = 0.066, balanced accuracy = 0.657%29. These findings demonstrate that integration of risk factors across multiple domains can improve HF prediction. Knowing that PGS combined with clinical, lifestyle, and SDOH risk factors is predictive of HF risk provides greater opportunity for the identification of individuals at risk of HF prior to disease onset with the goal of prevention or early intervention.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if adding genetic risk to medical, lifestyle, and social information helps predict who will get heart failure. They used data from 22,275 people and made a gene score (many small gene effects), a clinical score, and a lifestyle/social score, then tested models using them alone and together. The model that used all three predicted heart failure best (about 76% on a common prediction test) and beat the single scores. This could help find people at risk earlier so doctors can prevent or treat heart failure sooner.

pdr_abstract: Introduction: Alzheimer's disease %28AD%29 is the most common form of dementia. Studies have suggested prevalence is greater in individuals self-identifying as Hispanic. Population-specific results enable personalized and equitable interventions. Ethnicity as a stratifier co-occurs with genomic inflation due to heterogeneity.    Methods: We conducted genome-wide association studies %28GWAS%29 and meta-analyses among subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project %28ADSP%29 Umbrella whole genome sequencing %28WGS%29 dataset who self-identified as Hispanic and All of Us %28AoU%29 sub-cohorts matched to that cohort, using projected genetically-derived principal components.    Results: We identified a common variant in PIEZO2 on chromosome 18 protective for AD in ADSP subjects, with a p-value just beyond genome-wide significance %28p =      Discussion: We demonstrate a way to match subjects between large biobanks and small disease-specific cohorts, enabling novel findings.
lay_summary: This study looked for genes linked to Alzheimer's disease in people who identify as Hispanic. Researchers matched Hispanic participants from a focused sequencing study with similar people from a large health database by using their genetic patterns, then scanned all genes (the whole genome) and combined results. They found a common change in the PIEZO2 gene that appeared to lower Alzheimer's risk, though it fell just short of the strict cutoff scientists usually use. The work shows a new way to match groups, helping find genetic clues that could help make care and research fairer.

pdr_title: Association of genetic risk and physical activity with incident type 2 diabetes
pdr_journal_title: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
pdr_abstract: Objective: To assess whether daily step counts and genetic risk interact to influence the risk of developing type 2 diabetes.    Research Design And Methods: We analyzed data from 9,501 participants in the All of Us Research Program with both genetic and wearable device-derived physical activity data and without diabetes at baseline and median age of 56 years %2842-66%29. Physical activity was quantified using daily step counts. Genetic risk was assessed using a global polygenic score. Incident type 2 diabetes was identified using electronic health record-linked diagnostic codes. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios %28HRs%29 for type 2 diabetes across genetic risk and physical activity levels. We tested for additive interaction using the relative excess risk due to interaction %28RERI%29. In secondary analyses we used physical-activity intensity measures using wearable-derived and self-reported intensity levels.    Results: Type 2 diabetes incidence rates ranged from 4.1 per 1,000 person-years %2895% CI, 2.5-5.7%29 in individuals with high physical activity and low genetic risk to 18.4 %2895% CI, 15.2-21.6%29 in those with low physical activity and high genetic risk %28HR, 6.2 %2895% CI: 3.97, 9.6%29%29. A significant additive interaction was observed %28RERI, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.04-0.36; P = .007%29, with 15% %2895% CI, 2-27%29 of excess risk attributed to the interaction. Similar interaction patterns were found using device-based intensity metrics and self-reported physical activity measures.    Conclusions: These findings provide evidence of additive interactions between genetic risk and physical activity, underscoring the potential value of integrating genomic and device-derived data to identify individuals who would more likely benefit from increasing physical activity.

lay_summary: This study asked if daily walking and genes together change the chance of getting type 2 diabetes. Researchers followed 9,501 people without diabetes (average age 56) who wore activity trackers and had a genetic risk score (a measure of many diabetes genes). About 15% of the extra risk came from the combination. The result means being more active can lower diabetes risk, especially if your genes raise your risk.

pdr_title: Step counts over time with the burden of 105 non-communicable diseases in older adults from the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: As the impact of daily step counts on the risk and burden of various non-communicable diseases %28NCDs%29 in older adults remains unclear, we investigated this association using wearable device data from a large, diverse cohort.    Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort study using the All of Us Research Program, including 2969 older adults %28≥55 years%29 who wore Fitbit devices. Fitbit data were linked with electronic health records, and follow-up continued until July 1, 2022, to assess daily step counts and NCDs. We estimated the new-onset risks %28adjusted-hazard ratios [aHRs]%29 and burdens %28years lived with disability [YLDs]%29 for 105 NCDs.    Results: Of the 2969 participants aged ≥55, participants were categorized into a control group with ≥6000 step counts %28mean [SD] age, 66.4 [6.9] years; female, 1243 [62.7%]%29 and a low-step counts with <6000 steps %2867.9 [7.4]; 710 [72.1%]%29. Lower daily step counts were associated with increased risk and/or burden across various NCDs. First, for cardiovascular disease %28aHR, 1.17 [95% CI, 1.04-1.33]; YLD, 85.2 [28.9-141.4] per 100,000 populations%29, chronic respiratory disease %281.23 [1.08-1.40]; 138.5 [4.7-272.3]%29, digestive diseases %281.18 [1.04-1.34]; 116.9 [37.3-196.4]%29, and diabetes and kidney diseases %281.29 [1.11-1.51]; 186.3 [11.8-360.7]%29, lower step counts were linked to both increased risk and burden. Second, for neurological disorders, mental disorders, and substance use disorders, lower-step counts were associated with a higher risk but not burden. Third, for neoplasms and sense organ disorders, lower-step counts were linked to higher burden without changes in risk.    Conclusions: This study provides real-world evidence supporting the critical role of daily step counts in reducing the risk and/or burden of NCDs.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if daily step counts affect long-term diseases in older adults. They studied about 3,000 people aged 55  who wore Fitbits and linked their step data to medical records through 2022. People taking fewer than 6,000 steps a day had more risk or greater impact (how much a disease affects daily life) for many conditions. Fewer steps linked to more heart, lung, digestive, diabetes, and kidney problems. Some brain and mental disorders had more risk, and some cancers and eye/ear problems showed more impact. Walking more may help lower disease risk and harm.

pdr_title: Oropharyngeal Dysphagia in Parkinson's Disease: An Analysis of Prevalence, Swallow Therapy Utilization, and Complication Rates
pdr_abstract: Objective: Oropharyngeal dysphagia %28OD%29 is a common and challenging manifestation of Parkinson's disease %28PD%29, associated with risks of malnutrition, aspiration, and reduced quality of life. This study investigates interventions, complications, and factors associated with swallow therapy utilization in a national cohort of individuals with PD and OD.    Methods: In the All of Us database, we identified individuals with PD and OD using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes. Rates of swallow evaluation, swallow therapy, malnutrition and/or gastrostomy placement, and aspiration pneumonia were evaluated. Chi-square tests compared characteristics and complication rates among those with versus without swallow therapy.    Results: Of 2004 individuals with PD, 476 %2823.8%%29 underwent a swallow evaluation. Two hundred twenty-one individuals %2811.0%%29 were diagnosed with OD, with the majority being above 65years of age %2885.1%%29 and male %2871.0%%29. Among those with OD, 58 %2826.2%%29 received swallow therapy. Malnutrition and/or gastrostomy placement were documented in 44 %2819.9%%29 individuals with PD and OD, and aspiration pneumonia occurred in 25 %2811.3%%29 individuals. Factors associated with increased swallow therapy utilization were male sex %28p<0.001%29 and a history of malnutrition and/or gastrostomy placement %28p=0.04%29.    Conclusion: A small proportion of individuals with PD received swallow evaluation, and even among those with identified OD, few received swallow therapy. Complications including malnutrition, gastrostomy placement, and aspiration pneumonia were relatively common. These findings suggest a need for greater integration of swallowing evaluation and treatment into routine PD management.    Level Of Evidence: 3.
lay_summary: Researchers used national health records to see how often people with Parkinson's get swallowing tests, therapy, and related problems. Out of 2,004 people, 476 (24%) had a swallowing test and 221 (11%) had swallowing problems. Of those, 58 (26%) got swallow therapy. Forty-four (20%) had poor nutrition or needed a feeding tube and 25 (11%) had lung infections from food going into the lungs (aspiration). Most with problems were over 65 and male. The results mean doctors should check and treat swallowing problems more often to prevent poor nutrition and infections.

calc_abstract: Objective: Oropharyngeal dysphagia (OD) is a common and challenging manifestation of Parkinson's disease (PD), associated with risks of malnutrition, aspiration, and reduced quality of life. This study investigates interventions, complications, and factors associated with swallow therapy utilization in a national cohort of individuals with PD and OD.    Methods: In the All of Us database, we identified individuals with PD and OD using ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes. Rates of swallow evaluation, swallow therapy, malnutrition and/or gastrostomy placement, and aspiration pneumonia were evaluated. Chi-square tests compared characteristics and complication rates among those with versus without swallow therapy.    Results: Of 2004 individuals with PD, 476 (23.8%) underwent a swallow evaluation. Two hundred twenty-one individuals (11.0%) were diagnosed with OD, with the majority being above 65years of age (85.1%) and male (71.0%). Among those with OD, 58 (26.2%) received swallow therapy. Malnutrition and/or gastrostomy placement were documented in 44 (19.9%) individuals with PD and OD, and aspiration pneumonia occurred in 25 (11.3%) individuals. Factors associated with increased swallow therapy utilization were male sex (p<0.001) and a history of malnutrition and/or gastrostomy placement (p=0.04).    Conclusion: A small proportion of individuals with PD received swallow evaluation, and even among those with identified OD, few received swallow therapy. Complications including malnutrition, gastrostomy placement, and aspiration pneumonia were relatively common. These findings suggest a need for greater integration of swallowing evaluation and treatment into routine PD management.    Level Of Evidence: 3.

pdr_title: Post-traumatic stress disorder and social determinants of health among individuals with cancer: association with healthcare utilization and outcomes in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Cancer Survivorship : Research and Practice
pdr_abstract: Background: Individual effect of posttraumatic stress disorder %28PTSD%29 and social determinants of health %28SDoH%29 on healthcare utilization and well-being among cancer patients remains unclear. We sought to assess independent and combined effects of these factors on healthcare utilization and self-reported well-being.    Methods: All of Us Research Program was used to identify participants with cancer and/or PTSD, as well as individuals with neither. SDoH burden, healthcare utilization, and well-being were assessed relative to PTSD on multivariable logistic regression adjusting for sociodemographic factors.    Results: Among 16,261 participants, 11.6% %28n=1895%29 had cancer, 1.4% %28n=228%29 had cancer and PTSD, and 20.1% %28n=3281%29 had PTSD alone. PTSD was associated with higher odds of emergency room visits %28aOR 4.16, 95% CI 3.80-4.55%29, poor mental %28aOR 3.77, 95% CI 3.43-4.14%29, and emotional health %28aOR 3.76, 95% CI 3.41-4.16%29 %28all p<0.001%29. High SDoH burden independently predicted increased inpatient and emergency visits %28aOR 1.24, 95% CI 1.13-1.36%29, as well as greater risk of poor quality of life %28aOR 3.71, 95% CI 3.20-4.32%29 %28all p<0.001%29. Cancer patients with PTSD and high SDoH burden had substantially greater odds of poor mental health %28aOR 10.92, 95% CI 9.33-12.77%29 and poor emotional health %28aOR 12.20, 95% CI 10.33-14.41%29 %28all p<0.001%29.    Conclusion: Cancer, PTSD, and high SDoH burden were independently associated with greater healthcare use and worse well-being with combined exposures amplifying risk among cancer survivors.    Implications For Cancer Survivors: Survivors with PTSD and high SDoH burden are especially vulnerable. Integrating trauma-informed care and SDoH screening strengthens survivorship equity and outcome.
lay_summary: Researchers used a U.S. study of 16,261 people to see how posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD, a mental health reaction to trauma) and social determinants of health (SDoH—things like income, housing and access to care) affect people with cancer. About 12% had cancer, 20% had PTSD, and 1% had both. PTSD and high SDoH needs led to more ER and hospital visits and worse mental health. People with cancer who had both PTSD and high SDoH needs were about 11–12 times more likely to report poor mental health. Screening for trauma and social needs could help survivors get better support.

pdr_title: Higher lithium exposure in groundwater is associated with reduced stroke incidence and mortality
pdr_journal_title: International Journal of Stroke : Official Journal of the International Stroke Society
pdr_abstract: Background: Lithium, a naturally occurring element in drinking water, has demonstrated beneficial effects for stroke in prior research, yet its relationship with stroke risk in the general population remains uncertain.    Aims: To evaluate the association between environmental lithium exposure and stroke risk.    Methods: We assessed environmental lithium exposure across the US using monitoring data of 4,700 wells for drinking groundwater from the US Geological Survey. Ecological and individual-level analyses were conducted. Ecological associations between county level lithium concentration and stroke mortality %282015-2019%29 were evaluated in 3108 counties using multivariable linear regression adjusted for county-level socioeconomic factors. Individual level associations were examined in 303153 adults %28≥35years old%29 from the All of Us Research Program with electronic health records followed up through October 1, 2023 using stratified Cox models adjusted for individual-level sociodemographic, behavioral, and clinical factors. Lithium was analyzed per interquartile range %28IQR%29 increase and by quartiles.    Results: In ecological analysis, each IQR increase in lithium exposure corresponded to 8.2 fewer stroke deaths per 100,000 population %2895%CI:-9.8,-6.5%29. Compared with the lowest quartile %28≤6.6µg/L%29, the highest quartile %28>23.3µg/L%29 showed 22.6 fewer deaths per 100,000 %2895%CI:-27.4,-17.8%29; middle quartiles were not associated. In All of Us, each IQR increase was associated with a 23% lower incident stroke risk %28HR=0.77,95%CI:0.66,0.90%29. The highest exposure quartile %28>17.7µg/L%29 had a 52% lower risk %28HR=0.48,95%CI:0.34,0.67%29 versus the lowest; second %28HR=1.23, 95% CI: 0.73, 2.09%29 and third %28HR=0.92, 95% CI: 0.50, 1.69%29 quartile showed non significant associations. Results were robust to alternate exposure windows and residential stability restrictions.    Conclusion: Higher naturally occurring lithium concentrations in US groundwater are associated with reduced stroke mortality and incidence, whereas low to moderate levels confer no benefit.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether natural lithium in drinking water affects stroke. Researchers used lithium measurements from 4,700 US wells and death data in 3,108 counties, and followed 303,153 adults with health records. Areas with higher lithium had about 8 fewer stroke deaths per 100,000 people for a modest rise and about 23 fewer deaths in places with the highest levels. People in the highest lithium areas had about half the stroke risk compared with the lowest areas. The findings suggest natural lithium in water might lower stroke risk, but more research is needed before any changes are made.

pdr_title: Management and Consequences of Genotype-Positive Familial Hypercholesterolemia
pdr_abstract: Importance: Familial hypercholesterolemia %28FH%29 is a common genetic condition that causes hypercholesterolemia and increased risk for premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease %28ASCVD%29. The prevalence, management, and consequences of genetically confirmed FH across the US are poorly understood.    Objective: To identify genotype-positive FH in a national US cohort and describe its prevalence, consequences, and lipid-lowering management.    Design, Setting, And Participants: In the All of Us %28AoU%29 cohort study, whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic data from US adult participants enrolled between May 2018 and July 2022 were analyzed to identify and study genotype-positive FH. Data were analyzed between May 2024 and May 2025.    Exposure: FH variants %28pathogenic or likely pathogenic%29 in LDLR, APOB, and PCSK9 genes were manually classified with standard criteria.    Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcomes were demographic characteristics, lipid measurements, ASCVD, and prevalence of FH and noncarriers in AoU. Lipid management was then characterized among individuals with FH through lipid-lowering therapy %28LLT%29 documentation and guideline-based low-density lipoprotein cholesterol %28LDL-C%29 targets.    Results: A total of 245 388 participants were included, with mean %28SD%29 age of 56.5 %2816.9%29 years and 145 563 female participants %2859.3%%29. Genotype-positive FH was identified in 865 participants %28prevalence, 0.35%; 95% CI, 0.33%-0.38%; 1 in 287 participants%29. Among individuals with genotype-positive FH, 349 %2840%%29 were prescribed statins, and 332 %2838.4%%29 had LDL-C measured. Coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, and transient ischemic attack or stroke were significantly more common in genotype-positive FH carriers compared to noncarriers %28coronary artery disease: odds ratio [OR], 2.91; 95% CI, 2.34-3.58; peripheral artery disease: OR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.16-1.96; and transient ischemic attack or stroke: OR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.11-2.09%29. Only 30.1% of participants positive for FH variants had LDL-C less than 100 mg/dL at their most recent result compared to 48.2% of noncarriers %28P<.001%29. Of the total participants with ASCVD and LLT prescription, significantly fewer individuals with FH met the secondary prevention LDL-C target %28<70 mg/dL; 19.33% vs 43.12%; P<.001%29 compared to noncarriers.    Conclusions And Relevance: This cohort study finds a prevalence of genotype-positive FH in All of Us participants of 0.35% %2895% CI, 0.33%-0.38%%29, with state-level variation. A minority of individuals with genotype-positive FH met guideline-recommended LDL-C targets and had increased rates of ASCVD.
lay_summary: This study looked for people with a genetic form of very high cholesterol called familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) in 245,388 US adults using whole-genome sequencing and health records. It found 865 people with FH (about 1 in 287). People with FH had more heart disease and strokes. Only 40% were on statins and 38% had cholesterol measured. Just 30% reached LDL cholesterol below 100 mg/dL and only about 19% with heart disease reached the stricter target, compared to 48% and 43% of others. These results show many with FH are under-treated and need better care.

pdr_title: Loneliness, Anxiety Symptoms, Depressive Symptoms, and Suicidal Ideation in the All of Us Dataset
pdr_abstract: Importance: Although anxiety symptoms and depressive symptoms are linked with increases in suicidal ideation, they leave much of the variance in suicidal ideation unexplained. Loneliness may mediate the links between anxiety symptoms and suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation.    Objective: To analyze the mediating role of loneliness in the association between anxiety symptoms and suicidal ideation as well as in the association between depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation.    Design, Setting, And Participants: This cross-sectional study used data collected between May 31, 2017, and October 1, 2023, from 62 685 US adults who completed the self-report mental health survey portion of the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program.    Main Outcomes And Measures: Self-report surveys estimated anxiety symptoms %28using the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale%29, depressive symptoms %28using the first 8 items of the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire [PHQ-9]%29, loneliness %28using the UCLA Loneliness Scale%29, and suicidal ideation %28using item 9 of the PHQ-9%29. Analyses were conducted in August of 2025.    Results: The analytic sample of 62 685 individuals had a mean %28SD%29 age of 61.8 %2816.1%29 years and included 40 749 women %2865.0%%29. Anxiety symptoms %28r=0.33; P<.001%29, depressive symptoms %28r=0.39; P<.001%29, and loneliness %28r=0.31; P<.001%29 correlated with suicidal ideation. When controlling for gender and race and ethnicity, depressive symptoms %28B=0.017 [95% CI, 0.017-0.019]%29, anxiety symptoms %28B=0.004 [95% CI, 0.004-0.006]%29, and loneliness %28B=0.007 [95% CI, 0.007-0.008]%29 accounted for significant variability in suicidal ideation. Loneliness partially mediated the association between anxiety symptoms %28average causal mediation effect=0.01; proportion mediated, 0.25; total association, 0.03; P<.001%29 and suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms %28average causal mediation effect=0.003; proportion mediated, 0.10; total association, 0.02; P<.001%29 and suicidal ideation, indicating the associations of anxiety and depressive symptoms with suicidal ideation were in part mediated by loneliness.    Conclusions And Relevance: In this cross-sectional study of 62 685 participants from the All of Us Research Program, loneliness partially mediated the association between anxiety symptoms and suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation. Targeting and reducing loneliness may present a transdiagnostic approach to arrest the progression from anxiety and depressive symptoms toward suicidal ideation.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if feeling lonely helps explain why anxiety and depression can lead to thoughts of suicide. They used one-time surveys from 62,685 U.S. adults (average age 62; 65% women) who answered questions about anxiety, depression, loneliness, and suicidal thoughts. People with more anxiety, more depression, and more loneliness were more likely to have suicidal thoughts. Loneliness explained about 25% of the link from anxiety and about 10% of the link from depression to suicidal thoughts. This suggests that reducing loneliness could help lower the chance that anxiety or depression leads to suicidal thinking.

pdr_title: Development and validation of a trans-ancestry polygenic risk score for type 1 diabetes
pdr_abstract: Aims/Hypothesis: The high heritability of type 1 diabetes has enabled the development of polygenic risk scores %28PRSs%29 as disease risk screening tools. PRSs can identify individuals at the highest genetic risk in a population, who can benefit from autoantibody and metabolic surveillance, to avoid ketoacidosis at diagnosis and to access preventive therapies. However, PRSs for type 1 diabetes developed from European data perform less well in non-European ancestries. We aimed to develop a PRS with comparable performance among different ancestries.    Methods: Using the PRS-CSx method, and data from large European, East Asian, African American and Hispanic type 1 diabetes genome-wide association studies %28Ntotal_cases=29,469%29, we developed a trans-ancestry PRS %28TA-PS%29, combining a non-HLA component incorporating over a million variants with the HLA component of a published European PRS %28GRS2x%29. We tested the performance of the PRS using area under the receiver operating curve %28AUROC%29, sensitivity and specificity in a multi-ancestry type 1 diabetes case-control cohort %28Ntotal=4657; Nnon-European=556%29 from Montreal, Canada. We validated our results in two independent type 1 diabetes case-control cohorts %28Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Center for Applied Genomics [CHOP-CAG] and Genetic Risk Assessment for Chinese Eaglet-T1D [GRACE]%29 and two population-based cohorts %28All of Us and UK Biobank%29.    Results: In the multi-ancestry Montreal-based cohort, TA-PS showed an AUROC of 0.89 which was significantly higher than the respective measure obtained with GRS2x in the same population %28AUROC of 0.85%29. We obtained better overall sensitivity at the 90th percentile cut-off using TA-PS %280.71 in Europeans, 0.77 in South Asians%29, compared with sensitivity of 0.32 in African Americans and 0.56 in Europeans using GRS2x. The specificity obtained using TA-PS was slightly lower than that of GRS2x, albeit still acceptable %28≥0.83 across all ancestries%29. These results were validated in the four independent cohorts.    Conclusions/Interpretation: We developed a trans-ancestry PRS that outperformed the European-based GRS2x. Importantly, TA-PS provides a comparable prediction in various ancestries, which supports its use in population-wide screening programmes.
lay_summary: Researchers made a new genetic test (a polygenic risk score uses many genes) to better find people at high risk for type 1 diabetes because older scores worked worse in non‑European groups. They used genetic data from tens of thousands and tested it in several groups. The new score worked better across ancestries (0.89 vs 0.85), found 71% of high‑risk Europeans and 77% of South Asians at the top 10% cut‑off, and correctly ruled out at least 83% of people without the disease. This could help screening programs find people who need closer checkups or prevention.

pdr_title: Scalable discovery and validation of order-specific electronic health record event trajectories for interpretable adverse-outcome risk estimation
pdr_abstract: Objective: Clinicians must estimate patients' risk of adverse outcomes, yet many electronic health record tools represent health history as an unordered 'bag of codes,' discarding temporal order. Machine learning tools that leverage sequence order may offer better predictions but often lack interpretability for clinical audit. We introduce an interpretable, order-aware framework that mines frequent event pairs %28A → B%29 and tests whether their ordering provides prognostic information for estimating risk of adverse outcomes %28C%29 beyond the same codes without order.    Methods: Using the NIH All of Us Controlled Tier, 432,617 eligible participants were split 70/30 into discovery and confirmation. We combined 340,687 A → B pairs with nine outcomes %28C%29 to create 3,066,183 candidate trajectories and tested 85,535 trajectories in this pilot using observation-aware indexing, a 90-day latency and 5-year A → B gap, inverse-probability weighting, weighted competing-risk cumulative incidence, four prespecified comparators %28primary: B with no prior A%29, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate %28FDR%29 in a discovery/confirmation design.    Results: After discovery FDR, 663 unique trajectories advanced and 171 validated for ≥ 1 horizon in confirmation. At 5 years, the median risk ratio %28RR%29 was 2.02 versus the primary comparator and 3.89 versus a calendar-time baseline %28median absolute risk difference 2.49 percentage-points%29. Reverse-order checks were feasible for ∼ 87% of hypotheses %28median A → B → C vs B → A → C RR 1.18%29 at 5 years.    Conclusion: Ordered trajectories can provide interpretable, audit-ready signal beyond unordered features and can augment white-box risk estimation for adverse clinical outcomes.
lay_summary: This study tested whether the order of events in people’s medical records helps predict bad health outcomes. Researchers looked at records from 432,617 people and searched for pairs of events where one came before another. They tested many such ordered pairs and confirmed 171 that predicted problems within five years. Having event A then B about doubled risk compared to B alone, and nearly quadrupled risk versus a basic baseline, adding about 2.5% more absolute risk. These simple, ordered patterns could help doctors make clearer and checkable tools to find patients at higher risk.
calc_title: Scalable discovery and validation of order-specific electronic health record event trajectories for interpretable adverse-outcome risk estimation
calc_abstract: Objective: Clinicians must estimate patients' risk of adverse outcomes, yet many electronic health record tools represent health history as an unordered 'bag of codes,' discarding temporal order. Machine learning tools that leverage sequence order may offer better predictions but often lack interpretability for clinical audit. We introduce an interpretable, order-aware framework that mines frequent event pairs (A → B) and tests whether their ordering provides prognostic information for estimating risk of adverse outcomes (C) beyond the same codes without order.    Methods: Using the NIH All of Us Controlled Tier, 432,617 eligible participants were split 70/30 into discovery and confirmation. We combined 340,687 A → B pairs with nine outcomes (C) to create 3,066,183 candidate trajectories and tested 85,535 trajectories in this pilot using observation-aware indexing, a 90-day latency and 5-year A → B gap, inverse-probability weighting, weighted competing-risk cumulative incidence, four prespecified comparators (primary: B with no prior A), and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) in a discovery/confirmation design.    Results: After discovery FDR, 663 unique trajectories advanced and 171 validated for ≥ 1 horizon in confirmation. At 5 years, the median risk ratio (RR) was 2.02 versus the primary comparator and 3.89 versus a calendar-time baseline (median absolute risk difference 2.49 percentage-points). Reverse-order checks were feasible for ∼ 87% of hypotheses (median A → B → C vs B → A → C RR 1.18) at 5 years.    Conclusion: Ordered trajectories can provide interpretable, audit-ready signal beyond unordered features and can augment white-box risk estimation for adverse clinical outcomes.

pdr_title: Electronic Health Record-Linked Biobank Expansion Reveals Global Health Inequities
pdr_journal_title: Annual Review of Biomedical Data Science
pdr_abstract: Electronic health record %28EHR%29-linked biobanks are transforming biomedical research, enabling population-scale studies that integrate genomic, clinical, and phenotypic data. Yet as these resources proliferate, it remains unclear how their research outputs reflect global health priorities. This article presents a comprehensive review of five globally established EHR-linked biobanks: UK Biobank, the Million Veteran Program, FinnGen, the All of Us Research Program, and the Estonian Biobank. Drawing on 14,142 peer-reviewed publications from 2000 to 2024, we show how each biobank displays a distinct thematic profile, shaped by institutional mandates, population focus, and methodological design. We further evaluate alignment with global disease burden by mapping biobank-linked publications to 25 high-priority disease areas using World Health Organization disability-adjusted life years data. Our burden-adjusted gap scores and opportunity indices reveal striking underrepresentation of conditions such as malaria, tuberculosis, and diarrheal diseases when comparing biobank research output against high-priority diseases.
lay_summary: This study looked at five large EHR-linked biobanks (they link medical records and genetic data)—UK Biobank, Million Veteran Program, FinnGen, All of Us, and Estonian Biobank—by reviewing 14,142 research papers from 2000–2024. The researchers matched those papers to 25 top global diseases from the World Health Organization to see if research fits real health needs. Each biobank focused on different topics, but many big global problems like malaria, tuberculosis, and diarrheal diseases were under-studied. This means we need more research on diseases that hurt people most around the world.

pdr_title: Leveraging pleiotropy to improve genetic risk prediction across diseases
pdr_journal_title: Genetics in Medicine : Official Journal of the American College of Medical Genetics
pdr_abstract: Purpose: Polygenic scores %28PGSs%29 have shown promise in predicting disease risk, but their predictive accuracy remains limited for many complex diseases. Leveraging the shared genetic architecture among correlated traits may improve prediction performance.    Methods: We developed a flexible framework for constructing multi-trait PGSs by integrating candidate PGSs %28N=2,651%29 derived from 51 GWAS summary statistics using single-trait, MTAG-all, and MTAG-pairwise approaches. Multi-trait PGS models were trained using elastic net regression in the UK Biobank %28N = 307,230 individuals%29 and validated in both an internal set of UKB individuals %28N = 39,122%29 and All of Us %28N = 116,394%29 RESULTS: Multi-trait PGSs significantly improved risk prediction for eight diseases, with AUC gains ranging from 1.56% to 5.45% compared to optimal single-GWAS PGSs. Multi-trait PGSs further enhanced predictive performance when integrated with non-genetic factors. Significant interactions were identified between multi-trait PGS for peripheral artery disease %28PAD%29 and smoking and waist-to-hip ratio %28WHR%29. A clustering analysis uncovered genetically distinct subgroups with meaningful phenotypic variation, including a chronic kidney disease %28CKD%29 subgroup enriched for diabetes- and obesity-related traits.    Conclusion: Our multi-trait PGS framework improves disease prediction by capturing cross-trait genetic effects and enables personalized risk assessment through integration with non-genetic exposures, interactions, and subgroup identification.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to make genetic risk scores better by using shared genes that affect more than one disease (pleiotropy: same genes affect multiple traits). They used genetic data from over 300,000 people and tested their method in about 155,000 more. They combined 2,651 genetic scores from 51 studies and trained models. The new multi-trait scores improved prediction for eight diseases, raising accuracy by about 1.6% to 5.5%. Scores worked even better when added to non-genetic factors like smoking and body shape. This could help people get advice to lower their disease risk.

pdr_title: Precision Diagnosis in APOL1 Kidney Disease With the p.N264K M1 Protective Variant
pdr_abstract: Importance: The APOL1 M1 %28p.N264K%29 variant protects against G2-associated APOL1 focal segmental glomerulosclerosis %28FSGS%29 and chronic kidney disease %28CKD%29. However, the utility of knowing an individual's M1 status in guiding kidney disease diagnosis and other clinical scenarios remains underexplored.    Objective: To test 2 hypotheses: %281%29 in patients with APOL1 high-risk %28HR%29 genotype kidney disease with at least 1 G2 allele, M1 can distinguish APOL1 CKD from non-APOL1 CKD; %282%29 in people with APOL1 low-risk %28LR%29 genotypes, M1 is independently associated with protection against FSGS and CKD.    Design, Setting, And Participants: Retrospective case-control study using data from 2 tertiary care hospitals %28Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Mass General Brigham Biobank%29 and population-based data %28the UK Biobank [UKB], Electronic Medical Records and Genomics [eMERGE-III], and All of Us [AoU]%29. Participants were individuals with a diagnosis of FSGS or steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome %28SRNS%29, individuals with CKD, and controls.    Exposures: Exposures included the M1 variant %28p.N264K%29 obtained from exome or genome sequencing data, sex, and genetic ancestry.    Main Outcome And Measure: The main outcome was the presence or absence of kidney disease, defined as FSGS or non-FSGS CKD, compared with non-kidney disease controls. Association between the M1 variant and disease status was assessed using odds ratios %28ORs%29.    Results: A total of 107 696 individuals %2854 994 [51.1%] female; 8779 [8.2%] with African ancestry, 78 475 [72.9%] with European ancestry, and 16 129 [15.0%] with multiethnic ancestry%29, including 3460 with FSGS or SRNS, 24 382 with non-FSGS CKD kidney disease, and 79 854 controls were enrolled in the discovery cohort. In the APOL1-HR group %281413 participants%29, M1 was significantly inversely associated with FSGS or SRNS cases compared with controls without kidney disease %28OR, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.04-0.63; P=3.69×10-3%29. Among individuals with CKD with APOL1-HR genotypes, M1 was 4 times more frequent in those whose CKD was not due to FSGS or SRNS. Importantly, electronic health record and biopsy review identified an alternative, non-APOL1 cause for CKD in nearly all APOL1-HR-M1 cases. There was no association between individuals with APOL1-LR genotypes with M1 and protection against CKD or FSGS.    Conclusions And Relevance: In this case-control study of 107 696 individuals, presence of an APOL1-HR genotype M1 was significantly associated with protection against kidney disease, suggesting that it may have a role as a genetic modifier. Patients with CKD with an APOL1-HR genotype and M1 should be evaluated for an alternative and potentially treatable cause of their CKD.
lay_summary: This study asked if a gene change called M1 (a protective APOL1 variant) can help tell when kidney disease is due to APOL1. Researchers looked at genetic data and medical records from 107,696 people in hospitals and biobanks. They found that in people with high-risk APOL1 genes, having M1 was linked to much less FSGS (a type of kidney scarring) and was four times more common when the kidney disease had a different cause. This means doctors should check for other, treatable causes when a high-risk patient also has M1.

pdr_title: Barriers to Health Care Access and Use among Racial and Ethnic Minorities with Renal Cell Carcinoma
pdr_abstract: Background: Racial disparities in renal cell carcinoma %28RCC%29 outcomes are well-documented, yet the specific patient-reported barriers contributing to these inequities remain underexamined. This study investigates the barriers to healthcare access on minority patients with RCC.    Methods: We performed a cross-sectional study using version 8 of the All of Us Research Program. RCC cases were identified using electronic health record data. We analyzed patient-reported data regarding financial barriers, social determinants, and health literacy. Comparisons between White, Hispanic, and Black patients were conducted via chi-square tests, and adjusted logistic regressions controlled for age, sex, education, insurance, and income.    Results: Among 2,215 RCC patients, minority respondents were younger %28p<0.0001%29 and reported lower annual incomes %28p<0.0001%29. Hispanic patients more frequently cited inability to afford medications %2823.8% vs. 8.2% in White patients, p<0.0001%29 and mental health service costs %2812.6%, p=0.026%29, whereas Black patients reported difficulty taking time off work %28p=0.0018%29 and transportation issues %28p<0.0001%29. Additionally, 44.4% of both Black and Hispanic patients rated their general health as poor or fair, compared with 29.3% of White patients %28p<0.0001%29. In adjusted models, Black patients had twice the odds of being unable to afford medications %28aOR 2.09 [1.20-3.65], p=0.0096%29, and Hispanic patients were nearly four times more likely to delay care due to co-pays %28aOR 3.98 [1.87-8.47], p=0.00033%29.    Conclusions: Minority RCC patients face significant structural and financial barriers, including cost-related delays and lower self-rated health, even after adjusting for socioeconomic status. Addressing these patient-reported obstacles is essential to achieving health equity in urologic oncology.
lay_summary: Researchers studied why racial and ethnic minority people with renal cell carcinoma (kidney cancer) face worse care. Using medical records and surveys from 2,215 patients, they asked about money, social needs, and health understanding. Minority patients were younger and poorer. Almost 24% of Hispanic patients could not afford medicines versus 8% of White patients. 44% of Black and Hispanic patients rated their health fair or poor versus 29% of White patients. Costs, time off work, and transport stopped people from getting care, so health systems should fix these problems.

pdr_title: Defining Spiritual Wellbeing in Survivors of Stroke: A Convergent Parallel Mixed Methods Study
pdr_journal_title: Journal of the American Heart Association
pdr_abstract: Background: Stroke recovery involves adapting to physical impairments, emotional distress, and uncertainty about the future. Survivors of stroke may rely on spirituality and spiritual wellbeing practices to cope with illness. However, how survivors of stroke experience spiritual wellbeing remains unexplored. This study aimed to explore spiritual wellbeing in survivors of stroke and identify associated practices.    Methods: A convergent parallel mixed methods study using virtual focus groups with survivors of stroke and caregivers and survey data on spirituality using the All of Us research database was completed from October 2023 to February 2025. The framework method was used for qualitative data analysis and a 7-item spirituality survey completed by survivors of stroke was analyzed from the All of Us research database using descriptive statistics. Data sets were integrated through joint displays to assess coherence.    Results: A total of 41 participants completed 6 focus groups. In this context, spirituality was defined as trust in a higher power and maintaining emotional balance. Focus groups identified spiritual wellbeing practices, including mindfulness, prayer, and spending time in nature. These findings converged with survey data %28n=5428%29, with 70% of respondents endorsing connection with god/higher power. Spiritual practices extended beyond religious services, as 51.7% of respondents reported they did not attend religious services as a practice. Spending time in nature was a common practice, with 90.4% of respondents feeling spiritually touched by nature at least occasionally.    Conclusions: Spiritual wellbeing and its practices are important to survivors of stroke and can serve as a foundation for targeted interventions in poststroke care. Future research should investigate spiritual wellbeing in diverse populations to develop tailored interventions for survivors of stroke.
lay_summary: This study looked at how people who had a stroke feel about spiritual wellbeing and what helps them. Researchers held six online groups with 41 stroke survivors and caregivers and studied a survey of 5,428 survivors. Participants said spirituality meant trust in a higher power and staying emotionally balanced. Common practices were mindfulness, prayer, and time in nature. About 70% felt a connection with a higher power, 52% did not use religious services, and 90% felt nature touched them sometimes. These findings could help shape care after stroke.

pdr_title: Metabolic Risk Factors and Clinical Presentations of Metabolic Dysfunction-associated Steatotic Liver Disease Using Data from the I%28content=['All of Us']%29 Research Program
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Clinical and Translational Hepatology
pdr_abstract: Background And Aims: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease %28MASLD%29 affects approximately 32% of the US adult population. The present study aimed to utilize the All of Us electronic health record-linked large cohort to assess seven metabolic risk factors %28MRFs%29 simultaneously, the impact by ethnicity and age, and clinical presentations of MASLD.    Methods: This study included a MASLD group %28n = 15,060%29 and a frequency-matched control group %28n = 75,300%29. Multivariable analyses were performed to compare the frequencies of MRFs and clinical outcomes between the two groups. Type 1 diabetes was not included in the multivariable analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to race and ethnicity, as well as age.    Results: The overall frequency of MASLD was 6.0%. Compared with the control group, individuals with MASLD had significantly higher independent frequencies of obesity %2866.1% vs. 41.3%%29, type 2 diabetes %2839.5% vs. 16.9%%29, hypertension %2864.3% vs. 38.6%%29, hyperlipidemia %2859.8% vs. 37.3%%29, obstructive sleep apnea %2828.9% vs. 13.4%%29, and hypothyroidism %2821.2% vs. 13.4%%29. Obesity was identified as the strongest independent MRF among Asians, Whites, and Hispanics, particularly in individuals younger than 50 years, whereas hypertension was the strongest independent MRF in Blacks. MASLD was also associated with significantly higher frequencies of cardiac events, including coronary artery disease %2817.1% vs. 9.4%%29 and myocardial infarction %287.1% vs. 4.2%%29; hepatic events, including cirrhosis %287.5% vs. 1.1%%29 and hepatocellular carcinoma %280.5% vs. 0.1%%29; and elevated liver enzymes, including alanine aminotransferase %2827.7% vs. 10.1%%29, aspartate aminotransferase %2818.0% vs. 6.4%%29, and alkaline phosphatase %2819.8% vs. 13.1%%29, compared with the control group.    Conclusions: Our study demonstrated that obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, and hypothyroidism were independent MRFs for MASLD overall, but the ranking of these MRFs by odds ratios could vary by ethnicity and age. MASLD presents with significantly higher rates of alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase elevation, as well as cardiac and hepatic events.
lay_summary: Researchers used a large US medical record database to compare 15,060 people with MASLD (fatty liver from metabolic problems) to 75,300 without it. They checked seven metabolic risks and outcomes. People with MASLD had more obesity (66% vs 41%), type 2 diabetes (40% vs 17%), high blood pressure (64% vs 39%), high cholesterol (60% vs 37%), sleep apnea (29% vs 13%), and low thyroid function (21% vs 13%). They also had more heart disease and liver damage. Risk rankings varied by race and age. This means managing weight, blood pressure, diabetes, and cholesterol may cut liver and heart risks.

Conclusions: Our study demonstrated that obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, and hypothyroidism were independent MRFs for MASLD overall, but the ranking of these MRFs by odds ratios could vary by ethnicity and age. MASLD presents with significantly higher rates of alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alkaline phosphatase elevation, as well as cardiac and hepatic events.

pdr_title: Assessing data quality of rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis patients in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Purpose: Rheumatoid and Psoriatic Arthritis %28RA and PsA%29 are autoimmune diseases that cause debilitating joint pain. Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs %28DMARDs%29 are recommended for the treatment of both conditions. However, real-world evidence studies would help characterize compliance with these recommendations. The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model %28OMOP CDM%29 standardizes electronic health record %28EHR%29 data, allowing for research that incorporates multiple data sources. We are interested in determining whether OMOP CDM data on RA and PsA are fit-for-use.    Methods: We selected diagnosis codes for RA and PsA that were the basis for each phenotype. We used a data quality checklist to evaluate 5 domains systematically: conformance, completeness, concordance, plausibility, and temporality.    Results: Most phenotype-defining ICD source codes mapped to SNOMED. Both cohorts had low concept prevalences. Most concept correlations were weak %28ρ ≤ 0.5%29. The relative distribution of DMARD ingredients in both cohorts was consistent with prior studies. The proportion of the RA and PsA cohorts that had data for timing between event calculations ranged from 13% to 85% and 16% to 81%, respectively. Despite variability in concept sequence analysis, symptomatic treatment concepts for RA and PsA were preceded by rheumatoid factor concepts, followed by DMARD therapy and disease diagnosis concepts.    Conclusion: We have shown a novel implementation of our data quality framework on autoimmune disease cohorts.
lay_summary: Doctors studied health records of people with rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis to see if the data are good enough for research. They used a method that checks if records follow standards, are complete, match across sources, make sense, and have correct timing. Most diagnosis codes matched a standard system. Many specific items were rare and links between them were weak. Drug types matched what other studies found. Timing info was present in about 13%–85% of rheumatoid and 16%–81% of psoriatic patients. This means the records can help research but some info may be missing or uneven.

pdr_title: Atopic Comorbidities Associated With Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria: A Case-Control Analysis of the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Chronic spontaneous urticaria %28CSU%29 is a mast cell-driven condition defined by recurrent wheals and/or angioedema lasting over 6 weeks without an identifiable trigger. Though CSU is known to co-occur with atopic diseases and share Th2-dominant immunologic pathways, prior studies have not adequately addressed these relationships in diverse populations.    Objectives: To examine associations between CSU and atopic comorbidities in the All of Us %28AoU%29 research program, a diverse, nationwide National Institutes of Health cohort focused on increasing enrollment from historically underrepresented groups.    Methods: We conducted a matched, case-control study of AoU participants aged ≧18 years enrolled between May 6, 2018 and October 1, 2023. CSU cases were identified using SNOMED codes 51611005 and 42265009. Controls were matched 4:1 by age, sex, race, ethnicity, and smoking status. We compared rates of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, nasal polyps, food allergy, and drug allergy. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for hypothyroidism, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis given known associations with CSU.    Results: We identified 1171 CSU cases and 4684 matched controls with no significant demographic differences. CSU patients had significantly higher rates of atopic dermatitis %2812.6% vs. 1.7%, p<0.001%29, allergic rhinitis %2858% vs. 13.2%, p<0.001%29, asthma %2846.2% vs. 13.2%, p<0.001%29, nasal polyps %283.8% vs. 0.7%, p<0.001%29, and food and drug allergies %28p<0.001%29. These associations persisted after multivariable adjustment %28p<0.001%29.    Conclusions: This study demonstrates a strong association between CSU and atopic disease in a racially and socioeconomically diverse cohort. Our findings highlight shared Th2-driven pathways underlying CSU and atopy and reinforce the potential utility of type 2 targeted therapies %28e.g., dupilumab%29 in patients with CSU and comorbid atopic disease. Clinicians should screen CSU patients for atopic disease to help guide comprehensive, targeted therapy.
lay_summary: This study looked for links between chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), a condition with itchy hives or swelling lasting over 6 weeks, and other allergic diseases in a diverse U.S. group. Researchers compared 1,171 adults with CSU to 4,684 similar people without it. People with CSU had more eczema (12.6% vs 1.7%), hay fever (58% vs 13%), asthma (46% vs 13%), nasal polyps (3.8% vs 0.7%), and more food or drug allergies. This means doctors should check CSU patients for other allergies and some targeted medicines may help.

pdr_title: Time to Treatment Discontinuation and Cost Effectiveness of Third-Line Therapies in Advanced Colorectal Cancer: Real-World Evidence from the NIH All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Treatment options for patients with advanced colorectal cancer who progress after standard therapies remain limited, and real-world evidence on treatment durability and economic outcomes in later lines of therapy is needed to inform clinical and policy decision making. This study evaluated real-world outcomes, healthcare utilization, and cost effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors %28ICI%29 compared with regorafenib or trifluridine/tipiracil %28Rego/Tri%29 in third-line %283L%29 advanced colorectal cancer %28CRC%29, leveraging the nationally distributed NIH All of Us Research Program.    Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort cost-utility analysis using All of Us Version 8 Curated Data Repository. Eligible adults %28≥18 years%29 with advanced CRC initiated ICI %28pembrolizumab, nivolumab ± ipilimumab%29 or Rego/Tri during 2017-2023. Outcomes included time to treatment discontinuation %28TTD%29, healthcare utilization, costs, and quality-adjusted life years %28QALYs; base-case utility = 0.75%29. Costs were estimated from CMS 2023 schedules %28Part B ASP for infused agents, Part D unit costs for orals; inpatient/outpatient fee schedules for non-drug services%29, applied per cycle and proportionally for partial cycles. Analyses were conducted from the US Medicare payer perspective, with the time horizon limited to observed TTD and no discounting applied %28<1 year%29. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios %28ICERs%29, incremental net monetary benefit %28INMB%29, and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves %28CEACs%29 were estimated using nonparametric bootstrapping %281000 replicates%29. Sensitivity analyses varied utility weights %280.6-1.0%29.    Results: Among 82 patients %28ICI n = 50; Rego/Tri n = 32%29, median TTD was significantly longer with ICI %288.0 vs 1.4 months; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.30-0.79; p = 0.0037%29. Non-drug utilization costs were not significantly different, but ICI drug costs were higher %28US$207,558 vs US$119,805; p = 0.001%29. Mean total costs were US$476,729 for ICI versus US$264,225 for Rego/Tri %28p = 0.018%29. QALYs were higher for ICI %280.84 vs 0.43; p < 0.001%29. The ICER was US$518,000 per QALY gained. CEAC analysis demonstrated ~0% probability of cost effectiveness at US$150,000/QALY, ~50% at US$500,000/QALY, and ~80% at ≥US$1,000,000/QALY. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent findings.    Conclusions: In this exploratory analysis using the novel NIH All of Us Research Program, ICI therapy was associated with longer treatment duration and greater QALYs but substantially higher costs compared with Rego/Tri. ICI was unlikely to be cost effective at conventional US thresholds but may be favorable at higher willingness-to-pay values. These findings highlight both the promise of leveraging the All of Us Research Program for nationally distributed, demographically diverse pharmacoeconomic research and the challenges of interpreting real-world cost effectiveness in small cohorts. As the dataset matures and sample sizes increase, broader application of All of Us may provide valuable insights to inform precision oncology policy and value-based pricing strategies.
lay_summary: This study looked at 82 adults with advanced colorectal cancer who started third-line treatment from 2017–2023 to see how long treatments last and if they are worth the cost. It compared immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI, cancer immunotherapy) with regorafenib or trifluridine/tipiracil. Researchers checked treatment time, costs, and quality-adjusted life years (a measure of life length and quality). Patients on ICI stayed about 8 months versus 1.4 months, had higher quality-adjusted survival (0.84 vs 0.43), but much higher costs ($477k vs $264k). ICI may help patients more but costs a lot more and may not be judged good value.

pdr_title: Social determinants of healthy aging: An investigation using the all of us cohort
pdr_abstract: Introduction: The increasing aging population raises significant concerns about the ability of individuals to age healthily, avoiding chronic diseases and maintaining cognitive and physical functions. However, the pathways through which SDOH factors are associated with healthy aging remain unclear.    Methods: This retrospective cohort study uses the registered tier data from the All of Us Research Program %28AoURP%29 registered tier dataset v7. Eligible study participants are those aged 50 and older who have responded to any of the SDOH survey questions with available EHR data. Three different algorithms were trained %28logistic regression [LR], multi-layer perceptron [MLP], and extreme gradient boosting [XGBoost]%29. The outcome is healthy aging, which is measured by a composite score of the status for 1%29 comorbidities, 2%29 cognitive conditions, and 3%29 mobility function. We evaluate the model performance by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve %28AUROC%29 and assess the fairness of best-performed model through predictive parity. Feature importance is analyzed using SHapley Additive exPlanations %28SHAP%29 values.    Results: Our study included 99,935 participants aged 50 and above, and the mean %28SD%29 age was 74 %289.3%29, with 55,294 %2855.3%%29 females, 67,457 %2867.5%%29 Whites, 11,109 %2811.1%%29 Hispanic ethnicity, and 44,109 %2844.1%%29 are classified as healthy aging. Most of the individuals lived in their own house %2864%%29, were married %2851%%29, obtained college or advanced degrees %2874%%29, and had Medicare %2856.2%%29. The best predictive model was XGBoost with random oversampler, with a performance of AUROC [95% CI]: 0.793 [0.788-0.796], F1 score: 0.697 [0.692-0.701], recall: 0.739 [0.732-0.748], precision: 0.659 [0.655-0.663], and accuracy: 0.716 [0.712-0.720], and the XGBoost model achieved predictive parity by similar positive and negative predictive values across race and sex groups %280.86-1.06%29. In feature importance analysis, health insurance type is ranked as the most predictive feature, followed by employment status, substance use, and health insurance coverage %28yes/no%29.    Conclusion: In this cohort study, XGBoost model accurately predicted individuals achieving healthy aging, outperforming LR and MLP. Our findings underscore the significant role of health insurance in contributing to healthy aging.
lay_summary: Researchers studied 99,935 people aged 50 and older (average age 74) to see how social factors affect healthy aging. They used health records and surveys and tested three computer models to predict healthy aging (based on illnesses, thinking, and walking). About 44% were aging healthily. The best model (XGBoost, a computer algorithm) predicted well and worked similarly for different races and sexes. The top social factor was type of health insurance, then employment and substance use. This means having health coverage and steady work may help people age better.

pdr_abstract: In this retrospective study utilizing data from the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program, individuals with Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy %28n=548%29 exhibited a higher burden of cardiometabolic disease than matched controls %28n=5,480%29.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy (an eye disease that affects the clear front part of the eye) is linked to heart and metabolic illnesses. They looked back at health records from the NIH All of Us program and compared 548 people with Fuchs' to 5,480 similar people without it. People with Fuchs' had more heart and metabolism problems (cardiometabolic = heart, blood vessel, and metabolism illnesses). This means doctors and patients may want to watch for these conditions if someone has Fuchs'.

pdr_title: Wearable-derived REM sleep as a modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease: A multimodal prediction model in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Sleep is increasingly recognized as a modifiable factor for cardiovascular diseases %28CVDs%29, yet the roles of specific sleep stages, particularly rapid eye movement %28REM%29 sleep, and the utility of wearable-derived sleep parameters for CVD prediction remain unknown. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the associations of sleep with CVD risk and to develop multimodal prediction models for incident CVD. Using data from the All of Us Research Program, 23,413 adults who consented to share both Fitbit and electronic health record data between May 2018 and October 2023 were included in the analysis. Sleep data were obtained from Fitbit wearable devices, including sleep duration and stage-specific information such as REM sleep. Incident CVD was defined as occurring at least six months after the initiation of Fitbit monitoring. Cox proportional hazards models were applied to estimate adjusted hazard ratios %28aHR%29 with 95% confidence intervals %28CIs%29 for sleep duration and REM sleep in association with CVD. For the prediction of CVD within six years, two modeling strategies were implemented, including a non-invasive multimodal model using demographic, self-reported, and wearable-derived data and an invasive multimodal model that additionally incorporated laboratory measures. To compare real-world model performance, we applied and compared several conventional risk prediction models, including SCORE2, the Framingham Risk Score, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and the Pooled Cohort Equations. Among 23,413 participants %28mean [standard deviation] age, 56.7 [15.5] years; 70.9% female%29, both short %28<7 h%29 and long %28≥9 h%29 sleep durations were associated with higher risk of CVDs compared with 7 to 9 h of sleep %28short sleep: aHR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.07 to 1.27]; long sleep: aHR, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.10 to 1.58]%29, with U-shaped relationship. Individuals with less than 20% REM sleep had a greater risk of CVDs %28aHR, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.18 to 1.45]%29 compared with those with 20% to 25% REM sleep. These associations were consistent across CVD subtypes. In prediction analyses, soft-voting ensemble models with LightGBM and XGBoost integrating wearable, clinical, and laboratory data achieved high performance %28AUROC of non-invasive models, 0.748; AUROC of invasive models, 0.782%29, outperforming conventional risk scores %28SCORE2, the Framingham Risk Score, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and the Pooled Cohort Equations: AUROC range, 0.649 to 0.685%29. Short and long sleep durations, as well as reduced REM sleep, were associated with increased risk of CVD. We also derived and validated a multimodal model to predict the incidence of CVD within six years. These findings support the potential value of integrating objective sleep-stage measures and multimodal digital health data into future cardiovascular prevention strategies and guideline development.
lay_summary: Researchers used Fitbit and health records from 23,413 adults to see if sleep affects new heart and blood vessel disease. They tracked new cases starting six months after monitoring began. Sleeping less than 7 hours or 9 hours or more raised heart disease risk compared to 7–9 hours (about 16% and 32% higher). Having under 20% REM sleep (REM is the dreaming stage) raised risk by about 31%. Computer models that used wearable sleep data predicted heart disease better than older tools. Keeping regular sleep length and enough REM may help lower risk.

In prediction analyses, soft-voting ensemble models with LightGBM and XGBoost integrating wearable, clinical, and laboratory data achieved high performance (AUROC of non-invasive models, 0.748; AUROC of invasive models, 0.782), outperforming conventional risk scores (SCORE2, the Framingham Risk Score, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and the Pooled Cohort Equations: AUROC range, 0.649 to 0.685). Short and long sleep durations, as well as reduced REM sleep, were associated with increased risk of CVD. We also derived and validated a multimodal model to predict the incidence of CVD within six years. These findings support the potential value of integrating objective sleep-stage measures and multimodal digital health data into future cardiovascular prevention strategies and guideline development.
