pdr_title: Early change in daily step counts after antidepressant initiation among adults with depression: A within-person interrupted time series study
pdr_abstract: Objective: Early real-world activity changes after starting antidepressants are not well described. This study aimed to quantify short-term changes in daily ambulatory activity around antidepressant initiation using wearables.    Methods: We analyzed the All of Us Research Program CDR v8 %28data cutoff October 1, 2023%29. Adults with incident major depressive disorder and a first antidepressant %28ATC N06A%29 record within 90 days were included. Prior-year antidepressant use and history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder were excluded. Fitbit step counts were summarized daily from 60 days before to 60 days after the index date. Valid days required ≥600 min of non-missing minute-level heart rate data. We fit a within-person mixed-effects piecewise interrupted time-series model on log steps with breakpoints at day 0 and day 14, adjusting for day of week.    Results: Among 168 participants %28mean age 44.2 years; 78% female%29, steps declined in pre-index period %28-0.16%/day; p = 0.027%29. During days 0-14 after initiation, the slope increased versus pre-index %28p = 0.012%29, with predicted mean steps rising from 6634 %28day 0%29 to 7341 %28day 14; ~0.74%/day%29. After day 14, changes were minimal %28~0.07%/day%29. An immediate decrease at initiation was observed %28-9.7%; p = 0.031%29. After additionally adjusting for days 0-2, the increasing trend over days 0-14 remained.    Conclusions: Daily Fitbit step counts captured distinct activity patterns in the first two weeks after antidepressant initiation, suggesting wearables can support high-frequency monitoring during treatment start.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see how people’s daily walking changed when they started antidepressant medicine. They looked at 168 adults with new depression who wore Fitbits and counted steps for 60 days before and after starting treatment. Steps fell a little each day before starting and dropped about 10% on the day the medicine began. Over the next two weeks average steps rose from about 6,600 to 7,300 per day (about 700 more). After two weeks there was little change. This shows wearables can help track activity when treatment starts.
calc_title: Early change in daily step counts after antidepressant initiation among adults with depression: A within-person interrupted time series study
calc_abstract: Objective: Early real-world activity changes after starting antidepressants are not well described. This study aimed to quantify short-term changes in daily ambulatory activity around antidepressant initiation using wearables.    Methods: We analyzed the All of Us Research Program CDR v8 (data cutoff October 1, 2023). Adults with incident major depressive disorder and a first antidepressant (ATC N06A) record within 90 days were included. Prior-year antidepressant use and history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder were excluded. Fitbit step counts were summarized daily from 60 days before to 60 days after the index date. Valid days required ≥600 min of non-missing minute-level heart rate data. We fit a within-person mixed-effects piecewise interrupted time-series model on log steps with breakpoints at day 0 and day 14, adjusting for day of week.    Results: Among 168 participants (mean age 44.2 years; 78% female), steps declined in pre-index period (-0.16%/day; p = 0.027). After day 14, changes were minimal (~0.07%/day). An immediate decrease at initiation was observed (-9.7%; p = 0.031). After additionally adjusting for days 0-2, the increasing trend over days 0-14 remained.    Conclusions: Daily Fitbit step counts captured distinct activity patterns in the first two weeks after antidepressant initiation, suggesting wearables can support high-frequency monitoring during treatment start.

pdr_title: How Genomic and Structural Context Could Shape JAK-STAT Variant Pathogenicity
pdr_journal_title: Twin Research and Human Genetics : The Official Journal of the International Society for Twin Studies
pdr_abstract: The Janus kinase %28JAK%29-Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription %28STAT%29 pathway is essential for cellular signal transduction, regulating immune responses, hematopoiesis, and cell proliferation. Dysregulation of JAK-STAT signaling due to genetic variations, particularly missense mutations, has been implicated in autoimmune disorders, cancers, and hematological malignancies. This study investigates missense mutations in JAK and STAT genes, focusing on disease-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms %28SNPs%29 and ClinVar benign variants identified in the All of Us and COSMIC databases. We analyzed the distribution of these mutations across functional domains, their structural localization, and biochemical properties. We identified mutation hotspots within specific domains, highlighting their correlation with disease phenotypes. Structural mapping revealed that disease-associated SNPs predominantly localize in linker regions and at the boundaries of secondary structures, suggesting a significant impact on folding, stability, and function of JAK and STAT proteins. Additionally, we examined the genomic context of mutations and identified vulnerable sequences; for example, 'GATC'. Furthermore, our analysis found no predominant association between potential CRISPR-Cas9 target sites and ClinVar benign/disease-associated SNPs. The analysis of amino acid sequence patterns surrounding mutations uncovered an enrichment of hydrophobic residues leucine %28Leu%29, isoleucine %28Ile%29, methionine %28Met%29, and phenylalanine %28Phe%29 in close proximity to disease-associated mutations. Our findings emphasize the importance of structural and biochemical context in determining pathogenicity. In this study, we provide a bioinformatic strategy for refining variant classification and understanding the roles of JAK-STAT pathway mutations in disease.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see how changes in the JAK-STAT genes affect disease. They looked at single-letter gene changes (missense mutations) from large public datasets (All of Us, COSMIC, and ClinVar) and mapped them onto protein parts and DNA sequences. They found mutation hotspots in certain protein areas. Disease-linked changes were often in linker regions and at edges of folded parts, which can hurt protein shape and function. A short DNA pattern 'GATC' was often vulnerable. Certain nearby amino acids (Leu, Ile, Met, Phe) appeared more often. This work can help doctors better tell harmful from harmless gene changes.

pdr_title: Novel Systemic Associations of Idiopathic Epiretinal Membrane Identified via Machine Learning
pdr_abstract: Purpose: To discover novel systemic associations that may lead to idiopathic epiretinal membrane %28iERM%29 using interpretable machine learning models.    Design: Large data retrospective case-control study.    Subjects: All of Us Dataset, including a total of 10 380 patients: 2015 iERM patients with 2015 1:1 matched controls, 3175 secondary epiretinal membrane %28sERM%29 patients with 3175 1:1 matched controls.    Methods: Electronic health records of epiretinal membrane %28ERM%29 patients from the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide longitudinal cohort of US adults %28data from 6/2016 to 2/2025%29 were collected. Unsupervised clustering using principal component analysis was performed on the data set to identify distinct patient subgroups. Supervised machine learning models, including gradient-boosted decision trees and logistic regression, were trained to predict iERM.    Main Outcome Measures: Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve %28AUC%29, while feature importance was assessed using the Gini index for tree-based models and coefficient magnitudes for logistic regression. Additionally, odds ratios for comorbidities associated with both iERM and sERM were estimated using 2 × 2 contingency tables.    Results: Unsupervised clustering of iERM patients revealed 4 distinct subgroups characterized by unique systemic comorbidity profiles, including cardiometabolic, dermatologic, and joint disorder pathways. Clusters demonstrated significant associations with systemic conditions such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory skin conditions, osteoarthritis, and anemia. Supervised models, including logistic regression and gradient-boosted decision trees, achieved AUC values exceeding 0.679 on a testing set. Key predictors of iERM included knee osteoarthritis, hyperlipidemia, essential hypertension, and sensorineural hearing loss, each demonstrating high coefficient magnitudes, Gini importance, and statistically significant odds ratios.    Conclusions: This study challenges conventional distinctions between iERM and sERM, proposing systemic comorbidities as associations to ERM development. The observed associations with cardiometabolic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and joint and dermatologic disorders suggest that systemic mechanisms may significantly influence ERM pathogenesis. Future studies are necessary to establish causality and explore targeted therapeutic approaches, potentially incorporating anti-inflammatory treatments or cardiovascular risk management to prevent ERM formation. These findings highlight opportunities for personalized risk assessment and preventative interventions based on systemic comorbidity profiles. lay_summary: Researchers wanted to find health problems linked to idiopathic epiretinal membrane (iERM), a thin scar on the retina that can affect vision. They looked at medical records from 10,380 people in the All of Us database, including 2,015 with iERM, and used computer programs that learn patterns (machine learning). They found four patient groups and links between iERM and high blood pressure, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory skin conditions, osteoarthritis (joint wear), anemia, knee arthritis, and hearing loss. This suggests that treating these health issues might help doctors spot or lower the risk of this eye problem.

pdr_title: Biologics Use Disparities in Non-Infectious Uveitis: A National Study of Social Determinants of Health
pdr_abstract: Purpose: To determine whether insurance status, household income, race, sex, or age influence receipt of biologic therapy among U.S. patients with non-infectious uveitis.    Methods: We analyzed NIH All of Us data %282005-2022%29 in a nationwide retrospective cohort study. Patients were identified by ICD-9, ICD-10, and SNOMED codes. Multivariable logistic regression tested associations between race, sex at birth, income, insurance, and age and the primary outcome of biologic use. Individuals with missing data were retained as separate strata. Adjusted odds ratios %28OR%29 with 95% confidence intervals %28CI%29 were calculated.    Results: Out of 2911 patients, 244 %288.4%%29 received biologics. Treatment proportions varied across demographic and socioeconomic strata. The strongest predictor of reduced biologic use was uninsured status %28OR 0.23, CI: 0.037-0.728%29. Income below $35K %28OR 0.55, CI: 0.367-0.812%29 and $35K-$50K %28OR 0.46, CI: 0.237-0.840%29 were also associated with lower biologic use. Participants with missing household income data also demonstrated lower odds of receiving biologic therapy. African American and Hispanic patients demonstrated decreased odds of receiving biologics %28OR 0.58, CI: 0.399-0.839; OR 0.66, CI: 0.434-0.989%29. Females were more likely to receive biologics %28OR 1.46, CI: 1.089-1.962%29. Each incremental year in age exhibited decreased odds of biologics treatment %28OR 0.97, p < 0.001%29.    Conclusion: Access to biologic therapy for non-infectious uveitis varies by insurance, income, race, sex, and age. Insurance coverage exerted the greatest effect, indicating that payer policy is the main determinant of overall treatment allocation in the U.S. healthcare system.
lay_summary: This study looked at 2,911 U.S. patients with non-infectious uveitis using national health records from 2005–2022 to see who received biologic medications (advanced drugs that target the immune system). Only 8.4% (244) got biologics. People without insurance, with household incomes under $35,000 or $35,000–$50,000, Black or Hispanic patients, and older people were less likely to get these drugs, while women were more likely. The biggest factor was having insurance, so insurance rules decide who gets treatment and may leave some people without needed care.

pdr_title: Determinants of chromosome-specific telomere lengths among 2573 All of Us participants
pdr_abstract: Telomere length is a biomarker of aging and disease risk. Most human studies have assessed average telomere length, limiting our understanding of variability across chromosome arms. Using long-read sequencing data from >2500 All of Us participants, we estimate chromosome-specific telomere lengths and characterize sources of biological and technical variation. Telomere length varies by chromosome arm, accounting for 9.1% of total variance. Substantial variance %288.9%%29 in chromosome-specific telomere lengths is attributable to individual, independent of age, suggesting that inter-individual differences in length are established at birth and maintained through life. Age is inversely associated with length for all arms, but longer arms show stronger association. We demonstrate that chromosome-specific telomere estimates enable analysis of disease associations for individual telomeres and for individuals' shortest telomere. Overall, this work highlights the utility of long-read sequencing for population-scale analysis of chromosome-specific telomere lengths and provides a framework to guide future studies.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know why telomere length (telomeres are protective caps on chromosomes that shorten with age) differs between chromosome ends and people. They measured telomere length for each chromosome arm in long-read DNA data from over 2,500 All of Us participants. They found about 9% of variation comes from which chromosome arm it is, and about 9% comes from differences between people that seem set at birth and stay through life. Telomeres got shorter with age on all arms, especially the longer ones. This method can help link specific telomeres to disease risk and guide future health studies.

pdr_title: Genomic, phenomic and geographic associations of leukocyte telomere length in the United States
pdr_abstract: Leukocyte telomere length %28LTL%29 is associated with multiple conditions, including cardiovascular diseases and neoplasms, yet their differential associations across diverse individuals are largely unknown. We estimated LTL from blood-derived whole-genome sequences in the All of Us research program %28n=242,494%29 with diverse ancestries across the USA. LTL was associated with lifestyle, socioeconomic status, biomarkers, cardiometabolic diseases and neoplasms, with heterogeneity across genetic ancestries and sexes. Geographical analysis revealed that significantly longer LTL clustered in the West Coast and Central Midwest, while significantly shorter LTL clustered in the Southeast in the USA. Genome-wide association studies and meta-analyses with the UK Biobank %28n=679,972%29 found 234 nonoverlapping loci, of which 37 were novel. We identified six novel loci unique to non-European-like populations and one specific to women. Rare variant analysis uncovered nine novel genes, providing new functional insights. Our study highlighted underappreciated contextual heterogeneities of phenomic and genomic associations with LTL.

pdr_title: Leveraging Large and Diverse Biobanks to Evaluate Gene-Disease Associations in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
pdr_abstract: Background: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy %28HCM%29 is a common inherited disease and a leading known cause of sudden cardiac arrest in young adults and athletes. While genetic testing has advanced rapidly in the past decade, the yield of genetic testing remains low. The Clinical Genome Resource %28ClinGen%29 initiative has become a leading resource for defining the clinical relevance of genetic variants with expert groups focusing on evaluating the strength of evidence for each HCM implicated gene. With the rise of large biobanks and population databases, genetic discovery has been significantly advanced. However, whether these databases can be used to validate gene-disease associations curated by ClinGen and provide evidence for novel gene-disease associations remains unclear. Objectives: Here, we utilized a publicly available database containing 748,879 individuals across three large biobanks %28All of Us, UK biobank, Mass General Brigham biobank%29. Methods: We tested the association of rare coding variants in each gene in the HCM ClinGen panel with HCM. In total, 38 genes were tested, and Bonferroni correction was applied accordingly. Results: Of the 12 genes with definitive evidence for HCM %28e.g., MYBPC3, MYH7, TNNT2, ALPK3%29, 8 %2867%%29 demonstrated nominally significant association with HCM on a population level, and 5 %2842%%29 remained significant after Bonferroni correction, further supporting the validity of these genes in HCM panels. Several definitive genes which are much less commonly affected in HCM %28CSRP3, MYL3, ACTC1, TPM1, FHOD3, MYL2, and TNNC1%29 did not pass our Bonferroni corrected-significance threshold, but all had positively associated effect sizes with HCM. No genes deemed to have moderate or limited evidence had any significant associations with HCM even before Bonferroni correction. Conclusions: Altogether, we show that large biobanks and population databases generally recapitulate established gene-disease associations for HCM and support the ClinGen group's gene curations. The utilization of such publicly accessible databases represents an additional tool for assessing gene validity in monogenic cardiac disorders with an established phenotype, although it may have limited sensitivity and should not be solely relied on.
lay_summary: Scientists wanted to see if very large health databases can confirm which genes cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), an inherited heart problem. They looked at rare gene changes in 748,879 people from three big biobanks (large health databases) and tested 38 HCM-linked genes. Of 12 genes thought to be definitely linked to HCM, 8 (67%) showed a link and 5 (42%) still showed a link after strict checks. Genes with weaker evidence showed no clear links. This means big databases can help check gene links, but doctors should not use them alone.

pdr_title: Machine learning predicts hepatocellular carcinoma risk from routine clinical data: a large population-based multicentric study
pdr_abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma %28HCC%29 is a highly fatal tumor, for which risk stratification is crucial, yet remains challenging. Here, we develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for HCC risk stratification based on routinely collected clinical data. We utilize prospectively collected multimodal data from over 900,000 individuals and 983 cases of HCC across two population-scale cohorts: the 'UK Biobank study' %28development%29 and the 'All of Us Research Program' %28external testing%29. We assess individual and cumulative contributions of data modalities including demographics, lifestyle, health records, blood, genomics, and metabolomics. Our final, random-forest-based models significantly outperform all publicly available state-of-the-art risk-scores on both internal and external test sets. We demonstrate robustness across ethnic subgroups, provide comprehensive interpretability and release all code, model weights and a web-calculator for external validation and agentic integration. Our study presents PRE-Screen-HCC, a robust and interpretable machine-learning framework for HCC risk stratification and early detection.

lay_summary: This study made a computer program that uses regular health information to predict who might get liver cancer (HCC). Researchers used data from over 900,000 people, including 983 actual liver cancer cases, from two big studies. They trained and tested the program with things like age, lifestyle, medical records, blood tests, genes and small molecules in blood. calc_title: Machine learning predicts hepatocellular carcinoma risk from routine clinical data: a large population-based multicentric study
calc_abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly fatal tumor, for which risk stratification is crucial, yet remains challenging. Here, we develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for HCC risk stratification based on routinely collected clinical data. We utilize prospectively collected multimodal data from over 900,000 individuals and 983 cases of HCC across two population-scale cohorts: the 'UK Biobank study' (development) and the 'All of Us Research Program' (external testing). We assess individual and cumulative contributions of data modalities including demographics, lifestyle, health records, blood, genomics, and metabolomics. Our final, random-forest-based models significantly outperform all publicly available state-of-the-art risk-scores on both internal and external test sets. We demonstrate robustness across ethnic subgroups, provide comprehensive interpretability and release all code, model weights and a web-calculator for external validation and agentic integration. Our study presents PRE-Screen-HCC, a robust and interpretable machine-learning framework for HCC risk stratification and early detection.

pdr_title: The DNA virome varies with human genes and environments
pdr_abstract: Many viruses have adapted to persist in infected humans for life1,2. Variable host control of their ongoing abundance %28viral load%29 can lead to clearance or disease3-5. Here we analysed the viral DNA load of 31 common viruses in human blood and saliva using whole-genome sequencing data from UK Biobank %28n=490,401%29, All of Us %28n=414,817%29 and Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research for Knowledge %28SPARK; n=12,519%29. Viral DNA load varied markedly with age, time of day and season; most viruses were also present at greater abundance in men than in women. Human genetic variation at dozens of loci associated with DNA load of seven viruses: Epstein-Barr virus %28EBV, 45 loci%29, human herpesvirus %28HHV%29-7 %2837 loci%29, HHV-6B, Merkel cell polyomavirus and three anelloviruses. Variation at the major histocompatibility complex %28MHC%29 locus generated the strongest associations %28P = 5.8 × 10-9 to 2.5 × 10-1459%29, which were specific to each virus. The HLA-B*08:01 allele also exhibited a host-virus genetic interaction with EBV subtype %28P = 7.4 × 10-70%29. Other human genetic effects implicated genes encoding proteins that process peptides for antigen presentation, such as ERAP1 %28HHV-7, P = 2.7 × 10-78%29 and ERAP2 %28EBV, P = 4.6 × 10-111%29. Mendelian randomization analyses supported a strong causal effect of EBV DNA load on increased risk of Hodgkin's lymphoma %28P = 1.8 × 10-3%29, but not multiple sclerosis %28P = 0.52%29. This suggests that higher chronic EBV load increases lymphoma risk, whereas associations of EBV infection with autoimmune conditions reflect host immune responses to particular viral epitopes.
lay_summary: Researchers studied viral DNA in blood and saliva from about 900,000 people using whole-genome sequencing to see how genes and the environment affect 31 common viruses. Viral levels changed with age, time of day, season, and were generally higher in men. Dozens of human gene regions, especially the MHC (a key immune gene area), were linked to levels of seven viruses, including Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Genetic analyses suggested higher long-term EBV levels raise the chance of Hodgkin’s lymphoma (a cancer) but not multiple sclerosis. This means genes and daily life shape virus levels and can affect health risks.

pdr_title: Socioeconomic Correlates of Incident Heart Failure and Consequent Mortality: The All of Us Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Although socioeconomic status %28SES%29 is a known determinant of cardiovascular disease, the independent risks of incident heart failure %28HF%29 and consequent mortality portended by individual and neighborhood measures of SES remain less established.    Objectives: This study sought to evaluate the prospective associations of SES with HF in adults without HF and SES with all-cause mortality in those with HF.    Methods: The authors identified adults from the National Institutes of Health-run All of Us Research Program %282018-present%29 who consented to share their electronic health records. Among 280,431 participants free of HF and 10,550 participants with prevalent HF, Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations of income, education, and Area Deprivation Index %28ADI%29 with risks of incident HF and mortality.    Results: Over 41 ± 23 months, 6,783 of 280,431 participants developed HF. Compared with household income ≥$200,000, risk was higher for $100,000 to <$200,000 %28HR: 1.29; 95% CI: 1.12-1.48%29, $50,000 to <$100,000 %28HR: 1.82; 95% CI: 1.60-2.09%29, $25,000 to <$50,000 %28HR: 2.24; 95% CI: 1.95-2.57%29, and <$25,000 %28HR: 3.02; 95% CI: 2.63-3.47%29. Relative to college graduates, risk was higher for those with some college %28HR: 1.37; 95% CI: 1.28-1.46%29, General Educational Development %28HR: 1.46; 95% CI: 1.36-1.58%29, and less than high school %28HR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.26-1.55%29. Compared with the least deprived tertile of ADI, risk was higher in the middle tertile %28HR: 1.21; 95% CI: 1.14-1.29%29 and the most deprived tertile %28HR: 1.18; 95% CI: 1.11-1.26%29. Non-White participants and residents of the most deprived ADI tertiles experienced less benefit from higher education. Among those with prevalent HF, each $10,000 increase in income was associated with 3% lower all-cause mortality.    Conclusions: Lower income, education, and high neighborhood deprivation independently associate with incident HF, whereas only income was associated with mortality. Higher education was less protective in non-White participants and individuals residing in deprived neighborhoods. Addressing these disparities is essential to reducing HF burden and consequent mortality.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at health records from 280,431 U.S. adults without heart failure and 10,550 with heart failure in the All of Us study to see if income, education, and neighborhood hardship (how poor a neighborhood is) matter. Over about three and a half years, 6,783 people developed heart failure. People earning under $25,000 had about three times the risk versus those earning $200,000 or more. Less schooling and worse neighborhoods also raised risk. For people with heart failure, each $10,000 more income meant about 3% lower chance of dying. This shows poverty, lower education, and poor neighborhoods raise heart failure risk and need attention.

pdr_title: Conductive Hearing Loss Pathologies are Associated With Depression in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_journal_title: Otology & Neurotology : Official Publication of the American Otological Society, American Neurotology Society [And] European Academy of Otology and Neurotology
pdr_abstract: Objective: Prior cross-sectional analysis suggests an association between conductive hearing loss %28CHL%29 and depression. However, little is known about the potential impact of specific CHL pathologies on mood disorders. We investigate if there is an association between 3 potentially correctable causes of CHL %28otosclerosis, cholesteatoma, and tympanic membrane perforation%29 and depressive disorders in a national cohort.    Study Design: Cross-sectional epidemiologic study.    Setting: National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program.    Patients: Participants 18 years or older %28n=363,302%29. Exposures were CHL pathologies defined by ICD-10 code: otosclerosis %28H80.X%29, cholesteatoma %28H71.X%29, and tympanic membrane perforation %28H72.X%29.    Main Outcome Measures: Outcomes were depressive disorders defined by ICD-10 code: major depressive disorder %28MDD; F32-33%29 and dysthymia %28F34.1%29. Multivariable regression, adjusting for potential confounders %28age, sex, race, ethnicity, education, and smoking history%29, assessed the odds of depression in subjects with and without specific CHL pathologies.    Results: The median age %28interquartile range, range%29 was 57 years [41 to 69, 18 to 122]; 62% identified as female. Controlling for covariates, the odds of MDD were 1.5 times %2895% CI: 1.2-1.9; P<0.001%29 higher for those with otosclerosis compared with those without; no association was seen with dysthymia. The odds of MDD and dysthymia were 1.8 times %281.5 to 2.3; P<0.001%29 and 2.2 times %281.2 to 3.6; P=0.004%29 higher, respectively, for those with cholesteatoma, and 2.4 times %282.2 to 2.6; P<0.001%29 and 2.8 times %282.2 to 3.5; P<0.001%29 higher, respectively, for those with tympanic membrane perforation.    Conclusions: In the All of Us dataset, all CHL pathologies were associated with MDD and most with dysthymia. This adds evidence that sensory deprivation from a purely peripheral process may impact mood.

lay_summary: Researchers studied health records of 363,302 adults to see if three treatable ear problems that cause hearing loss—otosclerosis, cholesteatoma, and eardrum holes—are linked to depression. They used diagnosis codes to compare people with and without these conditions. Otosclerosis had about a 50% higher rate of major depression. Cholesteatoma had about an 80% higher rate of major depression and double the rate of long‑term low mood (dysthymia). Eardrum holes had about 140–180% higher rates of both depression types. This means doctors should check mood in patients with these ear problems.

pdr_title: Conductive Hearing Loss is Associated With Dementia in the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Objectives: Sensorineural hearing loss %28SNHL%29 has been associated with cognitive impairment and dementia. However, because SNHL contains a neural component, it is difficult to completely exclude reverse causation whereby dementia causes worse SNHL. Conductive hearing loss %28CHL%29, a purely peripheral phenomenon, would not have this mechanistic connection. We investigate the association between CHL and dementia in a large national cohort.    Methods: Cross-sectional study of ≥18-year-old %28n=338,048%29 voluntary participants from the NIH All of Us Research Program. The exposure was bilateral CHL defined by ICD-10 code %28H90.0%29. The outcome was dementia defined by ICD-10 codes %28F03, G30-32%29. The odds of dementia in subjects with and without CHL were assessed with multivariable regression, controlling for potentially confounding variables %28age, sex, ethnicity, race, education, and smoking history%29, as well as surgical and medical interventions for CHL.    Results: The mean %28SD, range%29 age was 54years %28±17%29. 62.9% %28n=212,623%29 of participants identified as female. The cohort included 393 %280.1%%29 individuals with CHL. 1.9% %28n=6597%29 had dementia. After controlling for covariates, the odds of dementia were 2.05 times %2895% CI 1.18-3.32; p=0.006%29 higher for those with CHL compared to those without CHL. The odds were variably reduced when surgical interventions %28stapedectomy, tympanoplasty, mastoidectomy, myringoplasty%29 %28OR=2.03, CI 1.17-3.29; p=0.007%29 or hearing devices %28hearing aids, implants%29 %28OR=1.98, CI 1.13-3.21; p=0.010%29 were added to the fully adjusted multivariable model.    Conclusion: In the All of Us Research Program, CHL was strongly associated with dementia and treatment of CHL, both surgically and non-surgically, minimally reduced the odds of dementia.

lay_summary: This study asked whether conductive hearing loss (CHL), a problem that blocks sound in the ear, is linked to dementia. Researchers looked at records from 338,048 adults in a national database. 393 people had CHL and 6,597 had dementia. After accounting for age, sex, race, education, and smoking, people with CHL were twice as likely to have dementia as those without. Treatments (surgery or hearing aids) only slightly reduced this link. Because the study looked at one point in time, it cannot prove CHL causes dementia. The result suggests checking and treating CHL may be important for brain health.

pdr_title: Extensive genetic interactions %28epistasis%29 linked to alcohol use disorder in a high-risk population
pdr_abstract: Alcohol use disorder %28AUD%29 is known to have a significant genetic component, yet there remains a gap between its heritability and findings from genome-wide association studies. One potential explanation for this could be genetic interactions, or epistasis, which remain largely unexplored in the context of AUD. We investigated the role of epistasis in AUD susceptibility among 742 American Indians. By analyzing 467K variants in 3,736 genes and regulatory elements linked to AUD, we identified 97 interacting gene pairs significantly associated with AUD severity in an American Indian cohort. Five of these gene pairs: CNTNAP2-GRM8, CSMD1-DLGAP1, CSMD1-ERBB4, CSMD1-MAML2, and KCNQ5-ROBO2 - were replicated in All of Us research American Indian cohort %28N=5,037%29. These genes were enriched for immune system, cell adhesion, neuronal, and disease pathways. Their expressions were particularly enriched in midbrain GABAergic neurons. This large-scale epistasis study of AUD suggests that epistasis may contribute to the development of AUD.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if interactions between genes (called epistasis, meaning genetic interactions) help explain alcohol use disorder (AUD). They studied DNA from 742 American Indian people and looked at many gene parts linked to AUD. They found 97 pairs of genes that work together and are tied to how severe AUD is. Five of those pairs were also found in another group of 5,037 American Indians. These genes affect the immune system, cell connections, and certain brain cells. This suggests gene interactions may help explain AUD and could lead to better tests or treatments.

pdr_title: Unraveling the genetic architecture of non-Huntington chorea: a biobank-scale study of rare variants and repeat expansions
pdr_abstract: Chorea can arise from genetic, metabolic, pharmacologic, and autoimmune causes. In clinical practice, however, non-genetic causes are rare. The most common genetic cause is a CAG repeat expansion in HTT, leading to Huntington's disease %28HD%29. Beyond HD, systematic studies have been lacking and many individuals with non-HD chorea remain without a molecular diagnosis. We conducted whole-exome and genome sequencing analysis on 190 non-HD chorea cases, leveraging data from the All of Us Research Program %28n=134%29, UK Biobank %28n=26%29, and a clinically ascertained multicenter Spanish cohort recruited by the Spanish Study Group for Genetics of Chorea %28SSGGC%29 %28n=30%29. Variant calling was performed without pre-filtering based on a disease or gene list, and variants were clinically contextualized using OMIM, ClinVar, and in silico predictions. We identified thirteen protein-altering variants, including six previously described as pathogenic or likely pathogenic. Notably, we identified a pathogenic JPH3 expansion in a patient of Black race and c9orf72 expansions in individuals of European and South Asian ancestry. These findings explained 23% of cases in the SSGGC, 12% in UK Biobank, and 4% in All of Us. Our results broaden the genetic architecture of non-HD chorea and highlight the value of multi-ancestry genomic approaches for rare movement disorders.
lay_summary: The study looked for genetic causes of chorea that are not Huntington's disease because many people with this movement problem have no diagnosis. Researchers sequenced genes from 190 people with non‑HD chorea from three groups: All of Us (134), UK Biobank (26), and a Spanish clinical group (30). They found 13 gene changes that affect proteins, including six already known to cause disease, and repeat expansions (extra copies of DNA) in JPH3 and C9orf72. Genetic causes explained 23% of Spanish, 12% of UK, and 4% of All of Us cases. This shows more diverse genetic testing can help diagnose patients and guide care.

We conducted whole-exome and genome sequencing analysis on 190 non-HD chorea cases, leveraging data from the All of Us Research Program (n=134), UK Biobank (n=26), and a clinically ascertained multicenter Spanish cohort recruited by the Spanish Study Group for Genetics of Chorea (SSGGC) (n=30). Variant calling was performed without pre-filtering based on a disease or gene list, and variants were clinically contextualized using OMIM, ClinVar, and in silico predictions. We identified thirteen protein-altering variants, including six previously described as pathogenic or likely pathogenic. Notably, we identified a pathogenic JPH3 expansion in a patient of Black race and c9orf72 expansions in individuals of European and South Asian ancestry. These findings explained 23% of cases in the SSGGC, 12% in UK Biobank, and 4% in All of Us. Our results broaden the genetic architecture of non-HD chorea and highlight the value of multi-ancestry genomic approaches for rare movement disorders.

pdr_abstract: Importance: Genetic diagnosis has become increasingly important to guide clinical decision-making for patients with dilated cardiomyopathy %28DCM%29. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic %28P/LP%29 missense variants in the gene RBM20 cause a highly penetrant arrhythmogenic DCM, but the role of RBM20 truncating variants %28RBM20tvs%29 is unclear.    Objective: To assess the contribution of RBM20 variants to arrhythmogenic DCM.    Design, Setting, And Participants: In this cohort study, participants in the genome-first UK Biobank %28UKB%29 and All of Us populations were evaluated to assess the etiologic fraction, natural history and penetrance of RBM20 variants. Retrospective data were collected from an international cohort of patients with DCM and RBM20 variants identified at centers of excellence for genetic heart disease and compared based on time to event. Study dates are not disclosed because the institutional review board did not authorize the sharing of this information.    Exposures: RBM20 variants were compared to known P/LP variants and variants of uncertain significance in RBM20 as well as titin truncating variants %28TTNtvs%29.    Main Outcomes And Measures: Major ventricular arrhythmias, end-stage heart failure, and heart failure hospitalization as measured by medical record review %28retrospective cohort%29 and diagnostic codes %28UKB%29.    Results: Two main cohorts were studied for this project. In UK Biobank, a cohort of participants with RBM20tvs, RBM20 synonymous variants, and TTNtvs was studied. Of these 4249 participants, 1869 %2844%%29 were male. The mean %28SD%29 age at enrollment was 56 %288.2%29 years. In the RBM20 registry, of 179 patients, 105 %2858.6%%29 were male, and the mean %28SD%29 age at enrollment was 43.8 %2819.1%29 years. A validation cohort from the All of Us biobank was also used. This consisted of 7002 participants, 4342 of whom %2862.0%%29 were male, and the mean %28SD%29 age was 52.7 %2816.7%29 years. The etiologic fraction of RBM20 variants in arrhythmogenic DCM was 0.53 %2895% CI, 0.32-0.67; P<.001%29. In genome-first biobanks, lifetime incidence of cardiomyopathy, heart failure, or major ventricular arrhythmia diagnosis was lower in participants with RBM20 variants than in those with TTNtvs %28hazard ratio, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.36-0.84; P<.001%29. Patients with RBM20tvs and DCM presented to referral centers later in life than those with P/LP RBM20 and DCM %28mean [SD], 53 [10] vs 34 [18] years; P<.001%29 and were less likely to have a family history of sudden cardiac arrest %282 of 10 [20%] vs 11 of 17 [65%]; P=.046%29 or cardiomyopathy %282 of 10 [20%] vs 14 of 18 [78%]; P<.001%29. lay_summary: This study asked whether RBM20 truncating variants (DNA changes that make a shortened protein) cause a dangerous heart problem called dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Researchers looked at genetic data and medical records from two large health databases and a patient registry. They found RBM20 variants explained about half of arrhythmia-related DCM cases. These variants can cause disease but are often milder, so families should still be checked for other risky genes.

pdr_title: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Risk of Stroke: Evidence From Over 800 000 Individuals Across 3 Cohorts
pdr_abstract: Background: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential %28CHIP%29 is a common age-related condition that increases risk for cardiovascular disease. However, its relationship with stroke remains uncertain.    Methods: To resolve these conflicting findings, we analyzed genomic and clinical data from 800160 participants with genetic sequencing and medical records across 3 large-scale cohorts: the Vanderbilt BioVU biobank %28United States; enrollment 2007-2022%29, the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program %28United States; enrollment 2018-2023%29, and the UK Biobank %28United Kingdom; enrollment 2006-2010%29. The median follow-up time was 4.4 years %28interquartile range, 1.8-10.2%29 in BioVU, 1.9 years %28interquartile range, 0.4-3.9%29 in All of Us, and 12.4 years %28interquartile range, 11.7-13.1%29 in UK Biobank. Stroke events were identified and classified as ischemic or hemorrhagic using International Classification of Diseases codes. Subgroup analyses were conducted by driver gene, clone size, sex, and menopausal status. Genetically predicted levels of 27 cytokines were assessed for modification of CHIP-associated stroke risk.    Results: CHIP was associated with increased risk of incident stroke in the meta-analysis %28hazard ratio [HR], 1.20 [95% CI, 1.14-1.27]; P=1.92×10-10%29. This association was observed for ischemic %28HR, 1.18%29 and hemorrhagic %28HR, 1.25%29 stroke subtypes. Gene-specific analyses showed strong associations for JAK2 %28HR, 2.52%29 and TET2 %28HR, 1.23%29. DNMT3A demonstrated weak but significant associations %28HR, 1.13%29. CHIP was associated with stroke risk in both sexes; however, among women, the association was evident in postmenopausal %28HR, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.16-1.92]; P=1.91×10-3%29 but not in premenopausal participants %28HR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.36-1.43]; P=0.33%29. Among participants with CHIP, but not among participants without CHIP, genetically predicted levels of IL-1RAP %28interleukin-1 receptor accessory protein%29 were predictive of risk for stroke, suggesting IL-1RAP as a modifier of the CHIP-associated risk for stroke.    Conclusions: Our large-scale, multicohort study establishes CHIP as a determinant of incident stroke risk and IL %28interleukin%29-1-mediated inflammation as a targetable pathway to reduce this risk.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at genetic tests and medical records from over 800,000 people to see if a common blood change called CHIP (clonal hematopoiesis) raises stroke risk. They found people with CHIP had about a 20% higher chance of stroke, for both blocked and bleeding types. One gene, JAK2, raised risk about two and a half times. Risk was higher in women after menopause. A protein linked to inflammation (IL-1RAP) may explain some risk and could become a target to help lower stroke chances.

pdr_title: Daily steps offset risks of sedentary behavior in the All of Us research program
pdr_abstract: Sedentary behavior is associated with increased mortality and chronic diseases, yet it remains unclear whether higher daily step counts can mitigate these risks. In this study, we analyzed longitudinal sedentary and step data from Fitbit devices in the All of Us Research Program to examine incident diagnoses of chronic conditions. We show that greater sedentary time was associated with higher risk of obesity, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, major depressive disorder, sleep apnea, and atrial fibrillation. Increasing daily steps offset the excess risk of high sedentary time %2814 vs. 8hours/day%29 for several conditions, with the additional steps required ranging from 1700 to 5500 per day. However, no step count fully offset sedentary risks for coronary artery disease or heart failure. These findings support personalized, behavior-based recommendations that consider both sedentary behavior and daily steps.
lay_summary: Researchers asked if walking more can undo harms of too much sitting. They used Fitbit data from thousands in the All of Us study and checked who later got health problems. More sitting raised the chance of obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, many heart and lung problems, kidney disease, sleep apnea, and depression. Adding about 1,700–5,500 extra steps per day could cancel the added risk of sitting 14 vs 8 hours for many conditions, but not for some heart diseases. People should sit less and try to walk more each day.

pdr_title: Association between GLP-1 receptor agonist use and substance use disorders among individuals with type 2 diabetes or obesity: a nested case-control study in the All of Us research program
pdr_abstract: Objectives    The current study evaluated the association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists %28GLP-1 RAs%29 and substance use disorders %28SUD%29 in type 2 diabetes and obesity.    Methods    We conducted a retrospective nested case-control study using the All of Us Research Program data. Cases were defined as diabetes/obese individuals with a new diagnosis of alcohol use disorder %28AUD%29, opioid use disorder %28OUD%29, nicotine use disorder %28NUD%29, or cocaine use disorder %28CUD%29. Control participants were drawn from individuals with diabetes or obesity who had no documented history of SUD. Conditional logistic regression was performed to estimate the association between SUD and GLP-1 RA exposure.    Results    The study included a total of 22,652 participants in the AUD group, 13,226 in the OUD group, 42,320 in the NUD group, and 9,296 in the CUD group; each group comprised both cases and matched control participants. GLP-1 RA use was associated with a 74% reduction in the odds of AUD %28odds ratio [OR] = 0.26; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.20–0.34%29, a 69% reduction in the odds of OUD %28 OR = 0.31; 95% CI: 0.23–0.42%29, a 68% reduction in the odds of NUD %28 OR = 0.32; 95% CI: 0.27–0.39%29, a 75% reduction in the odds of CUD %28 OR = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.16–0.40%29, and 75% lower odds of any SUD compared with non-users participants %28OR = 0.25, 95% CI 0.22–0.30%29.    Conclusions    GLP-1 RA use was consistently associated with lower odds of developing SUDs among individuals with type 2 diabetes or obesity. These findings suggest potential for GLP-1 RAs to help mitigate SUD in these populations.
lay_summary: This study checked whether GLP‑1 receptor agonists (diabetes and weight‑loss medicines) are linked to fewer addictions. Researchers looked back at records from a large U.S. database of people with type 2 diabetes or obesity and compared users to nonusers. Using these drugs was tied to about 70% lower chances of alcohol, opioid, nicotine, and cocaine addictions, and about 75% lower chance of any addiction. This suggests the medicines might cut the risk of addiction in these patients, but people should talk to their doctor.

pdr_title: Malignancy Risk Following Ophthalmic Herpes Infection Within a Diverse U.S. Cohort
pdr_abstract: Topic: We evaluated the malignancy risk following herpes zoster ophthalmicus %28HZO%29 and ophthalmic herpes simplex virus %28HSV%29 in a large, diverse U.S.    Clinical Relevance: There has been a longstanding contention as to whether HZO serves as a clinical marker of cancer risk, with discordant findings observed across epidemiologic studies worldwide. In contrast, the relationship between ophthalmic HSV infection and malignancy remains unknown.    Methods: This matched, retrospective cohort study analyzed electronic health record data from adults enrolled in the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program. Participants with incident diagnoses of HZO or ophthalmic HSV were propensity score-matched %281:3%29 to controls based on sociodemographic characteristics and pre-existing immune dysregulation %28i.e., autoimmune disease or immunodeficient states%29. Stratified Cox proportional hazards models were applied to estimate relative hazards of incident malignancy within 1-, 2-, and 3-year intervals and over the entire follow-up period. Effect modification was investigated based on age, sex, and baseline immune dysregulation.    Results: The HZO cohort comprised 327 cases matched to 981 controls %28mean follow-up=7.48 ± 5.33 years%29, and the ophthalmic HSV cohort included 292 cases matched to 876 controls %28mean follow-up=8.66 ± 5.89 years%29. For HZO, incident malignancy risk did not differ from controls within ≤1 year %28p=1.00%29, ≤2 years %28p=0.36%29, ≤3 years %28p=0.27%29, or across the full follow-up period %28HR=1.01, 95% CI=[0.76, 1.36], p=0.93%29. However, significant effect modification by immune dysregulation was observed, with HZO associated with an increased risk of malignancy among participants with autoimmune disease %28HR=2.91, 95% CI=[1.48, 5.74], p<0.01%29 or immunodeficient status %28HR=5.75, 95% CI=[2.16, 15.35], p<0.01%29. For ophthalmic HSV, no increased malignancy risk was observed within ≤1 year %28p=0.86%29, ≤2 years %28p=0.18%29, ≤3 years %28p=0.10%29, or across the full follow-up period %28HR=0.97, 95% CI=[0.72, 1.32], p=0.87%29, with no evidence of effect modification.    Conclusions: In this large, diverse U.S. cohort, ophthalmic herpes infections were not associated with an increased risk of malignancy in the overall cohort. However, HZO was associated with a higher subsequent risk of cancer among individuals with preexisting immune dysregulation, potentially warranting heightened oncologic vigilance in this patient demographic, thus refining the interpretation of a longstanding epidemiologic debate.
lay_summary: This study asked if herpes infections in the eye raise later cancer risk. Researchers used U.S. health records to compare 327 people with eye shingles (HZO) and 292 with eye herpes (HSV) to similar people without these infections and followed them about 8 years. Overall, neither HZO nor HSV raised cancer risk. But people who had HZO plus autoimmune disease (when the body attacks itself) had about three times higher cancer risk, and those with weakened immune systems had about six times higher risk. Doctors may watch these patients more closely for cancer.

pdr_title: Beware the Little Foxes that Spoil the Vines: Small Inconsistencies in Clinical Data Can Distort Machine Learning Findings
pdr_abstract: It is well known that Electronic Health Records %28EHR%29 data contain inconsistent and inaccurate data, the effect of which on predictive model performance and risk/benefit factor identification are often neglected. This study investigates how varying levels of random and non-random binary differences, often referred to as “noise”, affect modeling tools, such as logistic regression, support vector machines, and gradient boosting models. Using curated data from the All of Us database, we simulated different noise levels to mimic real-world variability. Across all models and noise types, increased noise consistently reduced classification accuracy. More importantly, noise diminished the variance of variable impact scores while leaving their means unchanged, suggesting a muted ability to identify key predictors. These findings imply that even modest noise levels can obscure meaningful signals. Measures like accuracy and hazard ratios may thus be misleading in noisy data contexts. The consistency of effects across models and noise mechanisms suggests this issue stems from inherent data variability rather than model brittleness, with broad implications for EHR data analyses.
lay_summary: This study tested how small mistakes in electronic health records (EHRs) affect computer models that predict health outcomes. Researchers used real data from the All of Us project and added different kinds of errors to mimic real life. They tried several common prediction methods and found that more errors made the models less accurate and made it harder to spot which health factors mattered. This means results from messy medical records can be misleading, so people should be careful and improve data quality.

pdr_title: Health literacy, healthcare access, and self-perception of health among intracranial tumor patients: an analysis of the National Institute of Health %28NIH%29 'All of Us' research program
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Clinical Neuroscience : Official Journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
pdr_abstract: Background And Objective: Racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic disparities in healthcare outcomes are well documented; however, their influence on health literacy, patient-reported health status, and access to care among intracranial tumor %28ICT%29 patients remains underexplored. This study aimed to characterize these disparities within a national cohort to inform equity-focused neurosurgical care strategies.    Methods: Using the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program %28NIH AoURP%29 dataset, this cross-sectional analysis included 2,295 ICT patients identified via OMOP code 4116092, encompassing both primary and secondary tumors. Participants were categorized into non-Hispanic White %28NHW%29, non-Hispanic Black %28NHB%29, and Hispanic/Latino %28HLA%29 groups. Data were derived from the All of Us Basics Survey, Healthcare Access and Utilization Survey, and Overall Health Survey, which include standardized patient-reported measures of sociodemographics, health literacy, and health status %28including pain and emotional distress%29. Group comparisons were performed using chi-squared and Fisher's exact tests.    Results: HLA and NHB participants demonstrated significantly higher rates of Medicaid enrollment compared to NHW participants %28p < 0.001%29. Both HLA and NHB groups reported greater difficulty understanding medical information and completing health-related forms %28p < 0.001%29 than NHW. Patient-reported pain severity and emotional distress were also more frequently reported among HLA and NHB participants %28p < 0.05%29 compared to NHW. Financial and transportation-related barriers to care were disproportionately reported in HLA and NHB cohorts %28p < 0.05%29 compared to NHW.    Conclusion: Significant disparities in health literacy, patient-reported health status, and healthcare access exist among ICT patients across racial and socioeconomic groups. These findings underscore the need for literacy-sensitive communication, financial navigation support, and targeted equity-focused interventions within neurosurgical care pathways.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at 2,295 people with intracranial tumors (brain tumors) in a national database to see if race and money affected how well patients understand health information, their health, and access to care. They used surveys about health, money, and care. Black and Hispanic/Latino patients had more trouble understanding medical information and filling forms, reported more pain and emotional distress, and more often had Medicaid and trouble paying or getting to care than White patients. This means hospitals should use easier communication and help with costs and transport to make care fair for all.

pdr_title: Health care discrimination and self-reported health in transgender, gender nonconforming, and nonbinary individuals with cancer
pdr_abstract: Background: There is limited information about care experiences and health outcomes among transgender, gender-nonconforming, and nonbinary %28TGNCNB%29 individuals with cancer. This study quantifies experienced health care discrimination among TGNCNB individuals living with cancer and its impact on their health.    Methods: This cross-sectional analysis used data from the All of Us Research Program on individuals with cancer. The authors performed propensity score matching %281:5%29 to balance TGNCNB and cisgender individuals by sociodemographic factors and cancer site. Health care discrimination and health were assessed using the Discrimination in Medical Settings Scale and the Overall Health survey. They used multivariable logistic regression models to adjust for sociodemographic characteristics.    Results: The cohort included 1476 participants, of which 246 %2817%%29 identified as TGNCNB. TGNCNB participants had greater odds of reporting feeling unheard by providers %28odds ratio [OR], 2.38; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.79-3.17%29, treated with less respect %28OR, 2.61; 95% CI, 1.91-3.57%29, receiving poorer service %28OR, 2.39; 95% CI, 1.73-3.31%29, and providers acting afraid %28OR, 2.32; 95% CI, 1.37-3.93%29 compared to their cisgender counterparts. In adjusted models, TGNCNB identity was associated with increased odds of experiencing any health care discrimination %28OR, 2.42; 95% CI, 1.81-3.25%29, and discrimination was associated with self-reported poor health %28OR, 3.24; 95% CI, 2.58-4.07%29.    Discussion: The findings of this study suggest that in the TGNCNB population, increased rates of health care discrimination are associated with poorer health outcomes, which may perpetuate medical mistrust and decrease patient-centric quality of care overall. Future research and policy efforts should identify actionable interventions to advance equitable cancer care for TGNCNB individuals.

pdr_title: Putting polygenic scores in context: How intersectional factors affect relative and absolute genetic risk
pdr_abstract: The clinical utility of polygenic scores %28PGSs%29 is known to vary when training and test samples differ in ancestry, with recent work suggesting that sociodemographic differences can also impact PGS performance. However, the impact of belonging to multiple intersecting contexts on genetic risk remains understudied. We analyzed lifetime disease odds ratio %28OR%29 and absolute risk %28AR%29 estimates in high-PGS individuals across 106 two-way intersections of sociodemographic factors %28sex, age, alcohol intake, smoking, income, and deprivation%29. Seven diseases were assessed: atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, asthma, obesity, and major depression. Primary analyses were performed in the UK Biobank %28UKB; n = 375,054, British-European-like ancestry%29, with replication in All of Us %28AoU; n = 36,552, African-like ancestry and n = 99,477, European-like ancestry%29. ORs varied significantly across contexts, with greater variation observed across intersectional contexts. On average, the maximal OR varied across two-way contexts by 56%. AR deviations were more moderate after adjusting for context prevalence but still showed intersectional effects. For example, high-PGS, low-income individuals had an average 1.0 percentage-point drop in estimated AR across phenotypes using a context-aware vs. context-unaware PGS, while those additionally reporting low alcohol intake had a 3.1-point lower AR estimate for major depression in the UKB. Results were generally consistent across datasets, with strongest replication in European-like AoU samples. Our findings show that intersectional contexts can have a sizable impact on genetic risk effect estimates. Future clinical applications may need to incorporate these contextual effects to improve accuracy and fairness for individual-specific genetic risk assessment.
lay_summary: They studied whether social and lifestyle context changes what a polygenic score (PGS, a genetic risk score) says about disease risk. They used data on seven diseases from 375,054 people in the UK and about 136,000 U.S. participants and compared pairs of factors like sex, age, drinking, smoking, income, and neighborhood poverty. Genetic risk estimates changed a lot by combined factors — around 56% variation — and absolute risk shifted by about 1 to 3 percentage points in some cases. This means doctors should use social and lifestyle context to make genetic risk predictions fairer and more accurate.

pdr_title: Barriers to Health Care and Cancer Screening
pdr_abstract: Importance: Identification of health care access-related factors associated with lower rates of cancer screening may help inform targeted interventions to mitigate barriers and ameliorate screening disparities.    Objective: To examine the multifaceted obstacles associated with screening for breast, cervical, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer in a diverse population.    Design, Setting, And Participants: This cohort study included longitudinal data from the National Institutes of Health's All of Us %28AoU%29 Research Program %282017-2023%29. Nonincarcerated individuals aged 18 years or older residing in the US were eligible to participate by enrolling either online or through 1 of approximately 67 health care organizations. Identified participants within the AoU Research Program met US Preventive Services Task Force screening criteria for breast, colorectal, cervical, lung, or prostate cancer. Data were analyzed from October 2024 to January 2026.    Main Outcomes And Measures: Participants self-reported whether 9 potential barriers delayed their medical care in the past year. Multivariable-adjusted odds ratios were estimated for the association between each barrier, the barrier burden, as well as for patterns of interrelated barriers identified using factor analysis and adherence to cancer screening recommendations.    Results: In total, 160 691 participants were eligible for cancer screening including 42 908 participants in the breast %28median age at last follow-up, 60 [IQR, 52-67] years; 100% female%29, 45 791 in the cervical %28median age at last follow-up, 46 [IQR, 35-56] years; 100% female%29, 55 986 in the colorectal %28median age at last follow-up, 66 [IQR, 57-73] years; 63% female%29, 3358 in the lung %28median age at last follow-up, 66 [IQR, 59-72] years; 53% female%29, and 12 648 in the prostate cancer %28median age at last follow-up, 63 [IQR, 59-66] years; 100% male%29 screening cohorts. Out-of-pocket costs, nervousness about seeing clinicians, and inability to get time off work were the most cited barriers. Participants reporting 3 or more barriers to care had significantly lower screening rates compared with those who reported no barriers for all cancer types, ranging from 18% %28odds ratio [OR],0.82; 95% CI, 0.76-0.88%29 for colorectal cancer to 32% %28OR,0.68; 95% CI, 0.46-0.97%29 for lung cancer. Three latent factors were consistently identified across cancer sites reflecting cost concerns, logistical barriers %28eg, transportation%29, and competing obligations %28eg, time off work%29. In multivariable analyses, cost concerns were associated with odds of screening for breast cancer %28OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.66-0.80%29, cervical cancer %28OR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.73-0.87%29, and colorectal cancer %28OR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.94%29 and logistical barriers for breast cancer %28OR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.63-0.89%29, cervical cancer %28OR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65- 0.93%29, and colorectal cancer %28OR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65-0.94%29.    Conclusions And Relevance: In this cohort study of participants eligible for cancer screening, barriers to access and barriers related to cost concerns and logistics were associated with lower screening rates. Policies and interventions must target multiple dimensions of access simultaneously to increase cancer screening.

Results: In total, 160 691 participants were eligible for cancer screening including 42 908 participants in the breast (median age at last follow-up, 60 [IQR, 52-67] years; 100% female), 45 791 in the cervical (median age at last follow-up, 46 [IQR, 35-56] years; 100% female), 55 986 in the colorectal (median age at last follow-up, 66 [IQR, 57-73] years; 63% female), 3358 in the lung (median age at last follow-up, 66 [IQR, 59-72] years; 53% female), and 12 648 in the prostate cancer (median age at last follow-up, 63 [IQR, 59-66] years; 100% male) screening cohorts. Out-of-pocket costs, nervousness about seeing clinicians, and inability to get time off work were the most cited barriers. Participants reporting 3 or more barriers to care had significantly lower screening rates compared with those who reported no barriers for all cancer types, ranging from 18% (odds ratio [OR],0.82; 95% CI, 0.76-0.88) for colorectal cancer to 32% (OR,0.68; 95% CI, 0.46-0.97) for lung cancer. Three latent factors were consistently identified across cancer sites reflecting cost concerns, logistical barriers (eg, transportation), and competing obligations (eg, time off work). In multivariable analyses, cost concerns were associated with odds of screening for breast cancer (OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.66-0.80), cervical cancer (OR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.73-0.87), and colorectal cancer (OR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.94) and logistical barriers for breast cancer (OR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.63-0.89), cervical cancer (OR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65- 0.93), and colorectal cancer (OR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65-0.94).    Conclusions And Relevance: In this cohort study of participants eligible for cancer screening, barriers to access and barriers related to cost concerns and logistics were associated with lower screening rates. Policies and interventions must target multiple dimensions of access simultaneously to increase cancer screening.

pdr_title: GLP1R expression and parkinson's disease and related disorders in GLP-1RA-treated type 2 diabetes
pdr_abstract: Preclinical and epidemiologic data suggest that glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists %28GLP-1RAs%29 may reduce the risk of Parkinson's disease and related disorders %28PDRD%29, yet clinical trial findings have been mixed, raising the possibility of biologically meaningful heterogeneity. We tested whether interindividual differences in systemic GLP1R expression are associated with PDRD risk among adults with type 2 diabetes initiating GLP-1RAs. We conducted an electronic health record %28EHR%29-based new-user cohort study in the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program, focusing on adults with type 2 diabetes aged 50 years or older who initiated a GLP-1RA between 2005 and 2023 and had no prior PDRD or Alzheimer's disease and related dementias %28ADRD%29. Systemic GLP1R expression was genetically proxied by a 15-variant cis-expression quantitative trait locus %28cis-eQTL%29 genetic risk score dichotomized at the cohort median. Follow-up ended at the earliest of incident PDRD, death, or October 1, 2023. Hazard ratios were estimated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models adjusting for baseline covariates, and incidence rates and rate differences per 1,000 person-years were estimated using Poisson models. Prespecified sensitivity analyses excluded early outcome events and short drug exposure; an exploratory analysis evaluated incident ADRD. The cohort included 7,039 initiators %283,520 high vs 3,519 low genetic score; mean age 61.7 ± 8.4 years; 59.8% female; mean follow-up 3.8 ± 3.1 years%29. Compared with the low-score group, the high-score group had a lower hazard of incident PDRD %28hazard ratio 0.78; 95% confidence interval 0.62 to 0.98%29 and a lower incidence rate %28rate difference -1.36 per 1,000 person-years; 95% confidence interval -2.51 to -0.20%29. Associations were consistent across sensitivity analyses. No association was observed for incident ADRD %28hazard ratio 1.02; 95% confidence interval 0.81 to 1.28%29. These findings link a mechanism-anchored genetic proxy for higher systemic GLP1R expression to a lower risk of incident PDRD among GLP-1RA-treated adults with type 2 diabetes. Systemic GLP1R-mediated pathways may be relevant to interindividual differences in observed PDRD risk, and genetic instruments for GLP1R expression may inform hypotheses for future PDRD trial design.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if people with higher levels of a protein called GLP-1 receptor (found by their genes) who start GLP-1 diabetes drugs have less chance of getting Parkinson's disease and similar disorders. They studied 7,039 adults age 50  with type 2 diabetes who began these drugs and followed them about 4 years. People with genes linked to more GLP-1 receptor had fewer new cases—about 1.4 fewer cases per 1,000 people each year. There was no link with Alzheimer's. This suggests genes may change how these drugs lower Parkinson's risk and can help future studies.

pdr_title: Genetics of Cholesterol and Coronary Disease Risk across Six Global Ancestries
pdr_abstract: Background: Clinical trials of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol %28LDL-C%29-lowering medicines have shown improvement in cardiovascular disease risk. However, representation across diverse communities in such trials is limited. We set out to study whether or not more diverse human genetic studies could provide an opportunity to test whether these trial results can be generalized to poorly populations poorly represented in drug clinical trials.    Methods: We included six cohorts across 967,325 individuals %2854.5% female%29, including 65,258 African, 45,393 admixed American, 179,521 East Asian, 616,045 European, 4686 Middle Eastern, and 56,422 South Asian individuals. Genetic ancestry was determined using genetic principal components and k-nearest neighbors. We constructed ancestry-specific LDL-C polygenic risk scores %28PGS%29 using genome-wide association study %28GWAS%29 summary statistics trained and externally validated on each ancestry. We associated each PGS with population LDL-C, scaled for a 40 mg/dl increase, and tested these scores against coronary artery disease %28CAD%29 risk using hierarchical Bayesian meta-analyses.    Results: The associations between genetically predicted LDL-C levels and observed LDL-C were consistent across ancestries, supporting the validity of our genetic proxy. When scaled to mimic a 40 mg/dl increase in LDL-C, the PGS showed positive but heterogeneous associations with CAD. Posterior odds ratios for CAD ranged from 1.35 %2895% credible interval, 1.05 to 1.68%29 in African populations to 1.82 %2895% credible interval, 1.33 to 2.97%29 in Middle Eastern populations. Bayesian analysis revealed that 97.9% of posterior samples showed all population means greater than 0 on a log scale with a between-ancestry posterior variance %28τ2%29 of 0.062 %2895% credible interval, 0.001 to 0.352%29.    Conclusions: Our findings demonstrated a consistent association between LDL-C and CAD risk across diverse ancestry groups that are often poorly represented in clinical trials, although effect magnitudes varied. %28Funded by the National Institutes of Health and others.%29.
lay_summary: This study asked if DNA-based risk scores for 'bad' cholesterol (LDL-C) work the same in different ancestry groups and if higher LDL-C raises heart disease risk. Researchers used genetic data from 967,325 people from six ancestry groups. They made and checked DNA scores to predict LDL-C and then linked those scores to coronary artery disease (blocked heart arteries). The genetic scores matched real LDL-C across groups. A 40 mg/dL higher LDL-C was linked to higher heart disease risk in all groups, ranging about 35% to 82% more risk. This means lowering LDL-C likely helps reduce heart disease in diverse populations.

pdr_title: Polygenic risk scores enhance LDL cholesterol-based risk stratification for coronary artery disease
pdr_abstract: Background: Genetic risk for coronary artery disease %28CAD%29 can be estimated using polygenic risk scores %28PRS%29, but greater clarity is needed on how PRS might inform clinical risk assessment and prevention. We assessed the risk for CAD jointly conferred by LDL-C and CAD PRS relative to established treatment thresholds.    Methods: This study followed 257,158 UK Biobank %28UKBB%29 participants and 67,668 from the All of Us Research Program %28AoU%29, a longitudinal U.S. cohort, without prior CAD, stroke, or diabetes. In UKBB, Cox proportional hazards models estimated CAD hazard ratios for each LDL-C × CAD PRS stratum relative to individuals with LDL-C < 100 mg/dL. The severe hypercholesterolemia %28LDL-C ≥ 190 mg/dL%29 group, the guideline-designated threshold for statin initiation, served as a benchmark against which groups were compared. Parallel analyses were performed in AoU cross-sectionally.    Results: Over a median %28IQR%29 follow-up of 13.5 %2812.8-14.2%29 years, 13,886 %285.4%%29 participants developed CAD in UKBB. Higher CAD PRS was associated with CAD risk that was comparable to, or in some strata exceeding, that associated with LDL-C ≥ 190 mg/dL by pairwise Wald tests at progressively lower LDL-C concentrations in both cohorts.    Conclusions: Individuals with high genetic risk and moderate LDL-C elevations, representing 14.8% of the study population, have CAD risk comparable to or greater than that of SH. Consideration of dynamic LDL-C thresholds among those with high CAD PRS may identify individuals with risk sufficiently high to warrant preventive therapy.
lay_summary: This study tested whether adding a polygenic risk score (PRS, a measure of genetic risk from many genes) to LDL cholesterol (LDL-C, 'bad' cholesterol) helps find people at risk for coronary artery disease (CAD). They followed 257,158 UK and 67,668 U.S. adults without prior heart disease for 13.5 years and tracked new CAD cases; about 5% developed CAD. People with high PRS and moderate LDL-C were 14.8% of participants and had risk similar to or higher than those with very high LDL-C (≥190). This suggests using genetics with cholesterol can better guide preventive treatment.

pdr_title: Derivation and validation of a widely accessible cardiovascular risk prediction model and derived heart age for the general UK and US populations
pdr_abstract: Background: There remains a need for tools leveraging widely accessible data compatible with mobile health platforms to provide simple and broadly comprehensible cardiovascular risk estimations.    Methods: We streamlined the previously published DiCAVA model, originally developed in the UK Biobank %28UKB%29, into a 30-feature tool %28DiCAVA-Lite%29 to predict incident myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, angina, and transient ischemic attack in primary prevention settings. We then validated DiCAVA-Lite in the All of Us %28AoU%29 using Cox proportional hazard regression models and an incident composite cardiovascular outcome. We then translate the DivCAVA-Lite score to heart age in both UKB and AoU, which communicates the age of a healthy person with equivalent cardiovascular risk to that of the index individual.    Results: In the UKB dataset %28n = 466,052%29, the mean age was 56 years %28SD: 8%29 with 55.9% females, while in AoU %28n = 216,985%29, the mean age was 50 years %28SD: 17%29 with 63.2% females. The DiCAVA-Lite model demonstrated moderate discrimination, with the area under the curve %28AUC%29 of 0.740 %2895% CI: 0.735-0.745%29 %28vs. 0.747 [95% CI: 0.744-0.748] for DiCAVA%29 in UKB and 0.770 %2895% CI: 0.765-0.773%29 in external validation in AoU. Heart age demonstrated discriminative performance equivalent to the DiCAVA-Lite model. In UKB, the mean heart age was 60 among individuals who developed events vs. 55 in those who did not. In AoU, the corresponding ages were 57 and 50, respectively.    Conclusion: These findings support DiCAVA-Lite and the corresponding heart age as an accessible and interpretable tool for CVD risk assessment and communication in the US and UK primary prevention populations.
lay_summary: This study made a simpler 30-item heart risk tool (DiCAVA-Lite) and tested it in 466,052 people in the UK and 216,985 in the US. It used basic health information to predict future heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, chest pain, or mini-strokes. The tool correctly identified who would have problems about 74% of the time in the UK and 77% in the US. It also gives a 'heart age': people who later had events had average heart ages of 60 versus 55 in the UK (57 vs 50 in the US). It could help doctors and patients understand heart risk.

pdr_title: Biobank-Scale Plasma Proteomics Identifies Novel Biomarkers in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
pdr_abstract: Background: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy %28HCM%29 is characterized by substantial heterogeneity in both clinical phenotype and risk of adverse outcomes, including heart failure and sudden cardiac death. This highlights the need for robust biomarkers for risk stratification, and while previous studies have identified the role of select plasma proteins, comprehensive large-scale proteomic analyses have been limited in HCM.    Methods: We performed a case-control analysis of 2922 plasma proteins in 49588 UK Biobank participants %28100 HCM cases%29 to identify proteins associated with HCM. External replication analyses were performed in the deCODE Genetics Icelandic study %2851 cases/38 904 controls%29 and All of Us %28546 cases/41 049 controls%29 data sets. Associations with adverse clinical outcomes and cardiac endophenotypes of disease severity were further identified, and causal relationships were evaluated using Mendelian randomization. Relative biomarker importance was also assessed by joint modeling via machine learning.    Results: We identified novel associations of ANGPT2 %28angiopoietin-2%29 and LTBP2 %28latent transforming growth factor-beta binding protein 2%29 with HCM, with both also showing prognostic utility for heart failure-related outcomes in HCM cases. We also confirmed the associations of established biomarkers %28eg, NT-proBNP [N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide], troponins I and T%29 with HCM cases, cardiac imaging markers of disease severity, and adverse outcomes. Mendelian randomization analyses supported a causal effect of HCM on increasing NT-proBNP and troponin T levels.    Conclusions: This biobank-scale plasma proteomic study in HCM identified ANGPT2 and LTBP2 as novel HCM biomarkers with potential diagnostic and prognostic utility. These findings highlight the potential for plasma proteomics to improve risk prediction and provide insight into HCM pathobiology.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at blood proteins to find signs of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM, a heart muscle disease) because people with HCM have different risks. They checked about 3,000 proteins in nearly 50,000 UK Biobank people, including 100 with HCM, and confirmed results in two other large groups. They found two new blood markers, ANGPT2 and LTBP2, and confirmed known ones (NT‑proBNP and troponins). These markers linked to worse heart scans and heart-failure problems, and genetic tests suggested HCM raises NT‑proBNP and troponin T. This could help doctors diagnose HCM and predict who needs more care.
