pdr_title: Efficient collaborative learning of the average treatment effect
pdr_abstract: In response to the growing need for generating real-world evidence from multisite collaborative studies, we introduce an efficient collaborative learning approach to evaluate average treatment effect %28ECO-ATE%29 in a multisite setting under data-sharing constraints. Specifically, ECO-ATE operates in a federated manner, using individual-level data from a user-defined target population and summary statistics from other source populations, to construct efficient estimator for the average treatment effect on the target population of interest. Our federated approach does not require iterative communications between sites, making it particularly suitable for research consortia with limited resources for developing automated data-sharing infrastructures. Compared to existing work data integration methods in causal inference, ECO-ATE allows distributional shifts in outcomes, treatments, and baseline covariates distributions, and achieves semiparametric efficiency bound under appropriate conditions. We conduct simulation studies to demonstrate the extent of efficiency gains achieved by incorporating additional data sources, as well as the robustness of our approach against varying levels of distributional shifts and overparameterization, compared to existing benchmarks. We apply ECO-ATE to a case study examining the effect of insulin versus non-insulin treatments on heart failure for patients with type II diabetes using electronic health record data collected from the All of Us program.
lay_summary: The researchers made a new way to study how treatments work using data from many places without sharing all patient records. They used one hospital's patient data and only shared simple summaries from other sites (federated learning). In tests and computer simulations, their method gave more reliable and precise estimates, worked well even when sites differed, and did not need repeated data transfers. They tried it on insulin versus non‑insulin in type 2 diabetes and got improved results. This helps scientists learn which treatments help, while keeping patient data private.

pdr_title: Uncovering the Roots of Inequity: Social Determinants and Racial Disparities Among Gastrointestinal Cancer Patients
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
pdr_abstract: Introduction: Social Determinants of Health %28SDoH%29 profoundly influence cancer outcomes, yet their distribution among racially diverse gastrointestinal %28GI%29 cancer patients remains understudied. This study examines racial differences in SDoH between non-Hispanic White %28NHW%29 and Non-White %28including Asian, African American, and Hispanic%29 patients with gastrointestinal %28GI%29 cancers using data from the All of Us Research Program.    Methods: A total of 6,620 participants with GI cancer were identified using ICD-10 and SNOMED codes, of whom 1,831 completed the SDoH survey and were included in the analysis. Descriptive statistics summarized SDoH constructs such as social cohesion, support, and neighborhood disorder. Variables were categorized using validated scoring tools or grouped into tertiles. Group comparisons used chi-square, t-tests, or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.    Results: Among the 1,831 participants included in the overall cohort, 80.7% %28n=1,478%29 identified as non-Hispanic White and 13.9% %28n=255%29 as Non-White, including Black or African American %286.2%%29, Hispanic or Latino %286.4%%29, and Asian %281.4%%29. NHW participants were older %2871.0 vs. 64.2 years%29 and reported greater social cohesion %283.9 vs. 3.6, p<0.001%29 and support %283.9 vs. 3.7, p<0.001%29. Non-White patients reported higher perceived discrimination %281.7 vs. 1.5, p=0.016%29, daily spiritual experience %284.5 vs. 3.7, p<0.001%29, neighborhood disorder %282.2 vs. 2.1, p<0.001%29, food insecurity %2823.6% vs. 5.8%, p<0.001%29, and housing issues %2841.8% vs. 21.8%, p<0.001%29. Delayed care %2847.1% vs. 26.8%, p<0.001%29 and unaffordability of care %289.9% vs. 3.4%, p<0.001%29 were also more common.    Conclusion: Significant racial disparities in SDoH were observed among GI cancer patients. Non-White individuals faced greater economic hardship, environmental disadvantage, and barriers to healthcare access.    Key Messages: WHAT IS KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC: Racial disparities in gastrointestinal cancer outcomes persist, but the social and structural factors underlying these differences are not routinely captured in oncology research. Many cancer datasets emphasize clinical characteristics while underrepresenting patient-reported social, economic, and neighborhood conditions. Addressing social determinants of health is increasingly recognized as necessary to advance equity in cancer care delivery.    What This Study Adds: This study provides a comprehensive, patient-reported assessment of social determinants of health among GI cancer patients in the All of Us Research Program. Non-White patients experience a higher burden of economic instability, neighborhood disadvantage, perceived stress,and barriers to accessing healthcare services. These findings identify concrete social risk domains that can inform equity-focused screening, care navigation, and policy interventions within oncology practice.

lay_summary: This study looked at social factors that affect health (SDoH) in people with digestive system cancer (stomach and bowel) to see if they differ by race. Researchers used medical records and surveys from 1,831 patients in the All of Us program. Non-White patients reported more discrimination, worse neighborhoods, more food insecurity (24% vs 6%), more housing problems (42% vs 22%), and more delayed or unaffordable care (47% vs 27% delayed; 10% vs 3% unaffordable). White patients had more social support. The findings mean Non-White patients face bigger social and economic barriers to cancer care and need targeted help.
calc_title: Uncovering the Roots of Inequity: Social Determinants and Racial Disparities Among Gastrointestinal Cancer Patients
calc_journal_title: Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
calc_abstract: Introduction: Social Determinants of Health (SDoH) profoundly influence cancer outcomes, yet their distribution among racially diverse gastrointestinal (GI) cancer patients remains understudied. This study examines racial differences in SDoH between non-Hispanic White (NHW) and Non-White (including Asian, African American, and Hispanic) patients with gastrointestinal (GI) cancers using data from the All of Us Research Program.    Methods: A total of 6,620 participants with GI cancer were identified using ICD-10 and SNOMED codes, of whom 1,831 completed the SDoH survey and were included in the analysis. Descriptive statistics summarized SDoH constructs such as social cohesion, support, and neighborhood disorder. Variables were categorized using validated scoring tools or grouped into tertiles. Group comparisons used chi-square, t-tests, or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.    Results: Among the 1,831 participants included in the overall cohort, 80.7% (n=1,478) identified as non-Hispanic White and 13.9% (n=255) as Non-White, including Black or African American (6.2%), Hispanic or Latino (6.4%), and Asian (1.4%). NHW participants were older (71.0 vs. 64.2 years) and reported greater social cohesion (3.9 vs. 3.6, p<0.001) and support (3.9 vs. 3.7, p<0.001). Non-White patients reported higher perceived discrimination (1.7 vs. 1.5, p=0.016), daily spiritual experience (4.5 vs. 3.7, p<0.001), neighborhood disorder (2.2 vs. 2.1, p<0.001), food insecurity (23.6% vs. 5.8%, p<0.001), and housing issues (41.8% vs. 21.8%, p<0.001). Delayed care (47.1% vs. 26.8%, p<0.001) and unaffordability of care (9.9% vs. 3.4%, p<0.001) were also more common.    Conclusion: Significant racial disparities in SDoH were observed among GI cancer patients. Non-White individuals faced greater economic hardship, environmental disadvantage, and barriers to healthcare access.    Key Messages: WHAT IS KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC: Racial disparities in gastrointestinal cancer outcomes persist, but the social and structural factors underlying these differences are not routinely captured in oncology research. Many cancer datasets emphasize clinical characteristics while underrepresenting patient-reported social, economic, and neighborhood conditions. Addressing social determinants of health is increasingly recognized as necessary to advance equity in cancer care delivery.    What This Study Adds: This study provides a comprehensive, patient-reported assessment of social determinants of health among GI cancer patients in the All of Us Research Program. Non-White patients experience a higher burden of economic instability, neighborhood disadvantage, perceived stress,and barriers to accessing healthcare services. These findings identify concrete social risk domains that can inform equity-focused screening, care navigation, and policy interventions within oncology practice.

pdr_title: Toward scalable early cancer detection: evaluating EHR-based predictive models against traditional screening criteria
pdr_abstract: Current cancer screening guidelines cover only a few cancer types and rely on narrowly defined criteria such as age or a single risk factor like smoking history, to identify high-risk individuals. Predictive models using electronic health records %28EHRs%29, which capture large-scale longitudinal patient-level health information, may provide a more effective tool for identifying high-risk groups by detecting subtle prediagnostic signals of cancer. Recent advances in large language and foundation models have further expanded this potential, yet evidence remains limited on how useful EHR-based models are compared with traditional risk factors currently used in screening guidelines. We systematically evaluated the clinical utility of EHR-based predictive models against traditional risk factors, including gene mutations and family history of cancer, for identifying high-risk individuals across eight major cancers %28breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, ovarian, liver, pancreatic, and stomach%29, using data from the All of Us Research Program, which integrates EHR, genomic, and survey data from over 865,000 participants. Even with a baseline modeling approach, EHR-based models achieved a 3- to 6-fold higher enrichment of true cancer cases among individuals identified as high risk compared with traditional risk factors alone, whether used as a standalone or complementary tool. The EHR foundation model, a state-of-the-art approach trained on comprehensive patient trajectories, further improved predictive performance across 26 cancer types, demonstrating the clinical potential of EHR-based predictive modeling to support more precise and scalable early detection strategies.
lay_summary: Researchers tested whether tools using electronic health records (EHRs) can find people at high risk of cancer better than current screening rules. They analyzed health records, genetic and survey data from over 865,000 people in the All of Us study. EHR-based models flagged 3 to 6 times more real cancer cases among people they labeled high risk than traditional risk factors did. A more advanced foundation model worked even better across 26 cancer types. This suggests EHR tools could help find cancer earlier and guide who should get screening, potentially catching more cancers sooner.

pdr_title: A dynamic risk prediction framework for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias with interpretability
pdr_abstract: Alzheimer's disease and related dementias %28ADRD%29 develop years before symptoms emerge, making early prediction critical. Electronic health records %28EHR%29 offer a scalable alternative to neuroimaging but are challenged by irregular encounters, data sparsity, and limited interpretability. We propose Gated Recurrent Unit with Decay & Attention %28GRU-DA%29, which integrates GRU-D missingness modeling with RETAIN-style attention for interpretable risk monitoring. The model was trained on the University of Texas Physicians EHR %2815,172 ADRD cases with 1:10 matched controls%29 and externally validated in the All of Us cohort. EHR data up to 10 years before diagnosis were used, with random follow-up initiation to reflect real-world encounters. Both GRU-DA and GRU-D outperformed competing models, particularly beyond 5 years of follow-up and achieved AUROC~0.7 after 8.5 years. Prediction performance depended more on data availability than follow-up length: 1 year with 15% data availability %28AUROC 0.75, Average Precision 0.5%29 was comparable to 7.5 years with 10% availability. For individual cases, GRU-DA produced stable risk predictions with some variability in timestep and feature-level attributions across folds. These results demonstrate EHR data can support dynamic ADRD risk monitoring up to 10 years before diagnosis, with effectiveness strongly influenced by data completeness.
lay_summary: This study made a computer model to find people at risk for Alzheimer's disease years before symptoms. Researchers trained the model on electronic health records from over 15,000 patients with dementia and matched controls and checked it in a national research dataset. The model learns from irregular and missing visits and gives simple explanations. It predicted risk up to 10 years before diagnosis and beat other methods. Having more complete records mattered most; one year with better data worked as well as many years with sparse data. This could help doctors monitor risk earlier if records are kept well.

pdr_title: Genetic architecture of postpartum psychosis: from common to rare genetic variation
pdr_abstract: Postpartum psychosis is a severe psychiatric condition marked by the abrupt onset of psychosis, mania, or psychotic depression following childbirth. Despite evidence for a strong genetic basis, the roles of common and rare genetic variation remain poorly understood. Leveraging data from Swedish national registers and genomic data from the All of Us Research Program, we estimated family-based heritability at 55% and whole-genome sequencing-based heritability at 46%. Rare coding variant analysis identified HMGCR as a gene in which rare damaging variants confer risk for postpartum psychosis %28FDR<0.05%29. Analyses of 240,009 participants from the All of Us Research Program and 58,990 participants from the Mount Sinai BioMe Biobank identified significant associations linking deleterious rare variants in HMGCR to vascular dementia and mental disorder, not otherwise specified, supporting the gene's broader psychiatric relevance. Additionally, among the top 200 genes ranked by association statistics, 17% of bipolar disorder, 21% of schizophrenia, and 16-25% of multiple autoimmune disorders exhibit a possible association with postpartum psychosis. These findings reveal unique genetic contributions and shared pathways, providing a foundation for understanding pathophysiology and advancing therapeutic strategies.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know why some women get postpartum psychosis, a severe illness after childbirth. They looked at family records in Sweden and whole-genome data from large US studies to study common and rare DNA changes. They found that about half of the risk is genetic (around 46–55%). A rare harmful change in a gene called HMGCR (a gene is a DNA instruction) raises risk and is also linked to other brain and blood vessel problems. This shows genes matter and could help future tests and better treatments, but genes are not the only cause.

pdr_title: Association of Depression in Patients With Chronic Rhinosinusitis Comorbid Asthma and Allergic Rhinitis: A Cross-Sectional Study With the All of Us Research Database
pdr_abstract: BackgroundChronic rhinosinusitis %28CRS%29 is a persistent inflammatory condition often coexisting with asthma, allergic rhinitis %28AR%29, and depression, impacting patients' quality of life. While the relationship between CRS and these comorbidities is recognized, their interaction with depression remains underexplored.ObjectiveThis study aimed to investigate the associations of comorbid asthma and AR with depression in CRS patients using the All of Us Database.MethodsA cross-sectional analysis was conducted of 27 077 CRS and 244 101 non-CRS patients. Conditions were identified through Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine codes. Generalized linear models were used to calculate adjusted odds ratios %28aORs%29 for associations. Stratified analyses were performed by age, sex, and income.ResultsCRS patients were more likely to have asthma %2832.8% vs 12.2%%29, AR %2852.1% vs 13.1%%29, and depression %2841.7% vs 20.4%%29. The adjusted GLM revealed significant associations with depression for CRS %28aOR=2.54, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.43, 2.65%29, asthma %28aOR=2.93, 95% CI: 2.84, 3.02%29, and AR %28aOR=2.67, 95% CI: 2.59, 2.75%29. Low socioeconomic status %28SES%29 in CRS patients was associated with higher odds of depression %28aOR range: [2.70-2.90]%29. Patients with both CRS and asthma or AR exhibited increased odds of depression %28aOR=1.88 and 1.42%29. The combination of CRS, asthma, and AR showed the highest risk %28aOR=2.15%29.ConclusionThis study highlights the significant impact of comorbid asthma and AR on depression in CRS patients, with low SES further increasing the likelihood of depression. Our findings underscore the importance of comprehensive management of CRS and its comorbidities, particularly in patients with lower SES.
lay_summary: This study looked at health records from the All of Us database to see if people with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS, long-term sinus inflammation) who also had asthma or allergic rhinitis (AR, nose allergies) had more depression. Researchers compared 27,077 CRS patients to 244,101 others using medical codes. CRS patients had more asthma (33% vs 12%), AR (52% vs 13%), and depression (42% vs 20%). Having CRS plus asthma or AR raised the chances of depression, and having all three raised it most. This means doctors should check mental health when treating these patients, especially if they have low income.

pdr_title: Wearable-derived sleep architecture and chronic musculoskeletal pain: a national cohort study
pdr_abstract: Aims: Sleep disturbances are associated with chronic pain risk, but most large studies rely on self-reported sleep duration. We evaluated whether wearable-derived sleep architecture predicts incident musculoskeletal pain in a large United States national cohort.    Materials And Methods: We analyzed 26,852 adults in the NIH All of Us Research Program with wearable sleep data. Average nightly sleep duration and percentage of deep sleep, a wearable-derived proxy for slow-wave sleep %28SWS%29, were estimated prior to a 12-month washout period before diagnosis. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated associations with incident chronic hip, low back, neck, and shoulder pain. False discovery rate %28FDR%29 correction was applied across site-specific models.    Results: During follow-up, 3,949 participants %2814.7%%29 developed chronic pain. Higher deep sleep predicted lower odds of hip pain %28OR 0.73; p=0.020%29 and low back pain %28OR 0.72; p=0.023%29. Longer sleep duration predicted hip %28OR 1.09; p=0.041%29 and neck pain %28OR 1.11; p=0.025%29. After FDR correction, only the associations between higher deep sleep and hip and low back pain remained significant.    Conclusions: Lower deep sleep was associated with higher risk of hip and low back pain. Wearable-derived sleep architecture may represent a potential marker associated with musculoskeletal pain risk, although these findings require prospective validation.
lay_summary: This study looked at 26,852 adults who wore sleep trackers to see if sleep patterns predict new chronic hip, low back, neck, or shoulder pain. Researchers used average nightly sleep and percent deep sleep (slow-wave sleep). Over follow-up, 14.7% developed chronic pain. People with more deep sleep had lower chances of hip and low back pain. Longer total sleep linked to some pain but did not hold up after stricter checks. Wearable sleep measures might help spot people at higher pain risk, but more study is needed.

pdr_title: Discrimination, Stress, and Substance Use Among Ethnoracial Minority Gay, Bisexual, and Other Men Who Have Sex with Men: Findings from the NIH All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background: Unhealthy alcohol, marijuana, and cocaine use are major public health concerns among ethnoracial minority gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men %28GBMSM%29, who experience compounded stressors related to sexual and ethnoracial minority identities. Guided by the Minority Stress Model, this study examined pathways linking everyday discrimination, perceived stress, and substance use among ethnoracial minority GBMSM.    Objectives: To examine whether everyday discrimination is associated with unhealthy alcohol use, whether perceived stress mediates the association between discrimination and unhealthy alcohol use, whether unhealthy alcohol use mediates the relationship between perceived stress and marijuana/cocaine use, and whether nativity moderates these associations.    Results: A secondary analysis was conducted using survey data from 683 ethnoracial minority GBMSM enrolled in the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program. Structural equation modeling was used to assess direct, indirect, and moderating pathways. Everyday discrimination was positively associated with unhealthy alcohol use %28β=0.25, 95% CI [0.03, 0.46]%29. Unhealthy alcohol use was associated with both marijuana use %28β=0.30, 95% CI [0.16, 0.43]%29 and cocaine use %28β=0.21, 95% CI [0.08, 0.34]%29. Evidence for perceived stress as a mediator of the discrimination-alcohol use association was inconclusive, and nativity did not demonstrate a conclusive moderating effect.    Conclusions: Findings suggest that discrimination may influence substance use through mechanisms beyond self-reported stress and that unhealthy alcohol use may serve as a pathway to other substance involvement among ethnoracial minority GBMSM. Clinical screening for discrimination experiences and polysubstance use risk may help identify individuals at elevated risk. Future research is needed to clarify the mechanisms linking discrimination and substance use in this population.
lay_summary: Many gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (GBMSM) from racial or ethnic minority groups face extra stress and more drug and alcohol use. To learn why, researchers studied survey answers from 683 ethnoracial minority GBMSM in the All of Us study and used statistical models to look at links between discrimination, stress, and substance use. They found everyday discrimination was linked to more unhealthy drinking, and drinking was linked to more marijuana and cocaine use. Stress did not clearly explain the link. Doctors could ask about discrimination and multiple drug use to help find people who need support.

pdr_title: Association Between Lifetime Hallucinogen Use and Valvular Heart Disease: Findings from the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Recent literature suggests potential associations between hallucinogen use and valvular heart disease %28VHD%29 due to prolonged activation of serotonin 5-HT2B receptors, which may lead to valvular fibrosis - a condition also linked to drugs including fenfluramine and pergolide. Despite these concerns, epidemiological studies exploring this association are lacking. This exploratory analysis investigated associations between lifetime hallucinogen use and VHD using cross-sectional data from US adults with linked electronic health record data in the NIH All of Us Research Program who completed the Lifestyle survey. This survey included questions about lifetime hallucinogen use %28lysergic acid diethylamide [LSD], mushrooms/psilocybin, 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine [MDMA]/ecstasy, ketamine, phencyclidine [PCP]%29. Multivariable logistic regression models examined the association between hallucinogen use and VHD, adjusting for sociodemographic factors and other confounding health conditions. Our sample comprised 286,842 adults %28mean age 50.8 [SD 16.7], 61.4% female, 60.6% White%29. Among them, 13.2% reported lifetime hallucinogen use. Individuals with lifetime hallucinogen use had lower unadjusted VHD prevalence compared to those without lifetime hallucinogen use %283.6% vs. 4.7%, p<.001%29. However, after adjusting for confounders, models revealed modestly increased VHD odds %28aOR=1.08, 95% CI: 1.01-1.55, p=.017%29. This exploratory study found that hallucinogen use was associated with modestly increased VHD odds after adjustment, requiring confirmation through longitudinal research.
lay_summary: Researchers asked if lifetime hallucinogen use is linked to valvular heart disease (problems with heart valves) because some drugs can affect a serotonin receptor. They used survey answers and medical records from 286,842 U.S. adults in the All of Us study; 13% had used hallucinogens. Before accounting for other factors, valve disease was in 3.6% of users and 4.7% of nonusers. After accounting for age, sex, and health differences, hallucinogen use showed a small increase in the chance of valve disease. This does not prove cause; more long-term studies are needed, and doctors and users should be aware.

pdr_title: Uncovering apparent incomplete penetrance of TSC1/TSC2 variants: Insights from multiple population cohorts and implications for newborn screening
pdr_journal_title: European Journal of Human Genetics : EJHG
pdr_abstract: Tuberous sclerosis complex %28TSC%29 is a genetic multisystem disorder regarded as having near-complete penetrance, a view largely derived from clinically ascertained cohorts. As genomic newborn screening is piloted internationally, robust estimates of penetrance and expressivity in unselected populations are urgently needed. We analysed genome sequencing data from >900,000 adults in UK Biobank %28UKB%29 and the All of Us Research Program %28AoU%29, representing multiple genetic ancestries, to identify individuals carrying high-confidence ACMG/AMP %28likely%29 pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variants. Electronic health records and self-reported data were interrogated for TSC-related phenotypes, including diagnostic codes, and evidence of epilepsy, chronic kidney disease and other hamartomas. We identified 61 adults with %28likely%29 pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variants and phenotype data available. Only 20/61 %2833%%29 had a recorded diagnosis of TSC and a further 8/61 %2813%%29 had at least one TSC phenotype; 33/61 %2854%%29 had no recorded TSC diagnosis, manifestations or suggestive medication history, despite median age ≥55 years %28UKB≥75 years%29 with extensive longitudinal healthcare data. Apparent reduced penetrance was observed for TSC1 in both cohorts %2846.6% UKB, 46.1% AoU%29, consistent with previously reported milder phenotypes associated with this gene. Apparent TSC2 penetrance was also incomplete %2827.8% UKB, 66.7% AoU, p=0.038, not significant after Bonferroni correction%29. Borderline significant apparent penetrance differences between UKB and AoU were not explained by gene, variant class, or ClinVar designation, but may reflect healthy volunteer bias in UKB. Overall, these findings challenge the assumption of near-complete penetrance for %28likely%29 pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variants and have important implications for genomic newborn screening, variant interpretation and counselling of asymptomatic carriers.

lay_summary: This study asked how often harmful changes in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes cause tuberous sclerosis (TSC). Researchers checked genetic data and health records from over 900,000 adults in two large studies and found 61 people with these changes. Only 20 of 61 (33%) had a TSC diagnosis, 8 more had at least one TSC sign, and 33 (54%) had no signs despite being older than 55. About half of TSC1 carriers showed signs. This means the chance of showing disease (penetrance) is lower than thought, so screening and counseling should not assume all carriers will get TSC.

pdr_title: The association of a common HFE gene variant with stroke disability utilizing predictive machine learning and electronic health records
pdr_abstract: Unlabelled: Animal studies demonstrate that the H67D HFE mutation is neuroprotective against intracerebral hemorrhage %28ICH%29, but whether the human analog, H63D HFE, confers a similar effect is unknown. We developed a machine learning algorithm to predict discharge Modified Rankin Score %28mRS≤2 functionally independent vs.≥3 moderate-severe disability%29 from electronic health records %28EHR%29 of stroke patients. This model was applied to large genetic databases to determine the association between the H63D mutation and predicted stroke disability. Four algorithms were trained on ICD-10 codes from 6,500 stroke patient records to predict dichotomized discharge mRS. The best model was applied to UK Biobank and AllofUs stroke cohorts, and the association of predicted mRS with H63D mutation was assessed by logistic regression. Although all models performed similarly, the gradient boosting model achieved the highest performance %28AUROC 86.66; AUPRC 89.51%29. ICH patients without the H63D mutation had significantly higher odds of predicted disability %28mRS≥3%29 compared to carriers %28OR 1.42, p=0.044%29. No association was observed in other stroke types. Our study presents evidence that the commonly found H63D HFE mutation is associated with decreased ICH disability. These findings highlight a potential genetic mechanism that could guide future therapeutic strategies for ICH.    Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-026-46129-1.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if a common gene change called H63D helps people do better after a bleeding type of stroke (intracerebral hemorrhage). They taught a computer program using 6,500 hospital records to predict if patients left the hospital with serious disability. They then checked two large genetic databases. For bleeding strokes, people without H63D were about 40% more likely to have moderate to severe disability than people with H63D. There was no link for other stroke types. This could help guide future treatments.

pdr_title: Meta-analysis across six global biobanks identifies recessive coding associations with complex traits and diseases
pdr_abstract: Rare bi-allelic variation is a major contributor to human disease risk, yet its effects are difficult to study at scale in population cohorts owing to the limited number of individuals with putatively deleterious bi-allelic genotypes and the challenges of accurately phasing low-frequency variants. Here, we present recessive, gene-based analyses of rare and low-frequency variants in up to 948,690 exome- or whole-genome-sequenced individuals across six biobanks with linked electronic health records. Through statistical phasing, we inferred putatively damaging compound-heterozygous genotypes, increasing the number of bi-allelic damaging genotypes by 19%. Restricting to predicted loss-of-function %28pLoF%29 variants, we identified 5,563 genes harboring bi-allelic genotypes, a 19.8% increase in putative knockouts. We then considered all low-frequency variants %28minor allele frequency [MAF] <5%%29 and performed gene-based recessive association testing using putatively damaging bi-allelic genotypes, identifying 58 significant associations %28false discovery rate [FDR] ≤1% or prec≤7.5 × 10-7%29 after meta-analysis and Cauchy combination of nonsynonymous annotations. Comparing recessive and additive models, we found 17 instances where recessive effects were more pronounced, including several previously unreported associations, such as HBB with heart failure %28prec = 2.6 × 10-14; padd = 0.98%29, LECT2 with height %28prec = 3.7 × 10-14; padd = 4.1 × 10-10%29, and ENSG00000267561 with height %28prec = 2.9 × 10-9; padd = 0.37%29. This study demonstrates the potential of federated approaches to study the effects of rare bi-allelic variation.

lay_summary: The researchers wanted to learn how rare two-copy (bi-allelic) gene changes affect health because these are hard to study. They looked at genetic and health record data from about 948,690 people in six biobanks. Using statistics to match rare gene variants, they found 19% more damaging two-copy genotypes and identified 5,563 genes with likely knockouts (loss of function). They found 58 gene-trait links and 17 where recessive (two-copy) effects mattered more, including genes tied to heart failure and height. This helps doctors and scientists find hidden genetic risks and improve care and research.

pdr_title: Risk Factors and Social Determinants of Health for Retinal Artery Occlusion in the National Institutes of Health All of Us Program
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Neuro-Ophthalmology : The Official Journal of the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society
pdr_abstract: Background: Previous studies have identified inequities in stroke epidemiology. Given retinal artery occlusion %28RAO%29 is a stroke equivalent, we investigated risk factors and social determinants of health %28SDOH%29 associated with RAO.    Methods: This was a retrospective case-control study. The case group consisted of all patients diagnosed with RAO in the National Institutes of Health All of Us database from November 1992 to November 2020. The control group consisted of all patients without a diagnosis of RAO during that time frame. Associations of predictors of RAO were estimated using logistic regression models.    Results: There were 384 patients with an RAO diagnosis and 328,639 participants in the non-RAO group. Median age at RAO diagnosis was 66 years %28interquartile range [IQR] 57-72%29. Median age at study was 74 years %28IQR 67-81%29 for the RAO group and 58 years %28IQR 42-69%29 for the control group. Age- and sex-adjusted multivariable analysis revealed factors positively associated with RAO, including older age {odds ratio [OR]: 2.19 %2895% confidence interval [CI]: 2.01-2.39%29, P < 0.001}, male sex %28OR: 1.54 [95% CI: 1.25-1.89], P < 0.001%29, Black race %28OR: 1.62 [95% CI: 1.24-2.09], P < 0.001%29, military/Veterans Affairs insurance %28OR: 2.44 [95% CI: 1.61-3.66], P < 0.001%29, and Medicaid %28OR: 1.51 [95% CI: 1.06-2.15], P = 0.022%29. Having a college/advanced degree %28OR: 0.76 [95% CI: 0.59-0.98], P = 0.031%29, annual household income between $50,000 and $100,000 %28OR: 0.72 [95% CI: 0.52-0.98], P = 0.035%29, and annual household income between $100,000 and $200,000 %28OR: 0.48 [95% CI: 0.32-0.70], P < 0.001%29 were protective against RAO.    Conclusions: These findings confirm previously described associations between RAO and cardiovascular comorbidities and identified novel associations between RAO and SDOH, including Black race and Medicaid insurance. Stroke risk around the time of RAO was high in this cohort.
lay_summary: The study looked back at health records in a large U.S. database to find who gets retinal artery occlusion (RAO), which is like an eye stroke. Researchers compared 384 people with RAO to 328,639 without. RAO patients were older (median age 66 at diagnosis). They found higher RAO risk in older people, men, Black people, and those with VA or Medicaid insurance. People with college degrees and higher incomes had lower risk. Stroke risk around RAO was high. This means doctors and patients should watch for heart and stroke problems and consider social factors that affect care.

pdr_title: Gene-gene interactions between a LMNA variant and common polymorphisms drive early-onset atrial fibrillation
pdr_abstract: Atrial fibrillation %28AF%29, the most common sustained arrhythmia, has a complex genetic basis; however, the molecular mechanisms linking rare and common variants remain poorly understood. Polygenic risk score %28PRS%29 analysis in the UK Biobank and All of Us cohorts reveals that carriers of protein-altering LMNA variants %28PAVs%29 have a significantly higher risk of incident AF than predicted by PRS alone, supporting an additive effect of common polymorphisms and LMNA variants. Induced pluripotent stem cell derived atrial cardiomyocytes %28iPSC-aCMs%29 from individuals carrying the pathogenic missense variant p.S143P in LMNA exhibit widespread disruption of chromatin architecture and perturbation of atrial gene regulatory networks, particularly at loci harboring AF-associated variants and transcription factors essential for atrial rhythm control and contractility. Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats %28CRISPR%29-based epigenetic editing validates the function of several AF-associated regulatory elements and their downstream targets. Notably, reduced accessibility at an intronic SCN10A enhancer harboring the AF-associated SNP rs6801957 is associated with reduced sodium current in p.S143P iPSC-aCMs. These findings are reproduced in iPSC-aCMs derived from an additional individual carrying a distinct pathogenic LMNA variant, supporting a broader mechanism in which rare LMNA variants and common polymorphisms converge on shared regulatory networks to influence AF susceptibility and highlighting the value of integrating both in arrhythmia risk assessment.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know how rare changes in the LMNA gene work with common DNA differences to cause early atrial fibrillation (AF). They studied health data from large groups and lab-made heart cells grown from people with LMNA changes, and used CRISPR (a gene-editing tool) to test DNA switches. They found people with LMNA changes had higher AF risk than expected, and their cells showed altered DNA folding and gene control at AF sites and lower heart sodium current. This suggests testing both rare and common DNA changes can better predict AF risk.

pdr_title: Development and evaluation of cardiovascular disease risk prediction models for patients with type 2 diabetes
pdr_abstract: Unlabelled: To facilitate treatment decisions in people at risk of Cardiovascular Disease %28CVD%29, several risk equations such as the Pooled Cohort Equations and Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events %28PREVENT%29 equations have been developed to estimate CVD risk for primary prevention patients. However, it is unclear whether these equations achieve high predictive accuracy and fairness in patients with type 2 diabetes %28T2D%29, and whether a T2D-specific risk equation is needed. Accordingly, we developed a Weibull Accelerated Failure Time %28AFT%29 survival model for predicting the 3-year CVD risk in 23,795 patients with T2D from the All of Us dataset, using sociodemographic information, physical measurements, medication, and CVD history. Among patients without CVD history, our Weibull AFT %28vs. PREVENT%29 achieved a greater C-index %280.646 vs. 0.465%29, greater Concordance Fractions %280.610–0.674 vs. 0.541–0.600%29, and comparable Concordance Imparity %280.006 vs. 0.002%29 across sex and race/ethnicity %280.065 vs. 0.058%29 subgroups. Our findings highlight the need for a T2D-specific CVD risk equation and demonstrate the value of diverse datasets for developing fair and accurate predictive models.    Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1038/s41598-026-45129-5.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if heart disease risk tools work well for people with type 2 diabetes and if a diabetes-specific tool is needed. Using health records from 23,795 people with type 2 diabetes, they made a new 3-year heart disease risk model using age, race, body measurements, medicines, and past heart disease. The new model was more accurate than a common tool (about 65% vs 47%) and was about as fair for men and women and for different racial groups. This suggests a diabetes-specific risk tool could better help prevent heart disease.

pdr_title: Metabolic syndrome severity is related to perceived discrimination and stress in the all of us cohort
pdr_abstract: Introduction    Metabolic-syndrome %28MetS%29 is influenced by underlying physiologic processes potentially worsened by social determinants of health. Our goal was to assess whether MetS severity was associated with scores on scales assessing perceived discrimination and stress.    Methods    We assessed data from 25,969 participants without diabetes in the All-of-Us cohort for how a MetS-severity-z-score %28MetS-Z%29 was related to SDoH scales for Everyday Discrimination %28EDS%29, Discrimination in Medical Settings %28DMS%29, and Perceived Stress %28PSS%29. Regression models adjusted for sex, self-reported race and ethnicity, income, education and age-group, and evaluated for potential interactions between score, sex, race and ethnicity and age.    Results    All three discrimination and stress scores were positively associated with MetS-severity %28slopes: EDS 0.071 ± 0.007, DMS 0.085 ± 0.009, PSS 0.006 ± 0.001, all p     Conclusions    Perceived discrimination and stress were consistently—albeit weakly—associated with MetS-severity, supporting potential connections with physiologic processes increasing cardiometabolic disarray. Unexpectedly, in this analytic cohort the relationship between everyday discrimination and MetS-severity by race and ethnicity was strongest among White and Other individuals.
lay_summary: This study asked if feeling discriminated against or stressed is tied to how bad people’s metabolic syndrome (a cluster of risk factors for heart disease and diabetes) is. Researchers looked at 25,969 adults without diabetes in the All of Us project and compared scores for everyday discrimination, discrimination in medical care, and perceived stress with a metabolic-severity score. People who reported more discrimination or stress had slightly worse metabolic health, with the everyday discrimination link strongest in White and Other groups. Lowering stress and discrimination may help protect heart and metabolic health.
calc_title: Metabolic syndrome severity is related to perceived discrimination and stress in the all of us cohort
calc_abstract: Introduction    Metabolic-syndrome (MetS) is influenced by underlying physiologic processes potentially worsened by social determinants of health. Our goal was to assess whether MetS severity was associated with scores on scales assessing perceived discrimination and stress.    Methods    We assessed data from 25,969 participants without diabetes in the All-of-Us cohort for how a MetS-severity-z-score (MetS-Z) was related to SDoH scales for Everyday Discrimination (EDS), Discrimination in Medical Settings (DMS), and Perceived Stress (PSS). Regression models adjusted for sex, self-reported race and ethnicity, income, education and age-group, and evaluated for potential interactions between score, sex, race and ethnicity and age.    Results    All three discrimination and stress scores were positively associated with MetS-severity (slopes: EDS 0.071 ± 0.007, DMS 0.085 ± 0.009, PSS 0.006 ± 0.001, all p     Conclusions    Perceived discrimination and stress were consistently—albeit weakly—associated with MetS-severity, supporting potential connections with physiologic processes increasing cardiometabolic disarray. Unexpectedly, in this analytic cohort the relationship between everyday discrimination and MetS-severity by race and ethnicity was strongest among White and Other individuals.

pdr_title: Development of polyphenotypic scores to prioritize detection of G6PD rs1050828 carriers in African and African American populations
pdr_journal_title: Genetics in Medicine : Official Journal of the American College of Medical Genetics
pdr_abstract: Purpose: The G6PD missense variant rs1050828 %28NP_000393.4:p.Val98Met%29 is common in African and African American populations. It lowers HbA1c levels independent of glycemia, increasing the risk of underdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis of diabetes. We aimed to develop polyphenotypic scores %28PPS%29 using routinely collected phenotypes to identify likely carriers.    Methods: Using data from 31,083 African or African American participants in the All of Us Research Program %28AoU%29, we developed sex-specific PPS through multi-stage variable selection. We validated the PPS in independent African or African American individuals from AoU %28N = 8,846%29, BioMe Biobank %28N = 8,839%29, and UK Biobank %28N = 6,811%29, and evaluated their utility among individuals without diagnosed diabetes.    Results: The PPS achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranging from 0.7614 to 0.8686 in identifying male hemizygotes and from 0.7378 to 0.8654 identifying female homozygotes. Among individuals without diagnosed diabetes and with HbA1c <6.5%, PPS-based screening reduced the number needed to screen for identifying male hemizygotes by 65-90% and female homozygotes by 80-90%, compared to random screening.    Conclusion: The PPS may help identify likely rs1050828 carriers in African and African American populations, supporting prioritization for confirmatory testing or alternative diagnostic approaches for diabetes.
lay_summary: This study aimed to find people who carry a common genetic change (G6PD rs1050828) that can make a diabetes test (HbA1c, a blood sugar average) read too low. Researchers used routine health data from over 31,000 African and African American adults to build separate scores for men and women. They checked the scores in about 24,000 more people and found they worked well. Using the scores cut how many people need testing by about 65–90% for men and 80–90% for women. This can help doctors pick who needs extra checks for diabetes.

pdr_title: Clinical Implications of the Duffy-Null Genotype in Patients on Azathioprine or Methotrexate in the All of Us Cohort
pdr_journal_title: The Journal of Applied Laboratory Medicine
pdr_abstract: Background: The Duffy null variant %28CC genotype%29 is associated with lower absolute neutrophil count %28ANC%29 and increased risk of early discontinuation or ineligibility for certain treatments. Our primary objective was to evaluate the change in ANC over time among individuals on azathioprine or methotrexate. We also evaluated normality status %28i.e., a designation of abnormal vs not%29 of ANC under genotype-adjusted and unadjusted thresholds.    Methods: We used the UK Biobank to calculate genotype-adjusted and unadjusted thresholds. We included participants reporting azathioprine or methotrexate use in All of Us to examine the primary and secondary objectives. The primary outcome was the log-mean difference in ANC between 1 year before and 2 years post medication initiation. The secondary outcome was the odds of normality of ANC under genotype-adjusted vs unadjusted thresholds.    Results: We found that in azathioprine users, those with the CC genotype had nonstatistically significant lower ANC %28log-mean difference, -0.017; 95% CI, -0.072 to 0.038%29. For methotrexate, those with the CC genotype had a statistically significant lower ANC %28log-mean difference, -0.042; 95% CI, -0.074 to -0.009%29. Evaluations of unadjusted ANC thresholds in those on azathioprine revealed that CC individuals were more likely to be abnormal %28odds ratio [OR], 7.51; 95% CI, 1.64 to 34.43%29. Findings were similar for methotrexate %28OR, 4.35; 95% CI, 1.48 to 12.79%29. However, under Duffy-adjusted thresholds, there were no significant differences between both genotypes in either treatment group: azathioprine %28P = .491%29 and methotrexate %28P = .269%29.    Conclusion: We conclude that Duffy-adjusted ANC reference ranges reduce the proportion of individuals classified as abnormal, with several implications for Duffy-null individuals.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to see if a common genetic change called Duffy-null (CC), which can lower white blood cell counts, affects people taking the drugs azathioprine or methotrexate. They studied people in the All of Us project and used UK Biobank data to set usual and Duffy-adjusted cutoff numbers. They found Duffy-null people on methotrexate had lower white cell counts and Duffy-null people on either drug were much more often labeled 'abnormal' using standard cutoffs. Using Duffy-adjusted cutoffs removed these differences. This means using adjusted ranges may prevent unnecessary stopping or changes in care.

pdr_title: Associations between neighborhood disorder and mental health service utilization in the All of Us study
pdr_abstract: Background    Neighborhood environment is critically important in shaping mental health outcomes. Among those with a history of diagnoses of anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder %28PTSD%29 the likelihood of ongoing visits and current medication/treatment can be influenced by social and physical neighborhood-related risk factors. Despite growing evidence, only a few large-scale studies have examined these associations. Using data from the All of Us Research Program funded by the National Institute of Health %28NIH%29, we examined the association between neighborhood disorders on mental health service utilization among adults in the United States.    Methods    The present study analyzed the All of Us Controlled Tier Dataset V7, which included self-reported survey data collected between May 31, 2017, and June 30, 2022. The 39,438 participants responded to the 'Basics' %28demographics%29, 'Social Determinants of Health' %28SDOH%29, and 'Personal and Family Health History' %28PFHH%29 surveys, all completed within 365 days of enrollment. The Neighborhood Disorder Scale was used to assess social and physical disorder in neighborhoods. Self-reported history of anxiety, depression, or PTSD were collected via questionnaire on additional measures of ongoing provider care and current treatment or medication use. Data were analyzed via chi-square tests, Wilcoxon rank sum tests, and t-tests, while univariable and multivariable binary logistic regression models estimated the association between neighborhood disorder and mental health care engagement.    Results    Greater neighborhood disorder was linked to higher odds of ongoing mental health care %28OR 1.18; 95% CI 1.12–1.24%29 and current medication or treatment %28OR 1.13; 95% CI 1.07–1.18%29. Mental health care engagement declined with increasing age, with participants above 75 years being significantly less likely to receive care %28OR 0.14; 95% CI 0.12–0.16%29 and treatment %28OR 0.19; 95% CI 0.16–0.21%29 when compared to those 18–44 years of age. Cisgender men had lower odds of care %28OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.54–0.61%29 and treatment %28OR 0.54; 95% CI 0.51–0.57%29 compared to cisgender women, while non-cisgender participants showed significantly higher odds of both. Non-Hispanic White participants were more likely to receive care %28OR 2.08; 95% CI 1.91–2.27%29 and treatment %28OR 2.21; 95% CI 2.03–2.42%29 when compared with Hispanic/Latino participants.    Conclusion    Findings underscore the importance of neighborhood conditions in receiving mental health care. These results emphasize the need for targeted public health interventions addressing structural determinants of mental health care utilization.    Supplementary Information    The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12982-026-02103-w.
lay_summary: Researchers studied whether run-down neighborhoods affect mental health care. They used surveys from 39,438 U.S. adults in the All of Us study to measure neighborhood disorder and whether people with anxiety, depression, or PTSD were seeing a provider or taking medicine. People in worse neighborhoods were about 18% more likely to be getting care and 13% more likely to be on treatment. Adults over 75, men, and Hispanic/Latino people were less likely to get care, while non-cisgender people were more likely. Fixing neighborhood problems and focusing outreach on these groups could help.

pdr_title: Designing a Multimodal Data Structure for Cognitive Decline Using All of Us Resources and Gemini Flash Thinking
pdr_journal_title: Studies in Health Technology and Informatics
pdr_abstract: Cognitive decline is not easily defined, as it can manifest across multilayered and heterogeneous data. Its understanding requires the design of data structures that integrate all relevant dimensions. In this study, we address the challenge of implementing artificial intelligence models in medicine, focusing on the 'Black Box' problem, and propose a conceptual and methodological framework to enhance interpretability. The framework integrates the All of Us Resource and applies Gemini Flash Thinking to move beyond correlation and explore causality. The proposed multilayer design establishes the foundation for dynamic modeling. Future work will refine this Gemini-based structure using All of Us data and develop interpretable visualizations and outputs for diverse populations.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to make it easier to study and explain memory and thinking problems. They designed a plan that mixes a big health database called All of Us and a new AI way called Gemini Flash Thinking (an approach to help AI look for causes, not just links). They built a layered data structure as a first step toward models that change over time and that people can understand. Next they will test it with real data and make clear visuals. This could help doctors and patients trust and use AI for brain health.

pdr_title: Perioperative CA19-9 and CEA Trajectories After Pancreatic Cancer Resection
pdr_journal_title: Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery : Official Journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract
pdr_abstract: Background: The prognostic utility of CA19-9 may vary based on the clinical and genetic factors %28e.g., FUT2/FUT3 mutation or UGT1A1 alleles%29. We sought to examine early post-operative changes in CA19-9 relative to prognosis following resection of PDAC.    Methods: Patients undergoing resection of PDAC were identified from the All of Us Research Program. Patients were categorized into neoadjuvant therapy followed by resection %28NAT→resection%29 and surgery-first. The primary endpoint was real-world time-to-treatment-failure %28rwTTF%29. Genomic and sensitivity analyses excluded post-treatment draws with total bilirubin >2mg/dL and restricted to CA19-9 producers.    Results: Among 283 resected patients, 48 underwent NAT→resection and 235 underwent surgery-first. Index years ranged from 1999 to 2023. Baseline CA19-9 distributions differed markedly by pathway: NAT→resection patients had median pre-treatment CA19-9 273U/mL with 10.0% normal values, whereas surgery-first patients had median pre-treatment CA19-9 19U/mL with 68.7% normal values. CEA was available pre-treatment in 88 patients and post-operatively in 41 patients; only 1 of 8 phenotypic CA19-9 non-producers had elevated CEA. In CA19-9 trajectory analysis, median rwTTF was 1185.5 days for normal→normal, 693 days for elevated→normalized, and 138 days for elevated→persistently elevated patients. After excluding planned adjuvant therapy from the rwTTF endpoint, higher pre-treatment CA19-9 and greater post-operative CA19-9 change were independently associated with rwTTF, whereas binary post-operative normalization alone was not.    Conclusions: Basing prognosis on a single CA19-9 value or percent drop may be insufficient, particularly because many surgery-first patients had normal baseline CA19-9. Perioperative CA19-9 trajectories provided a more clinically informative framework, with persistent postoperative elevation identifying the highest-risk group after PDAC resection.
lay_summary: Researchers looked at 283 people who had surgery to remove pancreatic cancer to see if changes in CA19-9 (a blood tumor marker) and CEA (another marker) after surgery could predict outcomes. They compared people who had chemotherapy before surgery (48) and those who had surgery first (235). Patients whose CA19-9 stayed normal did best (about 3.3 years), those whose high levels dropped did worse (about 1.9 years), and those with always-high levels did worst (about 0.4 years). This means doctors should watch marker trends over time, not rely on one single test.

pdr_title: Discordance Between Electronic Health Records and Self-Reported Data: Evidence from Traumatic Brain Injury and Colorectal Cancer
pdr_abstract: Background/Objectives: Discordance between electronic health records %28EHR%29 and self-reported survey data may reflect incomplete clinical documentation on the provider side, as well as sociodemographic differences among survey participants. Cancer conditions are frequently reported with the least discordance. Traumatic brain injury %28TBI%29 may be particularly prone to discordance. The aim of this study was to nationally investigate discordance between EHR and self-reported data for TBI and colorectal cancer. Methods: This cross-sectional study used data from the national All of Us Research Program, including participants with both linked EHR and self-reported survey data. Participants in each condition were stratified into four groups: EHR+/Survey+ %28concordant positive%29, EHR−/Survey− %28concordant negative%29, EHR+/Survey− %28discordant%29, and EHR−/Survey+ %28discordant%29. EHR-documented and survey-reported conditions were compared using a 2 × 2 classification framework to assess concordance. Agreement metrics, including sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, overall concordance/discordance, directional discordance, and Cohen’s kappa, were calculated. Logistic regression models were used to examine the association between the outcomes and sociodemographic factors. Machine learning models additionally investigated the predictive performance of these factors. Results: For TBI, concordance between EHR and survey was fair %28κ = 0.33%29, with sensitivity of 60.9% and specificity, 92.9%. In regression models, increasing age was associated with higher odds of both discordant groups %28EHR+/Survey− and EHR−/Survey+%29; lower educational levels and non-White participants had higher odds of discordance specifically in EHR+/Survey− group. Medicaid insurance had higher odds in the EHR−/Survey+ group. In contrast, colorectal cancer showed stronger concordance %28κ = 0.66; sensitivity 74.5%; specificity 98.6%%29 and fewer sociodemographic associations in regression models. The association between race and Medicaid coverage showed a similar pattern to TBI. Machine learning results were also consistent with logistic regression models. Conclusions: Concordance between EHR and self-reported data was fair for TBI. Older age, lower education, non-White race, and Medicaid insurance were associated with greater discordance. These sociodemographic patterns were less pronounced in colorectal cancer, except for race and Medicaid insurance. Policies are needed to improve concordance between EHR and self-reported data, particularly across certain sociodemographic groups.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if medical records and people’s survey answers matched for traumatic brain injury (TBI) and colorectal cancer. They looked at a large national database that had both medical records and self-reported surveys. For TBI, the match was only fair: about 61% of cases in records were also reported by people. For colorectal cancer the match was better at about 75%. Older people, those with less schooling, non-White people, and people on Medicaid had more mismatches, especially for TBI. This means we need better record-keeping and asking patients to get fair care and research.

pdr_title: Phenome-wide analysis of downstream health outcomes following second-line antidiabetic agent prescriptions in All of Us
pdr_abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists %28GLP-1 RAs%29 are increasingly prescribed for type 2 diabetes %28T2D%29 and weight management, yet their real-world health impacts remain understudied. Using a retrospective cohort design with electronic health record data from 17,267 adults with type 2 diabetes in the All of Us Research Program, we conduct propensity score-matched phenome-wide association studies comparing diagnoses following GLP-1 RA prescription %28including semaglutide-specific analyses%29 to those following sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor %28SGLT2i%29 and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor %28DPP4i%29 prescriptions between January 2018 and October 2023. We employ both intention-to-treat and per-protocol Cox proportional hazards models alongside restricted mean survival time analyses evaluating up to 974 phenotypes. We identify multiple phenome-wide significant and suggestive associations, including for cardiovascular, genitourinary, dental, and metabolic outcomes. Compared to SGLT2i, semaglutide demonstrates reduced risk for genitourinary infections in women %28e.g., candidiasis of vulva and vagina %28per-protocol hazard ratio 0.31, 95% confidence interval %280.17-0.55%29%29. Compared to DPP4i, GLP-1 RAs are associated with reduced risk of diseases of hard tissues of teeth %280.45 %280.33-0.61%29%29. Time-to-event analyses reveal modest delays for key diagnoses. These findings underscore differences in downstream diagnostic associations across second-line T2D therapies and highlight semaglutide's distinct profile, with implications for clinical decision-making and personalized prescribing.
lay_summary: Researchers studied 17,267 adults with type 2 diabetes using health records to compare health problems after starting second-line diabetes drugs from 2018 to 2023. They matched patients and checked nearly 1,000 diagnoses. They found drugs had different risks. GLP-1 drugs (a class of diabetes medicines, like semaglutide) were tied to fewer dental and metabolic problems. Compared with SGLT2 drugs, semaglutide showed about 70% fewer vaginal yeast infections in women. Compared with DPP4 drugs, GLP-1 drugs had about 55% fewer problems of the hard parts of teeth (like enamel and decay). This can help doctors choose medicines that fit patients.

We employ both intention-to-treat and per-protocol Cox proportional hazards models alongside restricted mean survival time analyses evaluating up to 974 phenotypes. We identify multiple phenome-wide significant and suggestive associations, including for cardiovascular, genitourinary, dental, and metabolic outcomes. Compared to SGLT2i, semaglutide demonstrates reduced risk for genitourinary infections in women (e.g., candidiasis of vulva and vagina (per-protocol hazard ratio 0.31, 95% confidence interval (0.17-0.55)). Compared to DPP4i, GLP-1 RAs are associated with reduced risk of diseases of hard tissues of teeth (0.45 (0.33-0.61)). Time-to-event analyses reveal modest delays for key diagnoses. These findings underscore differences in downstream diagnostic associations across second-line T2D therapies and highlight semaglutide's distinct profile, with implications for clinical decision-making and personalized prescribing.

pdr_title: Air pollution modifies clonal hematopoiesis-associated non-small cell lung cancer risk in non-smoking individuals
pdr_journal_title: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
pdr_abstract: Small particulate matter air pollution %28PM2.5%29 is a recognized driver of non-small cell lung cancer %28NSCLC%29, including in non-smoking individuals. Inhaled PM2.5 recruits pro-inflammatory macrophages to the air-lung interface, which promotes malignant lung epithelial cell growth and progression to overt cancer. Smoking is recognized to potentiate this process, though no factors potentiating risk among non-smoking individuals have been identified. We sought to determine whether clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential %28CHIP%29, a common age-related condition characterized by hyperinflammatory macrophages, synergizes with PM2.5 to promote NSCLC in non-smoking individuals using genetic, environmental, and phenotypic data from over 650,000 people in the UK Biobank and All of Us cohorts. In meta-analysis, CHIP was associated with a greater risk of NSCLC in never-smoking participants %28hazard ratio %28HR%29=1.76[1.07-2.89]%29. This risk is exacerbated in the setting of above-median PM2.5 levels %28HR=2.51[1.55 to 4.05]; p-interaction=0.02%29. The CHIP x PM2.5 interaction also associated with elevated markers of systemic inflammation %28CRP, IL-6, and IL-1β%29. Together, these results suggest CHIP and PM2.5 form a novel somatic gene × environment interaction promoting inflammation and NSCLC tumorigenesis in non-smoking individuals.
lay_summary: Researchers asked whether a common age-related blood change called CHIP (which makes immune cells more inflamed) makes air pollution more likely to cause lung cancer in people who never smoked. They used genetic, environmental, and health data from over 650,000 people in the UK Biobank and All of Us. Never-smokers with CHIP had about a 75% higher chance of non-small cell lung cancer, and that risk was more than doubled if they lived where air pollution was higher. These people also had higher blood inflammation. It means cutting air pollution and checking for CHIP could lower lung cancer risk.

pdr_title: Association of Common Ancestry-Enriched Variants With Cardiomyopathy and Arrhythmias
pdr_abstract: Background: Individuals of African ancestry are underrepresented in genetic studies, contributing to disproportionately higher rates of variants of uncertain significance %28VUS%29 and fewer actionable results in genetic testing for cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias. We aimed to determine whether ancestry-enriched VUS confer measurable cardiovascular risk among individuals of African ancestry.    Methods: We identified VUS enriched in individuals of African ancestry in 18 cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia genes. We defined enriched as allele frequency in gnomAD ≥2-fold higher than in European %28non-Finnish%29 individuals, and we confined the analysis to VUS with allele frequency >0.05% in individuals of African ancestry. Associations with cardiovascular phenotypes were assessed in 96 897 individuals of African ancestry from the All of Us %28n=65 481%29 and BioVU %28n=31 416%29 biobanks using fixed-effects meta-analysis. Analyses were stratified by heart failure %28HF%29 status and conventional cardiovascular risk factors.    Results: We identified 82 ancestry-enriched VUS. Exploratory analysis in All of Us identified 10 variants associated with composite cardiovascular outcome, 4 of which were associated with individual cardiovascular phenotypes in pooled meta-analysis across both cohorts. PKP2 p.Val558Ile was associated with a 4-fold increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death %28adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 4.02 [95% CI, 1.85-8.71]; P=0.004%29. ELAC2 p.Ile396Val was associated with HF %28aOR, 1.67 [95% CI, 1.17-2.39]; P=0.02%29 and atrial arrhythmias %28aOR, 1.88 [95% CI, 1.27-2.78]; P=0.02%29. FLNC p.Gly11Ser and PKP2 p.Val842Ile were associated with HF %28aOR, 1.96 [95% CI, 1.24-3.10]; P=0.02 and aOR, 1.99 [95% CI, 1.16-3.41]; P=0.039%29. The presence of cardiovascular risk factors was associated with earlier onset of HF %28adjusted hazard ratio, 1.71 [95% CI, 1.25-2.33]; P=0.0006%29 and atrial arrhythmias %28adjusted hazard ratio, 1.17 [95% CI, 1.06-1.29]; P=0.0019%29 in pooled variant carriers. PKP2 p.Val558Ile, SCN5A p.Gln1832Glu, and FLNC p.Gly11Ser demonstrated increased arrhythmia burden specifically in participants with HF. Using American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines, PKP2 p.Val558Ile met criteria for likely pathogenic classification, potentially affecting an estimated 24000 Black adults in the United States.    Conclusions: Large-scale biobank analysis identified variants classified as VUS that conferred increased risk of cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia in individuals with African ancestry. The risk associated with these variants was increased in the presence of cardiovascular risk factors and HF.
lay_summary: This study looked for gene changes common in people of African ancestry that might raise risk for heart muscle disease and dangerous heart rhythms. Researchers studied 82 uncertain gene changes in 18 heart genes in 96,897 people from two large health databases. They found four changes linked to more heart problems. One raised risk of life‑threatening heart rhythms about four times. Others were tied to higher risk of heart failure or irregular heartbeats. Having common heart risk factors made problems happen earlier. One change may affect about 24,000 Black adults and could help doctors interpret genetic tests.

pdr_title: Evidence for overlapping genetic architecture between lifestyle factors and severe mental disorders with different patterns across diagnoses
pdr_abstract: Background: Severe mental disorders %28SMDs%29 are associated with unhealthy lifestyle, contributing to increased risk of comorbid cardiovascular disease. Genetic factors influence both SMDs and lifestyle behaviours, but their genetic relationships remain unclear. Here, we aimed to unravel the shared genetic architecture of SMDs and lifestyle factors. Additionally, we assessed if genetic propensity to SMDs predicts body mass index %28BMI%29 and lipids through lifestyle factors.    Methods: We analysed genome-wide data on major depression %28MD%29 %28N = 480,359%29, schizophrenia %28SCZ%29 %28N = 130,644%29, bipolar disorder %28BIP%29 %28N = 353,889%29 and self-reported lifestyle factors %28N = 266,048-606,820%29, including food intake, physical activity, sedentary behaviours, and accelerometer-assessed activity from All of Us %28N = 30,132%29 and UK Biobank %28N = 91,105%29 to obtain objective measures for sensitivity analysis. We estimated the shared genetic architecture using bivariate MiXeR. Shared genetic loci were identified using conjunctional false discovery rate and mapped to genes, which were subject to enrichment analyses. We applied structural equation modelling %28SEM%29 to assess if lifestyle mediates the relationship between polygenic risk score for SMDs and BMI and lipids. People with lived experience were involved in the research.    Findings: There was extensive genetic overlap between lifestyle factors and SMDs, with different patterns of effects. MD was genetically correlated with less physical activity and more sedentary behaviour. SCZ and BIP displayed opposite patterns with genetic associations with less sedentary behaviour, more physical activity and healthier food intake. This divergent pattern across SMDs was largely consistent using accelerometer-assessed activity. We identified 551 shared loci, implicating biological processes related to neurodevelopment and synaptic and neuronal properties. Further analyses indicated that lifestyle factors partly mediate the relationship between genetic risk for SMDs and BMI and lipids.    Interpretation: The results show a genetic propensity towards unhealthier lifestyle behaviours in MD, while SCZ and BIP displayed a divergent pattern. The genetic correlations reflecting mixed effect directions may also imply subgroups with different genetic propensity, which can form the basis for risk stratification and more tailored lifestyle interventions and personalised treatment.    Funding: Research Council of Norway %28grants, 273291, 273446, 300309, 324252, and 326813%29, South-East Norway Regional Health Authority %28grants 2023-031 and 2022-073%29, NordForsk %28University Cooperation Grant 164218, PreciMENT%29, European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Programme %28grant 847776, CoMorMent; grant 964874, RealMent%29, and the National Institutes of Health %28grant R01MH125938%29.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if the same genes link severe mental illnesses and lifestyle habits like activity and eating. They studied genetic data from hundreds of thousands of people and compared gene patterns to self-reported and device-measured activity, diet, body weight, and blood fats. They found many shared genetic regions (551) and different patterns: genes for major depression linked to less exercise and more sitting, while genes for schizophrenia and bipolar linked to more activity and healthier eating. Lifestyle partly explained how genetic risk affects weight and blood fats. This could help target lifestyle support for people at risk.

pdr_title: Population Heterogeneity in Iron Biomarkers by Age, Sex, Menopausal Status, and Race in Healthy U.S. Adults: A Cross-Sectional Analysis from the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Background/Objectives: Blood iron biomarkers are commonly interpreted using fixed clinical reference intervals, although iron metabolism varies by age, sex, menopausal status, and race. This study aimed to characterize the distribution of iron biomarkers across demographic subgroups and to examine their distribution relative to commonly used reference intervals. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 7990 adults %28≥18 years%29 from the All of Us Research Program were classified as premenopausal women, postmenopausal women, men  56 years. Serum iron, ferritin, total iron-binding capacity, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and transferrin saturation %28TSAT%29 were summarized across groups and compared descriptively with commonly used reference intervals. Results: Iron biomarkers varied across demographic groups. Mean serum iron was 82.3 µg/dL overall, with lower levels in premenopausal women %2879.5 ± 36.7 µg/dL%29 and higher levels in men Conclusions: Iron biomarker distributions differ across demographic subgroups and may not be fully reflected by commonly used reference intervals. These findings highlight the importance of context-specific interpretation and underscore the need for further studies to evaluate the applicability of current reference intervals across diverse populations.
lay_summary: Researchers studied 7,990 U.S. adults from the All of Us program to see how blood iron tests differ by age, sex, menopausal status, and race. They measured several iron tests like serum iron and ferritin (stored iron). Average serum iron was about 82 micrograms per deciliter, lower in premenopausal women (about 80) and higher in men. The tests varied by group and common one-size-fits-all reference ranges may miss these differences. This means doctors may need to think about a person’s age, sex, and race when checking iron levels.

pdr_title: A Genome-First Study of Familial Hypercholesterolemia Comparing African and European Ancestry Individuals
pdr_abstract: Background: Familial hypercholesterolemia %28FH%29 is an inherited disorder characterized by lifelong elevated LDL-C %28low-density lipoprotein cholesterol%29 and increased risk for premature myocardial infarction. FH research has focused on European populations and, consequently, estimates of global FH burden primarily reflect this ancestry, with limited data available from other groups.    Methods: We examined the prevalence and clinical outcomes of FH among 104300 African ancestry individuals enrolled in 3 US-based cohorts: the National Institutes of Health's All of Us, Mount Sinai's BioMe, and Geisinger's MyCode. Genetic variants were evaluated according to standards provided by the Clinical Genome Resource's FH Variant Curation Expert Panel and grouped as pathogenic variants or variants of unknown significance %28VUSs%29. Participants were assigned to European and African ancestry groups based on genetic similarity to reference populations. Clinical outcomes were LDL-C and myocardial infarction. Analyses were adjusted for age and sex. Results were meta-analyzed across cohorts.    Results: The prevalence of a pathogenic variant was similar in the African %281 in 306%29 and European %281 in 273%29 ancestry groups. The LDL-C elevation associated with pathogenic variants was 20.81 mg/dL %2895% CI, 16.17-25.45%29 greater in individuals with African ancestry compared with their counterparts with European ancestry. Individuals with African ancestry had 1.61 %2895% CI, 1.42-1.83; P=1.2×10-12%29 higher odds of having a VUS compared with individuals with European ancestry and a 10.01 mg/dL %2895% CI, 6.13-13.88%29 greater elevation in LDL-C compared with individuals with European ancestry with a VUS. Although pathogenic variants in both ancestries conferred a 2- to 3-fold increased risk of myocardial infarction, having a VUS only conferred increased risk among the African ancestry group %28odds ratio, 1.91 [95% CI, 1.18-3.10]%29.    Conclusions: The prevalence of pathogenic variants did not significantly vary between African and European ancestry groups. VUSs were both more prevalent among individuals of African ancestry and associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction equivalent to that of a pathogenic variant. These findings suggest that dependence on existing resources for variant classification could contribute to underdiagnosis of FH in individuals of African ancestry.

lay_summary: This study looked at inherited high cholesterol (familial hypercholesterolemia, FH) in over 104,000 people of African and European genetic ancestry from three U.S. groups. Researchers checked DNA for known harmful changes and for unclear changes (VUS = variant of unknown significance). Harmful changes were about equally common (about 1 in 300) in both groups. Unclear changes were more common in African ancestry people and were linked to higher bad cholesterol (about 10–20 mg/dL more) and to more heart attacks. This means current DNA labels may miss risk in people of African ancestry.
