pdr_title: Long COVID risk by pre-infection symptoms and functional status: A retrospective cohort study of data from the All of Us Research Program
pdr_abstract: Importance    Over seven million U.S. adults experience persistent health issues after COVID-19, known as “long COVID”. Although multiple guidelines recommend the inclusion of functional status in long COVID diagnostic criteria, more evidence is needed to guide this recommendation. This study explored the adjusted odds of developing long COVID by pre-infection symptoms and functional status, and the feasibility of estimating functional status using health records data.    Design & Methods    Retrospective cohort study of U.S. adults with history of COVID-19 enrolled in a multicenter national cohort study through July 2022 %28 All of Us Controlled Tier CDR 7.0%29, using diagnostic, procedure, and billing codes from the health record, and baseline survey responses. The risk of long COVID was estimated using logistic regression by pre-infection %28−5 years%29 incidences of %28a%29 at least one symptom common in long COVID, and %28b%29 functional impairment, and adjusted for disease and demographic characteristics.    Results    n = 65,464 met inclusion criteria; n = 40,655 had post-infection occurrences of at least one symptom %28long COVID group%29, n = 24,809 had none %28recovered%29. Adjusted odds ratios of developing long COVID increased with older age, female sex, Black racial identity, earlier variant, non-vaccination, lower pre-infection self-reported mental and cognitive health, and number of pre-infection symptoms. Adjusted odds were not significantly affected by any single pre-infection symptom, self-rated physical ability, or EHR-derived indicators of prior functional impairment.    Conclusions    In this model, there were no significant differences in risk of long COVID based on either pre-infection total incidences of long COVID symptoms %28compared to the average of 4%29 or pre-infection functional impairment. This suggests that long COVID was associated with a change from baseline functioning and health, including in people with pre-infection incident symptoms and functional impairments. The impacts of co-occurring pre-infection symptoms requires further investigation. Both harmonized electronic health records data and patient-reported outcomes contribute important data for developing the diagnostic utility of functional status changes in long COVID.
lay_summary: Researchers wanted to know if symptoms or problems doing daily activities before getting COVID made long COVID more likely. They looked at health records and surveys from 65,464 U.S. adults with COVID through July 2022. About 62% (40,655) had symptoms after infection and 38% recovered. Being older, female, Black, infected by an earlier virus type, not vaccinated, having worse mental or thinking health before illness, or having more prior symptoms made long COVID more likely. But having single symptoms or trouble with daily activities before COVID did not change risk. This means doctors should look for new changes from a person’s earlier health because people with earlier symptoms can still get long COVID.

pdr_abstract: Objective    This study aims to assess the prevalence of head and neck %28ENT%29 symptoms in patients with sarcoidosis.    Study Design    1:4 matched‐case control study.    Setting    Patients with and without sarcoidosis who enrolled in the All of Us Research Program and consented to electronic medical record use.    Methods    Multivariate logistic regression examined the association between ENT symptoms and sarcoidosis, adjusting for autoimmune status, the Charlson Comorbidity Index score, and smoking status.    Results    A total of 2446 patients with sarcoidosis were matched to 9783 controls. Compared to age‐, sex‐, race‐, and ethnicity‐matched controls and after adjustment, patients with sarcoidosis are more likely to have a recorded diagnosis of sinonasal symptoms, including chronic rhinitis %28adjusted OR: 2.061 %2895% CI: 1.779‐2.387%29, P P P P P P P = .0018%29. Controls were more likely to have a recorded diagnosis of impacted cerumen %28aOR: 0.505 %280.405‐0.630%29, P     Conclusion    Patients with sarcoidosis are significantly more likely to be diagnosed with sinonasal symptoms, airway and swallowing symptoms, and cranial nerve pathologies with prevalence rates higher than previously reported. Sarcoidosis of the upper airway is likely underdiagnosed and consequently undertreated, necessitating greater awareness and further exploration of the etiology of upper airway symptoms in patients with sarcoidosis.
lay_summary: This study looked at whether people with sarcoidosis have more head and neck problems. Researchers compared medical records for 2,446 people with sarcoidosis and 9,783 similar people without it. They found people with sarcoidosis were more likely to have sinus and nose problems (sinonasal), chronic runny or irritated nose, breathing and swallowing troubles, and nerve problems in the head and neck. Earwax blockage was more common in people without sarcoidosis. This means these upper airway issues may be missed and should get more attention from doctors and patients.

pdr_title: Exome-wide association study of blood lipids in 1,158,017 individuals from diverse populations
pdr_abstract: Rare coding alleles have crucial roles in the molecular diagnosis of genetic diseases. However, the systematic identification of these alleles has been challenging due to their scarcity in the general population. Here we discovered and characterized rare coding alleles contributing to genetic dyslipidemia, a principal risk for coronary artery disease %28CAD%29, among 1,158,017 multi-ancestral individuals. Testing 2,997,401 rare coding variants, we identified 800 exome-wide significant associations %28176 predicted loss of function %28pLoF%29 and 624 missense variants%29. Associated alleles are enriched in functional variant classes, show significant additive and recessive associations, exhibit similar effects across populations and resolve pathogenicity for variants of unknown significance. Furthermore, we identified five lipid-associated genes associated with CAD. Among them, silencing RORC

pdr_title: Sociodemographic disparities and reasons for delayed healthcare among U.S. cancer survivors: an All of Us study
pdr_abstract: Objective    To examine how sociodemographic factors influence healthcare access among cancer survivors.    Methods    From the National Institutes of Health’s All of Us dataset %282018–2022, n = 27,589%29, we analyzed the relationship between characteristics like age, income, race/ethnicity, and insurance, and reasons for delayed healthcare, including affordability, transportation, and nervousness.    Results    Young adult cancer survivors %28ages 18–39%29, those on Medicaid, and individuals earning less than $25,000 annually consistently experienced higher rates of delayed healthcare. The top reasons for delayed healthcare were affordability issues %2812%%29, nervousness %288%%29, and transportation barriers %286%%29. Female survivors were more likely to delay care for all reasons except transportation. Work and caregiving-related delays were more common among minoritized racial/ethnic groups, while non-Hispanic White survivors more often delayed healthcare due to nervousness and socioeconomic factors.    Conclusions    Considerable differences in delayed healthcare were observed among cancer survivors by sociodemographic characteristics. Findings highlight the need for tailored interventions to effectively address the unique social needs of each cancer survivor, ultimately improving healthcare access for all.    Supplementary Information    The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00520-026-10880-y.
lay_summary: Researchers studied 27,589 U.S. cancer survivors from a national database to see who delays care and why. They found young adults (18–39), people on Medicaid, and those earning under $25,000 delayed care most. Top reasons were cost (12%), nervousness about care (8%), and lack of transportation (6%). Women delayed more than men for most reasons except transportation. Work and caregiving problems caused more delays in racial and ethnic minority groups, while White survivors more often delayed because of nervousness or money. This shows we need programs that help different groups get care on time.

pdr_title: Augmenting Missing Individual Social Determinants of Health with Area-Level Social Deprivation Index for Gene-Environment Interaction: Application to Opioid Use Disorder Prediction
pdr_journal_title: AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science Proceedings. AMIA Joint Summits on Translational Science
pdr_abstract: Detecting gene-environment %28G×E%29 interactions is challenging when individual-level social determinants of health survey responses %28iSR%29 are highly missing. We hypothesize that an area-level Social Deprivation Index %28aSDI%29, derived from ZIP3 codes with <1% missingness, can augment or substitute for iSR variables, which exhibit ∼62% missingness in the All of Us Research Program. We developed a generalized linear mixed-effects model framework incorporating ZIP3-level random effects, assessed concordance between iSR and aSDI through correlation and quintile analyses, and evaluated G×E interactions between polygenic risk scores and aSDI. We applied this framework to prediction of opioid use disorder %28OUD%29 in All of Us %28N = 123,325 opioid-exposed adults%29. Composite quintile concordance between iSR and aSDI was moderate %28r = 0.52%29. Models using aSDI alone %28AUC = 0.822%29 performed comparably to iSR-only models %28AUC = 0.825%29. Leveraging aSDI to address missing iSR expanded the analytic sample from ∼43,000 to ∼123,000 and enabled detection of significant gene-poverty and gene-income interactions. The full model integrating clinical, genetic, individual, and area-level social features achieved AUC = 0.835.
lay_summary: Researchers tested whether a neighborhood-level score (aSDI) can stand in for missing personal social data when studying how genes and environment affect opioid use disorder (OUD). They used data from 123,325 adults who had used opioids. Personal social surveys were about 62% missing, but aSDI from ZIP codes had almost no missing data. Using aSDI grew the study from about 43,000 to 123,000. Models with aSDI predicted OUD about 82% as well as survey models, and the full model was about 84%. This suggests ZIP-code social scores can help find people at higher risk when personal data are missing.

calc_abstract: Detecting gene-environment (G×E) interactions is challenging when individual-level social determinants of health survey responses (iSR) are highly missing. We hypothesize that an area-level Social Deprivation Index (aSDI), derived from ZIP3 codes with <1% missingness, can augment or substitute for iSR variables, which exhibit ∼62% missingness in the All of Us Research Program. We developed a generalized linear mixed-effects model framework incorporating ZIP3-level random effects, assessed concordance between iSR and aSDI through correlation and quintile analyses, and evaluated G×E interactions between polygenic risk scores and aSDI. We applied this framework to prediction of opioid use disorder (OUD) in All of Us (N = 123,325 opioid-exposed adults). Composite quintile concordance between iSR and aSDI was moderate (r = 0.52). Models using aSDI alone (AUC = 0.822) performed comparably to iSR-only models (AUC = 0.825). Leveraging aSDI to address missing iSR expanded the analytic sample from ∼43,000 to ∼123,000 and enabled detection of significant gene-poverty and gene-income interactions. The full model integrating clinical, genetic, individual, and area-level social features achieved AUC = 0.835.

pdr_title: Privacy-enhancing sequential learning under heterogeneous selection bias in multi-site electronic health records data
pdr_journal_title: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
pdr_abstract: Objectives: To develop privacy-enhancing statistical methods for estimating disease risk parameters across multiple electronic health record %28EHR%29 sites with heterogeneous selection mechanisms, avoiding individual-level data sharing. We illustrate their utility via a cross-biobank analysis of smoking and 97 cancer subtypes using NIH All of Us %28AOU%29 and Michigan Genomics Initiative %28MGI%29 data sites.    Materials And Methods: Distributed health platforms often render centralized algorithms infeasible due to patient privacy protection. We propose Sequential Pseudo-Likelihood %28SPL%29 and Sequential Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting %28SAIPW%29 to adjust for selection bias using summary statistics shared across sites and external population information. SAIPW employs flexible auxiliary models for multiple robustness. We compared SPL and SAIPW against unweighted and centralized/meta-learning benchmarks in simulations, applying them to harmonized MGI %28n=50 935%29 and AOU %28n=241 563%29 data.    Results: Unweighted estimators exhibited substantial bias. SPL and SAIPW yielded unbiased estimates with valid coverage, with SAIPW remaining robust to selection model misspecification. Both approaches showed negligible efficiency loss relative to centralized methods. Meta-learning methods proved unstable for rare outcomes. Real-data analyses consistently identified strong associations between smoking and lung, bladder, and larynx cancers.    Discussion: These findings highlight the necessity of adjusting for site-specific selection biases in distributed health networks. SPL and SAIPW offer practical, scalable solutions that bypass the instability of meta-analysis for rare events, successfully harmonizing diverse biobanks while strictly enhancing patient privacy.    Conclusion: Our framework enables valid, privacy-enhancing inference across EHR sites subject to heterogeneous selection, facilitating scalable, distributed research using real-world data.
lay_summary: Researchers made two privacy-friendly methods to estimate disease risk across hospitals when some people are more likely to be included (selection bias). They used summary data and external population information on two medical databases: All of Us (241,563) and MGI (50,935), studying smoking and 97 cancers. The new methods removed bias seen in simple approaches and matched full-data results, and one stayed reliable even when models were wrong. Standard combined analyses were unstable for rare cancers. This helps researchers use real medical records without sharing patient-level data, protecting privacy and giving more trustworthy results for patients.

pdr_title: Population-scale genomic medicine with the Hong Kong Genome Project
pdr_abstract: The Hong Kong Genome Project %28HKGP%29 aims to build a foundational resource for precision medicine in the Chinese population through large-scale genome sequencing and integrated analyses. Here we report findings from over 20,000 HKGP participants across two cohorts: a rare disease cohort including 2,227 patients with suspected genetic diseases and a population cohort including 18,261 participants undergoing genomic screening for medically actionable findings. The rare disease cohort achieved a diagnostic rate of 25%. When benchmarked against panels designed for European ancestries, the analysis revealed that 3.7% of the individuals in the population cohort had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with dominant disorders. While 48% of individuals were found to carry recessive disorder genes in the gene list based upon European ancestries, our analysis revealed that 38 additional clinically important genes would have been overlooked in the Chinese population. Pharmacogenomic analysis demonstrated that nearly all participants harbored at least one actionable phenotype, potentially informing nearly one million annual prescriptions in Hong Kong. The ongoing HKGP establishes a curated Hong Kong Chinese reference for clinically relevant genetic variation and serves as a blueprint for the implementation of precision medicine in underrepresented populations.

lay_summary: Researchers built a genetic map for Chinese people to improve medical care. They sequenced genomes from over 20,000 Hong Kong residents: about 2,200 patients with suspected rare genetic diseases and about 18,200 people screened for health risks. They looked for harmful gene changes and genes that affect medicines. They found a diagnosis for 25% of rare disease patients. About 3.7% had harmful changes that can cause dominant conditions. Nearly half carried genes for recessive conditions, and 38 important genes would have been missed using European-focused lists. Almost everyone had a gene change that could affect medicine choice. This work can help doctors give better diagnoses and safer drug choices for Chinese people.

pdr_title: Semaglutide and Risk of Adult-Onset Seizure: A Target Trial Emulation
pdr_abstract: Background And Objectives: Adult-onset seizure reflects the burden of acquired brain insults, but established disease-modifying preventive strategies are limited. We evaluated whether semaglutide initiation is associated with a lower incidence of adult-onset seizure compared with sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors %28SGLT2i%29 and other glucose-lowering drugs %28GLDs%29 in adults with type 2 diabetes.    Methods: Using the All of Us Research Program, we emulated a population-based target trial in new-user, active-comparator cohorts from January 2018 to October 2023. We compared semaglutide vs other GLDs and semaglutide vs SGLT2i. Incident epilepsy or seizure was identified from diagnostic codes. Effects were estimated using inverse probability of treatment weighting with weighted Cox models and targeted maximum likelihood estimation %28TMLE%29. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses with multiple outcome definitions and analytic approaches were conducted to assess the robustness of findings. We evaluated mediation through hemoglobin A1c %28HbA1c%29 and body mass index %28BMI%29 using the longitudinal Vansteelandt framework.    Results: We analyzed 10,213 patients in the semaglutide %28n = 2,586, mean age, 60.1 years; 56.8% female%29 vs other GLDs cohort %28n = 7,627, mean age, 63.7 years; 54.2% female%29 and 8,605 patients in the semaglutide %28n = 2,814, mean age, 60.5 years; 66.2% female%29 vs SGLT2i cohort %28n = 5,791, mean age, 64.4 years; 47.3% female%29. Semaglutide was associated with a lower risk of adult-onset seizure compared with other GLDs %28weighted HR 0.44 [95% CI 0.25-0.79]; 4-year risk difference -1.78% [95% CI -2.58 to -0.98]%29 and SGLT2i %28weighted HR 0.48 [95% CI 0.27-0.85]; 4-year risk difference -1.46% [95% CI -2.41 to -0.51]%29. TMLE estimated risk differences per 1,000 persons of -14.20 %2895% CI -18.33 to -10.07%29 vs other GLDs and -7.62 %2895% CI -11.65 to -3.60%29 vs SGLT2i, corresponding to numbers needed to treat of 70 and 131, respectively. Mediation was minimal for HbA1c %282.4% vs other GLDs; 6.5% vs SGLT2i%29 and BMI %280% vs other GLDs; 0.7% vs SGLT2i%29.    Discussion: Semaglutide initiation was associated with a lower risk of adult-onset seizure compared with SGLT2i and other GLDs in patients with type 2 diabetes, independent of glycemic and weight effects. Residual confounding, low event counts, and shorter follow-up limit causal interpretation.    Classification Of Evidence: This study provides Class II evidence that semaglutide use was associated with a lower risk of adult-onset seizures compared with other GLDs and SGLT2i.
lay_summary: This study asked whether starting semaglutide, a diabetes drug, lowers new seizures in adults with type 2 diabetes. Researchers looked at health records for over 10,000 people who began semaglutide or other diabetes medicines from 2018 to 2023 and checked who got new seizures. Fewer people on semaglutide had seizures over four years: about 1.8% fewer than with other drugs and about 1.5% fewer than with SGLT2 inhibitors (another type of diabetes drug). This suggests semaglutide might cut seizure risk, but more research is needed because there were few events and follow-up was short.
